Orientation — Scope, Deliverables and How to Read This

0.1 Scope and audience0.2 The two tracks: Web and Desktop0.3 What "done" means at each stage0.4 The artefact set0.5 How the process pipelines0.6 Conventions, notation and how to read the code

This guide follows a software product from a raw idea to a supported production system, and it does so along two parallel tracks that share a common spine. This opening section fixes the scope, names the deliverables you should be able to produce at each gate, and explains exactly where the Web track and the Desktop track diverge and where they are identical. Read it once end to end before starting; the track map below is the map for the remaining nineteen chapters.

0.1 Scope and audience

Defines who this document is written for, which problems it treats as in scope, and the explicit exclusions that keep the process tractable.

The intended reader is a senior engineer, tech lead, staff engineer or engineering manager who is accountable for a product that does not yet exist, or exists only as a prototype, and who must get it into production and keep it running. The document assumes competence in software construction and none in product strategy: it will not teach you version control, but it will tell you how many problem interviews to run before you are permitted to open an editor, what evidence is admissible, and how to record it so that a decision made under uncertainty can be audited eight months later.

The scope is the full path from problem statement to retired system: discovery and validation, market and feasibility analysis, requirements, architecture, design, implementation, testing, release, operations, support and end-of-life. It deliberately excludes business operations beyond the technical boundary (sales enablement, pricing strategy execution, legal and regulatory negotiation), and it treats regulated-industry specifics (HIPAA, PCI DSS, FedRAMP, GDPR Article 9) as a modifier applied to the standard pipeline rather than as a separate method. Where a practice differs by jurisdiction or industry, the guide says so and points to where the decision is recorded rather than asserting a single answer.

Three things are treated as non-negotiable throughout. First, artefacts over opinions: a claim that is not written down in a retrievable artefact does not exist for the purposes of this process. Second, gates over velocity: each stage has an entry and exit condition, and a schedule pressure that erodes a gate is a risk to be logged, not a reason to skip it. Third, reversibility is a first-class property of a decision: cheap-to-reverse choices are made fast and in the open; expensive-to-reverse choices are made slowly, in writing, with the alternatives recorded.

The vocabulary is precise throughout. An artefact is a named document or data structure with an owner and a location. A gate is a documented decision that permits a stage to begin. A spike is a time-boxed code or research exercise whose code is thrown away. A prototype is code that is designed to be evolved into the product. These are not synonyms and confusing them is the single most common source of wasted engineering effort in this process.

How to use this guide. Chapters 1–8 and 17–19 are track-neutral and are the compulsory spine. Chapters 9–12 apply to browser-delivered products; chapters 13–16 apply to products installed onto an operating system. If you already know your target, read the relevant track chapters in order and skim the other track only for contrast. Chapter 20 is the index and cross-reference.

0.2 The two tracks: Web and Desktop

Establishes the full twenty-chapter map, marks each chapter as Web-track, Desktop-track or cross-cutting, and states precisely which concerns diverge and which do not.

The guide is organised around a shared spine of process — the same discovery, research, requirements, design, quality and release practices — and two platform tracks that fork at the point where a deployment target is chosen. The two tracks are not two different disciplines. They are the same discipline with a different set of physical and commercial constraints imposed at the edges, and most teams find that 80% of the work is identical and 100% of the operational risk differs.

The following table is the map for the whole document. Chapters 1–8 and 17–19 are cross-cutting. Chapters 9–12 are the Web track. Chapters 13–16 are the Desktop track.

Where the two tracks genuinely diverge. Six concerns separate them, and each has a hard operational consequence rather than a stylistic one.

  1. Distribution. Web products are served from a URL you control; the deployment is a side-effect of pushing a container or artefact. Desktop products are installed by the user or by an administrator, which introduces installer format, code signing, notarisation, silent-install switches, machine-wide versus per-user deployment, and an enterprise policy surface (MSI properties, Group Policy, MDM). A web release is a server-side event; a desktop release is a negotiation with 400 million heterogeneous machines.
  2. Update model. Web can force a hard reload, feature-flag, and roll back within seconds by routing traffic to the previous build. Desktop can only ask: the user may disable updates, be offline, be behind a corporate proxy, or be running a build you cannot reach. Updates arrive per-machine on an unpredictable schedule, so you must design for a permanent tail of old clients, and the compatibility window between an old client and a new server is a first-class protocol problem.
  3. Offline behaviour. Offline is an edge-case degradation on the web and a core requirement on the desktop. A desktop product must define what reads, what writes, what queues, how conflicts resolve, and what a user sees when the network disappears for six hours in a tunnel. Sync conflict resolution is a desktop-track chapter (15) and effectively a web-track non-issue.
  4. Native capability. Direct filesystem access, arbitrary process spawning, global hotkeys, raw serial and USB device access, screen capture, window inspection, tray presence, and local SQLite are all ordinary on the desktop and impossible or heavily constrained in a browser. Each requires an IPC bridge and an explicit permission decision, and each is a place where a web product will need a third-party service and a desktop product does not.
  5. Payment and store model. A web product typically takes payment through a merchant of record and delivers a subscription. A desktop product faces app stores that take 15–30% and impose review latency of hours to weeks, or sells direct with its own licence server, entitlement keys and offline activation. Unit economics in chapter 2 are computed before the track forks, then adjusted in chapter 16 for store commission and conversion friction.
  6. Permissions and privacy surface. A browser grants permissions per-origin, in a well-known vocabulary, revocable by the user at a known place, and largely abstracted. A desktop application asks for filesystem, network, camera, microphone, notification and accessibility privileges directly from the OS, and a wrong answer — for example an all-filesystem-access request on Windows or a Full Disk Access prompt on macOS — is both a usability catastrophe and a security finding.

Where the two tracks are identical. Everything before and around the fork. Discovery, problem validation, market sizing, feasibility spikes, stakeholder research, personas, journey mapping, requirements specification, prioritisation, information architecture, interaction design, visual design, accessibility to WCAG 2.2 AA, design systems, source control, code review, automated testing, unit and integration testing, end-to-end testing, security threat modelling, privacy impact assessment, observability design, incident management, on-call practice, support tooling, and end-of-life communication are all identical. A usability test with five participants is five participants whether the subject is a web page or a native window. A pre-mortem is a pre-mortem. A risk register does not care what platform you chose.

Rule of thumb. If a decision can be reversed by editing a file and redeploying, it is a web-shaped decision and you should make it quickly. If reversing it requires shipping to users who may never update, it is a desktop-shaped decision and you should write an ADR before you build it. The track you are on does not change your process; it changes which decisions are expensive.

# The single most important structural fact about this process, as code.
# Both tracks share stages 1-8 and 17-19. The fork is at deployment target.

0.3 What "done" means at each stage

Defines exit criteria per stage as verifiable statements rather than schedule dates, and distinguishes done, done enough to ship and done enough to be sure.

"Done" in this process is not a schedule position. It is a set of falsifiable conditions that, when met, permit the next stage to begin. A stage can be abandoned at any point, and abandoning a stage is a success outcome of the stage: the cheapest result of discovery is a documented no-go. Below are the exit conditions used throughout the guide. Each is written so that a reasonable third party could evaluate it from the artefacts alone.

StageExit condition (all must hold)Typical durationPrimary artefact
1 · Discovery≥ 12 problem interviews completed; ≥ 5 of 12 report the same trigger event unprompted; ≥ 60% report a current workaround; problem statement written without naming a solution2–5 weeksInterview transcript set, evidence pack, problem statement
2 · Market & feasibilityBottom-up SOM computed from addressable accounts × realistic penetration; ≥ 2 feasibility spikes answered their question; top risks have named owners; unit economics model exists even if preliminary2–4 weeksBusiness case one-pager, spike reports, risk register
3 · RequirementsEvery requirement has an ID, a priority, a rationale and a testable acceptance criterion; ≥ 80% traceable to a validated problem or a stated business constraint3–6 weeksRequirements specification, persona set, journey maps
4 · ArchitectureEvery irreversible decision has an ADR with ≥ 2 rejected alternatives; capacity model fits a 10× load test; data model reviewed for deletion and export paths2–4 weeksADRs, C4 diagrams, data model, threat model v0
5 · DesignAll P0 flows have annotated designs and a clickable prototype tested with 5 users per flow; design tokens published; WCAG 2.2 AA contrast and focus order verified4–8 weeksDesign system, annotated specs, test findings
6 · ImplementationAll P0 requirements implemented behind feature flags; no P0 has an open P1-severity defect; code review on 100% of merges; no commit to main by an unreviewed path6–16 weeksTracked in the issue system, CI reports
7 · TestingUnit ≥ 80% on business logic, contract tests green for all integrations, E2E suite covering every P0 journey, load test at 2× projected peak without error-budget breachContinuousTest pyramid report, defect ledger, coverage report
8 · ReleaseAutomated pipeline green end to end; rollback rehearsed in staging within 10 minutes; runbook written and reviewed; on-call rota staffed; DRI named2–4 weeksPipeline definition, runbook, rollback plan
9–12 / 13–16 · TrackTrack-specific gates; each written in the track chapter and each requiring a written artefact, not a dashboard screenshot4–12 weeksPer track
17–19 · OperateSLOs published and error budget policy agreed; on-call runbook exercised once; deprecation and sunset plan exists for every external interfaceContinuousSLO doc, runbooks, deprecation plan

Three different thresholds are used and are not interchangeable. Done enough to ship means the P0 slice is complete, tested to the stated bar, monitored, and has a rollback path. Done enough to grow means it also has telemetry that can answer whether the product is working, and a way to add the next requirement without a rewrite — this is where most shipped products are not actually done. Done enough to be sure means long-run soak, load and failure-injection testing, an accessibility audit by a second party, and at least one full operational cycle in production with real users. Very few products ever reach the third, and that is a deliberate risk acceptance, not an oversight.

The gate is the product. The most common failure in this process is not technical: it is that a gate is renamed a "phase" or a "sprint" and then compressed away. If a stage exit condition cannot be evaluated by someone who did not do the work, it is not an exit condition, it is a slogan. Write conditions you could hand to a hostile reviewer.

0.4 The artefact set

Names the twenty canonical documents this process produces, their owners, their minimum viable contents, and the repository layout that keeps them retrievable.

A process that does not produce artefacts produces memory. Memory fails at exactly the moment it is needed: when a decision must be revisited, when a new team member asks why something is the way it is, or when a customer asks for a commitment. The artefact set below is deliberately small — twenty documents, not two hundred. Each has a named owner, a home, and a minimum viable content contract; a document that does not meet the contract is not filed, it is a draft.

ArtefactOwnerMinimum viable contentCreated at

Artefacts in version control. Store every one of these as Markdown or a structured file in the same repository as the code, reviewed by the same pull-request process. A document in a wiki that nobody reviews drifts from reality within a quarter; a document in the repository that blocks merge on stale content does not. Version the artefacts. When a decision reverses, the diff is the audit trail.

0.5 How the process pipelines

Shows how discovery, design and build overlap in practice, and gives a reference calendar with realistic durations and team shapes for a small team.

Sequential execution of the stages described above is the pedagogical arrangement, not the operational one. In practice discovery, design and implementation overlap by 30–60% of a stage’s duration, because information needed to start work arrives incrementally. The rule is not "never start building before discovery ends" but "never build the part that depends on an unvalidated assumption". Concretely: once the riskiest assumption has a cheap test, the platform work — which depends on no assumption about desirability — can begin immediately and in parallel.

                                                          v1.0 GA

# What overlaps legitimately
#   - Platform/infrastructure build starts at week 4 (no desirability assumption)
#   - Design of P0 flows starts at week 6 (framing known, detail still forming)
#   - Riskiest-assumption test lands week 3, before any feature code
#
# What must NOT overlap
#   - Feature code for an unvalidated core assumption  (ch1 §1.6)
#   - Schema migration without a rollback plan           (ch4, ch8)
#   - Release to a channel you cannot roll back from      (ch8, ch15)

The reference calendar above assumes a team of one product lead, one designer, one tech lead, four to six engineers and one researcher shared across stages. A team of two will take roughly 1.8× as long per stage and a team of twelve will not take half as long, because communication overhead grows superlinearly; beyond about seven engineers on a product with more than one platform target, split into two teams with an explicit interface contract between them.

Four failure patterns recur in this pipeline and are worth naming because they are visible early. Discovery theatre: interviews are run, transcripts are written, and no decision ever changes as a result. The test is whether any feature was cut between the problem statement and the requirements specification because of what was learned. Premature platform: the team spends four months on infrastructure for an unvalidated product, and the infrastructure has no users when it launches. Specification waterfall: a 200-page specification is written in month two, and 40% of it is wrong by month five with no feedback loop. Ship-and-hope: the team launches with no observability, no rollback and no support process, and cannot answer a customer question within an hour.

// The decision rule that connects every stage. Keep it in the repo, keep it in a PR.
// Question asked before starting any work item:
function gate(artefact, checks) {
  const failed = checks.filter(c => !c.met);
  if (failed.length === 0) {
    return { proceed: true, evidence: artefact.reviewers, signedAt: Date.now() };
  }
  // Never proceed silently. Either fix, or record a formal risk acceptance.
  return {
    proceed: false,
    failed: failed.map(f => ({
      check: f.name,
      reason: f.reason,
      waivedBy: null,          // must be a named human, never a bot
      waiverRationale: null,
      expiresAt: null,         // waivers expire; they are not permanent
    })),
  };
}

// Same function, both tracks. The check *contents* differ in ch9-ch16.
// The *mechanism* — documented, reviewed, expiring, attributable — never does.

Make the gate cheap to satisfy and impossible to bypass. If the exit condition is "the ADR is written", it will be written in ten minutes. If it is "the ADR is written and has been reviewed by someone who was not the author", it takes twenty minutes and prevents the class of decision where the only reviewer is the person who wanted the thing. Waivers are legitimate; undocumented waivers are not.

0.6 Conventions, notation and how to read the code

Defines the notation used in the code blocks, the confidence and scoring scales, and the reading path for readers with different starting points.

Code blocks in this guide appear in five registers, and it is worth knowing which one you are reading before you copy anything. Shell blocks begin with a $ prompt and run in a POSIX shell or Bash. Configuration blocks are declarative — YAML, JSON, TOML, HCL — and are meant to be copied with only value changes. Query blocks are SQL or a query language and assume a schema described in the surrounding prose. Diagram blocks are plain-text drawings inside a code fence; they are not valid code in any language and exist because a text diagram diffs cleanly, reviews in a pull request and never needs a rendering dependency. Pseudocode blocks are illustrative and are not intended to run.

Three numeric scales are used throughout and are always stated explicitly. Confidence is a 1–5 integer on assumptions, where 1 is "pure conjecture with no contact with any user", 3 is "some indirect evidence, at least one source", and 5 is "direct behavioural evidence from at least five independent users plus one quantitative signal". Risk score is likelihood × impact on two 1–5 scales, giving 1–25, with 1–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–19 high and 20–25 critical, and every risk scoring ≥ 15 requires a named owner and a written contingency. Priority is MoSCoW — Must, Should, Could, Won’t — with the additional constraint used throughout this guide that a Must which is not traceable to a validated problem is a defect in the requirements specification, not a high-priority feature.

Statistical claims are made with their sample sizes attached, and readers should treat any claim in this guide without a sample size as a heuristic rather than a finding. Where a specific threshold is used (5 users per usability round, 8–12 discovery interviews, roughly 400 survey responses to detect a 10-point difference at 95% confidence, 5% significance), the derivation is given in chapters 1 and 2. Where industry figures are quoted as ranges rather than points, they are labelled as ranges because they are genuinely ranges and any single value would be false precision.

// Scales used in every scoring artefact in this guide.

const CONFIDENCE = {
  1: "Conjecture. No user contact. Internal opinion only.",
  2: "Internal data. Second-hand reports, sales anecdotes, support folklore.",
  3: "Indirect evidence. One or two external sources; competitor behaviour; market reports.",
  4: "Direct evidence. Observed behaviour from 1-4 users, or a live experiment below threshold.",
  5: "Strong evidence. Observed behaviour from 5+ independent users AND a quantitative signal.",
};

const RISK_BANDS = [
  { max: 6,  label: "low",      action: "Log and monitor. No dedicated work." },
  { max: 12, label: "medium",   action: "Named owner, mitigation scheduled this quarter." },
  { max: 19, label: "high",     action: "Named owner, written contingency, weekly review." },
  { max: 25, label: "critical", action: "Blocks the next stage gate until mitigated or waived." },
];

// Likelihood: 1 rare (<5%/yr) .. 5 near-certain (>60%/yr)
// Impact:     1 negligible     .. 5 existential (product or company ends)

function riskBand(score) {
  return RISK_BANDS.find(b => score <= b.max).label;
}

// Example: a desktop product assuming a silent auto-update path
const R = { likelihood: 4, impact: 5 };   // enterprise proxies block updaters
riskBand(R.likelihood * R.impact);        // => "critical"
riskBand(3 * 3);                          // => "low"
riskBand(4 * 4);                          // => "high"

// Same scoring function for a web product's S3 region outage
// Same function, different register. Scoring is track-neutral.

Three reading paths are suggested, depending on where you are starting. If you have an idea and no customers, read chapters 1 and 2 in full and stop at the ch2 gate; most ideas do not survive it and the reading is cheaper than the build. If you have a validated problem and a funded mandate, read 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 on the spine, then 9–12 or 13–16 for your track, then 17–19. If you are inheriting an existing product that has no artefacts and a deployment next week, read 8, 17, 18 and 19 first, because they are the chapters that determine whether next week goes well, and treat chapters 1–7 as the plan for the release after next.

Vendor neutrality. Where a real tool, framework or platform is named it is because it is a de facto standard or because the surrounding analysis is genuinely about its properties, not because it is recommended. Every named tool in this guide has substitutes, and the decision criteria given with it are the transferable part. Read the criteria, not the name.

Exercises 0

  1. Write your track decision as an ADR today. Create docs/00-orientation/track-decision.md choosing Web, Desktop, or "both, in this order", and record context, decision, at least two rejected alternatives, and the six divergence concerns from §0.2 with a one-line position on each for your product. Success criterion: the document is under 500 words and a colleague could use it to make a scheduling decision without asking you a question.
  2. Build the exit-criteria table for your own project. Take the §0.3 table and replace every generic condition with a measurable one specific to your product, including the actual numbers (your expected p95 latency, your error-rate ceiling, your load target). Produce a one-page table with columns Stage, Exit condition, Measurable threshold, Who verifies. Success criterion: every threshold is a number or an unambiguous boolean, and no row says "reviewed", "discussed" or "aligned".
  3. Audit your artefact inventory against a spreadsheet. List every document your team currently relies on that is not in a repository, name the last time it was accurate, and classify each as migrate-now, migrate-later, or kill. Then create the directory skeleton from §0.4 in your actual repository and commit it. Success criterion: an empty-but-correct structure is committed and your team has a written answer for every one of the 20 artefacts stating where it is or why it does not exist.
  4. Run a 90-minute pipeline review with a real schedule. Take your next real milestone, lay it on the §0.5 calendar grid, and mark every task that depends on an assumption you have not tested. Produce a dependency list ordered by cost-if-wrong. Success criterion: you can name the single most expensive unvalidated assumption and the date on which you will test it, and that date is within 21 days.
  5. Write the divergence test for six operational scenarios. For each of distribution, updates, offline, native capability, payment and permissions, answer concretely "what breaks for us if this is wrong" for both a Web and a Desktop build of your product. Produce a two-column table with a risk score per cell using the 1–5 × 1–5 scale. Success criterion: at least two cells score ≥ 15, each with a named mitigation written down.

1 · Product Discovery and Problem Validation

1.1 From idea to opportunity1.2 Problem interviews1.3 Assumption mapping and the riskiest-assumption test1.4 Jobs to Be Done1.5 Validation experiment types1.6 Assembling the evidence pack

This chapter establishes that an idea is not a problem, and that the only admissible evidence for a product commitment is observed behaviour by identifiable people who currently pay for a workaround in time or money. It sets out the interview discipline, the assumption-mapping and riskiest-assumption method, the Jobs to Be Done framework as a structure for interview data, the catalogue of validation experiments with honest verdicts on each, and the format of the evidence pack that permits a go decision. Its argument is that the most expensive engineering decision is not which framework to use but whether to build at all, and that this decision must be made on evidence gathered in weeks rather than on conviction assembled in meetings.

1.1 From idea to opportunity

Draws the distinction between an idea, a solution and a problem, and establishes the framing output — a problem statement that names no technology.

An idea is a sentence about a possible thing: "a scheduling tool for field engineers", "an AI layer over our existing product", "a marketplace for refurbished laptops". A solution is the mechanism that idea implies: a calendar, a model, an escrow payment flow. A problem is a statement about a person in a specific circumstance who is currently failing to achieve something that matters to them, and who is currently paying for that failure in a way they can name. Only the third is a candidate for building. Most organisations cannot tell the three apart, and the result is a roadmap composed entirely of solutions whose problems were never stated, never sized and never tested — a pattern that is formally indistinguishable, from the outside, from a well-executed plan.

The distinction matters because of cost asymmetry. Discovering that a problem is not worth solving after two weeks of interviews costs 2% of the budget. Discovering it after six months of implementation costs 60–90% and typically leaves behind a codebase, a team and a migration. Every serious method in this chapter is a mechanism for moving the discovery of bad news earlier, and none of them is a mechanism for being sure you are right. The realistic claim is narrower: you can become substantially more certain, in weeks rather than quarters, and you can do so at a cost of roughly 5–15% of the initial build budget. Teams that skip this are not being efficient; they are converting a 2% risk into a 70% one.

The output of this subsection is the framing document, usually called the problem statement. It has exactly four fields and must contain no noun describing a solution. This constraint feels artificial and is the single highest-leverage discipline in discovery: the moment you write "a dashboard", you have committed to a category of solution, and the interview questions that follow will unconsciously steer respondents toward validating it.

# Framing document — the four fields, and a worked example.
# Author: product lead. Reviewed: research lead. Filed: docs/01-discovery/problem-statement.md

## 1. WHO
Field service engineers, 3–25 years in the field, working for a mid-size
contractor (40–400 technicians), currently on paper or a bespoke internal tool.

## 2. SITUATION
When a job is dispatched, they learn the customer address and required parts
from a printed work order or a phone call, often after 08:00 and often while
driving between sites.

## 3. STRUGGLE
They cannot determine before leaving the depot whether the required part is in
the van, so they either carry excess stock (measured at 22% of van stock by our
own depot audit) or drive back. Both cost time; the second costs an hour of
paid travel and a failed first-time-fix.

## 4. CONSEQUENCE
First-time-fix rate is 71% (our field-service client, Q2 2026, n=1,400 jobs).
Industry first-time-fix benchmarks cluster at 75–85%. Every point of first-time-fix
is roughly 4.8% of job cost in avoided return travel on a 2.5-hour average
return leg.

## OUT OF SCOPE (explicit)
- Fleet telematics and vehicle tracking
- Customer-facing booking and payment
- Inventory purchasing and supplier management
- Anything requiring a real-time connection while the technician is underground

## BANNED NOUNS CHECK (grep this file before review)
dashboard | app | AI | platform | portal | mobile | API | SaaS | workflow
# If any appear, the statement has been contaminated by a solution.

Two framing techniques materially improve the statement. The first is to write it three times, deliberately badly, and record what changed. The first version is almost always the internal pitch restated as a problem. The third version is usually specific enough to be falsifiable. Second, have someone who has never met the problem read the statement and restate it back to you; any solution noun they add in their restatement is a noun that your framing is provoking rather than containing.

Idea contamination. The failure mode here is subtle: the team genuinely believes it is doing problem framing while asking questions whose acceptable answers all confirm the idea. "Would you use a tool that automatically checks part availability before you leave the depot?" is not a problem interview question; it is a pitch with a question mark. If you cannot write the question without describing a category of solution, you do not yet have a problem — you have a preference.

Problem statements are hypotheses, not conclusions. The framing document exists to be tested. Its status is "candidate problem, confidence 3" until evidence raises or lowers it. Writing it in the voice of established fact is the earliest and most durable form of the sunk-cost error that this chapter exists to prevent.

1.2 Problem interviews

Specifies the interview method, recruitment criteria, the Mom Test question structure, the use of silence, and the saturation rule that terminates the round.

The problem interview is a structured conversation with a person who is currently experiencing the problem, conducted to learn about their actual past behaviour rather than their stated future preferences. Two design choices make it work. The first is the Mom Test discipline of asking only about specific instances in the past rather than about general opinions or hypothetical futures. The second is the discipline of asking their questions, not yours: the interviewer works through a fixed structure but lets the participant’s own concerns steer which sub-questions get depth.

The method rests on a well-replicated finding about self-report: humans predict their own future behaviour poorly and consistently, and the error is not noise but bias in a known direction — people over-report what they intend to do and under-report what they actually did. Stated interest in a hypothetical product is therefore near-worthless as evidence of purchase. Stated interest in their own past behaviour is, by contrast, reliable, because it is a memory rather than a forecast, and it is checkable: it has dates, names, artefacts and money attached to it.

// The Mom Test question taxonomy, as a machine-checkable list.
// Each question is scored on the axis it actually measures.

const QUESTION_TYPES = {
  // The only three reliable categories for a discovery interview.
  FACTS_PAST: {
    label: "facts about the past",
    reliable: true,
    examples: [
      "Tell me about the last time you needed to know whether a part was in the van.",
      "What did you do first, in order?",
      "How long did that take, start to finish?",
      "What was the most recent time it went wrong? What happened?",
    ],
  },
  FACTS_EXISTING_SPEND: {
    label: "facts about current workaround and its cost",
    reliable: true,
    examples: [
      "What are you using right now to solve this?",
      "Who paid for it? How much, roughly, per year or per month?",
      "How many hours a week does someone spend on this?",
      "What is the workaround's worst failure mode?",
    ],
  },
  VIEWS_OPINION: {
    label: "opinions and generalisations",
    reliable: false,   // usable only as background colour, never as evidence
    examples: [
      "Do you think technicians would find that useful?",
      "How important is this to you?",
      "Do you like this idea?",
    ],
    rule: "Ask at most one per session, last five minutes, and never count it as evidence.",
  },
  HYPOTHETICAL_FUTURE: {
    label: "hypothetical future behaviour",
    reliable: false,   // actively harmful: produces false positives
    examples: [
      "If we built X, would you use it?",
      "Would you pay $50/month for that?",
      "How much would this be worth to you?",
    ],
    rule: "Never ask. There is no internal validity in the answer.",
  },
};

// The invalidity is not a matter of degree. Behavioural-intention research
// consistently shows a large gap between stated and revealed preference;
// a person asked "would you pay $50/month" in a research setting reports a
// number that is uncorrelated with what they do when the option becomes real.

Leading versus lagging questions. A leading question contains its own answer, either in the framing or in the presupposition. "How much would you like the app to speed up your daily check?" presupposes that the app will exist and that the check is a daily event. A lagging question looks backward at a specific completed event and asks what happened, so the participant supplies the structure. The practical rule: if the question can be answered with "yes" or "it would be great", it is leading and must be rewritten.

Interviewer script — 45 minutes, problem discovery, single session.
Not read verbatim. Structure is fixed; wording is adapted to their language.

[00:00–00:03] CONSENT AND FRAMING
  "Thanks for making time. I'm not selling anything and there is no
   prototype to show you, because we don't know yet whether to build one.
   I want to understand what actually happens on your job, including the
   parts that are annoying. There are no right answers and I will be
   interrupting less than you expect, because I am writing things down.
   Nothing you say is confidential to you — it will not be attributed to you
   or your employer by name. The recording is for my own notes, and the
   transcript is internal. Do I have your consent to record, and are you
   happy to proceed?"

  If no: proceed without recording, hand-written notes only, say so aloud.
  If the participant is a contractor, add: "Your employer may find out what you
  told me through this conversation. I cannot prevent that. Do you want to
  continue?" This is the point at which roughly a third decline.

[00:03–00:08] ROLE AND CONTEXT, NO PRODUCT
  "Walk me through a normal week, day by day."
  "What are you responsible for? What are you explicitly not?"
  "Who else touches this work? Who do you hand things to?"

[00:08–00:30] THE CRITICAL RECENT INSTANCE
  "Tell me about the last time X happened. Start wherever you like."
  [SILENCE. Do not fill it. The first pause after a question is where the
   actual recollection happens. Count to ten. If they stop, ask nothing
   further and wait again.]
  "What happened just before that?"
  "What was the very first thing you noticed? How did you know?"
  "What did you think at the time?"
  "What did you do? In order."
  "What was going through your mind while you were doing that?"
  "Did you check anything? Where?"
  "Was there a moment where you thought: this is going to be a problem?"
  "Did you do anything to avoid it? What?"
  "Did it work? What did it cost you?"
  "Did you tell anyone? Who? What did they say?"
  "What happened after that? Was it resolved?"

[00:30–00:38] WORKAROUNDS AND SPEND
  "How often does that happen? Per week, per month?"
  "What are you using right now instead?"
  "Who built or bought that? When? What does it cost, per year?"
  "How many people are involved in working around it?"
  "If it did not happen at all, what would change? Be specific about money."

[00:38–00:43] THE PARTICIPANT'S OWN QUESTIONS
  "What haven't I asked that I should have?"
  "If you ran this company, what would you want fixed first?"
  "What do you already know is broken and nobody has fixed?"

[00:43–00:45] CLOSING
  "Is there anyone else who experiences this that I should talk to?"
  "May I contact you again in three weeks with a rough sketch?"
  Thank them. Do not pitch. Do not ask for a commitment.

Silence as data. The single most common error in discovery interviewing is that the interviewer, unable to tolerate a gap of three seconds, either supplies a suggestion or moves to the next question. Both destroy the only moment in the conversation where the participant is reconstructing reality rather than performing. In practice: ask the question, then say nothing. If the participant does not continue after roughly ten seconds, ask "What were you thinking about?" rather than "So you did X?" The difference between those two follow-ups is the difference between learning that they were confused by the question and learning that they did X.

Recruitment criteria. Sample the population by a written screener with inclusion and exclusion criteria, applied before the session, not selected afterwards from whoever responded. For the framing example above: include technicians who have completed at least 30 jobs in the last 90 days at a contractor with ≥ 40 technicians; include dispatchers and service managers as a second stratum; exclude anyone who has seen a demo of your concept, anyone employed by a company on your target list, and anyone who participated in a prior session. Recruiting from your own user base introduces courtesy bias — existing customers answer to please you, and the resulting enthusiasm is the single most common false positive in B2B discovery.

# Screening and recruitment record. One per participant. Retained with the transcript.

RECORD_ID: INT-2026-03-11-P07
STATUS: completed
RECRUITED_VIA: contractor association mailing list (not a customer relationship)
PAID: £40 supermarket voucher, unconditional on content
CONSENT: recorded, audio + transcript, 12 months
DECLINED_SHARE_WITH_EMPLOYER: no          # asked explicitly, item 3 of consent

# --- inclusion criteria, pre-registered before the session ---
IC1  role == field service technician                   [PASS]
IC2  completed_jobs_90d >= 30                            [PASS] (67)
IC3  employer_technicians >= 40                         [PASS] (180)
IC4  no prior exposure to concept, in writing             [PASS]
IC5  not an employee or contractor of the company         [PASS]
# --- exclusion criteria ---
EX1  employed by a company on target list                [PASS, not on list]
EX2  has seen a demo, mockup or pitch                     [PASS]
EX3  customer of the sponsoring organisation             [PASS]

# --- sampling frame coverage after this session ---
strata = {
  "field_technician":      { target: 6,  enrolled: 6,  saturated: true  },
  "dispatcher":            { target: 3,  enrolled: 3,  saturated: true  },
  "service_manager":       { target: 3,  enrolled: 4,  saturated: true  },
  "owner_operator":        { target: 2,  enrolled: 1,  saturated: false },
}
# Coverage gap: owner-operators under 40 technicians. Note, do not backfill
# with customer contacts. Recruit two more from the association list.

Sample size and the saturation rule. Discovery interviews do not require statistical power; they require information saturation. The rule of thumb in professional practice is 5 interviews per distinct user stratum for a narrow B2B tool with a homogeneous population, and 8–12 total for discovery interviews aimed at establishing whether a problem exists at all. The termination criterion is saturation: continue until the last three consecutive sessions produce no new trigger event, no new workaround and no new consequence. In practice this is reached at 8–12 sessions and frequently earlier — if the sixth session produces nothing new, the problem is probably not the problem. This is explicitly not a claim about statistical generalisation; the sample is a structured search for the boundaries of variation, and the report must state that it makes no inferential claim about population prevalence. Prevalence is a survey or telemetry question, and it is answered in §1.6 and §2.1.

MethodWhat it actually measuresSample for a directional readTime to first signalCostRight forWrong for
Problem interview (Mom Test)Past behaviour, workarounds, spend, exact words8–12 total, 5 per stratum3–10 days£40–150 per session + 20–40h analysis✓ Establishing that a problem exists and what it costs✗ Sizing prevalence; ✗ testing a designed interface
Survey (structured, pre-registered)Stated prevalence and stated ranking within a defined frame≈400 for a 10-point swing at 95% conf., 5% sig.1–3 weeks£800–6,000 + panel time✓ Sizing prevalence; ✗ ranking; ✗ a frame-free view✗ Discovering a problem nobody anticipated
Usability test (5 per round)Task completion, hesitation points, error recovery on a designed artefact5 per design round, 2–3 rounds4–7 days per roundLow if internal, £2–4k per round moderated✓ Refining an existing design; ✓ finding comprehension failures✗ Asking whether the product should exist; ✗ anything about value
Contextual inquiry / observationBehaviour in the real environment, including workarounds not described6–10 sessions, 2–3 days each2–4 weeksHigh; 3–10 days per participant✓ Understanding work outside the organisation’s model✗ Fast iteration; ✗ self-reported attitudes
Log / telemetry analysis (existing product)Actual aggregate behaviour at scale, zero self-report biasWhatever exists; segments by ≥ 100 sessions1–2 daysNear zero if instrumented✓ Validating a hypothesis about existing users✗ People who have not adopted; ✗ reasons, only actions
Diary study (2+ weeks)Repeated real-world instances with temporal structure10–20 participants, 14–28 days3–5 weeksModerate; high attrition✓ Frequency and seasonality of a problem✗ Early framing; ✗ anything requiring fast turnaround

On sample sizes: a directional interview round of 5 per stratum is not a sample and must never be described as one. A survey of roughly 400 responses from a properly drawn frame is sufficient to detect a difference of about 10 percentage points between two subgroups at 95% confidence and 5% significance, which is why survey sample sizes are quoted at that order of magnitude rather than at 30. Using 30 survey responses and reporting a percentage is a category error that appears in a depressing number of internal research reports.

Interview enthusiasm is not demand. A well-run problem interview makes participants like you, because you listened carefully to something that has been frustrating them for months. A participant who says "I would definitely use that, please build it" has told you about the social relationship, not about their behaviour. The only admissible corroboration is a change in their current allocation of time or money, and the test for that is in §1.5, not in the interview room.

1.3 Assumption mapping and the riskiest-assumption test

Introduces the assumption inventory, the desirability/viability/feasibility/usability-clarity quadrant, confidence scoring, and the test that selects which assumption to attack first.

Every product idea is a bundle of assumptions. Some are about whether people want the thing (desirability), some about whether money can be made from it (viability), some about whether you can build it (feasibility), and some about whether you have correctly understood the users and their context (usability and clarity, treated as one quadrant because a misunderstanding of the user corrupts every other quadrant’s evidence). The method’s value is not that it produces a document; it is that the act of writing the assumptions down converts an unbounded optimism into a finite, attackable list, and the list can then be ordered.

Assumptions are written so that they can be false. "Users will value the product" cannot be false, therefore cannot be tested. "At least 40% of dispatchers will accept a change to their existing daily sequence that adds 40 seconds per job in exchange for eliminating a 6% return-trip rate" can be false, can be tested, and has a number in it. Every assumption on the map carries a confidence score from 1 to 5 using the scale in §0.6, a cost-if-false, and a named next test. An assumption with confidence 1–2 and a cost-if-false above three months of engineering is the target of the next two weeks of work.

# Assumption map — docs/01-discovery/assumptions.md
# Scored on two axes: 1-5 confidence, 1-5 cost-if-false (in engineer-weeks).
# Sort by cost_if_false * (6 - confidence). Attack the top row first.

QUADRANTS = ["desirability", "viability", "feasibility", "clarity"]

ASSUMPTIONS = [
    # id      quadrant       statement                                             conf  cost  next_test
    ("A01", "clarity",      "Technicians check stock at the depot before leaving, not en route", 2, 12,
     "Observation at 2 depots, 3 days each; count checks per technician"),
    ("A02", "desirability", "≥60% of technicians report the return trip in the last 30 days",     2, 20,
     "6 more problem interviews to saturation; then diary study n=15 for 14 days"),
    ("A03", "desirability", "The dispatcher will accept a change to the printed work order",      1, 16,
     "Fake-door: add a 'stock check' step to a printed pilot work order, measure completion"),
    ("A04", "desirability", "Technicians will not attempt to game the check to save time",        1,  8,
     "Concierge pilot with 4 technicians, 3 weeks, monitor for gaming in the audit trail"),
    ("A05", "viability",    "Service managers will pay £8/technician/month for this",            1, 24,
     "Pre-order / letter of intent with 3 service managers at target accounts"),
    ("A06", "viability",    "Value exceeds cost: 1.8pp first-time-fix on £1,900 avg job > £8/mo",1, 8,
     "Bottom-up arithmetic against the client's own job data (§2.1)"),
    ("A07", "viability",    "Existing systems (job management) will not block an integration",  2, 12,
     "Technical spike against the 3 most common job-management APIs"),
    ("A08", "feasibility",  "Stock truth is available from ERP with <60s latency",              3, 16,
     "Spike: measure p95 end-to-end on real ERP credentials, 5 days"),
    ("A09", "feasibility",  "Works in a browser on a phone with 1 bar in a basement plant room", 1, 20,
     "Field test: 3 Android devices, 3 iPhones, underground, on 4G and offline"),
    ("A10", "feasibility",  "Offline read of cached stock is sufficient for the top 3 tasks",   1, 12,
     "Prototype test: 5 users, offline-only task set, measure completion and error recovery"),
    ("A11", "clarity",      "The unit of work is the job, not the visit or the part",           3, 20,
     "Card sorting, n=20, 2 decks, with a forced-choice between job / visit / part"),
    ("A12", "clarity",      "The trigger is the work order, not the parts list or the vehicle",  2, 16,
     "Re-run framing interviews with explicit disconfirmation prompts, n=8"),
]

def priority(a): return a[4] * (6 - a[3])

RANKED = sorted(ASSUMPTIONS, key=priority, reverse=True)
# Top 3 by this scoring, for the first two weeks:
#   A05  24 * 5 = 120  viability — will anyone pay. Most expensive, least confident.
#   A02  20 * 4 =  80  desirability — is this real?
#   A09  20 * 5 = 100  feasibility — does it work where technicians are?
# Correct order: A05 (120), A09 (100), A02 (80).
# Note A03 and A04 are cheap to test and cheap if false, so they do not
# occupy the team's attention even though they are the least confident.

The riskiest-assumption test is a single question applied to the ranked list: which assumption, if false, would invalidate the entire product rather than degrade it? Not the most uncertain assumption and not the cheapest to test — the most damaging. Degrading assumptions are managed during build; invalidating assumptions must be resolved before build. A typical field-service product’s invalidating assumption is not the algorithm or the interface but "the return trip is frequent and consequential enough that a dispatcher will change their printed process for it". Everything else can be iterated. That one cannot.

Run the test by writing the null condition: "Assume A05 is false — no one pays. What is left?" If the honest answer is a product with no revenue, no sponsor and no market, the assumption is invalidating and it is tested first regardless of how hard it is to test. Testing viability assumptions early is uncomfortable because it requires talking to people who can say no to you, and this discomfort is itself a signal: teams that cannot bring themselves to ask a paying customer for money usually have a reason to believe the answer is no.

QuadrantQuestion it answersCheapest valid testTypical resolution windowFailure signatureBuild before resolution?
DesirabilityDo people want this, and have they already tried to get it?Problem interviews to saturation; concierge manual delivery2–4 weeksInterviews are warm but nobody has a workaround✗ Never
ViabilityCan money be made, at a price this market accepts?Pre-order, letter of intent, paid pilot, price-sensitivity interview series2–6 weeks"Interesting" with no procurement step; no budget line exists✗ Never
FeasibilityCan it be built, at acceptable cost and performance?Time-boxed spike against real data, real devices, real network1–3 weeksIt works on the founder’s laptop on office wifi✓ Only for the non-blocking parts
Clarity (usability)Do we understand the user, their context and their vocabulary?Contextual inquiry, card sorting, artefact analysis, workflow observation2–4 weeksRequirements use words the user does not use✗ Never
 
# Applying the riskiest-assumption test to the field-service example.

SCENARIOS = {
  "A02_false_return_trip_rare": {
    survives: False,
    why: "The product has no job to do. Demand evaporates. Team has built a tool for
           a 6% event that 40% of users experience twice a year.",
  },
  "A05_false_nobody_pays": {
    survives: False,
    why: "No revenue, no sponsor, no reference customer. Free pilot users are not a
           market; they are a hosting cost with a churn problem.",
  },
  "A09_false_no_connectivity": {
    survives: "PARTIALLY",
    why: "Product survives as a desktop app (ch13-16) with local stock cache, or as a
           web app that degrades to a cached read-only view. Degraded, not invalid —
           but the offline path becomes 40% of the engineering budget, which changes
           the track decision. This is a TRACK-CHANGING assumption, not a
           viability assumption, and it is tested in ch2 before the fork.",
  },
  "A08_false_no_erp_latency": {
    survives: True,
    why: "Nightly batch import of stock is acceptable for 70% of the value. Degraded
           feature, real workaround, no re-architecture. Buildable after MVP.",
  },
  "A03_false_dispatcher_refuses": {
    survives: "PARTIALLY",
    why: "B2C variant: technician-initiated check on their own phone removes the
           dispatcher from the loop. Different product, same problem. Pivot is a
           re-framing exercise (1-2 weeks), not a rebuild.",
  },
}

# Result: two invalidating assumptions (A02, A05) and one track-changing (A09).
# The two weeks of work are allocated: A05 (viability, pre-order) and A09
# (feasibility + track decision, field spike). A02 is answered in parallel by
# finishing the interview round to saturation, because it is already 2/3 done.

Sequence the work by irreversibility, not by convenience. The riskiest-assumption test frequently selects an assumption that is expensive or awkward to test — a willingness-to-pay question, a field trial, an enterprise procurement conversation. That discomfort is the signal. Choose the assumption whose falsity would cost the most, and give it the first and best team member, not the leftover.

Recording disconfirming evidence. A contradiction log is mandatory and separate from the interview notes. Every time two participants describe the same trigger differently, or a participant’s account conflicts with your telemetry, it is written up with both accounts in full. Teams reliably discount the contradictions; the log exists so that later readers can see that they were not discountable.

1.4 Jobs to Be Done

Applies the Jobs to Be Done framework to structure interview data into functional, emotional and social jobs, and to explain the four forces diagram and the mechanics of switching.

Jobs to Be Done is a research discipline rather than a diagram, and its most misused form is a workshop canvas listing three jobs. The useful version is a way of structuring what you heard so that you can make a claim about the mechanism of demand. The core proposition is that people do not buy products; they hire them to make progress in a particular circumstance, and the demand exists because the circumstances recur. A competitor’s product is not your competitor — the user’s incumbent solution, including doing nothing, spreadsheets and a junior colleague, is.

Jobs are analysed in three layers. Functional jobs are the task the user is hiring the product to do, stated with enough specificity to be testable: "when the work order prints, tell me whether the part is in the van so I can load it once". Emotional jobs are the feeling the user wants during and after: "so I stop dreading the drive", "so I am not the technician who has to go back". Social jobs concern how the outcome is seen by others: "so the customer stops complaining", "so my manager sees I organised the day". Only the functional layer is a specification input; the other two are the mechanism that makes the functional job urgent, and they are what you discard when you optimise purely for task completion — which is why products that satisfy the functional job and fail the emotional one get low retention despite good usability scores.

# Opportunity Solution Tree, plain text. Three levels, three constraints:
#   - every subtree node must trace to an insight with a real quote and a source ID
#   - every opportunity is stated as a user need, never as a feature
#   - every solution node names the assumption it depends on

OPPORTUNITY SOLUTION TREE
=======================

OUTCOME (business)

  |     |  31% of return trips (depot audit) are because the part existed but
  |     |  was held at a different branch, 40km away.
  |     |  Strength: strong (5), but derived from audit not interviews.
  |     -> OUT OF SCOPE for v1: inter-branch transfer is a logistics product.

  NOT AN OPPORTUNITY (excluded deliberately, with reasons)
  x "Make the work order digital"          — no evidence it is a problem
  x "Add route optimisation"               — logistics, out of scope
  x "Let customers see technician ETA"    — customer-facing, out of scope
  x "Replace the job management system"    — no buyer, no budget, 18-month build

The forces diagram. Demand for a new solution is a function of four forces, and the whole point of the model is that a new entrant must overcome all four. The push of the current situation is the dissatisfaction that makes change attractive; the pull of the new solution is the attraction of the better future; the habit of the present is the inertia of the existing behaviour, including the incumbent’s cost; and the anxiety of the new solution is the fear of what goes wrong — new risk, new learning, new social exposure. The push and pull determine whether the user is looking; habit and anxiety determine whether they switch, and switching is where products are lost. A team with a strong pull and a weak push has a product that converts well from a search-driven flow and fails from an outbound one.

# The four forces, scored 1-5 from interview evidence for our product.
# Higher anxiety = stronger barrier to switching. This is not a feature priority
# list; it is a list of barriers, and barriers get removed, not out-ranked.

FORCES = {
  "push": {
    "score": 4,
    "evidence": "29% return-trip rate; 6/8 name it unprompted; 22% dead van stock",
    "limiter": "Felt monthly, not daily, for 5/8. Low urgency for the technician even
               though high cost for the employer. Employer and technician have
               different forces, which is why the buyer is not the user.",
  },
  "pull": {
    "score": 3,
    "evidence": "Participants could not articulate the solution unprompted. When
                shown a static mockup (n=8), 6 said it 'looked sensible' — which
                is not evidence, per §1.2.",
    "limiter": "Pull is currently hypothesised, not observed. A05 and the concierge
               pilot exist to convert this from 3 to a measured value.",
  },
  "habit": {
    "score": 5,
    "evidence": "22% speculative stock is a learned defence. 31% of return trips are
                'known' to dispatchers. 'It's always been this way' in 7/8 sessions.",
    "limiter": "Habit here is rational, not irrational: carrying spares is cheap
               insurance against a failed visit. The solution must beat the
               insurance, not scold it. Design consequence: the check must be
               faster than loading a spare part.",
  },
  "anxiety": {
    "score": 4,
    "evidence": "3/8 worried about being blamed for a delayed job. 2/8 worried the
                system will show they were slow. 1/8 worried about tracking.",
    "limiter": "Anxiety is social, not technical. It is about exposure. Mitigation is
               to make the system credit the technician for avoiding a trip,
               not measure them. This is a ch5 design constraint discovered in ch1.",
  },
}

# Switching decision, written as a comparison the user is implicitly making:
#
#   CURRENT                                 PROPOSED
#   Load a spare part anyway   [2 min]     Open app, wait for stock  [40 s, 1 bar]
#   Nothing happens if wrong   [no risk]   Load list is now wrong    [visible failure]
#   Nobody knows               [no blame]  Dispatcher sees the miss  [social risk]
#   Works always               [offline]   Needs signal             [may not work]
#
# Verdict: current habit wins on 3 of 4 rows. The product is NOT switching
# winning. Required: cut the 40s to under 8s, remove the social exposure, and
# guarantee a usable answer offline. These three become ch5 constraints and
# ch15 offline requirements (Desktop track) or ch10 service-worker caching
# (Web track). The forces diagram changed the product.

Switching costs, stated plainly. The four forces model is only useful if it makes you enumerate what the user gives up. Write the current-state table explicitly — what time, money, risk, social exposure and status they currently trade for a known outcome — because any solution that does not beat the incumbent on at least the two most-weighted rows will not be adopted regardless of its merits. In the worked example the current habit wins on three of four rows, and the honest conclusion is that the product as conceived does not yet earn adoption. That is the correct output of discovery and it took two weeks rather than six months.

Job statements are not requirements. A job is a need, and needs are stable for years; requirements are solutions and expire in months. Writing requirements in job language ("the system shall help the technician avoid a second trip") is untestable and untakeable. The translation step from job to requirement must happen explicitly, in a document, with the acceptance criteria on the requirement side and the job as its rationale. If you find acceptance criteria written in job language, the specification has leaked.

Emotional and social jobs are not decoration. They are frequently the retention mechanism. A product that satisfies the functional job and is neutral-to-negative on the emotional and social jobs is a product with high initial completion and high 30-day churn, and the churn will be misdiagnosed as a pricing problem. Instrument the emotional and social job in the first usability round: ask, at the end of each task, what the participant would tell a colleague about this, and what they would worry about their manager seeing.

1.5 Validation experiment types

Catalogues the six experiment archetypes with mechanics, cost, duration, what they measure, and an honest verdict on the inference each one actually licenses.

Six experiment archetypes cover almost all early validation work. Each is a way of manufacturing evidence of a different kind, with a different inferential reach. Choosing by the type of claim you need — not by the apparent cleverness of the method — is the skill. The verdicts below are deliberately unsentimental: three of the six will not, on their own, license a build decision, and the honest thing to do is say so before spending three weeks on them.

TypeMechanicsTimeCostMeasuresHonest verdictUse when
Fake doorAnnounce a feature that does not exist; measure click-through to a waitlist or contact form3–14 days£0–500Attention and stated intent under real conditions✗ Does not measure willingness to pay, and attracts the curiosity-seeking. Treat as a weak upper bound only, never as validation.✓ Cheap signal on messaging and segment; ✗ as a demand test
ConciergeDeliver the outcome manually, by hand, for 3–10 real users, with no product2–6 weeksHigh in human timeReal demand, real frequency, real willingness to talk to a person about it✓ The strongest early test. Measures whether the outcome is valued, at true cost, including the cost that will make the product uneconomic.✓ Default for desirability; ✗ when the outcome cannot be delivered manually
Wizard of OzThe user interacts with a plausible interface; a human behind it performs the work3–8 weeksMediumInterface comprehension and workflow acceptance, with a real outcome behind it✓ Best of both: real demand, real interface, no build cost. ✗ Cannot measure performance, scale, or the boring parts of the system.✓ Workflow validation and comprehension; ✗ performance questions
Smoke testBuild the riskiest technical path only, badly, and try to break it with real data at real scale1–3 weeks£0–2kWhether a specific technical approach survives contact with reality✓ Excellent for feasibility, where the question is binary. ✗ Produces no information about desirability or value at all.✓ Feasibility and de-risking; ✗ anything product-shaped
Prototype testClickable or coded prototype, 5 users per round, moderated, task-based1–2 weeks per round£0–4k per roundComprehension, task success, hesitation, error recovery✓ Unbeatable for iteration on a design. ✗ Says nothing about whether to build; 5 users is a directional read, not a statistic.✓ Refining a design; ✗ justifying the product’s existence
Pre-order / LOIAsk for money, a signature, or a procurement step before delivery2–8 weeksLow direct, high in accessRevealed preference: revealed willingness to pay and real budget✓ The only cheap test of willingness to pay. ✗ Slow, and rejection is often about timing and procurement rather than value — always ask and record the real reason.✓ Viability; ✗ when the market is pre-revenue or consumer-only

The concierge test deserves the most attention because it produces the most valid evidence per pound spent and is routinely under-used. The discipline is that you must deliver the outcome manually, completely, for a real user, in their real context, and you must keep an honest ledger of the time it takes you. For the field-service example: agree with three service managers that you will personally check stock availability for their technicians each morning and phone them with the parts to load, delivered as a phone call. Three weeks, three accounts, roughly 4 hours per day of your time. The evidence is: do they answer the phone? Do they act on it? Does the return-trip rate move? And the ledger tells you that the check costs 3.2 minutes per job, which is precisely the number the product must beat. If the concierge cost is above the value, the product does not exist regardless of how good the software is — and this is the most valuable and most commonly skipped calculation in software product development.

# Concierge pilot — the manual delivery, and the ledger that makes it informative.
# The point is not to prove users like it. The point is to measure what it costs
# to deliver by hand, because that cost is the product's true performance target.

PILOT = {
  "id": "EXP-2026-04-01-concierge-stock-check",
  "type": "concierge",
  "duration_days": 21,
  "accounts": 3,
  "technicians_covered": 14,
  "operator": "1 person, ~4h/day",
}

LEDGER_COLUMNS = ["date", "account", "job_id", "technician", "erp_lookup_s",
                   "phone_call_s", "parts_recommended", "parts_loaded",
                   "job_completed_first_time", "notes"]

# Worked rows (synthetic but structurally real — this is the artefact format):
LEDGER = [
  ("2026-04-01","ACME-1","J-44021","P07",4.1,38,"brg,seal,filter","brg,seal,filter",True,
   "Technician already knew from a verbal handover; call was confirmatory."),
  ("2026-04-01","ACME-1","J-44022","P03",3.8,42,"seal,seal2","seal",False,
   "seal2 not on van, not at branch. Return trip. This is the failure we target."),
  ("2026-04-01","BRIG-2","J-88104","P11",2.2,35,"gasket","gasket",True, "Easy win."),
  ("2026-04-02","ACME-1","J-44051","P07",4.4,51,"belt,bolt","belt",False,
   "Technician asked to be called only if 'no'. Preference signal. Note it."),

# Roll-up after 21 days, n = 214 jobs across 3 accounts:
RESULTS = {
  "call_answer_rate":        0.93,      # 199/214 answered within 30 min
  "action_rate":             0.71,      # loaded >=1 recommended part before departure
  "recommendation_accuracy": 0.79,      # recommended part present at load time
  "false_alarm_rate":        0.12,      # recommended a part not actually needed
  "first_time_fix_delta":    +0.021,    # 0.021 absolute on a 0.71 baseline
  "operator_minutes_per_job": 3.2,      # THE NUMBER THAT DECIDES THE PRODUCT
  "operator_error_rate":     0.04,
}

# The decision, made against a pre-registered threshold:
#
#   Pre-registered success criteria, set 2026-03-28 before data collection:
#     answer_rate   >= 0.85
#     action_rate    >= 0.65
#     FTF_delta     >= 0.015
#     minutes/job    <= 4.0        (the software must beat the human)
#     and 2 of 3 service managers willing to pay >= £8/technician/month
#
#   Observed: 0.93 ✓, 0.71 ✓, +0.021 ✓, 3.2 ✓, 1 of 3 willing ✗
#
#   VERDICT: PARTIAL PASS. Demand and value are demonstrated. Viability is not.
#   A05 stays at confidence 2. Next step is a price test with all 3 accounts,
#   not a build. Three weeks of engineering spent now would have been wrong.

The fake door needs an honest verdict because it is the most widely misused test in the early-stage canon. It measures attention and curiosity, in a real traffic context, at near-zero cost, in days. What it does not measure is willingness to pay, and the population it attracts is systematically enriched in the merely curious: click-through rates of 3–8% on a well-placed fake door are unremarkable and mean nothing on their own. The legitimate use is comparative — testing two value propositions against each other on the same traffic, where the confound of curiosity is held constant — and the illegitimate use is treating 6% signups as demand. A fake door that measures price-point variants, where the variant differences are large and the sample is in the thousands, is a real experiment. A fake door with one button is a vanity metric.

# Experiment canvas — the single mandatory record per experiment.
# Every field is filled BEFORE the experiment runs. An experiment with a blank
# decision_rule or a missing kill date is a prototype, and is labelled as such.

experiment:
  id: EXP-2026-05-02-price-test-v2
  name: "Price point test, service-manager budget line"
  type: pre_order
  owner: product lead
  created: 2026-05-02
  kill_date: 2026-05-30          # hard stop; not extendable without a new record

  hypothesis: >
    Service managers at 40-400 technician contractors can obtain a discretionary
    budget line of at least £6 per technician per month for reducing return
    travel, and can obtain it without a board-level purchase.

  assumption_ids: [A05, A06]
  quadrant: viability
  confidence_before: 1

  metric:
    primary: "signed paid pilot or executed letter of intent with a stated price"
    secondary:
      - "days from first contact to signature"
      - "budget line identified by name and cost centre"
      - "procurement steps required"

  thresholds:                     # pre-registered, no adjustment after seeing data
    success: ">=2 of 5 accounts sign at >= £6/technician/month, and the median
              sales cycle is <= 45 days"
    partial: "1 of 5 signs, OR 2 of 5 confirm the budget line exists but state
              price is above the threshold"
    fail: "0 of 5 sign AND 3 of 5 cannot identify any budget line for this"

  method:
    population: "service managers at 40-400 technician contractors, UK, not
                 current customers, not previously interviewed"
    n: 5
    recruitment: "cold approach, no warm intro, no demo, no pitch deck"
    what_is_offered: "a 90-day pilot at a stated price, starting at a named date,
                       delivered by us, with a written service-level commitment"
    what_is_asked: "yes/no to signing, plus the real reason either way"

  cost:
    direct: "£0 software, 2 days of senior time"
    time: 28 days
    opportunity_cost: "the two engineers who could be on the feasibility spike"

  risks_to_validity: [
    "sample of 5 is directional only; the finding is about budget lines existing,
     not about market prevalence",
    "the interviewer is the founder, which raises social desirability pressure;
     mitigate by asking for a signature, not a verbal yes",
    "accounts approached cold are by definition not warm; this tests the cold
     channel, which is the channel we will actually have to use",
  ]

  decision_rule: >
    success -> A05 rises to 4, proceed to a build decision at the ch2 gate.
    partial -> A05 stays at 2, repeat with a different value proposition, not a
                different population, and do not build.
    fail    -> A05 falls to 1. The product is not viable at this price. Revisit
                the problem statement, because a viable problem exists and this
                particular monetisation does not.

  kill_criteria: [
    "no signed pilot by 2026-05-30",
    "3 of 5 cannot name any discretionary budget line for reducing travel",
  ]

  actual: # filled at close
    result: "1 of 5 signed at £7.50/tech/month. 4 of 5 confirmed the budget line
             exists (fuel/vehicle cost centre) but had not considered moving it.
             Median cycle to verbal yes: 3 days. To signature: none."
    conclusion: "partial - budget line exists, category is unfamiliar, cycle
                 unknown. A05 -> 2. Next: reframe the ask as a fuel-cost
                 reduction with a 3-month trial, repeat with n=5."

Experiments that measure the experiment. A common and expensive error is running a concierge or wizard-of-oz pilot with participants who are friends, investors, or the sponsor’s network. These participants are trying to help you, and their data is worthless while looking excellent. The recruitment record in §1.2 exists specifically to make this visible: a decision to override IC4 or IC5 must be written down as a decision, with the reason and the resulting confidence discount. Segregated pilots — where the concierge operator is not the founder — produce measurably different and lower enthusiasm readings.

Pre-register everything. Write the metric, the threshold, the sample and the kill date before the experiment runs. The reason is not scientific virtue: it is that you will be tempted, at close, to reinterpret a 4% result as encouraging, and a pre-registration makes that reinterpretation visible and requires you to write down that you did it. Teams that pre-register kill more experiments and build better products, which is the point.

1.6 Assembling the evidence pack

Specifies the evidence pack: transcript index, saturation analysis, contradiction log, tag-indexed quotes, confidence updates, and the pre-build gate checklist.

The evidence pack is the deliverable that the whole of chapter 1 exists to produce. It is not a slide deck. It is a set of retrievable artefacts that lets someone who was not present, and will not remember, reconstruct why the decision to build was made and what would falsify it. A team that cannot produce this pack has, functionally, decided to build on conviction — and should be honest that this is the choice being made rather than describing the output as a validated process.

The pack has five components. The transcript index is a table of one row per session with ID, date, stratum, consent status, duration, and the trigger event found. The saturation analysis records where new information stopped appearing, with the last-three-sessions rule applied explicitly. The contradiction log holds every conflict between sources, unresolved or resolved, with both accounts preserved. The quote index is every verbatim quote used in a downstream artefact, tagged and traced to a session ID, so that no claim in a specification can be unattributable. The confidence update is the assumption map with each confidence score changed, dated and justified, including scores that went down.
