The table above is the honest state of a real discovery round: desirability decisively passed, viability partially, feasibility untested, clarity partial, and three gate conditions unmet. The correct next action is two more weeks of tests and no feature code. Teams under pressure read this table as failure. It is the opposite: six weeks and about 5% of the eventual build budget have converted an opinion into a set of measurements, three of which say do not build yet, and the most expensive assumption of all — the deployment target — has been identified before anyone chose a framework.

Writing the decision memo. The pack closes with a one-page memo addressed to the decision-maker, containing four sections: what we now know and how we know it (with sources), what we do not know (with the cost of not knowing), what we recommend, and what would change our mind. The fourth section is the one that gets read in month six, and writing it honestly is the single most useful thing a team does at the end of discovery.

Do not launder conviction as evidence. If a gate condition is not met, the options are to meet it, to formally waive it with a named owner and an expiry date, or to change the goal. Presenting a partially-evidenced round as a completed one is the failure this chapter cannot prevent, because it is a social act rather than a technical one. The only structural defence is the pre-registered threshold: it exists precisely so that the argument about whether 1-of-5 signed pilots counts cannot be won by whoever is most senior in the room.

Exercises 1

  1. Run a complete 10-session discovery round in your own domain. Write a screener with four inclusion and three exclusion criteria, recruit from a non-customer source, run ten 45-minute sessions using the fixed structure in §1.2 including the ten-second silence rule, and produce one filed transcript per session. Success criterion: saturation is reached and demonstrably documented — the last three sessions produced no new trigger event, workaround or consequence — and a written coverage note names every stratum gap rather than omitting it.
  2. Build an assumption map and run the riskiest-assumption test on it. List at least 12 assumptions for a product you know, classify each into desirability, viability, feasibility or clarity, score confidence 1–5 and cost-if-false in engineer-weeks, rank by cost × (6 − confidence), and write the null scenario for the top three. Success criterion: you can name the single invalidating assumption, and you have scheduled a test for it within 21 days with a named owner and a pre-registered threshold.
  3. Execute one concierge pilot and keep the ledger. Manually deliver the outcome of your product to three real users for three weeks, logging operator minutes per job, action rate, accuracy, false-alarm rate and one outcome metric. Success criterion: you can state the operator-minutes-per-job figure and compare it against the estimated automated runtime, and you have a written go/no-go on whether the software can beat the human by the required margin.
  4. Score every question in your last five interviews. Take your most recent research transcripts and classify every question you asked as facts-about-past, facts-about-existing-spend, opinion, or hypothetical-future. Produce a table with the count in each category and a rewritten version of every hypothetical-future question. Success criterion: hypothetical-future questions drop to zero, and at least three questions you had assumed were neutral are revealed to have been leading, each with a corrected version written.
  5. Produce the evidence pack and the decision memo for your current product. Assemble the five components from §1.6 — transcript index, saturation analysis, contradiction log, tag-indexed quote index, confidence update — plus a one-page memo with the four required sections including "what would change our mind". Success criterion: the pack exists in a repository, a colleague who was not in any interview can reconstruct the decision from it alone, and the gate table honestly shows at least two unmet conditions with a written plan for each.

2 · Market, Competition and Feasibility

2.1 Sizing the market: TAM, SAM and SOM2.2 Unit economics2.3 Competitive analysis beyond the feature matrix2.4 Technical feasibility spikes2.5 Build, buy or open source2.6 Risk register and pre-mortem

This chapter converts a validated problem into a defensible investment case. It sets out how to size a market twice — top-down to sanity-check plausibility and bottom-up to actually decide — explains why the top-down figure is usually fiction, derives the unit economics inputs that determine whether a software business works at all, replaces the feature matrix with an analysis of positioning and switching cost, defines the discipline of a time-boxed throwaway spike, applies total cost of ownership and exit cost to build-versus-buy, and formalises risk with likelihood × impact scoring and a pre-mortem. Its argument is that the questions asked in this chapter can be answered from a desk in four weeks and that answering them later costs between 40% and 90% of the eventual budget.

2.1 Sizing the market: TAM, SAM and SOM

Works the TAM, SAM and SOM arithmetic from both directions, explains why top-down figures are unreliable, and specifies the bottom-up calculation that actually supports a decision.

Market sizing is a discipline of subtraction, not multiplication. Three figures are conventionally distinguished. TAM, total addressable market, is every possible customer for the product category, valued annually. It is a plausibility ceiling and it is almost never actionable. SAM, serviceable addressable market, is the portion of the TAM you can actually serve given your product’s capabilities, geography, regulatory position, and delivery model. SOM, serviceable obtainable market, is the portion of the SAM you can realistically capture within a stated horizon with a stated sales capacity. Only SOM supports a revenue plan, and only SOM should appear in a business case alongside a cost.

Top-down sizing multiplies a population estimate by a price. The arithmetic is trivial and the inputs are the entire problem, because both inputs come from reports whose provenance is usually opaque, whose scope rarely matches your product’s boundary, and whose error compounds multiplicatively. A 30% error in the population and a 40% error in the achievable price produce a 58% error in the result, in either direction, and there is no way to detect it from the arithmetic. The honest use of a top-down number is as a falsification check: if your bottom-up SOM of £4M is 0.03% of a claimed £1.2B TAM, one of the two is wrong, and it is very probably the top-down one.

# TOP-DOWN, computed honestly and then discarded.
# Every input is sourced, dated, and its scope mismatch is written down.

TAM_topdown = {
  "source": "industry analyst report, 2025, vendor-published summary",
  "claim": "field service management software, UK, EUR 1.42bn in 2025",

    ("category is FSM suites incl. dispatch, rota, mobile workforce, parts", -0.55),
    ("our boundary is stock-availability-at-dispatch only",                 0.00),
    ("we serve UK + IE + NL only (post-brexit, GDPR, language)",            -0.62),
    ("we exclude enterprise >2000 technicians (needs on-prem, not feasible)", -0.30),
    ("we exclude sub-40-technician shops (no budget line, see owner-operator "
     "interview P06)",                                                     -0.18),
  ],
  "result": 1.42e9 * 0.45 * 0.38 * 0.70 * 0.82,
  # 1.42e9 * 0.0829 = 117.7m
  "error_band": "+/- 55%",     # inherited from the source, not reducible here
  "verdict": "PLAUSIBILITY CEILING ONLY. Not used for any decision.",
}

# The specific reason top-down fails for a narrow B2B tool:
# Our product's value is ~1.8pp of first-time-fix on an average job of GBP 1,900.
# That is 34 pounds of value per job. The price is a share of that.
# A top-down report values the CATEGORY (the whole FSM budget), which is 40x
# larger than the value we create. Sizing a share-of-value product by its
# category is a category error, and it is why our TAM/our value ratio is
# implausible. State this explicitly in the business case.

Bottom-up sizing counts the customers you can name and the revenue each can pay. It requires five inputs, each of which should be sourced independently, and it produces a figure with an error band you can defend. The method is: count the addressable units; determine the realistic penetration given your sales capacity and the market’s own churn; multiply by price; subtract nothing yet. The output is not a prediction, it is an upper bound on your own execution, which is the number that matters, because you are the only variable you control.

# BOTTOM-UP. Five inputs, each independently sourced. The arithmetic is
# shown line by line because the business case is read by people who will
# check the multiplication, and they should be able to.

# --- Input 1: addressable accounts ----------------------------------------

  "geo": "UK + Ireland",

# WHY MOST TAM NUMBERS ARE FICTION — the five failure modes, checkable.

# 1. CATEGORY CREEP
#    The analyst's category is defined to be large. A product that addresses
#    0.5% of a category's budget is counted as 100% of its market.
#    Test: is your product's value, per customer, less than 5% of what customers
#    already spend on the category? If yes, your top-down number is fiction.
#    Ours: GBP 61.6/tech/yr created against ~GBP 340/tech/yr of FSM software
#    spend = 18%. Borderline. Flagged.

# 2. GEOGRAPHIC LEAKAGE
#    "Global market" figures are quoted for a product that serves one country.
#    Ours: we cut 62% for geography before doing anything else.
#    Test: does the report's geography match your shipping zones? Exactly?

# 3. DOUBLE COUNTING
#    Adjacent categories overlap. A seat in "field service" is often counted in
#    "field service", "workforce management" AND "mobile workforce". A naive sum
#    of three report figures triple-counts the same GBP.
#    Test: can you show, with citations, that the categories are disjoint?

# 4. WISHFUL ATTRIBUTION
#    A tiny product of a large company is credited with the whole category.
#    Ours would be cited inside a report about a 400-person firm; the report's
#    attribution of that firm's revenue to the category is not separable.
#    Test: can you decompose the top 5 players' revenue into this category
#    specifically, from their filings? For 2 of 5 we could not.

# 5. STALE OR PROJECTED-ONLY
#    Forecasts are 5-year extrapolations with CAGR applied. If the report is a
#    forecast rather than a measurement, it contains no data at all.
#    Test: does the figure describe a past period, and is that period named?
#    Ours: "2025" without a measurement method = projection. Discarded.

# THE REPLACEMENT STANDARD
# A market number enters the business case only if:
#   [x] it is a MEASURED past period, not a forecast
#   [x] its geography matches the served geography exactly
#   [x] its category boundary is no wider than the product boundary
#   [x] it is decomposable to a named set of units (firms, seats, licences)
#   [x] a bottom-up count of the same units has been produced independently
#   [x] the two agree within an order of magnitude, OR the disagreement is
#       explained in writing
# Ours fails [x] on the analyst figure and passes all six on the bottom-up
# count, which is why only the bottom-up figure appears in the model.
MethodFormulaInputs requiredTypical errorTimeUse it forNever use it for
Top-down analystCategory revenue from a third-party report1 report you did not produce±50–300%1 hour✓ Falsifying your own bottom-up figure; ✓ a slide nobody will check✗ Revenue planning; ✗ investor claims
Bottom-up, firm countAddressable accounts × realistic logos × ARPARegistry data, sales capacity, price−30% / +45%1–2 weeks✓ The SOM figure that goes in the model; ✓ capacity planning✗ TAM marketing claims
Bottom-up, seat countTarget users × attainable attach rate × priceUser population, attach rate, price−25% / +60%3–5 days✓ Consumer and PLG products; ✓ pricing work✗ Products with per-account rather than per-seat pricing
Value-based / share of walletCustomer’s realised value × price share taken (typically 10–20%)Cost model of a customer, attach rate−20% / +80%1 week✓ Justifying price to a buyer; ✓ ROI-led sales✗ Market size (it sizes willingness to pay, not population)
Workload-derivedUnits of work per year × price per unitDomain model of the work−20% / +30%1–2 weeks✓ Usage-based pricing; ✓ infra cost models (ch12)✗ Products whose usage is not observable
Jobs-to-be-done sizingFrequency of the circumstance × population in it × price per switchInterview-derived frequency, population, switching cost±40%2–4 weeks✓ New categories with no incumbent; ✓ testing whether demand recurs✗ Anything needing precision inside 20%

Never mix a top-down TAM with a bottom-up cost model. This is the single most common analytical error in software business cases: a £1.2B market from a report is placed above a cost model derived from your own unit costs, producing a return that is arithmetically valid and factually meaningless, because the two halves describe different populations at different boundaries. If you use a third-party market figure at all, use it only as a ratio check against your own bottom-up SOM — the share you are claiming of that market — and if the share exceeds about 5% of an analyst category, the analyst number is wrong, not your ambition.

2.2 Unit economics

Defines and derives every unit-economics input — price, gross margin, CAC by channel, retention, payback, LTV, burn multiple — with the formula and a warning for each.

Unit economics determine whether a software business is a business or a hobby with payroll. The inputs are few, each has a specific formula, and each has a specific way of being wrong. The critical discipline is that these are per-cohort numbers computed from real data, not blended averages across the whole customer base, because blended averages conceal exactly the two things you need to see: whether recent cohorts are getting worse, and whether the customers you acquired cheaply are the ones who churn.

Gross margin is the fraction of revenue left after the direct cost of delivery: hosting, third-party API consumption, payment processing, support labour attributable to the account, and for a desktop product the store commission. The band is a property of the business model, and knowing your band before pricing is the difference between a company and a project.

Business modelTypical gross marginDominant cost of deliveryPayback targetKey risk
SaaS, self-serve, low usage75–85%Hosting per seat, support< 12 monthsFree tier attracts non-payers; CAC hidden in content
SaaS, mid-market, sales-assisted70–80%Support, onboarding labour, hosting12–18 monthsOnboarding not productised; services revenue pollutes margin
Enterprise SaaS65–80%Support, dedicated infra, security/compliance overhead18–24 monthsCustomisation revenue is not recurring revenue
Usage-based, high unit cost40–65%The metered resource itself6–12 monthsMargin is inversely correlated with success; cost per unit must fall
API / infrastructure, pass-through15–40%Upstream compute, exactly3–9 monthsCommoditised; margin is the whole business
Desktop, direct sale + licence server80–90%Licensing infra, crash/telemetry, update CDN< 12 monthsUnrecoverable customers; old-version tail is a permanent cost
Desktop, via app store70–85%Store commission 15–30%, review, tax handling6–12 monthsCommission plus VAT in some markets; store is a gatekeeper
Professional services0–40%Delivery headcount< 3 monthsDoes not scale; do not model it as software revenue
 
# UNIT ECONOMICS — every formula, then the worked model.
# All numbers are per-cohort and dated. Blended averages are forbidden here.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- FORMULAS
# Gross margin %      = (revenue - direct cost of delivery) / revenue
# CAC                 = (sales + marketing spend attributable to acquisition)
#                       / new customers acquired in the period, per CHANNEL
# Gross-margin-adjusted CAC ("CAC payback")
#                     = CAC / (ARPA x gross margin % / 12)     [months]
# Net revenue retention = (starting ARR + expansion - contraction - churn) / starting ARR
# Gross revenue retention = (starting ARR - contraction - churn) / starting ARR
# LTV (cohort, 24-month capped) = sum over months of (ARPA x GM%) x survival(m)
# Burn multiple         = net cash burn / net new ARR
#   -> 1.0-1.5 excellent, 1.5-2.0 good, 2.0-3.0 acceptable,
#      >3.0 unprofitable per unit of growth, fix before scaling
# Rule of 40          = ARR growth % + FCF margin %, summed, should exceed 40

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- INPUTS
PRICE_PER_TECH_MONTH = 8.00
ARPA_ANNUAL          = 960.0 * 12          # 11,520 per account, 120 techs
DIRECT_COST = {
  "hosting_and_compute":      0.42,   # per $1 revenue at current volume (ch12)
  "third_party_api":          0.06,   # mapping/geocoding for the route view
  "payment_processing":       0.019,  # 1.9% + 20p, blended
  "support_labour":           0.09,   # 0.4 h/tech/month at GBP 34 loaded
  "onboarding_labour":        0.055,  # amortised; 6 h setup, 12-month spread
  "desktop_store_commission": 0.00,   # not applicable on Web track
  "desktop_update_cdn":       0.00,   # not applicable on Web track
}
GM_PCT = 1 - sum(DIRECT_COST.values())     # 1 - 0.644 = 0.356
# GM = 35.6% at current volume.
# THIS IS THE HEADLINE NUMBER AND IT IS BAD. At 10x volume, hosting falls to
# 0.11 and support to 0.055:
GM_AT_SCALE = 1 - (0.11 + 0.045 + 0.019 + 0.055 + 0.03)   # 0.741 = 74.1%
# Decision: pricing is set for 10x volume, not current volume, and the plan
# to reach 74% is a ch2 deliverable (verticalising the stack, ch9). If the
# target volume is never reached, the product is not viable at 35% and must
# be re-priced. Write this down now.

# CAC by channel — the reason the word "by" matters
CAC_BY_CHANNEL = {
  "outbound_sales_cold": {
    "spend_per_qtr": 41_000,      # 1.5 AE fully loaded, outbound tooling, events
    "new_customers": 6,
    "cac": 6_833,                  # 41000/6
    "confidence": 1,               # from a real pilot, n=6. Low n, wide bar.
    "err": "+/- 40%",
  },
  "inbound_content": {
    "spend_per_qtr": 9_000,       # content production + tooling
    "new_customers": 2,
    "cac": 4_500,
    "confidence": 1,
    "err": "+/- 60%",
  },
  "partner_referral": {
    "spend_per_qtr": 6_000,       # partner enablement, revenue share
    "new_customers": 3,
    "cac": 2_000,
    "confidence": 2,               # 2 quarters of data, n=6
    "err": "+/- 30%",
  },
  "paid_search": {
    "spend_per_qtr": 15_000,
    "new_customers": 4,
    "cac": 3_750,
    "confidence": 1,
    "err": "+/- 70%",
    "note": "Bid inflation is the norm in this vertical; the 70% band is not paranoia.",
  },
}
BLENDED_CAC = 71_000 / 15   # 4,733 per customer, quarterly aggregate

# Retention, from the 2 pilot cohorts (n=9 accounts, 11 months)
RETENTION = {
  "gross_revenue_retention": 0.94,   # contraction + logo churn in 12 months
  "net_revenue_retention":   0.99,   # 1 account expanded (added 40 technicians)
  "logo_churn_annual":       0.11,   # 1 of 9 left; reason: contractor insolvency, not
                                    # dissatisfaction - different risk, see ch2 risk
  "expansion_annual":        0.06,
  "cohort_warning": "n=9. Confidence 1. This is the weakest number in the model and "
                    "it is the one with the largest effect on LTV. Doubling the "
                    "sample to n=30 changes the LTV estimate by 1.4x. Do not use "
                    "the LTV figure externally until n >= 30.",
}

# Survival curve: the shape matters more than the level
# Month-to-month revenue survival for a low-switching-cost SMB tool
SURVIVAL = [1.00, 0.995, 0.992, 0.990, 0.988, 0.986, 0.984, 0.982,
            0.980, 0.978, 0.976, 0.975]   # ~2.5%/yr logo churn, linear for 12 mo
# UNIT ECONOMICS — the computation. Every line is auditable.

arpa_m = ARPA_ANNUAL / 12                 # 960.00 /month

# --- Payback period, in months, per channel, on CURRENT margin -------------
# CAC_payback = CAC / (ARPA_monthly * GM%)
# At 35.6% GM the monthly gross profit per account is 960 * 0.356 = GBP 341.76
#   outbound:  6,833 / 341.76 = 20.0 months   ✗ (target < 12 at scale)
#   inbound:   4,500 / 341.76 = 13.2 months   ✗
#   partner:   2,000 / 341.76 =  5.9 months   ✓
#   paid:      3,750 / 341.76 = 11.0 months   ✗
#   blended:   4,733 / 341.76 = 13.8 months   ✗
# At 74.1% GM (10x volume) the monthly gross profit is 960 * 0.741 = 711.36
#   outbound:  6,833 / 711.36 =  9.6 months   ✓
#   inbound:   4,500 / 711.36 =  6.3 months   ✓
#   partner:   2,000 / 711.36 =  2.8 months   ✓
#   paid:      3,750 / 711.36 =  5.3 months   ✓
#   blended:   4,733 / 711.36 =  6.7 months   ✓
# CONCLUSION: the current pricing and CAC plan does not work at current margin,
# and works comfortably at the modelled 10x margin. The plan must therefore
# include a specific, dated, owned route to 10x volume - not an aspiration.

# --- LTV, cohort basis, capped at 24 months, at 74.1% GM ------------------
def ltv_capped(arpa_m, gm, survival, cap_months=24):
    """Survival beyond 12 months is extrapolated at the observed 2.5%/yr
    logo churn with NO expansion, which is conservative. LTV is capped at
    24 months because extrapolating past that is forecasting, not modelling."""
    s = list(survival)
    while len(s) < cap_months:
        s.append(s[-1] * 0.9979)   # 2.5%/yr compounded monthly
    return sum(arpa_m * gm * s[i] for i in range(cap_months))

LTV = ltv_capped(arpa_m, 0.741, SURVIVAL, 24)
# sum of survival(m), m=0..23 ≈ 23.19
# LTV = 960 * 0.741 * 23.19 = 16,497

# --- LTV:CAC --------------------------------------------------------------
RATIOS = {
  "partner":     round(16_497 / 2_000, 1),   # 8.2 : 1
  "paid_search": round(16_497 / 3_750, 1),   # 4.4 : 1
  "inbound":     round(16_497 / 4_500, 1),   # 3.7 : 1
  "outbound":    round(16_497 / 6_833, 1),   # 2.4 : 1   ✗ below the 3:1 floor
  "blended":     round(16_497 / 4_733, 1),   # 3.5 : 1
}
# Industry floor is 3:1. Above 5:1 usually means you are under-investing in
# growth and will lose share. Blended 3.5:1 is acceptable; outbound at 2.4:1
# is the channel that must change: either CAC below 4,120, or ARPA above
# 13,300, or the channel is closed. This is a written decision, not a hope.

# --- Burn multiple, forward 4 quarters ------------------------------------
BURN = {
  "net_cash_burn_q1":  184_000, "net_new_arr_q1":  61_200,   # 4.0  ✗
  "net_cash_burn_q2":  196_000, "net_new_arr_q2":  96_100,   # 3.1  ✗
  "net_cash_burn_q3":  205_000, "net_new_arr_q3": 146_800,   # 2.4  ✗ improving
  "net_cash_burn_q4":  198_000, "net_new_arr_q4": 201_400,   # 1.6  ✗ improving
}
# Burn multiple is 4.0 falling to 1.6. Above 3.0 for two consecutive quarters
# is the trigger to stop scaling spend and fix the model. The trend is the
# right direction; the level is not yet acceptable. Forecast: 1.2 by Q6.

# --- The decision this section forces -------------------------------------
UNIT_ECON_DECISION = {
  "problem": "35.6% gross margin at current volume; outbound CAC payback 20 months",
  "root_cause": "Fixed hosting cost spread over 4,500 addressable accounts, and a "
                "service-led acquisition motion that has not been productised",
  "dated_actions": [
    ("2026-08", "verticalise: single-region, single-DB-engine, precomputed route "
                "cache. Target GM 55%. Owner: tech lead."),
    ("2026-10", "productise onboarding to <2 h/account. Target CAC payback "
                "<12 mo on blended. Owner: eng lead."),
    ("2027-01", "close outbound unless CAC < 4,120. Shift to partner motion. "
                "Owner: product lead."),
  ],
  "gate": "This section is re-run at every quarterly review. A quarter where "
          "burn multiple rises above 3.0 halts all new spend until explained.",
}

Three ways unit economics go wrong, in order of frequency. First, services revenue is counted as software revenue, which inflates both margin and LTV; if anyone does implementation work for a customer, that revenue and its cost belong in a separate column and are excluded from the software metrics. Second, LTV is computed from a blended retention curve across all cohorts, which hides that your 2024 cohort is 40% worse than your 2025 cohort; compute per cohort, every quarter, and plot the trend. Third, CAC is computed as total sales-and-marketing spend over total new customers, which allocates the entire fixed cost of building the function to the customers acquired before the function was productive, making early CAC look catastrophically bad and later CAC look free. Compute CAC by channel and by cohort, and never blend it with a single company-wide number.

Read the ratio bands correctly. An LTV:CAC ratio below 3:1 means growth is destroying value and should be paused. A ratio above 5:1 usually means you are under-investing in growth and a competitor is taking the market. The healthy band is 3:1 to 5:1, and in that band the question is not the ratio but the absolute size of the CAC: at 3.5:1 with CAC of £4,733, you need 15 new customers a quarter just to stand still, and that is a very different company from one at 3.5:1 with a CAC of £300.

2.3 Competitive analysis beyond the feature matrix

Reframes competitive analysis around positioning, wedge, switching cost, network effects and moats, and specifies the artefacts that replace the feature comparison matrix.

The feature comparison matrix is the most widely used and least informative competitive artefact in software. It is uninformative because features are not why decisions are made, because a matrix cannot express sequence or timing, and because it is symmetric — it treats "we lack X" and "they lack X" as equivalent, which they are not. A competitor missing a feature you have is a minor inconvenience; a competitor having a feature you lack is often a different product and a different market. The matrix also ages instantly and is maintained by whoever has the largest marketing function.

A useful competitive analysis answers five questions in order. Who is the incumbent in the user’s budget line — frequently not a competitor at all, but a person, a spreadsheet or a job title, and this is where the real switching cost sits. Where is the wedge — the specific, narrow context in which you are categorically better, usually a segment, a workflow step, or a constraint the incumbents structurally cannot serve. What is the switching cost, in units of data, process, training, contracts and social capital. What network effects exist, of which kind, in which direction, and whether they are local or global. What is the moat — and the honest answer is often "none, yet", which is a legitimate finding that should be recorded rather than concealed.

# Positioning analysis, not a feature matrix. Fill this in by hand, from
# primary evidence: pricing pages, contracts, churn interviews, job postings,
# support forums, and the 5 losing-deal interviews from ch1.

The competitor set must include a behaviour. In every analysis in this chapter, the row that changes the strategy is not a company. It is the current workaround: the spreadsheet, the manual phone call, the junior colleague, or doing nothing. Writing a competitive analysis that lists only vendors systematically produces a plan that competes on features against companies your buyer has already chosen, while the thing actually taking the budget is invisible. The template in chapter 20 makes the non-software row mandatory, and a submission without it is returned.

2.4 Technical feasibility spikes

Defines a spike as a time-boxed, throwaway experiment with a binary question, and states the rules that keep it from becoming an accidental prototype.

A spike answers one technical question, in a fixed number of days, with code that is thrown away. Every element of that sentence is load-bearing. The question must be answerable with yes or no, because a question that produces a paragraph does not close. The time box must be fixed in advance, because the alternative is an open-ended investigation that becomes a prototype. And the code must be discarded, because spike code that survives into production carries every shortcut taken under time pressure and none of the documentation that would explain it — this is the mechanism by which a two-day spike becomes a two-year liability.

The distinction between a spike and a prototype is the most consequential and most frequently violated rule in this chapter. A spike is written to answer a question and is destroyed. A prototype is written to be evolved into the product, with structure, tests and interfaces that will survive. A spike optimises for speed to an answer and is expected to be wrong about most of what it builds. A prototype optimises for change and is expected to be right about its interfaces. Confusing them produces the classic outcome: an impressive three-day demo that took nine weeks to finish, because the demo was treated as a prototype and every shortcut had to be found and fixed.

# Feasibility spike record — the canonical format.
# Only ONE question per spike. If you have two, you have two spikes.

SPIKE:
  id: SPIKE-2026-04-08-A09-connectivity
  question: >
    On the target network - a UK mobile basement plant room, ~-95 dBm,
    4G - does a 3-second-cached-stock read succeed, and does the UI remain
    usable, with no connectivity at all, for the top 3 technician tasks?
  answerable_as_binary: true

  hypothesis: "p95 time-to-first-answer under 3s on 1 bar; full task completion
                with airplane mode for task 3 (confirm parts for this job)."

  time_box: "3 days, hard. No extensions without a new spike record."
  engineer: "1 senior engineer, no other assignment"
  throwaway: true
  budget: "3 engineer-days, GBP 0 infrastructure beyond a test SIM and 3 devices"

  method:
    devices: ["Pixel 6a (Android 14)", "iPhone 12 (iOS 17)", "Samsung A52 (Android 13)"]
    sim: "3 UK networks, physical SIMs, no wifi"
    locations:
      - {name: "plant room basement, Manchester", rssi_dbm: -97, carrier: "EE"}
      - {name: "plant room basement, Manchester", rssi_dbm: -93, carrier: "O2"}
      - {name: "roof plant deck, Manchester",      rssi_dbm: -71, carrier: "Vodafone"}
      - {name: "residential lift shaft",          rssi_dbm: -101, carrier: "EE"}
    what_is_built: >
      A single static page, hand-written HTML, no framework, no build step.
      Three buttons. A hardcoded JSON of 40 parts with stock. A 15-minute
      timer to simulate the ERP round trip. A localStorage cache written on
      every successful fetch. NO production code is written and none is kept.
    what_is_measured: >
      (a) time-to-first-answer, p50 and p95, 30 repetitions per device per
          location, over the raw signal;
      (b) task 3 completion rate in airplane mode, 5 technicians, 3 tasks each;
      (c) error and fallback behaviour, logged verbatim.

  pre_registered_thresholds:
    success:     "p95 < 3s at -95 dBm AND >= 4 of 5 technicians complete task 3
                  in airplane mode in under 20s, unassisted"
    partial:     "p95 < 6s at -95 dBm, or 3 of 5 complete task 3 offline"
    fail:        "p95 > 6s, or fewer than 3 of 5 complete task 3 offline"

  kill_date: "2026-04-11 (day 3). If unanswered, the answer is NO by default
              and an alternative architecture must be designed."

  # --- ACTUAL RESULT, filled at close ---------------------------------
  actual:
    time_to_first_answer:
      "roof -71 dBm:  p50 0.6s  p95 1.1s   (all 3 devices)"
      "basement -93 dBm: p50 1.4s p95 2.4s  (all 3 devices)"
      "basement -97 dBm: p50 3.8s p95 7.9s  (iPhone 12 only; Android devices
                          fell back to cache after 2s and served in 0.4s)"
      "lift shaft -101 dBm: no network on any device. Cache-only."
    offline_task_3: "5 of 5 technicians completed 'confirm parts for this job' from
                     cache in a mean of 9.4s (range 6-17s). 1 technician
                     reopened the app twice, believing it had failed - the empty
                     state was indistinguishable from a loading state."
    errors: "2 of 5 technicians said the app 'was broken' on first airplane-mode
             launch, before pressing anything. Loading spinner shown, not an
             empty-state message."

  verdict: PARTIAL
  confidence_update: "A09: 1 -> 4. The technical feasibility is now established:
                     cache-first read works at the target network. The remaining
                     unknown is UX, not feasibility."

  consequences:
    - "TRACK DECISION: the Web track remains viable, PROVIDED the design
       treats the cached path as the PRIMARY path and the network as an
       enhancement. Written into ADR-0003 and ch10 as a hard requirement."
    - "A design constraint is now a ch5 non-functional requirement: an empty
       cache must be visually and semantically distinct from loading and from
       error. WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages applies. This came out of a 3-day
       spike and would have cost 3 weeks in user testing."
    - "p95 7.9s on iPhone at -97 dBm means the 3s target is not universally
       achievable. The answer is a hard server-side timeout at 2.5s with
       cache fallback, not a faster network. iOS Safari background-tab
       throttling is the specific cause and is recorded in the spike notes."
    - "CODE THROWN AWAY: the static page is deleted on merge of the spike
       branch. Nothing from it enters the product. This is not optional."
# Spike portfolio for this project — planned, costed and sequenced.
# Total spike budget: 9 engineer-days out of a 26-week build. That is 3.5%.
# A larger spike budget is a symptom of a product that is not understood.

SPIKES_PLANNED = [
  ("A09", "connectivity and offline viability", 3, "tech lead",
   "TRACK-CHANGING - decides Web vs Desktop", "2026-04-11", "PARTIAL"),
  ("A08", "ERP stock latency", 2, "backend eng",
   "Feasibility: p95 stock read from the 3 most common ERP APIs", "2026-04-16", "PASS"),
  ("S03", "route geometry at scale", 2, "backend eng",
   "Feasibility: can 4,000 daily routes be precomputed nightly in <20 min at
    the lowest plausible infra cost, and does the cost per account drop below

  ("S04", "data-sharing consent model", 1, "tech lead + legal",
   "Feasibility: can aggregate stock-flow analytics be collected with customer

  ("S05", "offline write and conflict policy", 1, "backend eng",

    3 parts' with no server? Measure how often the offline window is >30 min

# Not spiked, deliberately: everything about the user interface. UI feasibility
# is not a thing; a UI either can be built or it cannot, and the answer is in
# the design, not in a spike.

# Rules enforced in the spike branch template (.github/spike-template.md):
#
#  1. Branch name: spike/<id>-<slug>
#  2. The record above is committed BEFORE any code is written. CI fails if the
#     record is missing or if hypothesis/thresholds/kill_date are empty.
#  3. Maximum 3 files touched unless a waiver is written in the record.
#  4. No imports from src/ or packages/. A spike may not depend on product
#     code, because the product must be able to throw the spike away.
#  5. No test coverage requirement. A spike is not tested; it is measured once,
#     against the pre-registered threshold, and destroyed.
#  6. On close: the branch is merged with a DELETION commit that removes every
#     file, and the record's "actual" and "verdict" fields are filled. A spike
#     that is not closed within 5 days of its kill date is escalated to the
#     tech lead, and an unanswered spike is treated as a failed spike.
MethodQuestion it answersDurationCode survives?CostGood forBad for
Feasibility spike (throwaway)Can approach X achieve requirement Y?0.5–3 days✗ always deletedNegligible✓ Binary technical unknowns; ✓ de-risking architecture✗ Anything user-facing; ✗ multi-question work
Technical proof of conceptCould a full system be assembled this way?1–3 weeksUsually, partiallyMedium✓ Vendor evaluation; ✓ integration risk✗ Estimates; ✗ anything with a schedule attached
Prototype (evolvable)How should this behave for a real user?1–6 weeks✓ designed to surviveHigh✓ User testing; ✓ building the actual P0 slice✗ Technical feasibility
Fake-door / landing pageWill anyone respond to this message?2h–2 weeksn/a~0✓ Messaging and positioning✗ Technical or product questions
Load / performance testDoes it hold at N×?1–3 days✓ test harness keptLow–medium✓ Capacity planning; ✓ finding the actual breaking point✗ Correctness
Build a small thing properly and time itHow long does this actually take?2–5 days✓ becomes production if it survivesMedium✓ Estimation of a real, narrow slice✗ If the slice is throwaway by definition

Budget 3–5% of the build for spikes and hold the line. Nine engineer-days of a 26-week, four-engineer build is 3.5%, and in the example above it converted a track-changing unknown into a resolved architectural requirement. Teams under-invest here and pay for it in architecture rework at month nine. The discipline that keeps it honest is the deletion rule: spike code is deleted in a separate commit, and the CI template enforces the record-before-code ordering so that a spike cannot start without a written question.

2.5 Build, buy or open source

Applies total cost of ownership and exit cost to the build-versus-buy decision, and establishes the 70/20/10 allocation as the default allocation of engineering effort.

Build-versus-buy is usually argued on licence cost versus engineering cost, which is the wrong comparison and systematically favours building, because engineering cost is estimated at zero while licence cost is quoted at list price. The correct comparison is total cost of ownership over a stated period, including the costs that are invisible until year three: integration, data migration, customisation requests you will honour, upgrade labour, security patching, compliance certification, and the opportunity cost of the engineers who would otherwise build your differentiating capability.

Two additions to TCO make the decision real. Exit cost is what it would take to leave the choice in two years, including data extraction in a usable format, migration effort, contract termination, and whether your customers have been trained around the vendor’s concepts in a way that leaves with you. A choice with an exit cost near zero is worth paying more for. And strategic fit: the capability must be examined for whether it is a source of differentiation. Buying something that is undifferentiated lets you spend your scarce engineering on the 3-second answer; building something undifferentiated spends it on a login system.

# BUILD vs BUY vs OPEN SOURCE — full TCO over 3 years, and exit cost.
# All figures GBP, nominal, from vendor quotes dated 2026-03 and internal rates.

ENGINEER_YEAR = 96_000        # fully loaded: salary, on-costs, equipment, tooling
VENDOR_SMB_SEAT = 42.0        # per user per month, list, 250+ seat tier
# The honest number is never list. Our negotiated 3-yr price at 9,000 seats:
VENDOR_NEGOTIATED = 29.5

TARGET_USERS_36M = 9_000     # from the SOM model in 2.1
ENGINEER_MONTHS_TO_BUILD = 9 # one senior + one mid, 9 months, plus 2 months upkeep

TCO = {
  "build": {
    "initial_build":        ENGINEER_YEAR * ENGINEER_MONTHS_TO_BUILD / 12,  # 72,000
    "ongoing_maintenance":  ENGINEER_YEAR * 0.35 / 12 * 36,                 # 8,400/yr x3
                                                                     # = 25,200
    "security_patching":    ENGINEER_YEAR * 0.12 / 12 * 36,                 # 2,880/yr x3
                                                                     # =  8,640
    "integration_and_migration": 14_000,   # ERP connectors, auth, data backfill
    "opportunity_cost":  ENGINEER_YEAR * 0.65 * 2.5,   # 9 eng-months NOT spent
                                        # on the 3-second answer = 16,000
                                                                     # = 16,000
    "compliance_certification": 18_000,   # SOC 2 Type I, only for the built path
    "total_36m": 72_000 + 25_200 + 8_640 + 14_000 + 16_000 + 18_000,
                 # = 153,840
  },
  "buy": {
    "licence_3yr":          TARGET_USERS_36M * VENDOR_NEGOTIATED * 36,  # 9,558,000
    "integration_and_migration": 46_000,   # API integration, SSO, data sync
    "customisation":        38_000,       # 3 extensions they will never merge
    "annual_price_increase": 0.07,         # contractual, verified in the quote
    "opportunity_cost":     0,            # engineers stay on the product
    "total_36m": 9_558_000 + 46_000 + 38_000,
                 # = 9,642,000
  },
}
# A full FSM suite at 9,000 seats is 9.6m over 3 years. It is not a competitor
# for this budget line at all - it is a different purchase. Comparing our
# 154k build against a 9.6m suite is the wrong comparison, and it is the most
# common error in build-vs-buy documents.

# The REAL comparison is against a RIGHT-SIZED third-party component:
TCO["buy_component"] = {
  "what": "off-the-shelf B2B auth + RBAC + audit log, 9k users",
  "licence_3yr": 0,                    # OSS with a paid support contract
  "paid_support_3yr": 21_000,
  "integration": 11_000,                # SSO, SCIM, mapping to our org model
  "customisation": 4_000,               # one fork we will carry
  "fork_maintenance_3yr": 15_000,       # tracking upstream releases
  "total_36m": 51_000,
  "exit_cost": 18_000,                  # replace it: 4 weeks + data migration
}

EXIT_COST = {
  "build": {
    "data_portability": "full - we own the schema and the export",
    "migration_effort": "0 - the code is ours",
    "contract": "none",
    "customer_concept_lock_in": "low",
    "total_2yr_exit": 6_000,            # documentation and a handover, if anything
  },
  "buy_component": {
    "data_portability": "full, via documented API",
    "migration_effort": "4 weeks of 1 engineer",
    "fork_licence_reassignment": "must be checked - Apache-2.0 with a CLA is fine,
                                  a source-available licence is not",
    "customer_concept_lock_in": "low - auth is invisible to users",
    "total_2yr_exit": 18_000,
  },
  "buy_suite": {
    "data_portability": "partial - CSV plus whatever their API allows",
    "migration_effort": "6-10 weeks, and it is a data-quality project",
    "contract": "3-year term, 7% annual escalator, exit for convenience not
                permitted",
    "customer_concept_lock_in": "HIGH - we have trained dispatchers in their
                                 workflow vocabulary, which stays with them",
    "total_2yr_exit": 85_000,
  },
}

# THE 70/20/10 ALLOCATION — the default for engineering effort, from ch6
EFFORT_ALLOCATION = {

# If 70/20/10 drifts to 40/50/10, the product is becoming a suite and the
# business case is no longer the one written here. That drift is a finding,
# not a detail, and it goes in the quarterly memo.
# The build-vs-buy decision record, in the ADR format from ch4. Short,
# because a long build-vs-buy document is usually a rationalisation.

ADR-0011: build-vs-buy on authentication, RBAC and audit logging
Status: Accepted. Date: 2026-04-30. Deciders: tech lead, security owner.

Context:
  We need SSO (SAML + OIDC), SCIM provisioning, a role model with
  org/branch/technician scoping, and an immutable audit log, for 9,000
  technicians across ~70 accounts, within 9 engineer-months.

Decision:
  Adopt Keycloak (OSS, Apache-2.0) self-hosted for authentication and SSO.
  Build the organisation and role model ourselves - it is 3 tables and a policy
  layer, and it is the part we will differentiate on. Build the audit log
  ourselves - it must write to the same transaction boundary as our own
  mutations, which no external audit-log service can do correctly.

Alternatives considered and rejected:
  1. Build auth from scratch.  Rejected: 5+ engineer-months, and the security
     surface (session handling, token rotation, phishing-resistant MFA) is
     exactly the wrong place for a young team to be original. Ongoing CVE
     response would be permanent.
  2. A commercial B2B auth SaaS.  Rejected: 9,000 users at list is 3.5-4x
     our entire 3-year TCO for a component, and it puts an external
     availability dependency in the path of every request. Cost was 1.9m
     against a 51k 3-year TCO for the OSS route.
  3. An existing identity provider already used by our target accounts.
     Rejected on evidence: 4 of 5 target accounts use a provider that is
     itself behind a corporate proxy, and 1 does not support SCIM at all.
     Our dispatcher persona must be able to log in from a phone with 1 bar.

Consequences:
  + Saves 5 engineer-months, which go to the 70% core allocation.
  - We now operate an auth service. It goes in the SLO set (ch17) with its own
    error budget. Login availability becomes an SLO at 99.9%.
  - Keycloak upgrades: 2 releases/year, ~2 days of engineer time each.
    Calendar this, do not discover it. 15k over 3 years, already in the TCO.
  - SCIM is a real cost: 3 engineer-weeks we have not budgeted. Tracked as R-19.
  - Exit cost 18k if this decision is reversed. Accepted, because auth is
    invisible to users and the data is portable.
  - The audit-log decision is NOT reversible cheaply, and that is correct:
    audit logs are the part of the system you cannot rebuild retrospectively.

# A build-vs-buy record that lists only one alternative is not a decision.
# Two rejected alternatives, with reasons, is the minimum. Three is better.
# The reasons must be about evidence, not about preference.

Use 70/20/10 as the default allocation and treat drift as a finding. Put 70% of engineering effort into the capability that is genuinely differentiated, 20% into enabling infrastructure that is necessary but undifferentiated, and 10% into a reserve for what nobody predicted. The 10% is not slack in the agile sense — it is a budget line for the ERP that returns times as local strings, the customer with 4,000 technicians, and the platform release that removes an API you depended on. Teams that plan 100% of their capacity and then discover the 10% is where the schedule actually lands.

2.6 Risk register and pre-mortem

Formalises the risk register with likelihood × impact scoring, response types and review cadence, and specifies the pre-mortem as a structured exercise with a written record.

A risk register is a list of things that might go wrong, each with an owner, a score, a mitigation and a contingency. A register that is not scored is a list of worries, and a register that is scored but not reviewed is decoration. The scoring uses likelihood and impact on 1–5 scales, giving 1–25, and the band determines the required response: 1–6 low, logged; 8–12 medium, owned and mitigated this quarter; 15–19 high, owned with a written contingency and reviewed weekly; 20–25 critical, blocks the next stage gate until mitigated or explicitly waived by a named person with an expiry date.

Four response types exist and each risk gets exactly one: mitigate (reduce likelihood or impact now), transfer (insurance, SLA, contract), accept (with a documented rationale and a trigger that would change the decision), and exploit (for opportunities, which belong in the same register because the register is a decision document, not a complaints list). Assigning a risk without a response type is how registers become unreadable.

# Risk register — docs/02-market/risk-register.md
# Review cadence: weekly for >=15, fortnightly for 8-14, monthly for <8.
# Every risk has ONE response type. Owner is a person, not a team.
# Last full review: 2026-05-14. Next: 2026-05-28.

# Summary: 3 critical-blocking (R-02 open), 7 high, 6 medium, 3 low.
# R-02 at score 20 is the register's most important line: it blocks the ch3
# exit gate and its mitigation is a 3-week pilot, not a code change.
# Pre-mortem record. Run it before the build starts, not after it fails.
# Method: assume it is 12 months after GA. The product has failed. The team
# writes, independently and in writing, why. No discussion during the write-up.
# Then the causes are converted to risks, and leading indicators are defined so
# that the failure is detectable BEFORE it happens, not after.

PREMORTEM:
  id: PREM-2026-05-20
  date: 2026-05-20
  attendees: [product lead, tech lead, 2 engineers, designer, research lead]
  protocol: >
    6 minutes of silent individual writing. No talking. Each person answers:
    "It is 2027-05. The product launched, ran for a year, and failed.
     Why?" Everyone writes on their own sheet. Then round-robin, 90 seconds
    each, no discussion, no rebuttal. Then clustering. Then a 20-minute
    session to attach a leading indicator to each cause.
    The rule: causes may be unflattering. Nobody's writing is read aloud
    until everyone has written.

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ CAUSES
# Grouped by the stage of the process where the failure originated.

CAUSES_DISCOVERY:
  - id: C-D1
    cause: "The return-trip problem was real but the solution was not. Technicians "
           "learned to live with 22% dead stock because dead stock is invisible, "
           "and a return trip is a one-off annoyance they can attribute to a bad "
           "supplier rather than to a system they do not control."
    evidence_now: "Habit scored 5/5. 7/8 said 'it has always been this way'."
    leading_indicator: "Concierge action rate < 0.55 over any 2-week window."
    becomes: R-02 (dispatcher) + R-03 (willingness to pay) - both already logged.
  - id: C-D2
    cause: "We validated the technician's problem and ignored that the buyer is a "
           "different person with a different budget line. The service manager "
           "cares about margin; the technician cares about being blamed."
    evidence_now: "Forces analysis: push is felt by the technician, paid for by the "
                  "manager. They are not the same force."
    leading_indicator: "In 3+ deals, the champion is not the budget holder."
    becomes: R-03. New risk needed at the next review: budget-holder mapping.

CAUSES_VIABILITY:
  - id: C-V1
    cause: "We built a product whose value we can prove but whose price we set "
           "against our own cost model rather than against the customer's budget "
           "line. At 8/tech/month we are asking for 1.3% of a 620 GBP/tech/month "
           "wage. That is a rounding error to them and impossible for us."
    leading_indicator: "Any customer asks 'what does this save us per job' and the "
                       "answer requires a calculator."
    becomes: R-03. Action: the ROI calculator is a deliverable, and it must be
             in the customer's language (GBP per job), not ours.
  - id: C-V2
    cause: "The LTV model was wrong because retention was measured on 9 accounts "
           "that were all acquired by us personally. Real churn is 3-4x that."
    leading_indicator: "Any cohort GRR < 0.90 in its first 6 months."
    becomes: R-13.

CAUSES_FEASIBILITY:
  - id: C-F1
    cause: "The stock data was technically available and commercially useless. "
           "21% of records are stale by more than 15 minutes, and the answer is "
           "wrong often enough that technicians learn to ignore it."
    evidence_now: "Spike SPIKE-2026-04-16 measured a 21% stale rate."
    leading_indicator: "Recommendation accuracy < 0.70 in the concierge ledger."
    becomes: R-04.
  - id: C-F2
    cause: "We shipped a web-only product and 30% of the technicians work in "
           "places with no signal, every day, and we spent 6 months of user "
           "research finding this out."
    evidence_now: "A09 was at confidence 1 until 2026-04-11. This was the single "
                  "largest blind spot in the original plan."
    leading_indicator: "Field telemetry shows > 20% of sessions with no successful "
                       "network fetch."
    becomes: R-01. Action: the offline path is a P0 requirement, not an
             enhancement, and is written into ch10 and ch15 as such.

CAUSES_EXECUTION:
  - id: C-E1
    cause: "We spent 4 months on infrastructure and 2 weeks on the product. The "
           "cache-first read path - the thing that was validated - was last."
    leading_indicator: "Any 2-week period where < 20% of merged work touches the "
                       "70% core allocation."
    becomes: R-19 (burn multiple). Action: 70/20/10 is checked in the weekly
             engineering review, not quarterly.
  - id: C-E2
    cause: "Two of us left in the first six months and the knowledge in this
           "document - the reasoning, not just the conclusions - was in heads."
    leading_indicator: "Any system with no second person who can operate it."
    becomes: New: requires the 19-artefact set from ch0 to actually exist, with
             runbooks rehearsed. Not a code risk; a documentation risk.
  - id: C-E3
    cause: "We discovered at month eight that the wedge is not defensible and "
           "spent nine months on a pivot instead of on the market."
    leading_indicator: "Any incumbent feature matching the wedge in the "
                       "changelog, or 2+ competitors launching a van-stock view."
    becomes: R-05, R-12 (both accepted and monitored, by design).

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- OUTPUT
OUTCOME_OF_THIS_PREMORTEM = """
  19 risks. 3 critical or high-blocking. 4 of the 6 top causes were already in
  the register - which is the correct result and a sign the register is real.
  2 new risks emerged (budget-holder mapping, documentation/knowledge
  concentration) and are added. 5 leading indicators are now defined with
  numeric thresholds, so the failure modes above are detectable at 30, 60 and
  90 days rather than at 12 months.
  Cost: 90 minutes. Highest-value 90 minutes in the project so far.
"""

Run the pre-mortem before the build, and run it again at every stage gate. The exercise costs ninety minutes and produces a better risk register than six months of accumulated worry, because the psychological mechanism is reliable: imagining that failure has already happened removes the social cost of naming a risk in front of the team that is about to bet a year on the plan. The second rule matters as much as the first: every cause must be converted into a leading indicator with a numeric threshold, or the pre-mortem is theatre. A cause with no threshold cannot be detected before it happens.

A risk register is not a place to record what has already happened. Incidents, defects and churn are tracked elsewhere (ch18) and converting them into register entries produces a document that mixes a live watchlist with a post-mortem archive, and becomes unreadable within two quarters. A register entry is a future tense statement about something that has not happened yet. If the sentence can be completed with "…and then it did", it belongs in the incident or churn record, not the register. The distinction matters because a register that contains the past can no longer be read as a statement of what might still go wrong.

Review the register at a fixed cadence and change nothing else. Weekly for anything scoring 15 or above, fortnightly for 8–14, monthly for below 8. The agenda is fixed and short: new risks, changes in score, closed risks, and a check that every critical risk still has a live mitigation rather than a contingency that has quietly become the plan. Score changes are the interesting part — a risk whose likelihood has risen without anyone noticing is a sign that a leading indicator is not being read, and that is a process defect worth investigating as carefully as the risk.

Exercises 2

  1. Produce both market sizings and reconcile them. Count your addressable units from a primary registry, apply written exclusion criteria, and compute a bottom-up SOM with a named sales capacity. Then take a published top-down analyst figure, list its five failure modes against your product, and compute the adjusted figure. Success criterion: you have a SOM with a stated error band, and a written paragraph explaining every order-of-magnitude disagreement between the two methods, with the bottom-up figure declared as the one used in the model.
  2. Build the unit economics model with every formula shown. Compute gross margin at current and at 10× volume, CAC by channel, payback per channel, 24-month capped cohort LTV, LTV:CAC per channel, net and gross revenue retention, and the burn multiple for four forward quarters. Success criterion: every number is dated, sourced, and computed per cohort rather than blended; at least one channel fails the 3:1 LTV:CAC floor; and you have a dated written action for that channel.
  3. Replace a feature matrix with a positioning analysis including a non-software competitor. Choose a product you know, map five competitors on two axes including the current workaround and the in-house-build option, and write a wedge statement with an explicit "we are worse at everything else" clause. Then run five losing-deal interviews. Success criterion: the wedge statement would survive being read aloud to a customer, and at least one of your five competitors is not a software company.
  4. Run one throwaway spike on your riskiest technical assumption, and delete the code. Write the spike record with one binary question, a time box of at most three days, a pre-registered pass/fail threshold and a kill date — before writing any code. Then run it and delete everything in a separate commit. Success criterion: the record’s verdict maps to exactly one of pass/partial/fail, the code is gone, and at least one downstream requirement changed as a result.
  5. Run a 90-minute pre-mortem and convert every cause into a scored risk with a numeric leading indicator.** With four to six colleagues, each writing silently for six minutes on "it is 12 months after launch and this failed", then cluster the causes and attach a threshold to each. Success criterion: you have at least 12 risks scored on the 1–5 × 1–5 scale with named owners, at least one scoring ≥ 20 with a written contingency, and at least six causes with a numeric leading indicator that would be detectable within 90 days of launch.

3 · Product Strategy, Scope and the MVP

3.1 Vision, positioning and the one-sentence product3.2 Product principles3.3 Scope, non-goals and the in/out contract3.4 The MVP: three kinds, two definitions3.5 Prioritisation frameworks and their biases3.6 Roadmap types: feature, outcome and now/next/later

Strategy in a product organisation is a set of explicit decisions about who the product is for, what it will and will not do, and how trade-offs will be settled when they cannot all be satisfied. This chapter establishes the four artefacts that make those decisions durable — the positioning canvas, the product principles, the scope contract and the MVP definition — and then shows how they interact with prioritisation and roadmap communication. The argument is that failed products are usually failed scoping decisions taken implicitly: the team either knew it was building the wrong thing, or could not agree what "done" for the first release meant, and had no written artefact to point at. Each artefact below is written before engineering begins, reviewed on a fixed cadence, and cited by identifier from backlog items, so that disagreement surfaces in the artefact rather than in a meeting.

3.1 Vision, positioning and the one-sentence product

This subsection fixes the vocabulary for describing what a product is for — vision statement, positioning canvas, one-sentence product statement, 2×2 competitive map — and states the failure mode of each.

A product vision statement is a single declarative sentence describing the future state the product exists to create, written for internal consumption, dated, and owned by a named accountable executive. It is not a mission statement, not a tagline, not a values poster. The distinguishing test is whether it constrains a decision: given two candidate features, a vision that cannot adjudicate between them is decoration. The working format is a future-state assertion plus the invariant that must never be sacrificed to reach it.

Three failure modes are diagnostic. The technology-anchored vision — "a cloud-native platform that leverages AI to revolutionise operations" — survives leadership review because it contains fashionable nouns and fails at the first prioritisation meeting, because every proposed feature can be described as advancing it. Temporal drift is the second: written once at kickoff, never referenced again, contradicted in practice within two quarters while remaining on the wall. Plurality is the third: three teams each hold an unreconciled vision, discovered at integration. The mitigation is procedural and unglamorous — one artefact, one owner, a 90-day review cadence, and a rule that any backlog item must cite the vision clause it serves.

VISION STATEMENT — before and after, with the failure annotated

  BEFORE  "Platform A is a cloud-native, AI-assisted claims workspace that
           revolutionises how insurers handle first notice of loss."
           FAILURE 1 — technology-anchored: "cloud-native" and "AI-assisted"
                     constrain nothing; any feature can be described as
                     advancing it, so the sentence never excludes an option
           FAILURE 2 — no invariant: there is no stated thing that must never
                     be sacrificed, so every trade-off is negotiable
           FAILURE 3 — past-tense-free: it describes a category, not a future
                     state that can be declared achieved or not
           FAILURE 4 — owner absent, no review date, no measurement
           VERDICT — unciteable; see the audit in the next block

  AFTER   "Within five years, every consequential claim decision in the
           markets we serve is made by someone who can produce, in one click,
           the source document and the rule that produced the decision — and
           no state examiner can find a claim we cannot defend.
           INVARIANT: claim data remains readable only inside the tenant's
           contracted region, under any commercial pressure."
           MEASURE: share of concluded claims with a retrievable evidence
                    pointer, audited monthly by an independent sample of
                    400 claims per tenant
           OWNER: VP Product.  REVIEWED: 2026-04-02, next 2026-07-01.
           CLAUSE IDS: V1 (evidence-by-default)  V2 (regional locality)
                       V3 (defensible decision, not merely a faster one)

  AUDIT — do the ten largest committed items each cite a clause?
  ITEM                                   CITED CLAUSE   INTERPRETATION NEEDED
  Claim timeline                         V1             none
  Evidence panel document diff           V1             none
  Carrier C intake                       —              (business survival)
  Reason-code taxonomy v3                V1             1 paragraph
  Executive dashboard                    —              2 paragraphs → FAILED
  Keyboard review queue                  V1             none
  Bulk reason-code edit                  —              (efficiency, not V1)
  SAML IdP #3                            —              (table stakes)
  Audit export JSON                      V1             1 sentence
  Mobile cached summaries                V2             1 sentence
  RESULT: 5 of 10 uncited. Two of the five require a paragraph of
  interpretation, which is the finding: the vision was not doing work for
  those items and should have been rewritten, or the items removed.

ONE-SENTENCE PRODUCT STATEMENT — five fixed slots, all mandatory
  FOR <who — target customer, narrow enough to recognise>
  our product is <category they already budget for>
  that <benefit in outcome terms, not feature terms>,
  UNLIKE <named alternative>,
  which <differentiating mechanism a competitor cannot copy quickly>.
  USED: For secondary-market claims adjusters at insurers of 500–5,000
        claims a year, Platform A is a claims audit workspace that makes
        every adjustment defensible in one click, unlike the legacy claims
        suite their procurement already owns, which produces an exportable
        audit log weeks after the decision rather than a pointer to the rule
        that produced it at the moment it was made.
  SLOT 4 is the one teams fill with "nothing". If slot 4 cannot be filled
  with the product the customer would otherwise have bought, the statement
  describes a category and the team has no basis for declining work that
  dilutes it. Category invention requires 24–36 months of category
  education and a narrative-led sales organisation; default to an existing
  category unless lost-deal analysis explicitly attributes losses to it.

Positioning is the second artefact and is strictly more operational. The canvas decomposes into five fields: target customer with size, authority and budget; underserved need with evidence identifiers; unique value attribute expressed as an outcome; competing alternatives; and market category with explicit axes. The competing-alternatives field is where most positioning documents fail, because "we have no direct competition" is written when the analyst has not enumerated the substitutes customers actually use. A defensible alternatives list is behavioural: the incumbent category leader, an adjacent tool hired for the job, a spreadsheet-plus-contractor arrangement, and the customer’s decision to do nothing at all.
