Warning. Vision statements drafted by an executive and never shown to the team are among the most reliable predictors of late-stage product failure. The tell is that no backlog item links to a vision clause. Audit it quarterly with a two-minute question: for each of the ten largest committed items, which sentence of the vision does it serve? If the answer needs a paragraph of interpretation, the vision is not doing work.

3.2 Product principles

This subsection defines what qualifies as a product principle, specifies the six-component format, and works two principles through real arguments to show the difference between a slogan and a decision rule.

A product principle is a standing decision rule: a conditional that, when two candidate actions conflict, determines which wins without escalation. The test is procedural, not rhetorical — give the principle to a team that has never met the product and ask whether it changes what they would build. A principle that describes a value does not survive that test. Every principle carries six components: the belief, the decision rule in conditional form, the acceptable consequence, the trade-off the team has agreed to accept, one worked precedent citing an actual shipped decision, and a falsifier — the observable condition that would prove the principle wrong. Three to five is the working maximum; beyond that the artefact supplies negotiation ammunition rather than adjudication, because any decision can be justified by selecting the favourable subset.

PRODUCT PRINCIPLES — Platform A
Version 3.1 | Effective 2026-07-01 | Owner: Head of Product
Review: every 90 days. Rules: max 5 principles, max 1 hour to read.

P1 — EVIDENCE BEFORE ASSERTION
  BELIEF        Decisions that change customer-visible behaviour rest on
                cited research or telemetry. Absent evidence, the default
                is the smallest reversible implementation.
  DECISION RULE If a proposal cites no evidence ID and is not reversible in
                under 2 person-weeks, ship it behind a flag at 5% and build
                no second surface until the flag has produced a decision.
  CONSEQUENCE    Slower visible progress; several proposals die quietly in
                review instead of failing in production.
  TRADE-OFF     Fewer complete features per quarter, in exchange for a
                measured hit rate on each one.
  PRECEDENT     Bulk CSV import (2019) shipped to 5%, withdrawn in 9 days;
                the full build would have cost 6 person-months.
  FALSIFIER     Two consecutive flags where measurement cannot distinguish
                the hypotheses → retire P1 and default to user research.

P2 — THE CLAIM FILE IS THE PRODUCT
  BELIEF        Every value the customer buys is the ability to point at the
                evidence for a decision. Features that cannot be attached to
                a specific claim transition are supporting cast.
  DECISION RULE If a feature cannot name the claim transition it improves,
                it is not scheduled in Now/Next/Later.
  CONSEQUENCE    Some high-revenue admin features are deprioritised.
  TRADE-OFF     Lower short-term revenue in exchange for retention in
                accounts of 500+ adjusters (churn target ≤ 4%/yr).
  PRECEDENT     Executive dashboard deferred; queue-wide assignment built
                instead (P-03, release 4.2).
  FALSIFIER     Expansion revenue from admin-only personas exceeds
                claim-workflow revenue for two consecutive quarters.

P3 — LOCALITY IS A PRODUCT PROMISE
  BELIEF        Claims data is regulated material in every state we sell in.
  DECISION RULE If an action would require production claim data to be
                readable outside the tenant's contracted region, the action
                is prohibited; redesign around in-region computation.
  CONSEQUENCE    No third-party experimentation platform, no shared data
                warehouse, no centrally trained model on tenant text.
  TRADE-OFF     3–5 extra weeks per analytics feature.
  PRECEDENT     Retention cohort analysis replaced a vendor export with an
                in-region aggregation job: +2 person-weeks.
  FALSIFIER     A regulatory change providing a compliant federated
                analytics programme (monitored quarterly).

The worked application matters more than the list. Consider a proposal to send claim data to a third-party analytics vendor for product telemetry, which three executives favoured because it would accelerate the retention analysis. Principle P3 decides it: the vendor would hold production claim data outside the tenant’s region to compute retention, the action is prohibited, and the architecture ships an in-region aggregation job instead. The principle specified the answer, named the party that would be unhappy, and produced a design that was arguably better — the in-region job turned out to be faster because it avoided the export. The second example concerns a ten-column bulk-edit screen for supervisors, which conflicts with P2: bulk editing cannot be attached to a claim transition, so it is not scheduled, and the team built a keyboard-driven sequential queue instead at 0.4 of the estimated person-months, which tested better with 5 users per round.

DECISION RECORD DR-003 — resolving the analytics-vendor argument
Status: accepted | Date: 2026-05-04 | Decider: VP Product (no escalation)

  CONTEXT      Retention analysis is blocked. 3 of 5 design partners churned
               or stalled on renewal for reasons the team cannot see, and the
               proposed vendor would identify claim-level behaviour patterns
               within 4 weeks. Effort: 0.6 person-months, one integration.
  ARGUMENT     Pro: fastest route to an answer that blocks $1.4M of renewal.
               Against (security, legal): claim data would be readable
               outside the tenant's region, and two of five partners have
               residency clauses in contract.
  PRINCIPLE    P3 — locality is a product promise. Rule is conditional and
               both sides agree on the facts, so the principle decides it
               without escalation. P1 (evidence before assertion) also
               applies: 0 of the vendor's findings are reproducible in-house.
  OPTIONS      A vendor export          0.6 pm, violates P3
               B in-region aggregation  2.2 pm, satisfies P3
               C sampled opt-in survey   0.3 pm, satisfies P3, weak signal
  DECISION     B, with C run in parallel as a corroborating signal.
  CONSEQUENCE   Retention answer moves from 4 weeks to about 11 weeks, and
               the renewal decision must be taken without it for Q2. Two
               partners were told the delay in writing. The vendor contract
               option is retained for a future federated analytics programme.
  WHAT WOULD   If a federated analytics regime becomes legally available,
  REVISIT      re-open and re-cost A; if churn correlates with a factor
               visible in option C's survey, promote C to the primary method.
  PROCESS NOTE The principle saved 3 weeks of escalation and produced a
               better artefact. The measurable benefit of a principle is the
               number of decisions that never reach an executive.

DECISION LEDGER — what a principle regime actually produces
  QUARTER  DECISIONS DECIDED BY A PRINCIPLE   REACHED EXECUTIVE   TIME SAVED
  2026-Q1  11                                4                  ~3 weeks
  2026-Q2  14                                2                  ~5 weeks
  2026-Q3   9                                1                  ~2 weeks
  EXERCISE  Count your own ledger for one quarter. A principles document
  nobody cites produces a ledger of zero, and the document should be deleted
  rather than maintained.

Tip. Write the falsifier first. If you cannot state the observable condition under which the principle would be retired, you are writing a belief, not a decision rule. Beliefs are allowed in the same document — label them and park them in a separate subsection — but they must never be cited in a decision record as though they settled the question.

3.3 Scope, non-goals and the in/out contract

This subsection turns scope from an aspiration into a written contract with enumerated exclusions, non-goals carrying disqualifying consequences, exit criteria with numeric thresholds, and a change protocol stating who may add work and at what cost.

The scope contract is the most cost-effective artefact in this chapter, because it is the only defence against the two most expensive behaviours in delivery: unbounded internal debate about what the release contains, and unbounded external commitment before the features exist. It lists three distinct things, and conflating the last two is why scope documents fail. Out-of-scope items are work that is legitimate but not now: they enter the backlog with a rough order and a revisit condition. Non-goals are assertions about what the product will never do, and they are what protects the architecture from erosion, because a non-goal is checked at design review rather than at backlog grooming.

A non-goal is only real if a disqualifying consequence is attached. "We will not build a general-purpose workflow engine" is a statement of intent; "if a requirement forces a general-purpose workflow engine into the release, the release is descoped by the product owner without further discussion" is a decision rule. Non-goals should be drawn from structural temptations rather than distant competitors: multi-tenancy beyond logical isolation, offline-first synchronisation, third-party write access, a public API before the first three enterprise design partners are live. Each is cheap to write and expensive to retrofit.

# SCOPE CONTRACT — Platform A, Release 1 "Ledger"
Version 1.2 | Approved 2026-07-14 | Product owner: R. Vance
Change authority: product owner for ≤ 5 person-months; VP Product + CTO
above that, or when a non-goal risk is introduced. Every delta appended.

## IN SCOPE (the release must contain all of it)
 1 Claim intake from two source carriers, nightly batch, ≤ 40,000 claims
   per month per tenant, with per-row acceptance or rejection reporting.
 2 Claim detail with an evidence panel: every adjustment carries a source
   document pointer and the rule identifier that produced it.
 3 Adjusting workflow: open → assign → investigate → conclude → appeal,
   with a mandatory reason code on conclusion.
 4 Audit export: immutable event log, filtered, CSV, ≤ 2 s for 30 days of a
   40,000-claim tenant.
 5 SAML 2.0 single sign-on and role-based access for 4 fixed roles.
 6 Evidence-linked navigation across claims of the same loss event.

## OUT OF SCOPE (backlogged, ordered, each with a revisit condition)
 - Carrier C integration. Revisit when Carrier C is ≥ 12% of intake volume
   in tenant telemetry for 2 consecutive months.
 - Bulk editing UI. Revisit only if the keyboard queue measures below 18
   claims per adjuster hour in production for 30 consecutive days.
 - Multi-language UI. Revisit at the first regulated-state expansion.
 - Public REST API. Revisit when 3 enterprise design partners request it
   in writing.
 AUDIT RULE: an out-of-scope item older than two quarters with no revisit
 condition and no rough order is deleted from the contract and competes in
 the ordinary backlog.

## NON-GOALS (release-blocking; owner may descope without discussion)
 NG1 No general-purpose workflow engine. Any requirement implying one
     blocks the release.
 NG2 No cross-tenant computation: federated analytics, shared model
     training, and any benchmark that aggregates across tenants are out
     for this release and the next two.
 NG3 No write access to source carrier systems. Read-only, batch only.
 NG4 No offline write path on mobile. Read-only cached summaries.
 NG5 No third-party script or pixel receiving tenant identifiers.
 NG6 No per-seat minimum on tenant pricing; pricing is per tenant and per
     claim volume. (Protects the axis chosen in §3.1.)

## EXIT CRITERIA (the release is done when all of these are true)
 - Every in-scope item meets its acceptance criteria in the traceability
   matrix (§5.5); zero uncovered requirements.
 - p95 claim-detail interaction ≤ 250 ms at a 40,000-claim tenant
   (REQ-QA-PERF-014), verified on the named baseline machine.
 - 30-day pilot: ≥ 4 of 5 design partners process 500+ claims with no
   support contact, and support contacts stay ≤ 12 per 1,000 claims.
 - Crash-free sessions ≥ 99.7% over the pilot window.
 - No open Sev-1 or Sev-2 defect at the release cut.

## CHANGE PROTOCOL
 - Product owner may add in-scope work up to 5 person-months by publishing
   a delta below with the work exchanged.
 - Above 5 person-months, or touching a non-goal, requires VP Product and
   CTO approval and a written statement of which exit criterion moves.
 - Deltas are appended, never rewritten, so that drift is visible.
 - Any delta older than 30 days unreviewed is escalated at the weekly.

## SCOPE DELTAS (append-only)
 2026-07-22 +1.5 pm  Evidence panel: added document diff view.
                        Exchanged: intake window nightly → every 4 h (0.5 pm).
 2026-08-04 +3.0 pm  SAML for 2 additional identity providers.
                        Exchanged: audit export CSV → JSON (0.75 pm).
 2026-08-19 −1.0 pm  Removed appeal status from scope: no design partner
                        required it and it touched NG1's risk profile.
                        Reinstated in the ordinary backlog at rank 41.
 NET AGAINST ORIGINAL SCOPE: +3.0 pm over an 18.2 pm release. The contract
 held because every addition published what it displaced.

## BURN-DOWN SIGNAL (reviewed weekly with the contract open)
  At the halfway date of a 2-week sprint, if more than 20% of committed
  items remain, the release is re-planned rather than squeezed. Signature
  two is unrequested surfaces: work appearing for audiences, locales or
  integrations not named in the contract. Both conversations are about the
  contract, not about individuals, which is the only way to run them.

Note. Non-goals are cheap to state now and expensive to retrofit later, and each one forecloses a design option — which is exactly why they must be written deliberately. Aim them at the temptation your own architecture creates: a flexible event model, a plugin seam, a generic permission layer. Those are the places where scope re-enters through the back door, one reasonable-looking ticket at a time, and where a written non-goal is the only thing that will hold.

3.4 The MVP: three kinds, two definitions

This subsection distinguishes the three MVP constructions — concierge, wizard-of-oz and landing-page — from the artefacts they are confused with, and sets the measurable thresholds at which each has done its job.

The minimum viable product is the smallest experiment that produces a decision about a key assumption with real users. It is a learning instrument, and the deliverable is a decision, not a release. Three constructions cover almost all first releases. The concierge MVP delivers the outcome manually behind a thin front end: the service is real, the automation is absent, and human labour stands in for code. The wizard-of-oz MVP presents a fully automated-looking interface while humans perform the work behind it, producing realistic usage data at realistic volume at the cost of a staffed operational floor that must itself be measured. The landing-page MVP tests demand before supply, presenting the value proposition and measuring intent, never touching the operational problem.

ConstructionWhat is realWhat is simulatedPrimary questionThreshold for a decisionSuitableNot suitable
ConciergeOutcome and customer relationship; manual fulfilmentAutomation; the back office entirelyWill anyone pay for this outcome?≥ 15 completed cycles and willingness to pay ≥ 2× the stated ceiling✓ High-ticket, low-frequency, bespoke workflows✗ Above ~50 active users; ✗ regulated records where manual custody is itself a finding
Wizard-of-ozInterface, data model, telemetry, real volumeThe automation behind the interfaceDoes the workflow hold at volume?≥ 4 weeks at ≥ 80% of projected volume; manual minutes per transaction ≤ 6✓ Workflow-heavy products where sequence matters more than automation✗ Safety-critical steps a human cannot leave unreviewed; ✗ anything needing sub-minute turnaround
Landing pageMessaging, visual hierarchy, signup pathEverything elseIs the value proposition understood and believed?≥ 200 qualified visitors and ≥ 5% single-call-to-action conversion, or ≥ 10 waitlist signups✓ Pre-demand, category education, pricing validation✗ Usability; ✗ willingness to pay; ✗ multi-session workflows
Single-feature sliceOne end-to-end path through the real systemAdjacent pathsDoes one workflow produce value on its own?≥ 5 real users complete it unaided per round, over 3 rounds✓ Existing products with an identified weak core workflow✗ Greenfield products with unvalidated demand
Prototype, spike, proof of conceptOne mechanism, shown to the team or a deciderEverything else, including realismIs this technically or commercially feasible?Explicit binary question answered inside the timebox, typically 5–10 person-days✓ De-risking unknown technology before funding✗ As evidence of demand from customers

Two adjacent definitions are used loosely and must be separated. The minimum viable product in its original sense is an experiment; the minimum lovable product is the quality floor below which adoption collapses, so a technically viable but unlovable release produces negative learning — users evaluate it as finished and never return. The difference is a small set of non-negotiable quality attributes: acceptable latency, no data loss, coherent error messages, and a design language consistent with the brand. State that floor as thresholds, not adjectives, because "polished" cannot be tested. A third distinction matters for planning: a prototype demonstrates a mechanism to the team, a proof of concept demonstrates feasibility to a decision-maker, a technical spike answers a bounded question with a throwaway artefact, and a pilot runs the real product with a limited, real audience under real obligations.

CONCIERGE MVP — OPERATIONS RUNBOOK (claims evidence pilot)
Hypothesis: H1 adjusters will pay for evidence-linked claim files.

   ≥ 15 completed claim cycles AND ≥ 8 accounts with a signed paid LOI
     → fund the build
   5–14 cycles → revise the offer and re-run
   < 5 cycles → stop, and record the kill reason
Owner of the manual work: Head of Ops — explicitly NOT the product manager.
Hard cap: 4 h/week of manual effort. Staffing is not a success metric.

  STEP 3  DELIVERY   A signed PDF claim file is emailed with the evidence
                      panel rendered as a table. No portal, no login.

  objection is artefact format, not automation. Next experiment is a portal,
  not a build. The automation decision is NOT yet due.

Two operational disciplines make these constructions work. First, cap the manual labour explicitly: a release with no stated cap serves whatever demand arrives, and the resulting queue will be misread as product–market fit when it is a capacity limit. Second, pre-commit the decision, including the decision to abandon. The experiment that ends with "let us discuss the findings" produces no learning, because the discussion is unanchored, and the sunk-cost argument arrives at week 14 with the full support of everyone who worked on it.

Warning. Manual work in an MVP is acceptable; manual work that touches regulated records without a custody trail is not. Concierge and wizard-of-oz constructions requiring a human to open, move or annotate a regulated document re-create the audit exposure the product exists to remove, and in several jurisdictions they create the reporting obligation as well. Where custody matters, the manual step must happen inside a system of record with logging, and the runbook must name that system.

3.5 Prioritisation frameworks and their biases

This subsection presents five frameworks in common use with formulas, inputs and known biases, shows the arithmetic for each so that scores can be reproduced rather than trusted, and gives the Kano instrument.

RICE exposes four factors in the open: reach (users or events affected in a stated period), impact (conventionally 3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal), confidence (a percentage reflecting the evidence behind the estimates) and effort in person-months, scored as ((Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort). ICE substitutes ease for effort on 1–10 scales: Impact × Confidence ÷ Ease. WSJF divides the cost of delay by job duration, where duration is a fractional estimate including queue time, so that small unblocking items outrank large ones. Kano classifies requirements into must-be, performance and excitement and shapes the quality profile rather than ranking a backlog. MoSCoW classifies by importance and orders only between classes, not within them.

Warning. A score is an argument, not a measurement, and the highest-scoring item is not thereby the right item. Scores are only meaningful when the inputs are visible and challengeable: publish the reach source, the impact multiplier and the confidence grade beside the score, and require the proposer to state the evidence ID for each. Where that is impossible, confidence should default to 20% — not to 80% because the proposer is sure.

3.6 Roadmap types: feature, outcome and now/next/later

This subsection distinguishes four roadmap artefacts, states what each promises and to whom, and sets the review discipline and the rollout mechanism that keeps an outcome roadmap honest.

A roadmap is a communication artefact with a contract attached, and the type determines the contract. The feature roadmap names capabilities with expected dates; it creates the strongest external expectation, the highest cost of a missed date, and — because dates are the unit of planning — padding followed by silent descope. Its legitimate uses are narrow: contractually committed scope for a named customer, a date fixed by statute, or an event-bound release such as a conference or an annual filing cycle. The outcome roadmap replaces features with the outcome sought, the measure, and timing expressed as Now/Next/Later with a confidence grade and the assumptions beneath. It commits to the sequence of problems and to the evidence to be gathered, not to the solution.

Roadmap typeUnit of contentAudiencePromisesFailure modeValid when
Feature roadmap, datedCapability plus dateCustomers, board, partnersThat a named capability exists by a dateDate padding then silent descope; scope enters as "must have for Q3"✓ Statutory deadline; ✓ contractual commitment; ✗ everything else
Outcome roadmap, Now/Next/LaterOutcome, measure, target, confidence, assumptionsCustomers, internal teams, investorsThat problems are worked in order and evidence gatheredVacuous outcomes nobody would call a miss; LATER becomes a graveyard✓ Any product with more than one plausible solution per problem
Release planItem, owner, sprint, dependencyDelivery team onlyNothing external; it is a working planLeaks into customer conversations and becomes a promise✓ Always, as the internal counterpart of an outcome roadmap
Vision statementFuture state plus invariantInternal; board on requestDirection and the thing never sacrificedBecomes wall decoration; cited by nobody✓ As the north-star artefact above the outcome roadmap
Product principlesDecision rule with trade-offEveryone who can make a decisionHow conflicts will be settled without escalationPoster treatment; more than five principles; no falsifier✓ Where decisions recur and must not each reach an executive

Delivery cadence interacts with roadmap type in a way that is often conflated. Continuous deployment, with several deploys per day behind flags, releases the outcome roadmap from date commitments because nothing waits for a train. A release train on a fixed cadence — typically every 4, 8 or 12 weeks — buys predictability for customers and operations and imposes a batching cost of up to one cadence on any fix, including hotfixes that carve out an exception. Whichever cadence applies, the rollout mechanism determines how much of an outcome roadmap is credible: if the only production deployment is monthly, a three-month Now/Next/Later horizon contains at most three changes, and the roadmap must say so on its face.

PROGRESSIVE ROLLOUT POLICY — the mechanism that makes the roadmap credible
  evidence_panel_v2:
    owner: claims-platform          created: 2026-09-22
    hypothesis: the diff view reduces document re-opens per audit by ≥ 20%
    stages: [ {pct: 5, min_days: 3}, {pct: 25, min_days: 5},
              {pct: 60, min_days: 7}, {pct: 100, min_days: 14} ]

      - metric: support_contacts_per_1k_claims abort_if: greater_than 18
      - metric: audit_export_error_rate       abort_if: greater_than 0.01
      - metric: killed_sessions_rate          abort_if: greater_than 0.003
    kill_switch: true                        # one toggle, no deploy needed
    rollback_runbook: RB-014                 # 4 steps, 12 min, drilled 09-20
    decision_by: 2026-10-20                  # see expiry policy below
    expiry: 2026-11-05                        # flag AND old path removed
  READING THE NUMBERS: 5% of tenants is 155 accounts — large enough for a
  support-signal read, small enough that a defect costs a week, not a
  quarter. Below 5% the telemetry is too thin to detect the effect the
  experiment was designed to measure.

FLAG EXPIRY POLICY (temporary by default, enforced by the platform)
  Required at creation: owner, created_on, hypothesis, decision_by, guardrails,
  rollback_runbook. A flag without a decision_by is refused at creation.
  At decision_by, the platform raises a ticket with three permitted outcomes:
    1 promote to 100% and delete the old path within the same release
    2 delete both paths
    3 re-file an RFC with a new decision_by (maximum two re-files)
  A flag older than 6 months cannot be promoted without VP approval, because
  the code it protects has almost certainly changed since.
  LIVE INVENTORY 2026-09-28: 11 flags, oldest 41 days, 0 without a date.
  COST OF IGNORING IT: a flag that outlives its experiment becomes a permanent
  branch, nobody can delete it safely, and the second-order decision — the one
  the experiment was for — is never made.

Tip. Score confidence honestly by counting how many of the assumptions under an outcome have actually been tested. Zero tested assumptions is LOW, one is MEDIUM, two or more with telemetry behind them is HIGH — and record the assumption IDs beside the grade, so a quarterly review can tell the difference between a team that gained confidence and a team that merely grew more certain of itself.

Exercises 3

  1. Produce a filled positioning canvas for your product: five fields, each carrying either an evidence identifier or the literal word ASSUMPTION. Draw the 2×2 on the two axes you believe are contested, place the named alternatives you actually lose deals to — including the one that wins when you lose — and mark the axis on which a customer scoring you 1 or 2 out of 5 would defect. Deliverable: one page plus a list of every field still carrying ASSUMPTION with the number of interviews needed to resolve each; the number, not the plan.
  2. Write a vision statement in the future-state plus invariant form with clause identifiers, then audit the ten largest committed backlog items and record which clause each serves. Deliverable: a ten-row table; any row needing more than a paragraph of interpretation is a finding. Then write the one-sentence product statement with all five slots filled, and name which of your named alternatives occupies slot 4.
  3. Write four product principles in the belief / decision rule / consequence / trade-off / precedent / falsifier format, then run each against the last three arguments your team actually lost. Deliverable: a table showing which principle would have decided each argument, and which arguments no principle reaches — the second column is the specification for what a fifth principle would have to cover, and an empty set is the real finding. Finish by opening a decision ledger and counting the decisions your current process sends to an executive for one quarter.
  4. Draft a scope contract for your next release: in-scope list, out-of-scope list where every entry carries a revisit condition, five non-goals each with a disqualifying consequence, five exit criteria with numeric thresholds, a change protocol with an authority threshold, and an append-only delta log. Then deliberately request one change above your own authority. Deliverable: the contract plus a signed delta entry recording who approved it, what left scope in exchange, and the person-month delta.
  5. Design one MVP experiment with a pre-committed decision: name the construction, the hypothesis, the instrument, the sample size, the numeric thresholds for continue, revise and stop, and the manual-effort cap in hours per week. Separately, score five candidate items on RICE, ICE and WSJF with impact split by persona. Deliverable: the experiment plan, the three scoring sheets, and 200 words naming the three points of disagreement between the frameworks and the one you will actually decide with.

4 · User Research, Personas and Journey Mapping

4.1 Research plans, methods and screeners4.2 Personas from evidence, and the fiction anti-pattern4.3 Jobs to be done and the forces diagram4.4 Journey maps: stages, emotion and pain points4.5 Service blueprints and lines of visibility4.6 Research operations, ethics and saturation

This chapter covers the discovery practice that converts the assumptions in the positioning canvas into evidence, and the synthesis artefacts that carry that evidence into design: research plans, screeners, personas, job statements, journey maps and service blueprints. The argument is that these artefacts earn their cost only when they are grounded — every attribute traceable to an interview, a telemetry query or a support export — because the dominant failure is not insufficient research but ungrounded synthesis, which produces confident artefacts that steer design away from the evidence that produced them. The chapter therefore specifies sample sizes and their statistical basis, the mechanics of a screener and why screening bias is fatal, the structure of each synthesis artefact, and the operational discipline of recruitment, consent, data minimisation and saturation.

4.1 Research plans, methods and screeners

This subsection defines the four-part research plan — question, method, sample, cadence — covers method selection with sample-size arithmetic, and shows screener construction including the disqualifying conditions.

Research should be commissioned against a decision, not a curiosity. The plan opens with the decision it informs, names the options it will distinguish, and states what will be done under each outcome — including the decision to stop. A question written as "what do users think about dashboards?" cannot be answered by any method and settles nothing; the same question written as "which of three claim-queue layouts reduces document lookups per claim from 6.4 to under 3, as measured in production?" can be answered, falsified and acted upon. Each question gets exactly one primary method, with secondary methods used only for triangulation, and the assignment is recorded so the evidence type is unambiguous at synthesis time: interviews support claims about motivation and reasoning, telemetry supports claims about behaviour, and usability tests support claims about learnability at a stated sample.

Sample size follows the claim type. For quantitative population claims it follows the confidence interval: roughly 385 responses give ±5 percentage points at 95% confidence, and 100 give ±10 points, both assuming the conservative 50% base rate. For qualitative discovery it follows saturation — the point at which new interviews yield no materially new codes — which for a single-domain product arrives between 5 and 8 interviews per segment, with the caveat that the first three are consumed by the frame itself and produce disproportionately weak data. For usability evaluation, 5 participants per round detects roughly 65–75% of the issues in a design, and because later rounds surface the deeper problems, three rounds of 5 reach the mid-90s in issue detection. Read operationally: one round of 5 users is a smoke test for catastrophic confusion, not an evaluation.

MethodAnswers which question typeSampleEvidence producedCost per sessionPrincipal weaknessSuitable
Discovery interviewMotivation, reasoning, workarounds, prior history5–8 per segment to saturationQuotes, codebook, theme frequencies60 min + 30 min synthesisSelf-report bias and social desirability; no frequency data✓ Understanding why a workaround exists
Contextual observationActual behaviour in context, including unclaimed work4–6 sessionsTask sequences, time on task, error counts90 min on siteObserver effect; explains no motivation✓ Jobs crossing tools or physical steps
SurveyDistribution, ranking, language for positioning385 for ±5 pts; 100 for ±10 ptsSegment sizes, preference sharesFielding plus 2 person-days analysisWording dominates; cannot ask why; satisficing✓ Sizing a segment, testing message resonance
Diary studyFrequency, duration and context of a behaviour over time6–10 participants × 10 daysEvent log with timestamps and context2 h setup plus participant burdenHigh attrition; participants self-curate entries✓ Infrequent, cross-session, emotionally loaded jobs
Moderated usability testLearnability and error recovery of a specific design5 per round; 3 rounds for coverageTask success, assistance counts, error taxonomy75 min per sessionMeasures no value, demand, or at-home behaviour✓ Deciding between two concrete designs
Unmoderated or benchmarkComparison against a fixed task set across releases≥ 60 per design for a directional readTask times, success rates, prior-release comparisonLow marginal cost after setupRecruits from the panel, not the population; cannot probe✓ Regression tracking once the task set is fixed
A/B test or staged rolloutCausal effect on a real metric with a real populationPower calculation; typically weeksLift with a confidence interval, on production behaviourEngineering cost, not research costAnswers only the question asked; exposes real users✓ Confirming a change moved the metric it targeted

The screener is the gate between the recruited pool and the study, and it is the artefact most often written badly. It has two halves: qualifying conditions, recruiting people with the relevant experience, and disqualifying conditions, removing people who would distort the findings. Both halves are usually written from the hypothesis rather than from the population, which introduces screening bias — the participants selected are the ones the hypothesis needs. The classical failure is recruiting exclusively for enthusiasts or exclusively for the persona that maximises the desired answer and reporting the result as the market. A subtler and more common failure is a qualifier requiring behaviour the target population does not perform, such as requiring enterprise plan ownership when the person experiencing the problem is an individual contributor two levels down.

RESEARCH PLAN — Q4/2026 — RP-2026-11
Decision this informs: which claim-queue layout to build in release 5.0.
Pre-committed actions per outcome:
   A (fewer lookups, more steps) → build A, re-plan effort at 3.2 pm
   B (fewer lookups, same steps) → build B as planned
   C (no measurable difference) → build neither; invest the capacity in
                                   carrier intake instead
   STOP: < 5 of 8 participants complete the task unaided in either layout,
   and lookups per claim differ by less than 25%.

  Q1  Is the out-of-band lookup mainly document retrieval?
      Method: contextual interview with observation | n=8 adjuster
      Sampling: max-variation on tenure, carrier mix, prior tool
      Cadence: 2 per week for 4 weeks                       Evidence: INT-0xx
  Q2  Does a filterable timeline reduce lookups per claim?
      Method: moderated task-based usability test | 15 participants
      Cadence: 1 round of 5 per fortnight, 3 rounds         Evidence: UT-4.0
  Q3  What do supervisors do outside the tool during review?
      Method: diary study | n=6 × 10 working days
      Cadence: daily entries, weekly 25-min interview        Evidence: DS-0xx
  Q4  How large is the out-of-band population in production?
      Method: telemetry query on the current release
      Cadence: one run, then monthly                    Evidence: TQ-2026-38
  NOTE: Q1–Q3 answer "why" and "how"; only Q4 answers "how many". A study
  of three questions about magnitude and none about motivation produces a
  confident design for a population nobody has measured.

SCREENER — SR-Q4-01 (pilot 2026-10-06, n=10, screen-out 3 of 10)
  QUALIFY (all must be true)
   Q1 In the last 30 days, have you personally worked a claim in the last
       stage of the claims lifecycle?          NO → DISQUALIFY
   Q2 About how many claims do you personally handle in a typical week?
       < 20 → DISQUALIFY   |   20–60 → stratum A (cap 5 per round)
       > 60 → stratum B (cap 5 per round)
   Q3 Which carrier supplies most of your claims?   [single select — used
       for quota only, never as a disqualifier]
   Q4 Do you use claims software other than ours?    [never disqualifies]
  DISQUALIFY (any one)
   D1 Employed in the product team, claims consulting, or insurance software
       sales within the past 12 months.
   D2 Took part in a usability study for this product in the past 6 months —
       carry-over depresses measured lookups by an estimated 20–30%.
  BIAS CHECK BEFORE LAUNCH: Q2 is the qualifier most likely to exclude the
  real population. Frame analysis: 4 of 5 people in the target frame report
  under 20 claims per week, yet all 5 report the out-of-band lookup. If the
  pilot reproduces this, Q2's floor drops to 10 and the strata are
  redefined BEFORE the study — never afterwards, from the findings.

Warning. Screener bias is fatal because it is invisible from inside the study. A study recruited through a qualifier that excludes 80% of the target population produces internally consistent findings — quotes, counts, saturation claims — describing a segment nobody intended to study, and the synthesis then confidently designs for it. Two checks catch most of it: pilot the screener on 10 responses and read every disqualification reason, and confirm against production telemetry that the recruited proportions match the real population on the two or three attributes that matter most.

INTERVIEW GUIDE — RP-2026-11, Q1, 55 minutes (read verbatim except ✱)
  0–5   "Thanks for making time. I work on the claim tool you use. I'm
         interested in how the work actually happens, including the parts
         that are awkward. There are no right answers and I will not be
         evaluating you. Anything about your process is fine, including
         things that reflect badly on us. Can I record? [consent]"
  5–12  CONTEXT, warm-up
       ✱ Tell me about your role — what does a normal week look like?
       ✱ Walk me through the last claim you worked from start to finish.
  12–30 THE JOB, past behaviour only, never hypotheticals
       ✱ When did you first realise this was a problem for you?
       ✱ What did you do about it the first time? Walk me through it.
       ✱ What did that cost you — time, money, rework, someone else?
       ✱ The last time something went wrong with that, what happened?
       ✱ Who else finds out when it goes wrong? Who do you have to tell?
       ✱ What have you already tried that did not work?
  30–45 THE OUT-OF-BAND WORK (the actual subject of this study)
       ✱ When you needed a source document last, how did you get it?
          [observe the actual steps, do not summarise them away]
       ✱ Show me where you keep notes. What is in this column?
       ✱ How do you know a claim is ready to decide?
       ✱ What happens if you get it wrong — who finds out, how quickly?
       ✱ If you could change one thing here, what would it be? Why that?
  45–52 THE OTHER TOOL
       ✱ Which other software do you use for this? What for exactly?
       ✱ What is the best thing about that one? What is the worst?
  52–55 CLOSE
       ✱ Who else does this job the way you do? May I contact them?
       ✱ Is there anything I should have asked and did not?
  PROBES AND BANS
    PROBE  "You said that took a while — how long? Show me where."
    PROBE  "You said it was fine — fine compared with what?"
    BAN    "Would you use a feature that…?"      → leads; ask for a past case
    BAN    "Don't you think…" and "Wouldn't it…" → acquiescence bias
    BAN    "How much would you pay for…?"         → move to E-01, the concierge
                                                  MVP, where payment is real
  NOTE: the question that has produced the most valuable evidence in this
  programme is the last one, "anything I should have asked", and it is free.

4.2 Personas from evidence, and the fiction anti-pattern

This subsection specifies the persona card format, the evidence-linking rule that distinguishes a research persona from an invented one, and the anti-pattern in which a fictional persona is ratified and then drives design.

A persona is a compression of a behavioural pattern observed in research, not a character. The distinguishing property is traceability: every attribute on the card carries either an evidence pointer — an interview identifier with a quotation, a telemetry query result, a support thread count — or an explicit ASSUMPTION marker. When the team cannot satisfy that rule for an attribute, the attribute is deleted, because an unsupported attribute is a guess wearing the authority of a research artefact. Count and selection are governed by decision structure: three to eight personas is the working range, chosen as one per key interaction — the set of decisions for which that persona is the decision maker — and each persona carries a named primary job, an owner, and a computed evidence strength. HIGH means three or more independent sessions plus supporting telemetry, MEDIUM two sessions or one plus telemetry, LOW a single account, and LOW personas are explicitly hypotheses that must be scheduled for discovery before they justify a release commitment.

PERSONA CARD — format v2 (one page, no adjectives, every field cited)

Persona typeBasisGood forDecision authorityFailure modeSuitable
Research persona, evidence-linkedPattern across sessions plus telemetryScope decisions, job prioritisation, release exit criteriaMay justify a committed itemSlow to build; goes stale as the population changes✓ Any team making scope trade-offs

Fictional persona, workshop characterImaginationNothing, once the workshop endsNone permittedUnfalsifiable; cited as if it were research; expensive to retract✗ Never as a decision input

The most expensive anti-pattern in this chapter is the fictional persona. It typically begins with a workshop that cannot recruit participants, a persona named after an archetype — "Sarah the overwhelmed operations manager" — described entirely in adjectives, ratified by a steering committee because it was the only artefact making the roadmap discussion concrete, and then cited for three quarters as though it were research. The damage is structural rather than immediate: adjectives cannot be tested, so the persona cannot be contradicted by evidence, and design decisions inherit its unearned certainty. Every subsequent study that contradicts it is treated as an outlier, because the artefact has become an identity. Recovery requires replacing the card with an evidence-backed persona and retracting the previous one explicitly in writing, which is socially expensive and is why teams that do not do it never do.

ANTI-PATTERN, documented for the record — "Sarah, the overwhelmed Ops Manager"
Retracted 2026-05-02 | Cost of retraction: 6 weeks of roadmap argument

  AS WRITTEN
    "Sarah is a 38-year-old MBA juggling six teams. She is passionate but
     overwhelmed and lives in spreadsheets. She wants a dashboard that gives
     her control at a glance and will champion our product to her CFO."

  FAILURE CHAIN, with the evidence that was never collected
    1. No interview, no telemetry, no observation. Invented in a planning
       workshop to fill an empty slot after recruitment fell through.
    2. "Overwhelmed" and "control at a glance" are not measurable, so no
       result can contradict them. The card cannot be wrong, which is the
       same as saying it cannot be right.
    3. Roadmap 2024 used it to justify the executive dashboard: 14 person-
       months, 3 engineers, 2 quarters.
       POST-LAUNCH: 3 of 9 supervisors used it weekly. They asked instead
       for queue-wide assignment — which became P-03 goal G1 and behaviour
       B1 once research was actually done, and cost 1.1 person-months.
    4. Because the card appeared in every steering deck, contradicting it
       read as attacking the plan. Two design reviews were lost to this.
    5. 6 weeks and one retracted document to correct a claim that one
       afternoon of recruiting would have prevented.

  RULES ADOPTED AFTER RETRACTION (both enforced by template validation)
    R1 No persona card enters a deck without an evidence ID on every
       attribute. A card that cannot cite is labelled PERSONA HYPOTHESIS
       and may not justify a release commitment.
    R2 No card is valid without a non-empty counter-evidence field. The
       act of writing "here is the evidence against me" is what stops a
       card from hardening into an identity.
    R3 Personas are reviewed against evidence at the same 90-day cadence as
       the vision and the principles. One demotion in the last audit cycle
       is the expected outcome, not an embarrassment.

Tip. Keep the counter-evidence field on every persona card and require the author, not a reviewer, to fill it. It is the cheapest available protection against the failure mode where a research artefact silently becomes an organisational belief, and in practice it takes one paragraph and produces the strongest counter-argument anyone in the room would have thought of.

4.3 Jobs to be done and the forces diagram

This subsection introduces job statements, the forces of progress diagram, the job story template and the importance–satisfaction scoring method, with worked examples and the switching estimate.

Jobs to be done reframes demand around the progress a person is trying to make in a circumstance, rather than around the person or the product. A job is stable over decades; products are hired and fired to do it. The statement takes the form "when [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]", and it is valid only when the situation is specific enough that the target user recognises it without explanation, and the outcome is something the person would still want if it were achieved by a completely different product. That last clause is the acid test: "so I can use the new platform" is a solution and invalidates the statement. Job statements also classify as functional, social or emotional, and the emotionally loaded one — defensibility in front of a regulator, being the supervisor who is never surprised — usually predicts purchase and churn better than the functional one.

JOB STATEMENT — P-03 claims supervisor (evidence: INT-021.3, INT-027, DS-004)
  When the daily claim queue exceeds 200 open items and a carrier filing
  deadline falls inside five business days,
  I want to reach a defensible decision on every assigned claim and be able
  to prove which decision rested on which source document,
  so I can close the queue before the filing cut-off without reconstructing
  my reasoning for a state examiner afterwards.
  CLASSIFICATION  functional (close the queue)
                + emotional (never be surprised, never be wrong)
                + social (be the supervisor who is never caught out)

JOB STORY TEMPLATE (filled) — the "so that" clause is mandatory
  As a claims supervisor with a filing deadline inside five business days,
  I want each claim in my queue to show its blocking state and its source,
  so that I can sequence 200 open items by what is actually decidable rather
  than by carrier arrival time.
  ACCEPTED BY 3 of 4 supervisors: INT-021, INT-027, INT-033
  REJECTED BY 1 who sorts strictly by age and would be slowed by a blocking
  state first (INT-030). Recorded, not averaged away — the disagreement is
  the reason the sort order is a per-user preference and not a default.
  SUBSTITUTION TEST "Would you still want this if a contractor did it?"
  → YES. Statement survives. (Compare: "…so I can use the new queue view."
    → NO. That is a feature wearing a job's clothes.)

COMPETING ALTERNATIVES SET — what the job is hired against today
  1 The carrier's own portal, used for the document retrieval the job needs
  2 The shared "week check" sheet, used as the memory that makes handover
    possible at all (INT-021.3)
  3 A phone call to the previous shift, used on Fridays (INT-021.3)
  4 Doing nothing: absorb the rework inside the existing adjustment hour
  5 Us, once shipped
  NOTE: alternatives 2 and 3 are not products. A job's competing set is
  almost always a bundle of workarounds, and the product that only competes
  against other software will lose to a spreadsheet.

SWITCHING ESTIMATE — sanity check on the opportunity
  Incumbent's customers who would move on a compelling alternative ≈ 26%
  (mature categories; the figure is a rule of thumb, not a measurement).
  Apply to the 3,100-account, 41,000-adjuster frame:
    naive plan in the brief: 100% of accounts in 24 months  → $2.9M
    with the switching rule applied: 26%                      → $0.75M
  A plan that assumes total movement is wrong by roughly 4×. Either fund
  the category-education effort explicitly, or plan against 26%.

The forces diagram explains switching, and it is the most useful single artefact for a team that has lost a deal and cannot say why. Four forces push the status quo. The push of the situation is the dissatisfaction that makes the moment arrive. The pull of the new solution is the attractiveness of the alternative. The habit of the present is the inertia of an existing arrangement, stronger the longer it has existed, and it includes familiarity, switching cost and the risk of re-learning. The anxiety of the new is the fear of a new arrangement, including the cost of evaluating it and the possibility of looking foolish. A sale occurs when push plus pull exceeds habit plus anxiety, and a well-run incumbent holds habit and anxiety high deliberately.

   no queue-wide view of unassigned claims    0.20   switching cost ~14 h           0.25
   month-end volume 3× normal                 0.10   Friday cut-off is social norm 0.15

   SUM = 1.00                                                    SUM = 1.00

              habit + anxiety = 1.00 + 0.20 = 1.20

IMPORTANCE / SATISFACTION (1–10, each score carrying its evidence ID)
   JOB                                        IMPORT  SATISF   DELTA   ACTION
   J1 close the queue before the cut-off         10       4      −6   opportunity

Note. The finding most teams do not expect is that the binding constraint is anxiety rather than appeal. Your product may be better than the status quo and still lose, because evaluating it is more expensive than tolerating the status quo. Treat the anxiety term as a design and onboarding requirement with a number attached — 0 hours of migration, 14 days of guided first run, a published residency guarantee — rather than as a marketing message.

4.4 Journey maps: stages, emotion and pain points

This subsection specifies the six rows of a journey map, the rules for emotion scoring and pain-point prioritisation, the opportunity backlog that follows, and the distinction between current-state and future-state journeys.

A journey map is a shared hypothesis about a sequence, and its value lies in forcing the team to commit to a specific structure that can then be contested row by row. Six rows are the minimum: stages, actions and behaviours, touchpoints, thoughts, emotions, and pain points with opportunities. Two further rows — the actor at each stage, and the system or channel — are frequently added and frequently skipped to their cost, because they expose where a stage has no owner or is owned by the customer as a workaround. Stages must be named from the participant’s point of view, in their own words, at a granularity at which something happens: "onboarding" is a stage, "waits three days for the carrier to accept the file" is an action, and only one of those belongs on the axis.

The emotion row is most often reduced to a decorative smiley scale, and it carries the most information about sequence. Emotions are rated plus to minus per stage, ideally captured from the participant rather than from the team’s imagination, and the curve is read for its shape: the peak is what the participant recommends to others, the end is what they remember, and a steep drop between two stages is a more reliable prioritisation signal than any absolute value. The peak-end rule is why the last impression disproportionately determines retention, and it is the justification for investing in an ending rather than only in a conversion step. An emotion claimed without an accompanying action, quote or metric is a projection and should be struck from the map.

   O-04 and O-05 score lowest but are the only two opportunities that change
   the END of the journey, so they are protected by the peak-end rule rather
   than by their score. Record that decision explicitly, because a scoring
   model that is overridden by a principle is only trustworthy if the
   override is written down.

  WHAT THIS VIEW EXPOSES: P5 (no handover) was invisible in the first four
  sessions and entered the map at P07 from one sentence about Friday. A
  journey map built before the seventh session would have shipped four of
  the five opportunities and left the retention risk in place.

Warning. Journey maps drift toward the design team’s interests because the team writes them after the design exists. Counter it by having the person who ran the research own the current-state map, requiring every cell to carry a session identifier or a telemetry query, and by mapping at least one journey for a persona the team does not intend to serve. The excluded journey frequently contains the constraint that explains why the intended persona behaves as they do.

4.5 Service blueprints and lines of visibility

This subsection covers service blueprint structure, the line-of-sight concept, handoffs and cycle time, failure demand, and the distinction between journey maps, blueprints and service processes.

A service blueprint extends the journey map backwards into the organisation, and its purpose is to make the customer’s experience visible as the output of internal work. It is used most effectively in exactly one pairing: identify the worst stage on the journey, blueprint the service behind it, and the recovery case usually appears in the backstage row. The structure is: user actions at the base, then the line of visibility, above which the customer can see or hear what is happening and below which they cannot; frontstage — the visible touchpoints, human and system; backstage — the actions and processes supporting them; then supporting infrastructure, people, guides, rules and regulations, and finally the time, volume and quality metrics that make the whole thing measurable.

The line of visibility does the most work, because it forces an explicit answer to "what does the customer know?" A step below the line that is invisible to the customer can be changed without a promise; a step above the line is a promise, and changing it is a change to the service. Many organisations do not know where their line sits — support believes it is below the line, product assumes the same, and the customer assumes the opposite — and the mismatch produces both missed expectations and missed opportunities to communicate progress. The disciplined practice is to draw the line with the whole cross-functional team present and reconcile disagreements about it explicitly, because the disagreements are the finding.

Tip. Quantify failure demand in the unit the business already reports — minutes per supervisor per day, or hours per claim — and put it on the blueprint. The first time a spreadsheet workaround appears as 4.2 FTE-equivalent on a diagram that the operations director drew, the conversation about whether to fix it stops being a design preference.

4.6 Research operations, ethics and saturation

This subsection covers recruitment funnels and incentive rates, consent and PII minimisation, the research repository and citation format, and the operational definition of saturation that authorises stopping.

Research fails operationally more often than methodologically. Recruitment is a funnel with known economics and the numbers should be planned, not hoped for: a screener response rate of 8–15% is typical for specialist B2B panels, a screen-out rate of 40–60% is normal, so a study needing 15 completed sessions from one stratum should recruit 150–200 screener responses. Incentive rates determine who shows up: consumer participants in the United States commonly receive $30–75, professional and practitioner participants $75–150, and regulated-domain practitioners $200 or more, paid on completion rather than on recruitment. Underpayment does not merely reduce volume; it over-recruits the recently unemployed, students and people with an unusually strong interest in the topic, which biases every finding toward the enthusiast.

Consent and data handling are part of the method, not the paperwork. Informed consent covers purpose, recording, the right to withdraw up to synthesis, and the absence of commercial benefit; it should be read aloud and acknowledged in the transcript header rather than assumed from a click. Data minimisation is the operative discipline: collect only what the question requires, assign a study-local identifier at screening, strip identifying fields from transcripts within 7 days, restrict access to named researchers on a least-privilege basis, and set a retention period with a deletion job rather than an intention — 90 days for raw transcripts and audio is a defensible default once synthesis is complete. Screenshots and screen recordings carry the same obligations as transcripts, which in practice means a seeded test tenant and never a production account.

The research repository is what makes evidence survive the researcher. Its minimum structure is a transcript per session named by study and participant identifier, a versioned codebook, a synthesis document in which every insight carries a quotation and its participant set, and a mapping from insight to the artefact that consumed it — persona attribute, journey pain point, job statement clause. Without that last mapping, the repository becomes an archive nobody reads twice and the next study repeats the previous one. Citation format must be short, stable and typed: INT-021.3 for a quote from session three, TQ-2026-38 for a telemetry query, DS-004.7 for a diary day, KB-0041 for an internal article, so that any claim in any artefact resolves to its origin in seconds.

Saturation is the operational licence to stop, and it should be written as a threshold rather than felt: two consecutive sessions producing no new codes against the current codebook, no new pain point above severity 2, and no contradicting evidence for a HIGH-strength attribute. Track the new-information rate per session as new codes divided by total codes raised, and treat a rate below roughly 10% across two consecutive sessions as the signal. Saturation is a property of a segment, not of the study: mature personas commonly saturate at 5–8 sessions each while an unfamiliar segment needs 15–20, and the usual failure is stopping when the first two participants happened to be articulate. Where research is already saturated, the correct action is not to re-interview the same people but to change the method — telemetry, a support-ticket audit, or an experiment.

Warning. Recruiting friends, colleagues and the accounts you like is the fastest way to produce findings you cannot use. Industry contacts convert at high rates and are disproportionately enthusiasts, so the study saturates in three sessions with everyone agreeing, and the artefact then describes a segment that does not exist. Two mitigations: cap direct contacts at 20% of the sample, and compare the recruited sample’s attribute distribution against production telemetry before writing any conclusion.

Exercises 4

  1. Write a complete research plan for one decision you are currently facing: the decision, the three options it distinguishes, and the action under each outcome including the stop condition. Then assign a method and a sample size per question, justified in writing — 385 for ±5 points if quantitative, saturation criteria if qualitative, 5 per round if usability. Finish with a recruitment plan showing response rate, screen-out rate, show rate and the resulting cost per completed session. Deliverable: one document, four pages maximum, with the numbers.
  2. Write a screener for that study with four qualifying and four disqualifying questions, pilot it against ten responses, and log the stated reason for every disqualification. Then identify the single qualifier most likely to exclude your true target population, compare the recruited distribution against production telemetry on two attributes, and state the adjustment you would make before the study. Deliverable: the screener, the rejection log, and a one-paragraph bias assessment naming the residual risk.
  3. Reconstruct three personas from evidence you already hold — interviews, tickets, telemetry. For each attribute attach a session identifier with a verbatim quote or the literal marker ASSUMPTION, then fill the counter-evidence field. Delete every attribute you cannot cite. Deliverable: three one-page cards plus a changelog listing what the evidence removed from the previous version, because the deletions are the finding.
  4. Write four job statements for one persona, classify each as functional, social or emotional, and score importance and satisfaction out of 10 with the evidence for each score. Then build a forces diagram with the four forces weighted to 1.0 per side, state which side dominates, and name the one action that changes the outcome. Deliverable: the four statements, the two scores, the forces diagram, and one sentence saying whether you are currently adding pull or removing anxiety.
  5. Map one journey in two states, with the current state carrying six rows and every cell carrying a session identifier, and the future state stated as deltas rather than features. Then blueprint the worst stage, draw the line of visibility explicitly, count the handoffs, and quantify the failure demand in minutes per user per week. Deliverable: the current-state map, the future-state delta list, the blueprint, and a numeric estimate of the failure demand you would fund against.

5 · Requirements Engineering and Traceability

5.1 Functional and non-functional requirements5.2 Quality attribute scenarios and the non-UI budget5.3 User stories that survive an estimator5.4 Acceptance criteria: Given/When/Then and alternatives5.5 Traceability from requirement to test5.6 Change control, RFCs and deprecation

This chapter covers the requirements artefacts that convert strategy and research into engineering commitments, and the mechanism that keeps them true over time. It distinguishes functional requirements, quality attributes and constraints; specifies quality attribute scenarios with stimulus, environment, artefact, response and measure, including the latency, offline, install-size, cold-start, memory and battery budgets that a desktop product must treat as first-class requirements rather than aspirations; defines user stories at a level of detail that survives estimation; fixes acceptance-criteria conventions and their alternatives; and specifies bidirectional traceability from requirement through design, code and test. It closes with change control, since a requirement system without a change protocol is a snapshot, and snapshots become fiction. The recurring theme is that a requirement is only real when it is testable, so every quality statement in this chapter ends in a measure and an environment.

5.1 Functional and non-functional requirements

This subsection separates functional requirements, quality attributes and constraints, explains why "the system shall be fast" is unusable, gives the rewriting rules that convert an aspiration into a verifiable assertion, and shows the derivation of quality requirements from business objectives.

A functional requirement specifies what the system does, in terms observable at an interface: an input is accepted, a state changes, an output is produced, and the behaviour can be demonstrated without reference to implementation. A quality requirement specifies how well it does it — the attribute, the measure and the threshold. A constraint bounds the solution space independently of behaviour: the operating system, the deployment topology, a dependency’s licence, a regulatory regime, a contractual interoperability obligation. The three take different modal verbs, and the distinction matters at review: RFC 2119 language applied carefully makes "shall" a mandatory obligation, "should" a strong recommendation with documented exceptions, and "may" genuinely optional. Requirements that use "shall" for a preference and "should" for an obligation are not reviewable, because reviewers cannot tell which disagreements are legitimate.

The canonical non-functional failure is "the system shall be fast". It fails on four counts at once: it names no attribute, so fast for whom and for what; no measure, so there is no threshold and no way to fail; no environment, so the number is meaningless without hardware, dataset size, concurrency and cache state; and no verification method, so no test can be written and no defect can be raised. Its replacement follows a fixed recipe — attribute, stimulus, environment, measure, threshold: "when an operator changes any filter on the claim queue, the system shall re-render the result table within 250 ms at the 95th percentile, measured from the click event to the first paint, on a client with 4 logical cores and 8 GB RAM, with 50,000 claims loaded and a cold cache."

5.2 Quality attribute scenarios and the non-UI budget

This subsection defines the five-field quality attribute scenario and the six-scenario set, works three examples — latency, availability and modifiability — and specifies the budgets a desktop product must state and enforce.

A quality attribute scenario is the smallest coherent description of a quality: stimulus, environment, artefact, response, measure, with an explicitly named actor for the stimulus. The six fields exist to close the loopholes adjectives leave open, and naming the environment is what converts a preference into a test. Where an attribute carries real risk, six scenarios are specified per attribute covering normal, load, stress, recovery, stability and change, because "fast" behaves differently at rest, at peak and immediately after a deployment, and a threshold that holds only at rest is not a service level.

Latency deserves particular care because averages hide everything. Thresholds are stated at a percentile, and the percentile must match the density of interactions: for a filter control used thousands of times per day, p95 is meaningful; for a once-per-session action, the p99 and the maximum are what users report. Latency budgets are decomposed rather than asserted end-to-end, because a single composite threshold cannot be diagnosed: a 250 ms interaction budget typically allocates roughly 20 ms to input handling, 60 ms to data fetch on the warm path, 120 ms to render and paint, and 50 ms to margin, each separately instrumented so that regressions point at a layer. The error in writing "the page shall load in under 2 seconds" is not the number but the absence of decomposition; a team that owns four sub-budgets finds the regression in one afternoon.

QUALITY ATTRIBUTE SCENARIOS — three worked, complete, five fields each

  1. LATENCY — interactive response on the claim queue
     STIMULUS   An operator clicks a queue filter control.
     ENVIRONMENT Production; client with 4 logical cores and 8 GB RAM;
                 Chrome, or desktop client build 4.2; 50,000 claims in
                 scope; cold cache; third-percentile network for the region.
     ARTEFACT   The queue view and its filter controls.
     RESPONSE   The result table re-renders with the filter applied; no
                 intermediate inconsistent state; focus remains in place.
     MEASURE    p95 ≤ 250 ms and p99 ≤ 600 ms, click timestamp to first
                 paint of the result rows, measured client-side with a
                 performance mark and reported to the telemetry service.
     BUDGET     input 20 ms | query 60 ms warm | render and paint 120 ms |
                 margin 50 ms — each segment instrumented separately.

  2. AVAILABILITY — continuity of the claim-detail journey
     STIMULUS   Any user request to /claims/{id} or its desktop equivalent.
     ENVIRONMENT Production, single region per tenant; monitoring at 60 s
                 intervals from 3 independent probes.
     ARTEFACT   The claim-detail service and its dependencies.
     RESPONSE   A response, or a documented degradation; never a blank error
                 and never partially rendered claim data.
     MEASURE    99.95% of measured wall-clock minutes per calendar month,
                 excluding announced maintenance ≤ 4 h/year inside a 72 h
                 notice window = 21.9 min/month of unavailability.
     RECOVERY  Zonal loss → ≤ 90 s above 0.5% errors, ≤ 5 min to full.
                 RPO 5 min, RTO 30 min, rehearsed quarterly with a signed
                 record (drill DR-07).

  3. MODIFIABILITY — adding a carrier adapter
     STIMULUS   A product decision to support a new source carrier with a
                 documented file schema and no change to the claim model.
     ENVIRONMENT The claim-processing service and the desktop client that
                 renders intake results; one engineer familiar with the
                 codebase but new to the carrier.
     ARTEFACT   The adapter interface, the intake pipeline, the intake
                 report view.
     RESPONSE   The adapter implements the existing interface; no change to
                 the queue, detail or audit code paths.
     MEASURE    ≤ 3 person-days elapsed; ≤ 5 modules changed; ≤ 400 changed
                 lines; zero changes to the paths named above; the four
                 existing adapter conformance tests pass unmodified.
     BASELINE   The last three additions took 6, 4.5 and 5 person-days
                 across 9, 7 and 8 modules. The current architecture FAILS
