    change     the threshold still holds when the feature is extended

DESKTOP-TRACK BUDGETS — these are requirements, not aspirations
Each becomes a measurable assertion in the test harness, with a threshold and
a machine to run it on. Each is enforced in CI nightly and on the
release-candidate build. A requirement checked once, by hand, during a
release, is a wish with a number in it.

  REQ-DESK-INST-001  Installer size       ≤ 120 MB downloaded and ≤ 340 MB
                       installed on a clean machine. Enforced by CI against
                       the packaged artefact; growth above 5 MB per release
                       requires an approval recorded against this ID.
  REQ-DESK-START-002 Cold start           ≤ 1.8 s from process launch to
                       first interactive frame, measured on BASELINE-01
                       (4-core, 8 GB, SATA SSD, no discrete GPU, Windows 11
                       23H2) with a warm OS file cache and a cold app cache,
                       p99 over 20 consecutive launches. A regression above
                       150 ms blocks the release.
  REQ-DESK-MEM-003   Resident memory      ≤ 450 MB RSS after a 30-minute
                       soak covering 2,000 claims opened and 40 filter
                       changes; growth slope ≤ 5 MB per 10 min, which is the
                       leak signature; hard transient ceiling 600 MB.
  REQ-DESK-CPU-004   CPU                  Idle below 1.5% of one core;
                       below 18% average while rendering 2,000-row tables.
  REQ-DESK-PWR-005   Battery impact       Below 3% of a 50 Wh battery per
                       hour of active use; below 0.5 W while idle-syncing.
                       Any feature that adds continuous polling must be
                       costed against this number before it is scheduled.
  REQ-DESK-OFF-006   Offline behaviour    Reads served from cache with a
                       visible staleness indicator and its timestamp; writes
                       queued locally and synchronised on reconnect;
                       read-your-writes guaranteed for the writing client;
                       per-field last-write-wins with an explicit conflict
                       surface, never a silent overwrite; no queued write
                       may be lost on a kill -9. Verified by a crash test.
  REQ-DESK-UPD-007   Update size          Incremental update ≤ 20 MB; an
                       update may not interrupt an unsaved form, verified by
                       a draft-preservation test.
  REQ-DESK-INST-008  Privileges           Runs as a standard user: no
                       elevation, no service installation, no administrator
                       rights. Verified by an automated install test in a
                       locked account on the CI runner.
  REQ-DESK-REL-009   Crash-free sessions  ≥ 99.7% over a rolling 30-day
                       window, from client telemetry with a declared
                       denominator: a session is an app run longer than 60 s.
  REQ-DESK-LOC-010   Local data           All claim content cached to disk is
                       encrypted at rest with a key derived from the user
                       credential, and the cache is purged on sign-out and on
                       7 days of inactivity.

  WHY THESE ARE HARDER THAN WEB BUDGETS
    There is no network boundary to hide behind: every millisecond of cold
    start is paid once per launch, on hardware the vendor does not control,
    with a disk that may be a spinning drive. The measurement environment is
    therefore part of the requirement, the baseline machine is version-
    controlled, and every threshold carries an explicit regression band. A
    desktop requirement without a baseline machine is unenforceable, and
    the first person to upgrade their laptop will quietly rewrite it.

Tip. Fix one named baseline machine per requirement — specific CPU generation, RAM, storage type, OS build — and change it only through a change request against the requirement. The most common form of requirement decay is not ignoring a threshold but quietly upgrading the measurement environment, so the number still looks satisfied on the newest hardware in the lab and fails on the oldest machine a customer owns.

Warning. The average is the most damaging number in a latency requirement. It is dominated by the fast cases and blind to the slow ones: a distribution of 5 ms and 2,000 ms in equal proportion averages just over a second and passes any 1.5 s threshold, while one user in ten waits two seconds on every interaction. Always state the percentile, and for high-frequency interactions state the maximum as well.

5.3 User stories that survive an estimator

This subsection explains why most user stories are too vague to estimate, specifies the four-part form that survives an estimating session, covers splitting patterns, and gives the calibration data behind the team’s numbers.

A user story is a promise of a conversation, not a specification, and it is frequently written as a placeholder the team later discovers has no content: "as an operator I want to filter claims so I can find what I need" contains no data, no behaviour, no boundary and no error handling, and any estimate attached to it is a guess dressed as a number. The version that survives an estimating session names the actor as a specific persona performing a specific job, states the capability in domain language, names the data and its constraints, states the business rule, states the permission model, and states what happens at the edges — empty, oversized, conflicting, unauthorised.

The actor must be a role and a job, not a person and not a title. The value clause must be an outcome the persona would want if it were achieved by a competitor or a contractor, which is the substitution test from §4.3; a value clause naming the solution is the single most common defect, because it smuggles features past prioritisation. Splitting is the primary skill, and the patterns are worth memorising: workflow steps, business rule variations, data variations, mandatory/optional/optional variation, and effort. A split piece must be independently valuable and independently shippable; if a split produces something that cannot be released alone, it is a task rather than a story.

STORY THAT SURVIVES AN ESTIMATOR — US-412 (one of five split from US-396)
  As a claims supervisor clearing a filing queue before the carrier cut-off,
  I want to see which of my assigned claims are blocked on a source document,
  so that I can sequence the queue by what is actually decidable rather than
  by carrier arrival time.

  DATA          claim.blocked_on_document : document_id (nullable, FK to the
                document index) plus blocked_since (timestamp), populated by
                the resolver service and never by the client.
  RULE          A claim is "blocked" when blocked_on_document IS NOT NULL
                AND the document index entry is missing or older than 24 h
                (the TTL). A present, fresh document does not block.
  PERMISSIONS   supervisor: read across their own tenant; adjuster: read only
                for claims assigned to them; auditor: read, never unblock.
  STATES        empty (none blocked) | normal | loading | stale (index older
                than 24 h, show the timestamp) | error (resolver unreachable,
                show last known state with a staleness warning).
  BEHAVIOUR     default sort changes to blocked-last when any blocked claim is
                in scope; the change is per-user, persisted and reversible.
  NON-GOALS     no bulk unblock; no cross-tenant view; no notification.
  ESTIMATE      5 (relative). Split from US-396 (15) into US-411 to US-415.
  CRITERIA      7 Given/When/Then clauses, worked in §5.4.

INVEST CHECK — the items that fail most often, and the fix
  I Independent   cut it if it can be bundled without coupling
  N Negotiable   explicitly negotiable; write the trade-off into the story
  V Valuable      value clause from a persona's job, never a feature
  E Estimable    has data, rules, permissions and states, or split or spike
  S Small        ≤ 2 days of focused work, else slice by workflow step
  T Testable      has acceptance criteria before it is pulled into a sprint
  T Trackable     one backlog item, one ID, one owner, visible on the board

SPLIT LOG — US-396 "operators can see claim status" (estimated 15, ran 24)
  US-396  by WORKFLOW STEP       → 411 queue list, 412 blocking state,
                                 413 claim detail header, 414 export
                                 column, 415 bulk unblock (deferred)
  US-397  "adjuster uploads a document" (estimated 8, ran 13)
          by BUSINESS RULE       → 397a required-document rules,
                                 397b optional-document rules,
                                 397c evidence-quality rules (deferred)
  US-398  "tenant admin manages roles" (estimated 13)
          by DATA VARIATION      → 398a single tenant, 398b multi-tenant,
                                 398c bulk role assignment (deferred)
  RULE OBSERVED a split piece must ship alone and be valuable alone. US-415
  and 397c were moved to the backlog as candidate non-goals rather than
  stories, because neither produces value without the others.
  ESTIMATION LESSON the 24 that US-396 actually took was not 24 days of
  coding: it was 9 days of specification discovered during the build, in
  the states row above, which nobody had written down at estimation time.

ESTIMATION REFERENCE — team claims-platform, 2026-Q3 calibration, 47 items
  A story point is a relative unit of complexity, uncertainty and effort
  combined. It is never an hour, and the conversion below is valid only
  inside this team and this quarter.

  ANCHORS  1  single field validation change, known pattern, 1 day
           2  one screen, no new query, states enumerated, ≤ 2 days
           3  one screen plus one new query plus one edge state, ≤ 3 days
           5  new service integration with permissions and 3 edge states
           8  cross-cutting change touching 3 modules, ≤ 8 days
           13 more than 1 week for one person, or 3+ modules with unknowns

  CONVERSION 8 points ≈ 5 person-days for this team. Measured over the last
           three iterations: actual 4.4, 5.1, 5.8 — mean 5.1, σ 0.7.
  RULES OF THUMB  one person-month = 20 person-days of available effort,
           not 30. A release plan that uses 30 is planning capacity the
           organisation does not have, and will slip.
  DRIFT CHECK   re-derive the conversion every quarter from delivered items.
           If the ratio moves more than 20%, the anchors are stale, not
           the team, and the anchors are what get rewritten.

  STORY-VERSUS-TASK DECISION (a cheaper alternative to cards)
    Use cards when the outcome and its acceptance are negotiable with a
    customer and the estimate carries uncertainty the team wants visible.
    Use a task list when the work is specification-driven with a known
    sequence — migrations, packaging, compliance sweeps. Teams that convert
    tasks into stories to satisfy a process rule get 5-point cards that
    measure nothing, and their velocity number stops meaning anything.
  EXAMPLE this release: 9 of 31 items are packaging and compliance work
  tracked as tasks with owners and dates; the remaining 22 are stories with
  criteria. Velocity is reported for the stories only, and the task effort
  is subtracted from capacity at the start of each iteration rather than
  discovered at the end.

Warning. The value clause is where feature creep enters the backlog disguised as intent. "so that I can use the new filtering engine" states the solution, commits the team to it, and removes the ability to meet the job more cheaply. Every story should pass the substitution test before it is accepted: if a competitor or a contractor delivered this outcome, would the persona still want it? If not, the clause names a feature and must be rewritten as the underlying job.

5.4 Acceptance criteria: Given/When/Then and alternatives

This subsection specifies acceptance-criteria quality, works Given/When/Then against a checklist and an examples-first BDD alternative, and gives the mandatory edge cases that most criteria omit.

Acceptance criteria are the contract between the person who wants the behaviour and the person who will build it, and their quality determines whether the estimate made at refinement was an estimate of anything. Three properties are required. They must be written before implementation, because criteria written afterwards describe what was built and therefore agree with it by construction. They must be testable by someone who did not write the story and who is not the implementer, which is the operative definition of done. And they must cover the edges, because a criterion set that only describes the happy path produces a system that is correct exactly once: for each story, criteria are needed for the empty state, the single-element boundary, the oversized maximum, the unauthorised case, the failure case, and the concurrent or duplicate case.

The dominant defect is implementation coupling. Criteria written as clicks — "click the filter, wait for the spinner, assert the row count" — pass against the first design and fail after the first legitimate refactor, and the team then discovers that the specification is a barrier to improvement rather than a record of intent. When/Then with concrete examples is preferable for exactly that reason: it is stated in domain terms, survives a change of interface, and converts directly to an automated test. The convention should be used strictly: Given establishes state including data and permissions, When is exactly one event, Then is the observable outcome, and each clause is a single assertion.

Criteria styleShapeBest forStrengthWeaknessAutomationSuitable
Given / When / ThenOne clause per assertion, domain languageBehaviour with states and edgesSurvives refactoring; reviewable by non-implementers; reads as specificationVerbose; penalised for trivial checksDirect, usually no glue✓ Default for feature work
Examples-first BDDNamed examples per rule, classes declared up frontDense rule sets, domain language, auditForces the complete rule inventory before coding; reusable as documentation and as support macrosRequires domain fluency; expensive to retrofitDirect✓ Regulated logic, eligibility, pricing
ChecklistVerifiable items, no narrativePackaging, configuration, compliance sweepsCheap, unambiguous, mechanically automatableDoes not express edges or orderingMechanical, one check per item✓ Non-behavioural work
Property-based or invariantsUniversal statements over the input spaceRules that would need dozens of enumerated casesCovers the space rather than the samples; shrinks the case listPoor diagnosis on failure; needs domain insight to state the propertyDirect, with generators✓ Money, totals, permissions, sorting
Click-path scriptsUI interaction stepsLegacy regression suitesFamiliar to non-engineers; cheap for trivial flowsCoupled to the interface; fails on every refactor; tests the UI, not the ruleBrittle✗ As the primary criteria for any story
Performance criteriaMeasure, percentile and environmentEvery story touching a quality attributeMakes the quality requirement part of doneFlaky without a controlled harness; needs a baseline machineLoad harness, nightly✓ Mandatory wherever a QA exists
 
ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA — US-412, Given/When/Then, one assertion per clause

  AC1  GIVEN  a claim assigned to me is blocked on a document missing from
               the document index
       WHEN   I open the queue
       THEN   the claim appears with a "blocked" marker
  AC2  GIVEN  a claim's document was indexed less than 24 hours ago
       WHEN   I open the queue
       THEN   that claim does NOT appear as blocked
  AC3  GIVEN  at least one in-scope claim is blocked
       WHEN   the queue is displayed
       THEN   the default sort places blocked claims last
  AC4  GIVEN  I changed the sort and then reloaded the page
       WHEN   the queue is displayed again
       THEN   my sort choice is restored
  AC5  GIVEN  I am an auditor
       WHEN   I open any claim in my tenant
       THEN   no unblock control is rendered
  AC6  GIVEN  the resolver service is unreachable
       WHEN   I open the queue
       THEN   the last known blocking states are shown with a staleness
               warning carrying the timestamp of the last successful read
  AC7  GIVEN  a 4-core / 8 GB client with 50,000 claims in scope, cold cache
       WHEN   I click any filter control
       THEN   the result table re-renders within 250 ms at p95, measured
               click-to-first-paint and reported to telemetry
  COVERAGE CHECK against the mandatory edge list:
    empty state    AC3's negation, plus a dedicated test asserting the
                   "none blocked" state renders without the marker
    maximum        the AC7 load test at 50,000 claims, all blocked
    unauthorised   AC5
    failure        AC6
    concurrent     out of scope for this story; covered by the REQ-QA-MOD-011
                   conformance suite, recorded here so it is not forgotten
  WHAT WOULD MAKE THESE FAIL — a deliberately hostile review question:
    "AC2 and AC6 both depend on the 24 h TTL. If the resolver service returns
     a document with no timestamp, what does the client believe?" Answer: the
     card is incomplete, and the field must become non-null with an explicit
     unknown value. Found at review, not in production.

DEFINITION OF DONE — the same clause for every story on this team
  1  Every Given/When/Then clause is implemented and green in CI.
  2  Every criterion that references a requirement ID resolves in the
     catalogue, and the reverse trace exists from code to requirement.
  3  Any criterion carrying a measure passes on the baseline machine, and
     the measurement is recorded, not assumed.
  4  Empty, boundary, unauthorised and failure states have tests.
  5  No new console errors or unhandled rejections on the exercised paths.
  6  Telemetry emitted for the new behaviour, visible in the staging board.
  7  Release note entry generated from the commit identifiers.
  8  Reviewed by someone who did not write the criteria.

ALTERNATIVE A — CHECKLIST, for the story type where narrative costs more
  CONFIGURATION ACCEPTANCE — desktop packaging, no behavioural edge cases
    [ ] Packaged installer ≤ 120 MB on a clean baseline machine  (INST-001)
    [ ] Installs and runs as a standard user, no elevation       (INST-008)
    [ ] Cold start to first interactive frame ≤ 1.8 s p99        (START-002)
    [ ] RSS ≤ 450 MB after the 30-minute 2,000-claim soak        (MEM-003)
    [ ] Idle CPU below 1.5% of one core                         (CPU-004)
    [ ] Battery impact below 3% per hour of active use          (PWR-005)
    [ ] Runs on the 6 configurations in matrix M-01, verified in the
        nightly compatibility job; a failure blocks merge
    [ ] Licence scan reports no reciprocal-licence component     (CON-002)
    [ ] Incremental update ≤ 20 MB and preserves an open draft   (UPD-007)
  WHY HERE each line is independently verifiable, none involves a business
  rule, and the cost of a narrative clause would exceed the cost of the check.

ALTERNATIVE B — EXAMPLES-FIRST BDD, for the rule inventory
  Written before implementation, so every rule is forced into the open.

  Feature: Claim blocking state
    Rule: a claim is blocked only if no fresh indexed document exists

      Example: missing from the index
        Given claim C-88213 is assigned to supervisor S-04
        And the document index contains no entry for C-88213's source PDF
        When S-04 opens the queue
        Then C-88213 is marked blocked

      Example: stale index entry
        Given C-88213's document was indexed 26 hours ago
        And no document has been fetched since
        When S-04 opens the queue
        Then C-88213 is marked blocked

      Example: fresh index entry
        Given C-88213's document was indexed 3 hours ago
        When S-04 opens the queue
        Then C-88213 is not marked blocked

      Example: missing timestamp is not freshness
        Given C-88213's document was indexed with no timestamp
        When S-04 opens the queue
        Then C-88213 is marked blocked with reason "unknown"

    Invariants (property-based, hold for every claim in the tenant)
      - every blocked claim has a reason drawn from {missing, stale, unknown}
      - the count of blocked claims never exceeds the count of in-scope claims
      - unblocking a claim never changes its assignment or its reason history
      - the set of blocked claims is monotonic within a session: a claim
        blocked at open stays blocked unless its document resolves

  NOTE the examples are the specification, the test code is generated from
  them, and the same examples appear in the support macro library so that
  support and engineering read one version of the rule. The fourth example
  exists because AC2 and AC6 in the main criteria left that case open.

Note. Keep criteria in version control next to the code, not only in the tracker. A tracker field is convenient for reporting and poor for review: it is not diffable, it has no history, and it is unreachable from the pull request where a reviewer needs it. Examples-first BDD in particular only works when the examples and the tests are the same reviewable change.

5.5 Traceability from requirement to test

This subsection defines the two directions of traceability, the identifier scheme, the coverage checks that catch gaps and orphans, the machine-readable export, and the artefact comparison showing what each tool actually proves.

Traceability answers two questions that must both be answerable on demand. Downward: if this requirement is implemented, where? Requirement to user story, to design element, to code artefact, to automated test, to release. Upward: if this code or this test exists, which requirement justifies it? The second direction is the one teams omit, and it is the one that prevents waste, because a large fraction of production code traces to no requirement at all — accumulated "while we were in there" changes, defensive branches, one-off reports. Upward trace also surfaces duplicate and contradictory requirements, where two identifiers specify overlapping behaviour and the two implementations disagree in production.

Traceability is only as good as its identifier scheme. A stable scheme with type and sequence — REQ-FUN-014, REQ-QA-PERF-004 — survives reordering, is greppable, sorts usefully, and separates obligations of different kinds for coverage reporting. Requirements carried only as backlog titles cannot be traced, because titles are edited freely; the title is a display artefact and the identifier is the identity. The identifier is never reused, never renumbered, and never retired without a supersession record, so a reference in a two-year-old test still resolves to the requirement actually in force.

      "status": "verified", "verifiedOn": "2026-06-11", "owner": "desktop"
    }
  ],
  "summary": {
    "total": 16, "functional": 3, "qualityAttribute": 12, "constraint": 0,
    "businessRule": 1, "compliance": 1,
    "verified": 16, "stale": 3, "gaps": 0, "orphanTests": 14,
    "lineCoveragePercent": 94.1,
    "note": "lineCoveragePercent is informational and is not requirements coverage"

}

Spreadsheet or document RTMRequirement to design, testDownward, manualHigh; stale within two releasesNo link to code; invisible in a pull request✗ As the system of record; ✓ as a periodic audit snapshot
Commit-message identifiersThat each change cites a requirementBothNear zero, enforced by a commit hookProse quality varies; no roll-up without parsing✓ Always; the cheapest real mechanism

Generated coverage reportWhich requirements lack a test; which tests lack a requirementBothGeneratedOnly as good as the link conventions✓ The authoritative artefact
Code line-coverage reportWhich lines executedNeitherGeneratedMistaken for requirements coverage; blind to load, chaos and drill verification✗ For coverage claims; ✓ for finding dead code
Release-note generatorRequirement to shipped releaseDownwardGeneratedRequires disciplined commit footers✓ Aligns communication with the catalogue

Warning. Do not report code coverage as requirement coverage, in either direction. An availability requirement verified by a quarterly chaos drill, a latency requirement verified by a load harness and a rollback requirement verified by an operational drill have no unit tests at all, and can be fully satisfied while the line-coverage report shows them as untested. Coverage is a property of obligations, not of lines, and the two numbers answer different questions.

5.6 Change control, RFCs and deprecation

This subsection specifies the change request and RFC process, roles and service levels, change impact analysis, the supersession record, and the deprecation discipline that makes a published commitment safe to revise.

A requirement catalogue without a change protocol is a snapshot, and snapshots become fiction within two releases. Change control is the mechanism by which an organisation distinguishes the change it has decided to make from the change it has merely discussed. The instrument is the RFC, and its discipline is that the author states the problem and the decision required rather than the solution, and reviewers respond to the problem statement before reading the proposal. The RFC carries a decision state — draft, proposed, accepted, rejected, withdrawn — and a deadline at which the state resolves, because an unresolved RFC taxes every subsequent decision touching the same area.

Roles should be explicit, because the common failure is a review that is technically rigorous and procedurally void. The author owns the problem statement and the impact analysis; reviewers are chosen for the area affected rather than for seniority, and each answers only for their domain; approvers are the one or two people with authority to accept, and do not review the detail; informed parties are told the outcome and do not gate it. Service levels keep the process from becoming a bottleneck: a small change within 5 working days, a large change within 10, a change touching a data model or public interface within 15, and anything requiring a compliance decision routed out of band. Every accepted RFC produces a supersession record: the old identifier is retired with a pointer to the new one, never renumbered and never deleted.

RFC TEMPLATE — RFC-2026-31 "Replace SFTP intake with an object-store drop"

CHANGE CONTROL AS CI ENFORCEMENT — the process that does not rot
  ci/require-requirement-id.sh — runs on every pull request
    fails the PR when: the branch name matches no pattern
      feat|fix|chore/REQ-[A-Z]+-[0-9]{3}-
    or when: the commit footers contain no REQ- identifier
    or when: no REQ- identifier in the footers resolves in the exported
      catalogue (export/requirements.json from the previous build)
    exempt paths: docs/, infra/charts/, .github/ — listed explicitly, never
    by a wildcard, because a wildcard exemption is how the rule dies

  ci/coverage-gate.sh — nightly, publishes to the release dashboard
    gate 1  every requirement with status "accepted" in the current release
            has at least one trace in the matrix, else FAIL the release cut
    gate 2  every test in suites/ that references no REQ- identifier is
            listed in the orphan report and requires a one-line justification
            in .test-orphans.yaml or is excluded by an explicit pattern
    gate 3  every requirement whose verifiedOn predates its last modified
            date is listed as stale and blocks the release until re-verified
            or until an owner records a documented decision not to
    gate 4  line coverage is reported and NEVER used as a gate for
            requirements; it is used only to find dead code

  ci/requirements-export.sh — build step
    regenerates export/requirements.json from catalogue/requirements.yaml
    runs the schema check, fails on an unknown type, a missing measure on a
    quality-attribute entry, or a threshold that is not numeric
    publishes the export as a build artefact so the compliance archive keeps
    the exact version that shipped, not the current version of the file

  WHAT THIS BUYS: the discipline of citing an identifier stops being a
  matter of memory or reviewer diligence and becomes a matter of the build
  passing. Teams that reach this state report that RFC review time drops by
  roughly half, because the impact analysis has already been generated.

  RESIDUAL RISKS TO MANAGE EXPLICITLY
    A lint rule forces the citation but not its honesty: an author who cites
    REQ-FUN-001 for an unrelated change breaks nothing. Countered by gate 3
    (staleness) plus quarterly sampling of 20 changes against their cited
    requirement, reviewed by someone outside the team.

Tip. Publish the catalogue as an export — JSON or YAML with the fields in §5.5 — and make the build depend on it. Once the link-linter, the coverage reporter and the release-note generator all consume the same file, the catalogue becomes infrastructure rather than documentation, and citation stops being a habit. The single highest-value version control is the schema check that refuses a quality attribute with a non-numeric threshold.

Exercises 5

  1. Take your five most recent requirements and classify each as functional, quality attribute, constraint, business rule, data or compliance. Find every quality requirement lacking a measure, a threshold or an environment and rewrite it in the stimulus / environment / artefact / response / measure form. Deliverable: a five-row table showing original text, the defect and the rewrite, plus a count of how many of your existing quality requirements would fail review against this standard.
  2. Write a complete scenario set for latency, availability and modifiability on your product: six scenarios each — normal, load, stress, recovery, stability, change — with named thresholds, then decompose one latency budget into segments with the instrumentation that proves each. Deliverable: three scenario tables, one budget diagram, and an effort estimate in person-days for each harness you would have to build.
  3. Write the desktop-track budget set for your client: install size, cold start to first interactive frame, memory ceiling with a soak profile, idle and active CPU, battery impact, offline behaviour including conflict policy, update size, privileges and crash-free session rate. For each, name the baseline machine, the measurement method and the cadence, and say where in the pipeline it is enforced. Deliverable: nine requirements in catalogue format with verification fields, plus a CI design showing which jobs run per merge and which run nightly.
  4. Rebuild one story your team estimated last quarter: persona and job as the actor, capability in domain language, data and constraints, business rule, permissions, and the empty, boundary, unauthorised and failure states. Split it until every piece ships alone, then re-estimate against your anchors. Deliverable: the rewritten story, the split log with a reason per split, original and new estimates, and an explanation of which part of the original estimate measured specification ambiguity rather than work.
  5. Build a traceability matrix for your last release: every requirement identifier with its story, design element, code module, test and release, plus a test-side sweep for tests referencing no requirement. Produce a coverage report separating requirement coverage from line coverage, identify every stale requirement whose verification predates its last modification, and state the mechanism that would generate the matrix rather than maintain it by hand. Deliverable: the matrix, the orphan list, and a one-page description of the commit, branch and test-link conventions you would enforce in CI.

6 · Interface Design: Wireframes, Prototyping and Usability Testing

6.1 Lo-fi to hi-fi6.2 Prototyping methods6.3 Usability testing6.4 Information architecture6.5 Accessibility as an upstream constraint6.6 Design-to-engineering handoff

Interface design is a sequence of increasingly expensive commitments, and the discipline of the discipline is matching the fidelity of the artefact to the question being asked. A lo-fi wireframe answers whether the structure is right, a mockup answers whether it looks right, and a coded prototype answers whether it feels right; conflating the three is the most common source of wasted design effort. This section moves from the fidelity ladder through prototyping media, a repeatable usability-test protocol, information architecture, accessibility treated as an upstream design constraint rather than a closing audit, and the handoff artefacts — including design tokens — that form the contract between design and engineering. Both delivery tracks in chapters 9–16 inherit everything here; the questions do not change, only the medium in which the artefact is produced.

6.1 Lo-fi to hi-fi

The fidelity ladder orders wireframe media by how much of the product they simulate, and each rung costs an order of magnitude more than the one below. Choosing a rung is choosing which class of question you are permitted to ask.

Fidelity is a set of independent variables — visual polish, behavioural realism, data realism, and system completeness — and the useful discipline is to raise them only as far as the question requires. A hand-drawn box-and-arrow sketch is visually low fidelity but can be behaviourally complete for a checkout flow if every state is drawn. A Figma component mock-up wired with real transitions is visually high fidelity and behaviourally nearly empty. Teams routinely build the second kind and then draw architectural conclusions from it, which is how "it felt good in the prototype" becomes a mandate for a rendering approach that does not survive contact with 10,000 rows of data.

The dominant shorthand is the 1/10/100 rule: rough sketches are worth roughly a tenth of a mid-fidelity clickable wireframe, which is worth roughly a hundredth of a coded, production-quality prototype — that is, the effort escalates by about two orders of magnitude per rung. Use it to argue for cheap answers to cheap questions, and to resist the "we need a coded prototype" request that is really a request for confidence. The confidence is better obtained by a usability test, which costs a fraction as much and produces stronger evidence.

Every rung should answer exactly one question class. A common discipline that works: the artefact-per-question table below is written into the design brief for every feature, and the artefact named in column two is the only artefact permitted to carry the decision in column three.

Wireframes are also the right medium for a specific, underrated artefact: the state inventory. Before any layout work, enumerate for each screen the states it can occupy — default, loading (skeleton and spinner), partial, empty, error, permission-denied, offline, over-quota, success — and draw each. Empty and error states are where most production interfaces are weakest because they are the states nobody prototypes.

<!-- Lo-fi wireframe: structure only, semantics exposed for review -->
<section aria-labelledby="w-search-h">
  <h2 id="w-search-h">Find a record</h2>

  <form role="search">
    <label for="w-q">Query</label>
    <input id="w-q" name="q" type="search"
           aria-describedby="w-q-hint" autocomplete="off">
    <p id="w-q-hint">Searches title and body. Press / to focus.</p>
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
  </form>

  <ul role="list">
    <li><a href="/r/1">Record one</a> <span>edited 2h ago</span></li>
    <li><a href="/r/2">Record two</a> <span>edited 1d ago</span></li>
  </ul>
</section>

The ASCII sketch below is the same screen at fidelity zero, drawn in any text editor in under ten minutes. Its value is that it forces decisions about grouping and order without committing a single pixel of styling, and it can be printed, annotated by hand, and thrown away without ceremony.

+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| Find a record                                      [ ? Help ]  |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Query [__________________________]  [ Search ]  [/ to focus]|
|                                                               |
|  Results (2)                              Sort: [Newest v]     |
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------+|
|  | Record one                            edited 2h ago       ||
|  | Record two                            edited 1d ago       ||
|  +-----------------------------------------------------------+|
|                                                               |
|  [< 1 ]  Page 1 of 1  [ 1 >]                                  |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+

  [ clear input ]      [ reset filters ]      [ save this search ]
ArtefactQuestion it answersSignal it givesTypical costReuse potential
Paper sketch / whiteboardIs this the right structure?Structural only; zero visual biasMinutesNone — disposable
ASCII / block wireframeIs the content hierarchy correct?Grouping, order, label wordingUnder 1 hourLow; survives as a spec
Static wireframe toolDoes layout hold at these sizes?Reflow, density, breakpoint behaviourHalf a dayMedium; becomes layout spec
Clickable wireframeIs the flow navigable without help?Task completion, no dead ends1–3 daysHigh; flow underpins build
Visual mockupDoes this look right?Aesthetic, brand, tonal targets2–5 daysMedium; tokens extracted
Coded prototypeDoes this feel right?Latency, input feel, real data volume1–3 weeksLow unless promoted to code

Why the artefact matters. Each rung has a different failure mode. Paper cannot show density, so overstuffed layouts look fine. Mockups cannot show latency, so a 900 ms perceived response feels instant on click. Only a coded prototype exposes the interaction costs that real users will feel, and even it exaggerates them if it is not connected to realistic data volumes.

The fidelity trap. Stakeholders review whatever is most polished and infer that the polished part is the most decided. Teams get trapped building a beautiful coded prototype for a question that a ten-minute sketch would have answered, and then discover the answer was no. Constrain the review: state on the artefact which question it is for, and mark undecided areas as open rather than rendering them confidently.

6.2 Prototyping methods

Prototypes are experimental apparatus. The choice of medium determines which variables are held constant, and therefore which conclusions the artefact is entitled to support.

Three media dominate, and they are not interchangeable. A paper prototype simulates behaviour with participants moving cut-out components; it is unbeatable for testing navigation and information architecture, and it costs almost nothing to change, which is exactly why it exposes structural mistakes early. A clickable wireframe in a design tool simulates screen-to-screen transitions with fixed content; it is the workhorse for flow validation and for stakeholder alignment, and it will systematically flatter anything involving input, scrolling, or latency. A coded prototype simulates real interaction against real components; it is the only medium that can honestly answer questions about input responsiveness, gesture handling, focus behaviour, data volume, and accessibility, and it is the only one that produces code you can keep.

Beyond the three, two specialised forms earn their place. A Wizard of Oz prototype fakes the intelligence of a feature behind the scenes while using the real interface — a human operator answers the queries a search or recommendation engine is supposed to answer. This lets you test the interaction and the perceived quality of a system capability long before the capability exists, and it isolates the genuinely risky question: do users trust and act on the output? A horizontal slice is a coded prototype built from real components on real infrastructure, but vertical in the sense of going all the way down only for one narrow slice of the domain. It is the most expensive artefact and the most persuasive, because nearly nothing about it is fictional.

Whatever the medium, prototype with a written assumption ledger: each interaction is paired with the assumption it tests and the evidence that would refute it. Without this, prototypes accumulate decisions nobody remembers making.

<!-- Coded prototype: a component, not a mockup.
     Real focus handling, real ARIA, real reduced-motion path. -->
<button id="invite-open" type="button" onclick="openInvite(this)">Invite</button>
<dialog id="invite-dialog" aria-labelledby="invite-h">
  <h2 id="invite-h">Invite a teammate</h2>
  <form method="dialog">
    <label for="invite-email">Email address</label>
    <input id="invite-email" name="email" type="email" required autocomplete="email">
    <p id="invite-status" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p>
    <menu><button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
      <button value="send">Send</button></menu>
  </form>
</dialog>
<p id="live" class="visually-hidden" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p>

<script>
  const dlg = document.getElementById('invite-dialog');
  let restoreTo = document.getElementById('invite-open');   // the element that opened it
  function openInvite(trigger) {
    restoreTo = trigger;
    dlg.showModal();                       // native focus trap, Esc, inert background
    document.getElementById('invite-email').focus();
  }
  dlg.addEventListener('close', () => {
    restoreTo.focus();                     // focus returns where it came from
    document.getElementById('live').textContent = 'Invite dialog closed';
  });
  dlg.addEventListener('submit', async (ev) => {
    ev.preventDefault();
    const s = document.getElementById('invite-status');
    s.textContent = 'Sending invite…';
    s.setAttribute('aria-busy', 'true');
    try {
      const r = await fetch('/api/invites', { method: 'POST',
        body: new FormData(ev.target) });
      if (!r.ok) throw new Error(String(r.status));
      dlg.close();
    } catch (err) {
      // Announced, not merely coloured red.
      s.textContent = 'Invite could not be sent. Check the address and retry.';
    } finally { s.removeAttribute('aria-busy'); }
  });
</script>
MethodBest forHolds constantBreaks down onCostKeep as artefact?
Paper, cut and shuffleNavigation, IA, terminologyNothing — fully simulatedAnything involving input or timingVery low✓ No, photograph and discard
Static wireframeLayout, density, breakpoint orderLayoutInteraction feel, input, latencyLow✓ Yes, as layout spec
Clickable wireframeFlow completeness, dead-end huntingScreen transitionsInput feel, real data volume, a11yMedium✓ Yes, as flow spec
Wizard of OzTrust, expectation, feedback designReal interfaceNothing much, by designMedium, needs an operator✗ No, but keep the protocol
Coded component prototypeFeel, focus, keyboard, data volumeReal componentsFull-system integrationHigh✓ Yes, promote to code
Horizontal sliceWhole-system feasibility, stakeholder buy-inAlmost everythingNothing, but it is no longer cheapVery high✓ Yes, this ships

Clickable prototypes lie about input. A design-tool transition is instantaneous and a design-tool text field accepts any string. Neither reflects IME composition, autofill, paste, drag-and-drop, validation timing, or the 120 ms it takes a real keystroke to feel native. Never let a clickable prototype be the evidence for a decision about an input-heavy screen; a keyboard test on coded components costs an hour and finds the problems.

Keep the prototype honest. Seed prototype data with worst-case volumes — 200 table rows, a 40-character name in every language you sell in, a zero-value numeric field, a 3 MB attachment. Prototypes that only ever show three tidy rows teach the team nothing about the layout they will actually ship.

6.3 Usability testing

A usability test is a controlled observation, not a demonstration. The protocol below is designed to elicit honest, task-level behaviour rather than polite endorsement of whatever is in front of the participant.

The purpose of a usability test is to find out what a person who has not seen the product before will do, and to notice where they stop, backtrack, or ask for help. Everything else — validating a hypothesis, comparing two designs, gauging vocabulary — is secondary. The most common failure is designing a session that cannot embarrass the design, because a session that cannot embarrass the design produces no findings.

Recruit. Five to eight participants from the target population, recruited through the same channel your customers come from. Screen for domain experience separately from product experience: a domain expert who has never used your product is an excellent participant, and an internal colleague is usually a poor one because they already know the answer. Recruit 1–2 participants per key persona, and reserve at least one slot for someone at the edge of the range — oldest, least technical, or slowest network — because they are the ones who break the assumptions.

Prepare tasks. Write 3–5 tasks in the participant’s language and goal, never in your interface’s language. "Find the invoice for the March hosting charge and download it as a PDF", not "click the Billing tab then Export". Each task needs a success criterion that can be judged objectively, an expected path only so you can classify detours, and no hint text. Prepare the seeded data so every task is achievable and the first attempt at a task is not blocked by a missing record.

Run the session, 60–90 minutes. Standard shape: 5 minutes introduction and consent, 5–10 minutes warm-up, 40–60 minutes on tasks, 10 minutes debrief. Present the study as testing the interface, never the participant. Ask them to think aloud, and use neutral prompts — "What are you thinking?" or "What would you try?" — rather than evaluative ones like "That is the right button, isn’t it?". Do not answer questions during a task; if asked, note the question as a finding. Observe behaviour, not faces: hesitation, backtracking, cursor drift to screen edges, and reading aloud from the screen are all stronger signals than satisfaction ratings.

Record and prioritise. Capture audio or screen video, and log every instance of hesitation, error, wrong path, and request for help. Then rank findings. The standard model multiplies severity by frequency: severity 4 (task-blocking, no workaround) × frequency 3 (most participants) outranks severity 3 (slow, confusing) × frequency 1. Fix the top of that ranked list first; the tail of a five-participant test is noise.

// Usability test plan — the document you actually write
const test = {
  id: 'UT-2026-04-invoice-export',
  hypothesis: 'Users can locate and export an invoice without assistance.',
  // Pass criterion set BEFORE the session, not after seeing the data.
  pass: {
    taskSuccessRate: '>= 0.8',      // 4 of 5 participants unassisted
    medianTimeOnTask: '<= 90s',
    assistanceRequests: '<= 1',
    severity4Findings: 0
  },
  participants: {
    n: 6,
    screen: [
      { id: 'P1', domainExpert: true,  productNovice: true,  edge: false },
      { id: 'P2', domainExpert: true,  productNovice: true,  edge: false },
      { id: 'P3', domainExpert: false, productNovice: true,  edge: false },
      { id: 'P4', domainExpert: false, productNovice: true,  edge: false },
      { id: 'P5', domainExpert: true,  productNovice: false, edge: false }, // regression check
      { id: 'P6', domainExpert: false, productNovice: true,  edge: true  }  // oldest, slowest net
    ]
  },
  tasks: [
    { id: 'T1', goal: 'Find last month's hosting invoice and download it',
      success: 'A PDF of the correct invoice is on disk',
      seed: 'Account with 14 months of invoices' },
    { id: 'T2', goal: 'Change the billing email on the account',
      success: 'Confirmation shown and new address persisted after reload',
      seed: 'Account with a verified billing contact' }
  ],
  protocol: {
    intro: 5, warmup: 8, tasks: 50, debrief: 10, total: 75,
    thinkAloud: true,
    forbiddenPrompts: ['Do you want to click Export?',
                       'That is the right button, right?',
                       'Most users do it that way.'],
    neutralPrompts: ['What are you thinking?',
                     'What would you try next?',
                     'What do you expect to happen?']
  },
  findings: [
    // severity x frequency, ranked
    { obs: 'Export button hidden in overflow menu on 1280px',
      tasks: 'T1', participants: 5, severity: 4, frequency: 5, score: 20,
      action: 'Move export to the toolbar primary slot' },
    { obs: 'Invoice list has no sort; users scroll to find March',
      tasks: 'T1', participants: 3, severity: 3, frequency: 3, score: 9,
      action: 'Default sort newest-first, add column headers as buttons' }
  ]
};
// Ranked order is the only order the team reads. Score = severity * frequency.

The 5-user rule. Nielsen’s heuristic is that five users will reveal roughly 65–75% of a user interface’s usability problems, and another five will raise coverage to around 85%. It is a planning heuristic, not a law, and it has limits that matter. It applies to a single, stable design tested against a homogeneous population; it does not apply to zero-findings claims, to comparing designs where the difference of interest affects fewer than one user in five, or to safety-critical or accessibility work. Accessibility conformance is verified by testing every user, not by sampling users — a screen-reader user is not a 1-in-20 segment to be discovered statistically.

// Session-type selection — pick by the question, not by the budget.

SESSION TYPE      N        DURATION   ANSWERS                    DOES NOT ANSWER
----------------  ------  ---------  -------------------------  -----------------
Formative, feature 5       60-90 min  Where does this break?    Whether the feature
                                                        is wanted at all
Formative, whole  8-12     2 sessions Which tasks fail, how    Anything below the
                often                    surface of each task
Comparative A/B   10-20    90 min     Which variant performs     Why; needs a
               per variant             better                   follow-up interview
Accessibility     2-3 exp  Half day   Keyboard, screen-reader,   Whether it meets
  walkthrough     + 2-4 AT            zoom paths                WCAG — that needs a
                                                           criterion audit
Summative         300+     Weeks      Task success at scale,     Why users struggled
  benchmark                             comparable over time

CADENCE: per feature · quarterly · per contested decision ·
         every release · once or twice a year respectively.

Ask about yesterday, not tomorrow. A closing question worth using: "Think of the last time you did this task with your current tool — walk me through it." Past behaviour produces far better design signal than hypothetical intent, and it exposes the workarounds people have invented, which are the cheapest usability findings you will ever get.

Do not run a test to approve a decision already made. This is the most common misuse. If the finding that matters cannot change the roadmap, the session is theatre and participants will sense it. Write the pass criteria into the plan before recruiting, and hold the team to the result even when it is inconvenient.

6.4 Information architecture

Information architecture decides what the product calls things and how they nest, and it is the layer where terminology decisions get expensive because they leak into code, URLs, analytics events and support scripts.

IA has three separable components: the organisation system (how content is divided — subject, task, audience, geography, or time), the labelling system (what things are called), and the navigation system (how a person moves between them). They fail independently and are usually fixed independently. An organisation that is chronological is fine for an event log and useless for a reference library; a label that says "Workspace" in the UI and "Project" in the API costs a translation layer forever.

Start from a content inventory and a task analysis, in that order of confidence. The inventory lists every distinct thing the product holds with the fields that describe it; the task analysis lists what people are actually trying to accomplish, phrased as verbs. If the object model and the verb model disagree — you have "Documents" and people say "find the spec" — the disagreement is a design finding, not a wording problem.

Two empirical techniques settle IA questions faster than argument. Open card sorting asks participants to sort candidate labels into groups of their own creation and name the groups; it yields the user’s own taxonomy. Closed card sorting offers a fixed set of groups and measures agreement with a fit statistic such as agreement, average matching, or a simple percentage — use it to compare a proposed structure against an incumbent. Tree testing removes the visual layer entirely by presenting the sitemap as a nested list and asking where a participant would look for X; a tree test can find a broken hierarchy using plain HTML with no design work at all, which is why it belongs so early. A reasonable starting target is a direct-hit rate of ≥ 60% and a first-click accuracy of ≥ 70% on the top-level structure; below those figures the labels, not the layout, are usually the problem.

User flows must include the states that are not the happy path. A flow diagram that ends at "success" is a diagram of a demo. Every flow needs explicit branches for validation failure, permission denial, network loss mid-transaction, duplicate submission, and the partial-success case where a bulk operation completed on 900 of 1,000 items. Drawing these forces the engineering estimate, because the partial case is where the cost lives.

<!-- User flow, exhaustive. Rendered as text for review, not as a diagram. -->
FLOW  Checkout (guest, single item)

  [cart]
    ├─ valid ──────────────> [address form]
    │                          ├─ invalid ──> [address form]   ✗ 0
    │                          │              shows 2 inline errors,
    │                          │              focus to first, aria-describedby set
    │                          ├─ address blocked ──> [address form] ✗ 1
    │                          │              "Not serviceable at this address"
    │                          └─ valid ─────> [payment]
    │                                          ├─ card declined ──> [payment] ✗ 2
    │                                          │                  inline, code preserved
    │                                          │                  3 retries then switch provider
    │                                          ├─ gateway timeout ─> [payment pending] ✗ 3
    │                                          │                  DO NOT retry automatically
    │                                          │                  poll for 30s, then offer resume
    │                                          └─ authorised ───> [receipt]
    │                                                             ├─ 2xx ──> [confirmation] ✓
    │                                                             └─ webhook lost ─> [pending] ✗ 4
    │                          show order as "Processing" for up to 24h
    ├─ empty ─────────────> [empty cart]  "Your cart is empty." + [Browse] ✓
    └─ item no longer in stock ─> [cart, adjusted] ✗ 5
                             preserve the rest of the cart, mark the line, require
                             explicit confirmation before proceeding

The naming discipline that follows from IA is a vocabulary register: one table of every user-visible term, its singular and plural, its permitted synonyms, the code identifier it maps to, and the analytics event it maps to. It is unglamorous and it is the single most effective defence against the three-way naming drift that makes analytics untrustworthy two years after launch.

| UI label (en-GB) | Plural | Synonyms (use) | Synonyms (ban) | API field     | Analytics event    |
|------------------|--------|----------------|-----------------|-------------|--------------------|
| Invoice          | Invoices| bill, statement  | receipt          | invoice_id   | invoice.viewed     |
| Workspace        | Workspaces| project, team   | org, tenant      | workspace_id | workspace.created |
| Member           | Members| user, teammate  | employee, contact | member_id  | member.invited    |
| Subscription     | Subscriptions | plan, licence | seat, tier    | subscription_id | sub.updated  |

Test the labels before the layout. A five-minute unmoderated test that shows only the navigation labels and asks "where would you look for the billing history?" costs almost nothing and regularly reveals that your primary noun is not a word your users use. This is the highest ratio of finding to cost in interface design.

Two navigation models at once. Hierarchical navigation with a left rail, plus a global search, plus a command palette, plus breadcrumb trails, is three competing answers to "where am I". Pick one primary model per surface. Anything else is progressive disclosure for expert users, and must be visually and semantically subordinate — which is exactly the property that is lost the moment four navigation affordances are given equal weight.

6.5 Accessibility as an upstream constraint

Accessibility that begins as a pre-launch audit is remediation; accessibility that begins as a design constraint is a design input. The technical criteria are knowable in advance, which means there is never an excuse for discovering them late.

The governing standard is WCAG 2.2, Level AA, which adds to 2.1 the criteria 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum). The 2.5.8 criterion sets a minimum target size of 24×24 CSS pixels with exceptions for spacing, inline links, and cases where a larger equivalent control exists — but note that 24 is a floor for conformance, not a design target. Use 44×44 CSS pixels (or 44 points on a desktop track where points and pixels diverge under display scaling) as the design minimum for anything touch- or click-driven, with adequate spacing so adjacent targets do not crowd.

The contrast requirements are non-negotiable and should be expressed as design tokens, not as a QA finding: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18.66 px bold or 24 px regular and above), and 3:1 against adjacent colours for the boundaries of user-interface components and graphical objects. Non-text contrast is the one most often missed: a 1px border that defines an input must itself meet 3:1 against its background, or the input has no perceivable boundary to a low-vision user.

Semantic HTML is the whole strategy. A <button> is focusable, operable by keyboard, announced as a button, and activated by both Enter and Space with no code. A <div onclick> is none of those things and must be made all of them manually, usually incompletely. Element choice precedes ARIA, and the first rule of ARIA is not to use ARIA: an element that already has the semantics you need needs no role, no tabindex, and no key handler.

Four mechanisms carry most of the remaining work. Focus order must follow the visual and logical order, must be visible at all times via a focus indicator meeting 3:1 against adjacent colours, and must never trap a keyboard user except inside a modal, which must then restore focus to its opener on close. Live regions — role="status" for polite updates such as "12 results", role="alert" for assertive interruptions such as "Payment failed" — are the only way non-visual users learn that something happened without a page load. Names and roles come from accessible names computed from content, aria-label, or aria-labelledby, in that order of preference. Keyboard-only operation is the cheapest proxy test available: unplug the mouse, and complete every task. If a control is unreachable, invisible, or inert, that is the finding.

/* Accessibility is a constraint on the design token set, not a later audit. */
:root {
  /* 4.5:1 on --surface-1 · 3:1 for large text and UI boundaries */
  --fg-on-surface-1:        #16181d;   /* 16.9:1 */
  --fg-on-surface-1-muted:  #4a4f5a;   /* 8.1:1  still AA at any size */
  --fg-on-surface-1-subtle: #6b7078;   /* 4.6:1  AA — floor, not comfort */

  /* Non-text: 3:1 against the surface it sits on */
  --border-subtle:   #c3c7ce;  /* 1.7:1 — decorative only, never a control edge */
  --border-control:  #8a9099;  /* 3.1:1  minimum for input boundaries */
  --focus-ring:      #1a5fd0;  /* 3.2:1 on --surface-1 and --surface-2 */

  /* Status colours are always paired with a shape and a word */
  --danger:          #b3261e;
  --danger-surface:  #fdecea;
  --danger-fg:       #8c1d18;   /* 7.4:1 */
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --fg-on-surface-1:        #e9ebef;  /* 14.2:1 */
    --fg-on-surface-1-muted:  #a7adb8;  /* 8.4:1  */
    --fg-on-surface-1-subtle: #8b929d;  /* 5.6:1  */
    --border-control:         #6f7681;  /* 3.2:1  */
    --focus-ring:             #7fb0ff;  /* 5.8:1  */
    --danger-fg:              #ffb4ab;  /* 8.9:1  */
  }
}

/* Focus is never removed, only restyled. */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
  border-radius: 2px;
}

/* Motion is decorative; honour the user. */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

/* Text-only alternative to any 3:1 non-text indicator. */
.sr-only {
  position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px;
  padding: 0; margin: -1px; overflow: hidden;
  clip-path: inset(50%); white-space: nowrap; border: 0;
}

/* Touch target: 44x44 minimum, enforced by the component, not by discipline. */
.icon-btn {
  inline-size: 44px; block-size: 44px;
  display: inline-grid; place-items: center;
  min-inline-size: 44px; min-block-size: 44px;
  padding: 0; border: 0; background: none; cursor: pointer;
}
.icon-btn > svg { inline-size: 20px; block-size: 20px; }
WCAG 2.2 criterionLevelWhat it demands in designCheapest test
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)AA4.5:1 text · 3:1 large textToken audit, once, then CI
1.4.11 Non-text ContrastAA3:1 on control boundaries, icons, focusGreyscale screenshot review
2.4.7 Focus VisibleAAVisible focus on every interactive elementTab through the screen
2.4.11 Focus Not ObscuredAASticky headers must not cover focused itemsTab at 320px and 400% zoom
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)AA24×24 CSS px, design at 44×44Measure the smallest target
3.3.7 Redundant EntryANever re-ask for information already givenWalk the longest form
3.3.8 Accessible AuthenticationAANo cognitive function test, no forced transcriptionTry to log in without a mouse
1.4.4 Resize TextAA200% zoom without loss of contentZoom to 200% at 1280px

The screen-reader smoke test. Once per design review, not once per release: put on a screen reader, load the primary screen, and attempt one task using only the accessibility tree. Ninety seconds of this catches more real problems than an hour of automated scanning, because it exercises the announcement order, the accessible names, and the live regions that automated tools cannot judge. Target pairing — VoiceOver or NVDA on Windows, and on the desktop track verify the same on both platforms — should be explicit.

Colour is never the only signal. A red field border with no text and no icon fails 1.4.1 Use of Colour even at perfect contrast, and it fails for roughly 1 in 12 men with a deuteranopia or protanopia. Every status, every diff, every severity and every chart series must be distinguishable by at least one redundant channel: text, shape, position, pattern, or weight. This is a design decision made in the component, not a fix applied by an auditor afterwards.

6.6 Design-to-engineering handoff

Handoff is a contract negotiation, and the artefacts that survive it are machine-readable specifications rather than annotated images. Design tokens are the spine of that contract because they make the design system executable.

The historical handoff artefact — a 300 px-wide PNG of a screen with red annotation arrows and comments attached in a proprietary tool — has a structural problem: it is a picture, so it is ambiguous at exactly the points where precision matters. It cannot express a state machine, a responsive rule, a focus order, or the difference between a token and a one-off value. It also describes a single moment, so every state other than that moment is unspecified.

The modern handoff is a set of complementary artefacts, and it is worth naming each one precisely. Annotated component specs state anatomy, permitted states, and which properties are token-driven versus fixed. State tables enumerate every state and its transitions. Redlines give exact measurements in the same coordinate system as the implementation. Interaction specifications define trigger, preconditions, behaviour, duration, and the accessibility announcement. Content specifications give real copy at real lengths, with truncation and wrapping behaviour. Prototype links give a working reference for feel. And tokens give the shared vocabulary.

Design tokens are named, decision-carrying values in three layers: primitives (the raw palette — blue-600), semantic (role — color-action-primary), and component (a specific override — button-primary-bg). The semantic layer is the one that makes theming possible: a dark theme, a high-contrast theme, a tenant-branded theme, or a dense-data variant all re-point semantic tokens and leave components untouched. A component-token layer should be used sparingly; each one is a place where the system stops being consistent.

Deliver tokens in a format that is both human-reviewable and machine-consumable. JSON or DTCG (Design Tokens Community Group) JSON is the interchange format; Style Dictionary or Tokens Studio compiles it to CSS custom properties, TypeScript constants, iOS and Android resources, and documentation. A hand-maintained parallel pair of JSON and CSS files will drift; a generated pair will not.

// tokens/core.json — DTCG format. Primitives only, no meaning attached.
{
  "color": {
    "blue": {
      "50":  { "$type": "color", "$value": "#eef4ff" },
      "600": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#1a5fd0" },
      "700": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#174ea6" }
    },
    "neutral": {
      "0":   { "$type": "color", "$value": "#ffffff" },
      "100": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#f4f5f7" },
      "400": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#8a9099" },
      "900": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#16181d" }
    },
    "red":   { "700": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#8c1d18" } },
    "green": { "700": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#1a6b3c" } },
    "amber": { "700": { "$type": "color", "$value": "#8a5300" } }
  },
  "space": {
    "0": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "0px" },
    "1": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "4px" },
    "2": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "8px" },
    "3": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "12px" },
    "4": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "16px" },
    "6": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "24px" },
    "8": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "32px" },
    "12":{ "$type": "dimension", "$value": "48px" }
  },
  "font": {
    "family": {
      "sans": { "$type": "fontFamily", "$value": ["Inter", "system-ui", "sans-serif"] },
      "mono": { "$type": "fontFamily", "$value": ["JetBrains Mono", "ui-monospace", "monospace"] }
    }
  }
}

The contract is only useful if it is enforced. The realistic outcome of a handoff is that engineering implements approximately 70% of the spec, and the remaining 30% is either deliberately deviated from or quietly lost. The mitigations are unglamorous: automated visual regression against the reference designs, component-level contract tests, and a single named owner for each component who reviews deviations. A design system without a named owner degrades within two quarters.

// Handoff artefact selection — what each one is entitled to specify.

ARTEFACT                  SPECIFIES                  MACHINE-CHECKABLE   COST
------------------------- -------------------------- ------------------  ------
Annotated static image    Visual intent, mood        no                make: low
                                                                    trust: high
Redline, exact measures   Geometry, spacing          yes, visual        medium
                                                  regression
State table               Every state, transition    partly, storybook  medium
Interaction spec          Trigger, timing,           partly,            medium
                          announcement               interaction tests
Token set (DTCG JSON)     The shared vocabulary      yes, in CI         low once
                                                                    generated
Coded component           Everything, exactly        yes                high up
  (living spec)                                                    front

SKIP ONE AND YOU GET: ambiguity and no unspecified states (image);
  guessed values in production (no redline); unstyled edge states at 3am
  (no state table); keyboard and AT breakage (no interaction spec);
  one-off hex values everywhere (no tokens); permanent divergence between
  design and build (no coded component).

Design in the real medium. If the shipping target is a desktop application, design the window at its minimum supported size from the first mock-up, not at a browser width. Real users maximise, resize, dock to a 13-inch display, run at 150% display scaling, and use a 1024×640 window. A design that only exists at 1440×900 in a 1× editor is a design that has not met its own product.

The annotation that says "use existing component". This is where most accessibility defects enter a codebase: a design that specifies a custom control because the existing library’s default styling did not match the mock-up. The correction is procedural — style the existing component from its tokens before proposing a new one, and require a written justification naming what the existing component cannot do. Custom controls are permanent maintenance liabilities: focus handling, keyboard bindings, ARIA, and platform text behaviours must all be implemented by hand.

Exercises 6

  1. Produce an artefact-per-question matrix for one feature of your product — at least eight user questions. For each, name the artefact you will build, the fidelity rung, the estimated hours, and the decision it is entitled to settle. Then find three questions in the list that you would otherwise have answered with a coded prototype and replace those prototypes with something cheaper; state the savings in hours and the loss of evidence you accept.
  2. Draw a complete state inventory for one screen: every data state (default, loading-skeleton, partial, empty, error, permission-denied, offline, over-quota), every input state (pristine, valid, invalid, validating, submitting), and every overlay state. Produce 18–25 ASCII or block wireframes, one per state, and mark the three states the current production build handles incorrectly. Deliverable: a state table with, for each state, the entry trigger, the announcement for assistive technology, and the recovery action.
  3. Write and run a five-participant formative test of a single task. Produce: three task scripts in the participant’s language with objective success criteria; a pass threshold fixed in advance; a moderator script containing only neutral prompts; a findings log capturing hesitation, backtrack and assistance for every participant; and a severity × frequency ranking. Deliverable: a ranked list where the top three items are each traceable to a named observation with a participant count.
  4. Run an open card sort on 25 candidate navigation labels from your product with at least eight participants, then a tree test on the resulting structure asking participants to locate five specific items. Deliverable: the label set, a similarity matrix or dendrogram, the first-level grouping that emerges, and a revised navigation tree with a written justification for each change — including any label you decided to keep despite the data, and why.
  5. Perform a full keyboard-only and screen-reader pass on the three highest-traffic screens of your product, then a WCAG 2.2 AA self-audit of those screens against at least eight named criteria. Deliverable: a defect list with severity, the criterion each defect fails, a manual reproduction path, and a proposed fix for each — plus a written decision on which defects block release and which are accepted with justification.

7 · Visual Design: Typography, Colour, Spacing, Motion and Responsive Strategy

7.1 Visual hierarchy7.2 Typography and the type scale7.3 Colour systems7.4 Spacing, density and tokens7.5 Motion7.6 Responsive strategy

Visual design is the conversion of an information hierarchy into a perceptual one, and it succeeds when the first glance produces the intended reading order without the reader being told what to look at. This section works from that hierarchy through type, colour, spacing, motion, and responsive strategy, and it treats each as a tokenised system rather than a set of individual decisions. Two arguments run through it. First, constraints beat taste: a scale, a grid, and a token set make a hundred screens consistent for free, whereas manual judgement does not scale past the first month. Second, the web track and the desktop track need different responsive models, because a browser viewport is a property of the user’s intent whereas a desktop window is a property of the user’s manipulation. Chasing "responsive" as if the two were the same is a category error that costs a redesign in both tracks.

7.1 Visual hierarchy

Visual hierarchy is the set of cues that determine where the eye goes first, and a screen without an intentional hierarchy has one imposed by accident — usually by whatever is largest or most saturated.

The eye reads a screen in a predictable order: top-left first, then top-right, then a downward sweep in the dominant reading direction. Within a region, attention is captured first by the largest element, then by the highest contrast against its background, then by the most saturated colour, then by the sharpest edge, then by the only element in a position that is not otherwise occupied. This is not a metaphor; it is the practical reason that a 28 px bold heading in a 16 px field set reads as more important than a 40 px pale grey label, and it is why increasing the size of everything by a fixed ratio produces a screen where nothing is important.

Hierarchy is built from a deliberately small number of levels — five or six is more than a screen can carry. Each level should be distinguishable along at least two of the following channels simultaneously, so that no single channel’s failure collapses the structure: size, weight, colour contrast, vertical space, container or rule, alignment, and case or letter-spacing. Space is the most under-used channel and the cheapest: a heading separated from its body by 24 px and its body separated from the next block by 8 px is unambiguously grouped, regardless of colour or size.

Layout grids supply the structural channel. The 12-column grid at a maximum content width of 1200–1320 px with 24 px gutters remains the default because it divides by 2, 3, 4 and 6, which covers almost every real layout. Optical alignment — the deliberate small corrections that make a shape look aligned when it mathematically is not — matters most for circles, rounded corners and icons, which appear to overshoot their bounding boxes.

/* Hierarchy by construction: a card, five levels, no hard-coded one-offs. */
.card {
  display: grid;
  gap: var(--space-2);                 /*  8px — internal rhythm            */
  padding: var(--space-4);              /* 16px — container inset           */
  background: var(--surface-1);
  border: 1px solid var(--border-subtle);
  border-radius: var(--radius-2);       /*  8px                              */
  box-shadow: var(--elevation-1);
}

.card__eyebrow {                        /* L1  micro-label, wide tracking      */
  font: var(--text-2xs);
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  color: var(--fg-on-surface-1-subtle);
}

.card__title {                          /* L2  the only strong element        */
  font: var(--text-xl);
  color: var(--fg-on-surface-1);
  text-wrap: balance;                   /* even rag, no orphan words          */
}

.card__body {                           /* L3  body, high contrast, no bold   */
  font: var(--text-md);
  color: var(--fg-on-surface-1-muted);
  text-wrap: pretty;
}

.card__meta {                           /* L4  supporting data, one level down */
  font: var(--text-sm);
  color: var(--fg-on-surface-1-subtle);
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;    /* columns of numbers must align     */
}

.card__action {                         /* L5  affordance: shape, not colour */
  align-self: start;
  margin-block-start: var(--space-2);
  min-block-size: 44px;                 /* target size, not decoration       */
  padding-inline: var(--space-4);
  font: var(--text-md);
  font-weight: 600;
  border-radius: var(--radius-1);
  background: var(--action-primary-bg);
  color: var(--action-primary-fg);
}

Three rules of restraint keep hierarchy intact across a large surface. Cap the number of accent colours per screen to one; accents are punctuation, and a screen with seven of them has no punctuation. Reserve the highest-emphasis treatment for the single most important action, and if a screen argues for two, the screen has two primary actions and one of them should be demoted. And keep the reading order the same as the DOM order — a visual order that contradicts the DOM order is both an accessibility failure under 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence and a maintenance trap.

Test hierarchy by degradation. Squint at the screen, or view it at 25% zoom, or convert it to greyscale. If the intended reading order survives, the hierarchy is carried by size, weight and space, and it will survive a bright sun, a cheap monitor, a colour-blind user, and a monochrome print. If it collapses, the hierarchy was being carried by colour alone.

Depth is not emphasis. Every extra shadow, border and gradient adds a level of visual difference without adding meaning, and after four or five levels the surface becomes noise that the eye reads as "important" everywhere. Express elevation through surface colour and a single shadow token per level, and reserve raised surfaces for genuinely floating things — dialogs, popovers, dragged items, sticky headers.

7.2 Typography and the type scale
