Type is the primary carrier of hierarchy and the primary carrier of readability, and a modular scale with declared line heights and measure limits solves most of typography before any individual choice is made.

Start from a base size and a ratio. A base of 16 px remains the correct default for both tracks — it is the browser default, it survives user font-size preferences, and on desktop it maps cleanly to 12 pt at 96 DPI while remaining legible at high display scaling. Use 1.200 (minor third) for dense application UI, where the number of steps you need is small and the range is narrow, and 1.250 for content-rich products that need a stronger editorial voice. Ratios above 1.333 produce steps too large to mix on a single screen; ratios below 1.125 produce steps too close to distinguish. The defensible band is 1.200–1.500, and the discipline is to use named steps, never computed ones.

Line height must be set per step, not globally: large text needs proportionally less leading than small text, because a small glyph with generous leading reads as disconnected and a large glyph with tight leading reads as cramped. Body text at 1.5 to 1.6, headings at 1.1 to 1.25, and dense UI labels at 1.35 to 1.45 is a workable ladder. The measure — line length — is the other half of readability: aim for 60–75 characters per line for continuous prose, 45–75 for most UI, and accept wider only for tables and code. If the container allows more than 90 characters, insert a measure constraint on the text block itself, not on the layout.

Weight and size are not independent channels at small sizes. Below about 14 px, weight 400 and 600 become hard to distinguish on a low-quality display, so use colour and spacing to carry emphasis instead of weight. Above 24 px, weight differences are over-amplified and the heavier weight looks clumsy — drop to 600 and let size do the work. Tabular numerals for any column of figures, and proportional for running text. Sentence case for all UI text; title case is a marketing convention, not an interface convention, and its inconsistent application is a visible quality signal.

/* Type scale — 1.250 major-ish scale, base 16px, declared line heights.
   Fluid between 360px and 1280px viewport with clamp(); capped below. */
:root {
  --font-sans: "Inter", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
  --font-mono: "JetBrains Mono", ui-monospace, "Cascadia Code", monospace;

  --step--1: clamp(0.800rem, 0.760rem + 0.190vw, 0.889rem);  /* 12.8 → 14.2 */
  --step-0:  clamp(0.938rem, 0.900rem + 0.190vw, 1.000rem);  /* 15.0 → 16.0 */
  --step-1:  calc(var(--step-0) * 1.250);                     /* 18.8 → 20.0 */
  --step-2:  calc(var(--step-0) * 1.563);                     /* 23.4 → 25.0 */
  --step-3:  calc(var(--step-0) * 1.953);                     /* 29.3 → 31.3 */
  --step-4:  calc(var(--step-0) * 2.441);                     /* 36.6 → 39.1 */

  /* Semantic roles with their own leading, not a single global line-height */
  --text-2xs: 500 var(--step--1) / 1.45 var(--font-sans);
  --text-xs:  500 var(--step--1) / 1.45 var(--font-sans);
  --text-sm:  500 var(--step-0)  / 1.40 var(--font-sans);
  --text-md:  400 var(--step-0)  / 1.55 var(--font-sans);   /* body            */
  --text-lg:  400 var(--step-1)  / 1.45 var(--font-sans);
  --text-xl:  600 var(--step-2)  / 1.25 var(--font-sans);   /* card title      */
  --text-2xl: 600 var(--step-3)  / 1.18 var(--font-sans);   /* page title      */
  --text-3xl: 600 var(--step-4)  / 1.10 var(--font-sans);   /* rare, one per screen */
  --text-mono: 400 var(--step--1) / 1.6 var(--font-mono);

  --measure: 68ch;      /* ~68 characters, the readability ceiling        */
  --measure-tight: 46ch; /* for dense UI and list descriptions            */
}

/* A page must opt in to its measure. Layout width and text width are
   different problems, and conflating them is how 120-character lines ship. */
.prose { max-inline-size: var(--measure); }
.prose > * + * { margin-block-start: var(--space-4); }
.prose h2 { font: var(--text-2xl); margin-block-start: var(--space-8); }
.prose h3 { font: var(--text-xl);  margin-block-start: var(--space-6); }
.prose ul { padding-inline-start: var(--space-4); }

/* Long unbroken strings must not break layout or overflow a panel. */
.wrap-anywhere { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }
.truncate      { overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap; }
.line-clamp-2  { display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 2;
                 -webkit-box-orient: vertical; overflow: hidden; }
// The type scale, tabulated for review. The CSS above is canonical.

// STEP    SIZE 360 to 1280px   ROLE                          WT  LH   MEASURE
// ------  -------------------  ----------------------------  ---  ---  ---------
step--1  12.8 to 14.2 px       meta, labels, badges,         500 1.45 ~90ch dense
                               table headers
step-0   15.0 to 16.0 px       body, default UI              400 1.55 68ch
step-1   18.8 to 20.0 px       lead paragraph, large         400 1.45 62ch
                               control label
step-2   23.4 to 25.0 px       card title, section heading   600 1.25 46ch
step-3   29.3 to 31.3 px       page title                    600 1.18 40ch
step-4   36.6 to 39.1 px       empty-state hero,             600 1.10 32ch
                               one per screen

// RULES
//  - every margin is a --space-* token, never an arbitrary number
//  - body prose is capped at --measure (68ch) regardless of layout width
//  - tabular-nums on any column of figures, proportional on running text
//  - sentence case everywhere; title case is a marketing convention
//  - layout in rem; no px height on any text container

Specify copy, not placeholders. Design every screen with real sentences at realistic length, including the longest translation. German runs roughly 30% longer than English and compounds to 50% in some locales; Finnish is longer still. A layout that only survives "Lorem ipsum" will need reworking in every language you add, and the rework always lands after a release date.

Users change their font size. Browser zoom, OS text scaling, and minimum-font-size settings all change the effective size of your type, and WCAG 1.4.4 requires the design to survive 200% text zoom without loss of content or function. Layout in rem rather than px for anything typographic, never set a height in px on a text container, and test at 200% and at 400% browser zoom on a 1280px window. A design that fails at 200% fails for a real and growing population of users.

7.3 Colour systems

Colour is the most abused channel in interface design, and the fix is structural: separate raw palette from meaning, make meaning themeable, and enforce contrast in the token layer rather than auditing it later.

Build colour in two layers. Primitive tokens are the raw palette with no semantic content — blue-600, neutral-100, red-700. Semantic tokens carry meaning and are the only layer a component may reference — fg-on-surface-1, action-primary-bg, danger-border, focus-ring. Components that reference primitives break the moment a theme changes, which is why color: var(--blue-600) in a component is a defect, not a style choice. The same three-layer idea appears in section 6.6 and is what makes the theme, the density variant, and a tenant brand all a token swap rather than a redesign.

The dual-theme model is not an inversion: a dark theme ≠ a programmatically lightened light theme, and the two must be authored separately. A dark theme is a separate set of semantic token values, checked on its own surface values, and hues are re-specified rather than transformed — a neutral of hue 0°, saturation 0% is a useful axis, and a blue of hue 210°, saturation 65% should become hue 212°, saturation 45% on a dark surface, not the same pair. Deep surfaces must not be pure black (pure black against pure white text produces halation on OLED and a harsh edge that is uncomfortable over a long session); a near-black such as #0f1115 with elevated surfaces stepping upward by roughly 3–5% lightness each level reads better. Saturation must be reduced in dark themes because a saturated colour on a dark background appears brighter and more intense than the same colour on white. Every semantic token needs a defined value in both themes, and the token set should fail a build if a semantic token is undefined in either theme.

Three constraints govern the palette. Contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text, 3:1 for the boundaries of UI components and meaningful graphics — enforce all three in the token layer and verify by script in CI, not by eye. Colour-vision deficiency: roughly 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have a red-green deficiency, and around 4% of the population has some form of colour-vision deficiency, so a palette that encodes meaning in hue alone excludes a meaningful minority. Simulate deuteranopia, protanopia, tritanopia and achromatopsia on every chart and every status indicator. And the never-only-hue rule: colour must never be the sole carrier of meaning, per WCAG 1.4.1 — pair every status colour with an icon, a word, or a position.

/* Colour tokens — semantic layer, both themes defined, no primitive leaks. */
:root {
  /* primitives exist but are not referenced by components */
  --blue-600: #1a5fd0;  --blue-700: #174ea6;  --blue-050: #eef4ff;
  --red-700:  #8c1d18;  --red-050:  #fdecea;  --red-300: #f2b8b5;
  --amber-700:#8a5300;  --amber-050:#fff6e6;  --amber-300:#f3d19e;
  --green-700:#1a6b3c;  --green-050:#e8f5ee;  --green-300:#a8d9bd;
  --neutral-0:#ffffff;   --neutral-100:#f4f5f7;  --neutral-200:#e6e8ec;
  --neutral-300:#d4d7dd;  --neutral-400:#8a9099;  --neutral-600:#4a4f5a;
  --neutral-900:#16181d; --neutral-950:#0f1115;

  /* semantic — light theme. Contrast annotated against its own surface. */
  --surface-0: var(--neutral-0);            /* app background   */
  --surface-1: var(--neutral-0);            /* cards            */
  --surface-2: var(--neutral-100);          /* inset, table zebra */
  --surface-overlay: var(--neutral-0);

  --fg-on-surface-1:        #16181d;       /* 16.9:1 */
  --fg-on-surface-1-muted:  #4a4f5a;       /*  8.1:1 */
  --fg-on-surface-1-subtle: #6b7078;       /*  4.6:1 */

  --action-primary-bg: #1a5fd0;  --action-primary-fg: #ffffff;   /* 6.4:1 */
  --action-primary-bg-hover: var(--blue-700);
  --action-primary-bg-active: #123f86;
  --action-secondary-bg: transparent; --action-secondary-fg: #174ea6;
  --action-secondary-border: #8a9099;   /* 3.1:1 non-text */

  --danger-bg: var(--red-050); --danger-fg: var(--red-700);      /* 7.4:1 */
  --warn-bg:   var(--amber-050); --warn-fg: var(--amber-700);
  --success-bg:var(--green-050); --success-fg: var(--green-700);
  --info-bg:   var(--blue-050);  --info-fg:  var(--blue-700);

  --border-subtle: #c3c7ce;  /* decorative only */
  --border-control: #8a9099; /* 3:1 minimum for control edges */
  --focus-ring: #1a5fd0;      /* 3.2:1 on both light surfaces */
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --surface-0: var(--neutral-950);
    --surface-1: #171a20;     /* +4% lightness per level */
    --surface-2: #1f232b;
    --surface-overlay: #23272f;

    --fg-on-surface-1:        #e9ebef;      /* 14.2:1 */
    --fg-on-surface-1-muted:  #a7adb8;      /*  8.4:1 */
    --fg-on-surface-1-subtle: #8b929d;      /*  5.6:1 */

    /* desaturated: a saturated hue reads hotter on a dark surface */
    --action-primary-bg: #3d7ff0;  --action-primary-fg: #06111f;
    --action-primary-bg-hover: #5590f5;  --action-primary-bg-active: #2e6ed6;
    --action-secondary-fg: #8fb8ff;
    --action-secondary-border: #6f7681;   /* 3.2:1 */

    --danger-bg: #2b1614;  --danger-fg: #ffb4ab;   /* 8.9:1 */
    --warn-bg:   #2b2010;  --warn-fg:   #f5c37b;
    --success-bg:#10251a;  --success-fg:#8fd6ac;
    --info-bg:   #12203a;  --info-fg:   #9dc2ff;

    --border-control: #6f7681;
    --focus-ring: #7fb0ff;   /* 5.8:1 */
  }
}

/* Status is never hue-only: swatch + word + shape, in every theme. */
.badge {
  display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5ch;
  padding-inline: var(--space-2); padding-block: 2px;
  border-radius: 999px;
  font: var(--text-xs); font-weight: 600;
  border: 1px solid currentColor;
}
.badge[data-status="error"]   { color: var(--danger-fg);   background: var(--danger-bg); }
.badge[data-status="warning"] { color: var(--warn-fg);     background: var(--warn-bg);   }
.badge[data-status="ok"]      { color: var(--success-fg);  background: var(--success-bg);  }
// Contrast is verified by script, in CI, from the token file — not by eye.
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const tokens = JSON.parse(readFileSync('tokens/semantic.json', 'utf8'));
const rgb = (hex) => {
  const h = hex.replace('#', '');
  return [0, 2, 4].map((i) => parseInt(h.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255);
};
const lum = (hex) => rgb(hex)
  .map((c) => (c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4))
  .reduce((a, c, i) => a + c * [0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722][i], 0);
const ratio = (a, b) => {
  const [hi, lo] = [lum(a), lum(b)].sort((x, y) => y - x);
  return (hi + 0.05) / (lo + 0.05);
};

const surfaces = ['surface-0', 'surface-1', 'surface-2', 'surface-overlay'];
const fail = [];
for (const theme of ['light', 'dark']) {
  for (const [name, fg] of Object.entries(tokens[theme].fg)) {
    for (const s of surfaces) {
      const r = ratio(tokens[theme][fg], tokens[theme][s]);
      // 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text
      if (r < 4.5) fail.push({ theme, pair: `${fg} on ${s}`, r: r.toFixed(2) });
    }
  }
  // 3:1 non-text: control boundaries, focus ring, meaningful graphics
  for (const name of ['border-control', 'focus-ring', 'action-primary-bg']) {
    const r = ratio(tokens[theme][name], tokens[theme]['surface-1']);
    if (r < 3) fail.push({ theme, pair: `${name} non-text`, r: r.toFixed(2) });
  }
}
if (fail.length) {
  console.error('Contrast failures:\n' + fail.map((f) => JSON.stringify(f)).join('\n'));
  process.exit(1);              // fails the build
}
console.log('All token contrast pairs pass WCAG 2.2 AA.');

Verify with a script, once, in CI. Compute every documented foreground/background pair in the token file, report the ratio, and fail the build below threshold. This takes an hour to write and permanently removes the most common accessibility regression. Add a rendering test for the colour-vision deficiency simulations, because those are visual judgements that a ratio check cannot make.

Semantic tokens are a contract, and contracts leak. Once a component hard-codes #1a5fd0 for its own button because it "looked better", the theme is broken for that component only, which is the most expensive kind of breakage because it looks like a bug report rather than an architectural fault. Enforce it with lint — a rule that fails a build when a hex literal appears in a component stylesheet — and give every exception an explicit, dated token rather than an inline override.

7.4 Spacing, density and tokens

Spacing is the skeleton of the layout and the cheapest channel for hierarchy, and an 8-point grid with a named token set is what keeps forty screens looking like one product.

Adopt an 8-point base grid and express all spacing as multiples of it, with a 4 px half-step available for tight internal component padding where 8 is too coarse. The scale should be small and named for intent: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128. Beyond about 64 the values are page-level rhythm rather than component internals. The alternative — arbitrary values chosen per screen — is precisely the source of the 13 px gap beside a 15 px gap that makes a finished-looking product look unfinished, and it is unfixable after the fact at scale.

Separate three spacing concepts that are frequently conflated. Internal padding is space inside a container and should follow the density of its content: 8 px for chips, 12–16 px for cards, 24 px for panels. External gap is space between siblings and carries grouping: related items get less separation than unrelated ones, and the ratio that matters is roughly 1:2 — 8 px inside a group, 16 px between groups, a factor of ≈ 2 that is small enough to read as order and large enough to read as structure. Layout rhythm is space between page sections, in the 48–96 px range. Getting the internal/external ratio wrong is what makes an interface feel either cramped or adrift, and no amount of colour work fixes it.

Density is a first-class variant, not a preference to be hard-coded. Compact, default, and comfortable row heights — 28/32/40 px for data tables — cover most professional products, and the density choice should be a user setting that maps to spacing and type tokens only, never to component logic. Elevation completes the surface hierarchy: a small set of shadow tokens from 0 (flat) to 4 (modal), each defined per theme because shadows on a dark surface must be replaced by surface lightness rather than by blackening, since black on near-black is invisible.

/* Spacing, radius, elevation and density — the whole structural token set. */
:root {
  --space-0: 0px;   --space-1: 4px;   --space-2: 8px;   --space-3: 12px;
  --space-4: 16px;  --space-5: 24px;  --space-6: 32px;  --space-8: 48px;
  --space-10: 64px; --space-12: 96px; --space-16: 128px;

  --radius-0: 0px;  --radius-1: 4px;  --radius-2: 8px;
  --radius-3: 12px; --radius-pill: 999px;

  --elevation-0: none;
  --elevation-1: 0 1px 2px rgb(16 20 28 / 0.06), 0 1px 1px rgb(16 20 28 / 0.04);
  --elevation-2: 0 2px 4px rgb(16 20 28 / 0.08), 0 4px 12px rgb(16 20 28 / 0.06);
  --elevation-3: 0 8px 24px rgb(16 20 28 / 0.12);
  --elevation-4: 0 16px 48px rgb(16 20 28 / 0.20);

  --density-row: 40px;      /* overridden by [data-density] below */
}

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    /* on dark, elevation is expressed as surface lightness, not shadow */
    --elevation-1: 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / 0.06);
    --elevation-2: 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / 0.09), 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.4);
    --elevation-3: 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / 0.12), 0 8px 24px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5);
    --elevation-4: 0 0 0 1px rgb(255 255 255 / 0.16), 0 16px 48px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6);
  }
}

/* Density is a token swap, never a component fork. */
[data-density="compact"] {
  --density-row: 28px;
  --space-2: 6px;  --space-3: 10px; --space-4: 12px; --space-5: 18px;
}
[data-density="comfortable"] {
  --density-row: 48px;
  --space-2: 10px; --space-3: 16px; --space-4: 24px; --space-5: 32px;
}

/* 12-column grid, 24px gutters, 1200px maximum content width. */
.shell {
  --gutter: var(--space-5);
  --cols: 12;
  inline-size: 100%;
  max-inline-size: 1200px;
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding-inline: var(--space-4);
}
.shell__grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(var(--cols), minmax(0, 1fr));
  gap: var(--gutter);
}
.col-3  { grid-column: span 3;  }
.col-4  { grid-column: span 4;  }
.col-6  { grid-column: span 6;  }
.col-12 { grid-column: span 12; }

/* Vertical rhythm: every margin is a token, never an arbitrary number. */
.stack       { display: grid; gap: var(--space-4); }
.stack-tight { display: grid; gap: var(--space-2); }
.cluster     { display: flex; gap: var(--space-2); align-items: center;
               flex-wrap: wrap; }
Token formatHuman-editableMachine-consumableThemingMulti-platform outputVerdict
Hand-written CSS custom properties✓✓✓ via media query✗ Manual per platformFine for web-only, weak contract
DTCG / W3C JSON✓✓✓✗ Needs a build✓ Best interchange format
Style Dictionary source✓✓✓✓ Generated✓ Best build-time pipeline
Figma Variables + Tokens Studio✓✓✓✓ Exported✓ Keep design and code in sync
TypeScript constantsMedium✓✗ Runtime objects✓Supplementary only, not canonical
 
// One canonical source, one build, six outputs. Never six hand-maintained copies.
// style-dictionary.config.mjs
import StyleDictionary from 'style-dictionary';

const themes = {
  // A theme is a value map keyed by token name, applied over the base.
  light: {
    'color.surface-1':            { value: '#ffffff' },
    'color.fg.on-surface-1':      { value: '#16181d' },
    'color.action.primary.bg':    { value: '#1a5fd0' }
  },
  dark: {
    'color.surface-1':            { value: '#171a20' },
    'color.fg.on-surface-1':      { value: '#e9ebef' },
    'color.action.primary.bg':    { value: '#3d7ff0' }
  }
};

const sd = new StyleDictionary({
  source: ['tokens/core.json', 'tokens/semantic.json'],
  platforms: [
    { transformGroup: 'css', buildPath: 'build/css/', files: [
      { destination: 'tokens.css', format: 'css/variables',
        options: { outputReferences: true } }          // keep var() references
    ]},
    { transformGroup: 'ts', buildPath: 'build/ts/', files: [
      // Typed constants: the compiler rejects a misspelled token at build time.
      { destination: 'tokens.d.ts',
        format: 'typescript/declarations',
        options: { outputReferences: false } }
    ]},
    { transformGroup: 'android', buildPath: 'build/android/', files: [
      { destination: 'colors.xml', format: 'android/resources' }
    ]},
    { transformGroup: 'ios', buildPath: 'build/ios/', files: [
      { destination: 'Tokens.h', format: 'ios/macros' }
    ]},
    { transformGroup: 'sass', buildPath: 'build/scss/', files: [
      { destination: '_tokens.scss', format: 'scss/variables' }
    ]},
    { transformGroup: 'html', buildPath: 'build/docs/', files: [
      // Rendered documentation: every swatch with its computed contrast ratio,
      // so the docs can never drift from the tokens they describe.
      { destination: 'tokens.html', format: 'html/documentation' }
    ]}
  ]
});

await sd.cleanAllPlatforms();
await sd.buildAllPlatforms();

// Semantic theme values are emitted as [data-theme] attribute maps, so the
// OS default and a user override resolve to the same generated block.
for (const [name, map] of Object.entries(themes)) {
  const rules = Object.entries(map)
    .map(([k, v]) => `  --${k.replace(/\./g, '-')}: ${v.value};`)
    .join('\n');
  await writeTheme(name, rules);
}

Generate, do not duplicate. One canonical token source, one build step that emits CSS custom properties, TypeScript types, Android XML, iOS asset catalogue entries, and a documentation page with rendered swatches and computed contrast ratios. Six hand-maintained copies of a palette will diverge within a quarter, and the divergence is invisible until a stakeholder notices the marketing site is a slightly different blue.

Off-grid values are not automatically wrong, but they must be deliberate. Optical corrections — a 2 px optical nudge on a 44 px icon button, a 1 px hairline at 1× that must be 2 px at 2× — are legitimate. The failure is off-grid values appearing by accident, which is what makes a design look unconsidered. Introduce a documented escape hatch: a --space-half token, or a rule that all non-grid values must appear in a single, reviewed exception list.

7.5 Motion

Motion earns its place by explaining change — where something came from, what state it is in, and whether the interface is responding — and it is a liability when it is decoration on a 200 ms budget.

Two classes of motion exist and must be treated separately. Functional motion explains a state change: a dialog entering from its trigger, a panel sliding from the edge it belongs to, a list item moving to its new sorted position. It is part of the interface’s grammar and users depend on it, because an unexplained jump is disorienting in exactly the way WCAG 2.3.3 and the general principles around animation address. Decorative motion — parallax, ambient animation, entrance flourishes on content the user did not ask for — is optional by definition and must be removable without loss of meaning.

Duration is bounded by perception, not taste. Below about 100 ms a transition reads as instantaneous and, on a frequently repeated action, as flicker. Between 100 and 300 ms is the range in which motion reads as responsive and remains smooth. Between 300 and 500 ms it begins to feel sluggish and is acceptable only for large surfaces such as a full-screen sheet. Beyond 500 ms a transition is being interpreted as a delay, and users will start clicking again. The related thresholds are about response rather than transition: 100 ms is the limit below which an interaction feels directly manipulated, 1 second is the limit at which attention drifts, and 10 seconds is the point at which the user has completely lost the thread and needs a progress indicator with real information in it.

Easing must be asymmetric. Things entering should decelerate — ease-out, fast start, soft landing — because they are arriving. Things leaving should accelerate — ease-in — because they are being dismissed. Things moving within the screen should use a standard curve such as cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) for a material feel or a symmetric ease for small movements. Using ease-in for an entrance or ease-out for an exit is the single most common motion error, and it makes every transition feel subtly wrong without anyone being able to say why.

/* Motion specification as tokens. One place, one budget, one opt-out. */
:root {
  --dur-instant: 100ms;  /* state that must feel like a direct manipulation  */
  --dur-fast:    150ms;  /* hover, focus, checkbox, small repaint            */
  --dur-base:    200ms;  /* dropdowns, tooltips, popovers, tab underline     */
  --dur-slow:    300ms;  /* dialogs, drawers, expandable regions             */
  --dur-sheet:   400ms;  /* full-screen surfaces; never above this           */

  --ease-decel:  cubic-bezier(0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1);      /* entering         */
  --ease-accel:  cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0.8, 0.15);     /* leaving          */
  --ease-std:    cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1);          /* moving in place  */
  --ease-linear: linear;                               /* progress only    */
}

.popover {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(-4px) scale(0.98);
  transform-origin: top center;
  transition: opacity var(--dur-base) var(--ease-decel),
              transform var(--dur-base) var(--ease-decel);
}
.popover[data-open="true"] { opacity: 1; transform: none; }

.drawer {
  transform: translateX(100%);
  transition: transform var(--dur-slow) var(--ease-decel);
}
.drawer[data-open="true"] { transform: none; }
/* Exits use the accelerating curve and the same duration, so the
   interruption is never visible. */

.list-item {
  transition: transform var(--dur-base) var(--ease-std),
              background-color var(--dur-fast) var(--ease-std);
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  /* Collapse to cross-fade: the state change is still communicated,
     nothing moves. Never set display:none, and never remove the
     transition outright on a list reorder — the reorder is information. */
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 1ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 1ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
  .drawer, .popover, .list-item { transform: none !important; }
  .spinner { animation: none !important;
             border-top-color: currentColor; opacity: 0.6; }
}

/* Never animate anything the user did not ask to move. Progress bars and
   spinners are exempt from the 300ms budget — they may run for seconds,
   but they must be determinate wherever the answer is knowable. */
Motion typeDurationEasingReduces toJustified?
Hover / focus feedback100–150 msease-outInstant state change✓ Yes
Tooltip, popover, dropdown150–200 msease-out, from triggerCross-fade 100 ms✓ Yes, explains origin
Dialog, drawer, sheet200–300 msease-out, from edgeCross-fade 100 ms✓ Yes
List reorder, layout shift150–250 msStandard curveInstant reposition✓ Yes, only if not continuous
Skeleton shimmer1.2–1.6 s looplinearStatic placeholder⚠ Only if load > 1 s
Determinate progressMatches real ratelinearStatic percentage✓ Required for > 10 s
Page / route transition150–250 msease-outNone — instant swap✗ Usually not
Entrance animation on content300–500 msease-out, staggeredNone✗ No — delays reading

Motion is a vestibular trigger, and the preference is real. Vestibular disorders affect a large minority, and parallax plus large-scale motion is a documented trigger. prefers-reduced-motion: reduce is a media query, not a suggestion, and it must be honoured for the entire system, not for the hero animation only. Also respect the platform-level setting on the desktop track — macOS "Reduce motion", Windows "Animation effects" — which maps to the same intent. And never autoplay motion: nothing moves unless the user caused it or explicitly enabled it.

Perceived response has a separate budget from transition. The moment a key is pressed or a button clicked, the system has 100 ms to show a response — a pressed state, a cursor change, a skeleton. If the operation takes 1.5 seconds, the wait must be filled with a determinate indicator and, past 10 seconds, with real information about what is happening. An animation that covers a 2-second wait is not a transition, it is an apology.

7.6 Responsive strategy

Responsive strategy is the set of rules by which one layout system serves many viewport sizes, and on the desktop track the problem is not a different one but a genuinely different one, because the viewport is a user decision rather than a device property.

Start from content, not devices. The industry habit of naming breakpoints after hardware — 768 for tablets, 1024 for laptops — dates from a period when that mapping was roughly true and has been wrong ever since. Instead, find the natural widths at which each layout breaks: add content until the measure exceeds 90 characters, until the sidebar falls below 220 px, until a card grid cannot hold three columns at a readable measure, and put a breakpoint just before each break. This yields 2–4 breakpoints for most products instead of five arbitrary ones, and it survives hardware that does not exist yet.

Mobile-first versus desktop-first is a real decision with real costs. Mobile-first CSS writes the narrow case as the base and adds complexity upward, which naturally produces progressive enhancement, puts the common case in the base layer where it is served to every client, and makes the narrow layout the hardest one to keep correct because it gets attention first. Desktop-first is faster to build when the primary audience is desktop, but it produces base styles that most traffic then downloads and re-declares. For either track, the honest position is that the implementation direction and the design direction are independent — you can design desktop-first and build mobile-first — and what matters is that both widths are designed, not derived by hope.

Fluid type and fluid spacing replace breakpoint jumps with clamp() — a minimum, a preferred value that scales with the viewport, and a maximum. This gives continuous scaling between breakpoints, which is what makes a fluid layout feel designed rather than assembled from three fixed states. The discipline is to put a real number in all three positions: an unbounded clamp() will render 60 px type on a 4K display.

Container queries change the unit of responsiveness from the viewport to the component. A card that appears in a 2-up grid and a 4-up grid should respond to the width it was actually given, and a media query cannot express that because it only knows the window. Container queries have been broadly available since 2023 and should be the default for component-level adaptation, with media queries reserved for page-level concerns such as navigation model and column count. Note that @media breakpoints continue to be the right tool for print, for device capabilities, and for user preferences.

Now the desktop case, which is a different problem. A web page’s viewport is chosen implicitly by the user through their device, is generally stable while they read, and is not manipulated during a task. A desktop application’s window is explicitly resized by the user, continuously, often while reading, frequently below the size anyone designed for, and simultaneously constrained by the operating system’s window manager, the desktop’s available work area, the number of monitors, the display scale factor, and the presence of a taskbar. "Responsive" in this context means: the layout must remain usable at every width from the declared minimum window size up to multi-monitor spans; the minimum window size is an enforced product decision, not something that happens; content-driven reflow must degrade to a single column rather than to a two-column layout with a 90 px sidebar; and state — scroll position, selection, open panel, focused field — must survive a resize, which is a genuine engineering requirement with no web equivalent.

/* Component-level responsiveness: container queries, not viewport queries.
   Breakpoints are content-derived, named for what breaks, not for devices. */
.card-grid { container-type: inline-size; container-name: cardgrid;
            display: grid; gap: var(--space-4);
            grid-template-columns: 1fr; }

/* @container queries react to the space the component was actually given */
@container cardgrid (min-width: 320px) {
  .card-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr)); }
}
@container cardgrid (min-width: 560px) {
  .card-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr)); }
  .card__meta { font: var(--text-2xs); }   /* density rises with width */
}
@container cardgrid (min-width: 820px) {
  .card-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(4, minmax(0, 1fr)); }
}

/* The shell responds to the window, not the component. Content-derived. */
.app-shell {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-areas: "nav main";
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);
  min-inline-size: 320px;   /* the layout floor, not a device assumption */
}
@container appwindow (min-width: 700px) {      /* rail can stand alone   */
  .app-shell { grid-template-areas: "nav main";
               grid-template-columns: 220px minmax(0, 1fr); }
}
@container appwindow (min-width: 1100px) {     /* inspector fits beside */
  .app-shell { grid-template-areas: "nav main inspector";
               grid-template-columns: 220px minmax(0, 1fr) 320px; }
}
/* Below the floor the inspector does not shrink to 60px — it is removed
   from the layout and reachable as an overlay. */

@container appwindow (min-width: 700px) {
  .prose { max-inline-size: var(--measure); }
}

/* Fluid spacing and type: bounded in all three clamp() positions. */
:root {
  --space-fluid: clamp(16px, 1vw + 12px, 28px);
  --text-fluid:  clamp(15px, 0.28vw + 14.1px, 17px);
}

/* Desktop-specific: honour the OS display scale and the user's text
   preference independently. A 1px hairline is wrong at 150% scaling. */
@media (min-resolution: 144dpi) {
  :root { --hairline: 0.5px; }   /* crisp on scaled desktop displays */
}
@media (prefers-contrast: more) {
  :root { --border-control: #4a4f5a; --fg-on-surface-1-subtle: #4a4f5a; }
}
@media print {
  :root { --surface-0: #fff; --surface-1: #fff; }   /* force light theme */
  .app-shell { display: block; }
  nav, .inspector, .toolbar { display: none; }
}
ConstraintWeb trackDesktop trackImplication for design
Who controls widthDevice, implicitlyUser, explicitly, continuouslyEvery intermediate width is a designed state
Minimum size320 px is a conventionEnforced by the window managerDeclare and enforce a minimum window size
State across resizePage state resets, rarely noticedScroll position, selection, focus, open dialogsRestore UI state on resize, do not re-layout under the user
Display scalingMostly fixed, 1×/2× zoom100–300% per monitor, mixed-DPI setupsTest at 100%, 150% and 200% on each target display
Multi-monitorNot applicableWindow can span; window can move between displaysTest a window dragged from a 150% to a 100% display, live
InputPointer, touch, keyboardPointer, keyboard, often trackpad with momentumHover is unreliable on trackpads — no hover-only affordances
Resizing gestureNone, apart from browser chromeContinuous drag at the window edgeLayout must not thrash; debounce expensive reflow by 100 ms
Safe area / insetsNotches, dynamic browser barsTaskbar, menu bar, window chromeNever assume the full window rect is usable

Design the middle widths, not the extremes. The extremes get attention because they are the marketing screenshots. The widths that break products are 900 px, 1180 px and 1440 px — the sizes that appear when someone undocks from a laptop, halves a wide monitor, or opens two windows side by side. For the desktop track, build a test harness that resizes the window continuously and screenshots at every 20 px from the minimum to the maximum; you will find more layout defects in an hour than in a week of normal use.

Resizable, not responsive. The two words describe different things: responsive design optimises for a set of discrete states selected by the author for a viewport the user did not choose, while a desktop window demands a continuum the user drags at will. Teams that port a web design into a desktop shell and add a "min-width" of 1024 ship a product that is unusable on a 13-inch laptop at 150% scaling — a 1280 px physical display providing roughly 853 px of usable layout width. Enforce and test the minimum window size as a product requirement, and derive it from the narrowest realistic content, not from the shortest screen.

Exercises 7

  1. Build a complete type system for a content product: choose a base size and a ratio, generate eight steps from a 1.200–1.500 modular scale, assign a semantic role and a line height to each, and express all of it as CSS custom properties. Then set one page in it and verify at 200% browser zoom on a 1280 px window with no loss of content. Deliverable: the token block, a rendered specimen table showing every role at three lengths (short, typical, and 120-character worst case), and a written statement of the maximum measure you permit and why.
  2. Produce two complete colour systems for the same product — a light theme and a dark theme — using primitive and semantic token layers only. For each pair of foreground/background tokens, compute and record the contrast ratio, and mark every pair failing 4.5:1, 3:1 for large text, or 3:1 for non-text UI boundaries. Then simulate deuteranopia, protanopia, tritanopia and achromatopsia over every status indicator and chart. Deliverable: two token files, a contrast audit table, a simulation screenshot set, and a list of every meaning currently carried by hue alone, each with a proposed redundant channel.
  3. Define a structural token set for a data-dense professional application: an 8-point spacing scale, three density variants, a radius scale, and five elevation levels for each theme. Then build one data table that honours all three densities purely by token swap, with no component fork, and verify row heights of 28/40/48 px. Deliverable: the token files, the single table component, and a written off-grid exception list stating every value that does not sit on the 8-point grid and the optical justification for each.
  4. Write a complete motion specification for one product: durations, easing curves, and enter/exit behaviour for dialogs, drawers, tooltips, popovers, list reorders, toasts, skeletons and progress indicators, with a stated upper bound on any transition. Then produce a reduced-motion variant that preserves every state change as a cross-fade and demonstrate it with prefers-reduced-motion forced on. Deliverable: a motion token block, a before/after recording of each interaction type, and a written justification for every motion you have classified as decorative and therefore removed.
  5. Take a real screen from your product and rebuild it across nine viewport widths from 360 px to 1920 px, plus three desktop window states including a 640×480 minimum window, a window spanning two monitors at mixed display scaling, and a window dragged live from a 150% display to a 100% display. Produce a media-query or container-query stylesheet that handles all of them. Deliverable: nine annotated screenshots, the stylesheet, a defect list of every width at which the layout broke, and a stated minimum window size with the content measurement that justifies it.

8 · Technical Architecture and Design Records

8.1 Architectural styles8.2 C4 diagrams8.3 Architecture decision records8.4 Technology selection under uncertainty8.5 Quality attribute architecture8.6 Technical debt and reversibility

Technical architecture is the set of decisions that constrain every subsequent decision, and the purpose of writing it down is not the diagram — it is to make the constraints and their reasons recoverable by people who were not in the room. This section covers the selection of an architectural style with its honest costs, the C4 hierarchy of diagrams, architecture decision records as the durable artefact, technology choice under genuine uncertainty, quality attribute architecture where every quality is forced to become a measurable scenario, and technical-debt management grounded in the reverse-dependency rule. It closes by separating the architectural decisions both delivery tracks share — identity, data ownership, synchronisation, telemetry — from those that are track-specific, and that separation is the hinge of the whole guide: chapters 9–12 and 13–16 diverge precisely along the boundary drawn here.

8.1 Architectural styles

An architectural style is a family of structural decisions about coupling, distribution and dependency direction. Choosing one is choosing which costs you accept, and every style is a good choice in some circumstances and a mistake in others.

Six styles cover the realistic range for a new product, and they are better understood as points on a spectrum of distribution than as mutually exclusive options. A layered architecture separates presentation, domain and persistence with one-directional dependencies; it is nearly universal as an internal discipline even when the deployment is a single process. A monolith — one deployable unit, in-process calls, shared database — minimises operational surface and maximises the blast radius of a bad deployment. A modular monolith keeps one deployable unit but enforces boundaries between modules with explicit interfaces and no shared mutable state, so that the modules can later be extracted into services with minimal friction. Hexagonal (ports and adapters) inverts the dependency: the domain defines ports as interfaces, and adapters depend on the domain rather than the reverse, which is what makes the domain testable without infrastructure.

Two styles move the boundary across processes. Event-driven architecture publishes facts and lets consumers react, which decouples producers from consumers in time and lets independent components scale separately; it introduces eventual consistency, at-least-once delivery, duplicate handling, ordering questions, and debugging that no longer fits in a stack trace. Microservices combine independent deployment with independent data stores, which is the only way to get true autonomy — and they import a distributed-systems bill for every network call: latency, partial failure, retries, idempotency, and the loss of a single coherent transaction. The honest position on microservices is that they are an organisational and scaling strategy, not a technical one, and that adopting them without independent deploy capability and independent data ownership converts a monolith into a distributed monolith, which is strictly worse than either.

flowchart TB
  subgraph client["Client — shared across both tracks"]
    UI["Interface layer<br/>presentation, forms, routing"]
    SP["State container<br/>client-side store, cache, sync queue"]
  end

  subgraph core["Core — identical in both tracks"]
    API["Interface adapter / API surface<br/>HTTP+JSON, or IPC + typed messages"]
    AUTH["Identity & access<br/>OIDC, sessions, capability checks"]
    APP["Application services<br/>use-case orchestration, transactions"]

  end

  subgraph adapters["Adapters — the only layer that knows the outside"]
    PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>system of record")]

    TEL["Telemetry<br/>traces, metrics, logs, audit"]
  end

  UI --> SP
  SP -->|"requests carry auth context"| API
  API --> AUTH
  API --> APP
  APP --> DOM
  APP --> PORTS
  PORTS -->|"implemented by adapters"| PG
  PORTS --> OBJ
  PORTS --> EXT

  classDef shared fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#1a5fd0
  classDef boundary fill:#fff6e6,stroke:#8a5300

Note the asymmetry in the diagram: everything inside core is identical for the web track and the desktop track, and only adapters differs. That is the structural payoff of ports and adapters, and it is the reason to adopt it in the shared layer regardless of track — a domain tested without a database is a domain that can be tested, and that property is worth more than the layering overhead.

StyleDistributionDeploy independentlyData couplingOps costBest forSuitable
MonolithSingle process✗ NoShared schemaLowest ✓Small team, unclear domain, changing fast✓ Default for < 20 engineers

A structured score is better than an argument. Weight each criterion for the specific product — an internal tool with three users and an 18-month life weights observability at 1 and deploy-frequency at 1; a consumer product with a mobile team that must ship weekly weights them at 5 — and score 1 to 5. The weighted total is not the decision; it is the beginning of a document that records the decision, which is section 8.3.

# tech-selection.yaml — weighted scorecard for the architectural style

context:

  domain_stability: low        # the domain is still being discovered
  expected_life: 7y

  data_sensitivity: high
  offline_requirement: true    # both tracks need local-first behaviour
  rationale: "Team is smaller than the number of services a
              distributed design would need to own. Offline support
              makes the sync boundary the most important architectural
              fact, and it is far easier to design inside one process."

totals: { monolith: 22, modular_monolith: 34, layered: 27,
          hexagonal: 34, event_driven: 26, microservices: 24 }

decision: modular_monolith with hexagonal internal structure
rationale: "modular_monolith and hexagonal tie at 34; modular_monolith
            wins because it additionally delivers team_scaling_fit=5
            and migration_risk=5, and it defers the distributed-systems
            tax until a measured constraint — a named service with a
            named independent scaling requirement — actually forces it."

Premature distribution is the most expensive architectural mistake. Splitting into services before the domain is understood multiplies the cost of every mistake, because a wrong concept is now wrong in four places with a network hop and a retry policy between them. Two signals justify distribution: a component that demonstrably needs to scale or be deployed on a different schedule from everything else, and a team boundary that cannot be drawn inside a single codebase. Until one of those is named specifically, distribution is a cost with no evidenced benefit.

8.2 C4 diagrams

The C4 model organises architecture communication into four levels of zoom, and the value of the model is not the notation but the rule that each level answers one audience’s question and no diagram tries to serve two.

Simon Brown’s C4 model defines Level 1 — System Context: the system as a single box, its users, and the external systems it depends on. This is a one-page diagram with maybe seven elements, and it is the diagram that executives, non-engineering stakeholders, and new joiners need. It is also the diagram that makes security and data-residency conversations concrete, because external systems are where data leaves the building. Most projects draw this and stop, and that is the correct behaviour for a small system.

Level 2 — Container decomposes the system into deployable or runnable units: web application, API, background worker, database, message broker, and in the desktop track the application binary, the updater, and the local database. This is the level at which deployment, scaling and ownership are decided, so it should carry the technology choices and the data each container owns. For a modular monolith, the container diagram will show fewer boxes than a typical microservices diagram, and that is honest rather than disappointing.

Level 3 — Component zooms into a single container and shows its internal modules and their dependencies, and it is the diagram that catches the two rules that matter most: dependencies point inwards toward the domain, and no module reaches into another module’s tables. Level 4 — Code shows classes or functions and is generated from source, not drawn by hand; maintain it if your toolchain can, and otherwise do not maintain it, because a hand-drawn code diagram is wrong within a sprint.

Two practical rules make diagrams survive contact with a codebase. Name every element with the name used in the repository and the deployment configuration, never with a friendly synonym — a diagram that says "Data Service" when the repo says billing-api is worse than no diagram, because it cannot be looked up. And version the diagram with a date and a link to the decision that produced it, so a reader can tell whether it describes the current system or an aspiration.

@startuml
' L1 — System context. One box. Everyone can read this.
title L1 · System context — "Ledger"
skinparam rectangle {
  BackgroundColor #eef4ff; BorderColor #1a5fd0
}
actor       Member      as M
actor       Admin       as A
rectangle   "Ledger" as L {
  backgroundColor #e8f0fe
}
rectangle "Email provider" as E
rectangle "Payment provider" as P
rectangle "Object storage" as O
rectangle "Identity provider (OIDC)" as I

M  --> L : uses, via browser
A  --> L : administers
L --> E : sends transactional email
L --> P : authorises payments
L --> O : stores exported statements
L --> I : authenticates via OIDC
