// Every mutation has five terminal states. A form that handles only
// success and error is missing three.
//   1. idle      — nothing submitted yet
//   2. pending   — submitted, in flight; the submit control must be disabled and
//                the user must be told why they cannot click again
//   3. success   — the reset, the navigation, the confirmation
//   4. failure   — the message, and whether the input is preserved
//   5. conflict  — someone else changed it. A 409 with the current state, shown
//                as a diff for the user to resolve. This is the one that is
//                always missing and always causes a support ticket.

10.5 Accessibility in the implementation

Accessibility is a property of the markup, not an audit. Anything that can be expressed in native HTML elements should be, and a great deal of the accessibility work then disappears because the platform already did it correctly across every browser, every screen reader and every input method.

// The decision that removes most accessibility work: use the native element.
// A div with a click handler is a button that the platform cannot see.

// ✗ Not focusable, no role, no keyboard activation, unannounced.
<div className="btn" onClick={submit}>Save</div>

// ✓ Focusable, Enter and Space activate it, announced as a button,
//   and it participates in form submission for free.
<button type="submit" disabled={pending}>
  {pending ? 'Saving…' : 'Save'}
</button>

// A live region must exist in the DOM BEFORE the message arrives, or the
// screen reader has nothing to observe. Adding the container at the same
// time as the text is a well-known mistake.
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
  {message && <p>{message}</p>}          // polite: waits for a pause
</div>
<div role="alert">{error && <p>{error}</p>}</div>   // assertive: interrupts

// Errors must be associated with their field, or a screen reader user
// hears "edit text, blank" and learns nothing.
<label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
<input
  id="email"
  type="email"
  required
  autoComplete="email"          // ← a real autofill hint, free value
  aria-invalid={!!errors.email}
  aria-describedby={errors.email ? 'email-error' : undefined}
/>
{errors.email && <span id="email-error" role="alert">{errors.email}</span>}

// Focus management on route change. Without this, a keyboard or screen
// reader user is left at the top of a page whose content has changed,
// and focus falls back to <body> — which some browsers scroll to the top.
const ref = useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
useEffect(() => { ref.current?.focus(); }, [pathname]);
<main ref={ref} tabIndex={-1} aria-labelledby="page-heading">
  <h1 id="page-heading">{title}</h1>

// tabIndex={-1} makes it programmatically focusable WITHOUT adding it to
// the tab order. A positive tabIndex is worse than none: it overrides the
// document order and produces a focus sequence nobody can predict.

// The three things to check before shipping, in this order:
//   1. Unplug the mouse. Can you complete the primary flow?
//   2. Tab from the top. Is the order the visual order? Can you see focus?
//   3. Read it with a screen reader. Does it make sense with the screen off?

Do not fake it with ARIA. role and aria-* overwrite the semantics the platform already provides, and a wrong ARIA override is worse than none, because assistive technology now believes something that is not true. The first rule of ARIA is: do not use ARIA if a native element with the right semantics exists. A button written as <div role="button" tabindex="0" onkeydown="…"> will be missing the native keyboard handling, the native disabled state, the native form participation and the native accessibility announcement, and you will have reimplemented three of the four incorrectly.

10.6 Core Web Vitals and performance budgets

Core Web Vitals are three field metrics that together approximate whether a page felt fast. They are a proxy for a user judgement, not the judgement itself, and the useful way to use them is as a budget that CI enforces rather than a number to optimise after launch.

MetricMeasuresGoodPoorWhat moves it
LCP — Largest Contentful PaintWhen the largest visible element finishes rendering≤ 2.5 s> 4.0 sServer response time, render-blocking resources, image size and priority, font loading, client-side data fetching
INP — Interaction to Next PaintLatency from input to the next frame, at the 98th percentile≤ 200 ms> 500 msLong tasks, oversized hydration, expensive event handlers, layout thrash, too much main-thread work
CLS — Cumulative Layout ShiftUnexpected movement of visible content during load≤ 0.1> 0.25Images without dimensions, fonts swapping in, content inserted above existing content, ads and banners
// A performance budget, expressed as assertions that fail the build. This is
// the only form of budget that survives; a document describing a target is
// not a budget.
//   bundle-budget.json
//   {
//     "route": "/orders",
//     "budgets": [
//       { "type": "initial",   "maxSize": "180kb" },   // JS + CSS on first load
//       { "type": "total",     "maxSize": "420kb" },   // everything, all routes
//       { "type": "thirdParty","maxSize": "80kb" }     // analytics, tag manager, chat
//     ]
//   }

// Two budgets, two different meanings. Mixing them is how a team ends up
// with a 2 MB "total" that nobody notices because the home page ships 90 KB.
//   per-route initial  → what a first-time visitor on a phone actually pays
//   total across app    → what a long session accumulates, and what CI guards

// The specific fixes, in the order they usually pay off:
//
// 1. LCP: find the LCP element, then serve it as early as possible.
//    <img src="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"
//         width="1600" height="900" alt="…">   ← fetchpriority, AND dimensions
//    AVIF with a WebP fallback; sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 50vw"
//    Never lazy-load the LCP element — lazy-loading delays it deliberately.
//
// 2. LCP: do not fetch content in a client effect. If the text is the LCP
//    element, it must be in the HTML the server sent.
//    This is why "server-render above the fold, hydrate the rest" is the rule.
//
// 3. CLS: every media element gets width and height. A font gets a
//    size-adjust fallback so the swap does not reflow.
//    @font-face {
//      font-family: 'Inter';
//      src: url('/fonts/inter.woff2') format('woff2');
//      font-display: swap;          ← but pair it with the metric override below
//    }
//    @font-face {
//      font-family: 'Inter Fallback';
//      src: local('Arial');   // metrics-matched placeholder
//      size-adjust: 107%;    // so the swap moves nothing
//    }
//
// 4. INP: the long task is the problem, not the framework.
//    Yield to the main thread between units of work:
//    await scheduler.yield?.() ?? new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));
//    Break a 400 ms synchronous loop into slices the browser can interrupt.
//
// 5. INP: defer what is not needed for the first interaction.
//    Dynamic import on intent — on hover, on focus, on idle — not on load.
//    el.addEventListener('pointerenter', () => import('./editor'), { once: true });
//
// 6. Third parties are the most common cause of a regression nobody made.
//    Load them after interaction, and measure their cost separately.

Measure on a real device profile, not on localhost. Field data comes from real users on real devices and is the only number that predicts experience. Lab data on an unthrottled laptop is roughly the experience of a developer on a workstation, which is not a user. Use both: lab for regression detection in CI, because it is deterministic, and field for the verdict, because it is true. A team optimising only lab data will make every number worse and the actual experience no better.

Exercises 10

  1. Take a route that loads over 500 KB of JavaScript. Convert a discriminated-union state to a typesafe shape, replace a global store with URL params, and delete three abstractions that were one component each. Record bytes removed at each step and whether the component count changed.
  2. Audit one form end to end. Write a Zod schema, use it on both client and server, and implement all five terminal states including the 409 conflict. Then write a test that asserts the server rejects a payload the client accepted, because they are the same code and this should be impossible.
  3. Complete your primary flow with the mouse unplugged and the screen not visible. Record every focus failure, every unlabelled control, and every status message a screen reader would not announce. Fix them and add a CI check that fails on any new div-with-onClick over a native button.
  4. Find your LCP element on the three slowest routes. Serve it with explicit dimensions, fetchpriority="high", and no lazy-load. Measure LCP before and after on a throttled 4G profile and record the delta.
  5. Add a bundle budget to CI with initial, total and thirdParty thresholds per route. Set each threshold at today’s value minus ten percent, then confirm the build passes. Add a deliberately heavy import and confirm the build fails.
  6. Profile one long task with the browser performance panel. Find the frame that blocks input, split it with a yield, and measure INP at the 98th percentile before and after on a mid-range Android device profile.

11 · Web Track: Backend, APIs and Data

11.1 API design and the resource model11.2 REST, GraphQL and gRPC11.3 Errors, pagination and the shape of a good response11.4 Authentication, authorisation and session handling11.5 Data layer, caching and background work11.6 Logging, tracing and the operational surface

Web track. The backend is where a web product’s guarantees are actually made. The frontend can be rebuilt in a week; a badly designed API is a decade of compatibility obligations, and a badly designed identity model is a breach. This chapter covers the design decisions that are expensive to reverse, in roughly the order you discover you got them wrong.

A backend is a compatibility surface before it is a computation. Every endpoint you publish is a promise to clients you cannot upgrade in lockstep, and every promise costs something to keep. This chapter is organised by reversibility: the decisions that are nearly free to change, the ones that are expensive, and the one that is effectively permanent.

11.1 API design and the resource model

The resource model is the part of API design that determines whether the API ages well. Endpoint shapes can change; the model underneath them can be replaced only by versioning, and a versioned API is two APIs forever.

// Model the domain, then derive the URL space from it. The reverse order —
// designing URLs for screens — produces an API shaped like a UI, which
// means every UI change is an API change.

// ✓ Resource-oriented: nouns in the path, verbs implied by the method.
GET    /v1/orders?status=open&placed_after=2026-09-01    list with filters
GET    /v1/orders/{orderId}                                  one
POST   /v1/orders                                          create
PATCH  /v1/orders/{orderId}                                 partial update
DELETE /v1/orders/{orderId}                                 delete (or 409 if not allowed)

// ✓ A sub-resource that is genuinely a resource with its own identity
//   and its own lifecycle. It is not a field on the parent.
GET    /v1/orders/{orderId}/lines
POST   /v1/orders/{orderId}/lines
PATCH  /v1/orders/{orderId}/lines/{lineNo}

// ✗ The failure mode: the API named after the click.
GET    /v1/getDashboardData?userId=123&tab=orders&page=2
POST   /v1/createOrderAndNotifyCustomer
PUT    /v1/updateCustomerProfileWithAvatar
// Every one of these is a screen frozen into a URL. The second one is
// especially bad: it makes "notify the customer" unreplaceable, because
// a client that needs the order without the notification cannot express it.

// The one place a verb belongs: actions that are not CRUD on a resource.
POST   /v1/orders/{orderId}/cancel     { reason: "customer_request" }
POST   /v1/orders/{orderId}/refund     { amountMinor: 4999 }
POST   /v1/orders/{orderId}/shipments  { carrier: "dhl", trackingNo: "..." }
// Model as a sub-resource POST when the action creates something with an
// identity (a shipment). Model as a state transition when it does not
// (a cancellation is a state of the order, not an entity).

Do not model "create and do three other things". POST /createOrderAndNotifyCustomer makes a future where the notification is user-configurable impossible to express without a new endpoint, and a future where the notification is asynchronous impossible to implement without breaking the contract. Write the order, then write an outbox event in the same transaction, and let a worker do the rest. The API says what the caller asked for; everything else is a consequence.

11.2 REST, GraphQL and gRPC

Three protocols solving overlapping problems, chosen on a small number of axes that are usually clear in advance and expensive to reverse afterwards. The most consequential question is not capability — it is who is the client and whether you control it.

AxisREST / JSON over HTTPGraphQLgRPC / protobuf
ShapeFixed per endpoint, decided by the serverDeclared by the client per requestFixed per service, generated from .proto
Over-fetchingCommon — a dedicated endpoint per viewEliminated by constructionCommon; needs per-call wrappers
Round tripsMany, for composed viewsOne, for arbitrary compositionOne, for a composed RPC
Payload efficiencyVerbose; gzip helps a lotVerbose; gzip helps a lotBest by an order of magnitude — binary, field-numbered, delta-friendly
CachingNative via HTTP semantics and CDNDifficult. POST-per-query breaks shared cachesPoor. Not HTTP-cacheable without a gateway
Human debuggabilityBest — curl worksGood — a query is textPoor — needs grpcurl and a descriptor set
Schema evolutionAdditive by conventionType system, checked per clientBest — field numbers and optionality are explicit
StreamingWebSocket or SSE, bolted onSubscriptions, nativeNative bidirectional and server-streaming
Browser support without a proxyYesYesNo — needs gRPC-Web or an Envoy proxy
Who the client isAnyone, including third partiesFirst-party apps, mostlyFirst-party services you deploy
Best fitPublic APIs, mixed clients, cacheable contentComplex first-party clients with varying needs, e.g. mobileInternal service-to-service, high volume, polyglot orgs
// gRPC: the schema is the contract, and the generated code is why it holds.
// Note field numbers, not field names, are the wire contract. Renaming a
// field is safe; reusing a number for a different field is unrecoverable.
syntax = "proto3";
package orders.v1;

service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder(GetOrderRequest) returns (Order);          // unary
  rpc ListOrders(ListOrdersRequest) returns (ListOrdersResponse);
  rpc WatchOrders(WatchOrdersRequest) returns (stream OrderEvent);  // server-stream
}

message Order {
  string id          = 1;
  string customer_id = 2;
  OrderStatus status    = 3;   // enum, 16 bytes, not a string
  int64  total_minor = 4;   // money as an integer, never a float
  string currency   = 5;
  int64  placed_at_unix_ms = 6;  // explicit epoch, no tz ambiguity
  repeated LineItem lines = 7;

  // Adding a field later is wire-compatible. Removing field 4, or
  // renumbering it, breaks every deployed client at once.
  reserved 8, 9;                 // never reuse these
  reserved "old_field";
}

enum OrderStatus {
  ORDER_STATUS_UNSPECIFIED = 0;  // required: zero must be the safe default
  DRAFT  = 1;
  PLACED = 2;
  PAID   = 3;
}

// Deadlines. gRPC propagates a deadline across the call chain, and every
// hop must respect it. This is the single most valuable property of the
// protocol and the one most often left unused by hand-rolled clients.
const ctx = metadata.AppendToOutgoingContext(ctx, 'x-request-id', id);
const c   = orders.NewOrderServiceClient(conn);
const call = c.GetOrder(ctx2, &GetOrderRequest{Id: id});
order, err := call.Header(), call.Err()   // respects the propagated deadline

11.3 Errors, pagination and the shape of a good response

Error responses, pagination and versioning are the three areas where an API is either careful or expensive, and they are almost always decided lazily. Deciding them once, in a written standard, costs an afternoon; fixing them after a hundred integrations costs a quarter.

// An error response that a client can act on. Three properties: a stable
// machine-readable code, a human message, and structured context.
{
  "error": {
    "code": "order_line_sku_duplicate",      // stable, machine-readable, snake_case
    "message": "SKU 'ABC-9' already appears on this order.",  // for a human, safe to show
    "status": 409,
    "target": "lines[0].sku",            // what to highlight in the form
    "details": { "sku": "ABC-9", "lineNo": 0 },
    "requestId": "01J8Z…",              // quote this in a support ticket
    "docs": "https://docs.example.com/errors/order_line_sku_duplicate"
  }
}
// ✗ { "error": "Bad Request" }  — the client can only show a string.
// ✗ Never put a stack trace, SQL fragment, or internal hostname in here.

// The status code set, and what each one licenses the client to do.
//   200  success with a body
//   201  created; MUST include a Location header
//   204  success, no body; do not return 200 with null
//   400  malformed request the client cannot fix by retrying
//   401  not authenticated — the client should send credentials and retry ONCE
//   403  authenticated but not permitted — retrying will never help
//   404  not found; also use it for a resource the caller may not see, so that
//        the existence of another tenant's order is not disclosed
//   409  conflict — the caller must re-read and reconcile, not blind-retry
//   422  syntactically valid, semantically rejected; carries field errors
//   429  rate limited; MUST include Retry-After
//   500  our fault. The client may retry with exponential backoff
//   503  temporarily unavailable, e.g. shedding load. MUST include Retry-After

// Keyset pagination. Offset pagination has cost proportional to depth and
// silently skips or repeats rows when the underlying set changes between
// page requests, which on an actively-written table is most of the time.
GET /v1/orders?status=open&limit=50&after=cur_eyJpZCI6ODgxNywicGxhY2VkQXQiOiIyMDI2LTA5LTAxVDEwOjAwOjAwWiJ9

{
  "data": [ … ],
  "page": {
    "hasMore": true,
    "nextCursor": "cur_eyJpZCI6ODg4OSwi…",   // opaque: the client must not parse it
    "limit": 50
  }
}
// The cursor encodes the sort key of the last row returned, so page 2
// costs the same as page 1 and no row is ever skipped or duplicated.

11.4 Authentication, authorisation and session handling

Authentication answers who; authorisation answers what. Conflating them is the most common and most expensive security error in a web backend, and the design below keeps them structurally separate so that forgetting a check produces a denied request rather than a data breach.

// OAuth 2.1 / OIDC: the browser flow for "log in with a third party". The
// critical property in 2026 is PKCE, which removes the need for a secret
// in a public client and closes the code-interception attack class.

// The browser never sees a client_secret. It generates a verifier, sends
// its SHA-256 hash as the challenge, and proves possession of the verifier
// when redeeming the code. An attacker who steals the code cannot redeem it.
const verifier = base64url(crypto.randomBytes(32));
const challenge = base64url(await crypto.subtle.digest(
  'SHA-256', new TextEncoder().encode(verifier)
));
sessionStorage.setItem('pkce_verifier', verifier);   // survives the redirect

// state is a CSRF defence AND a session-binding defence. Generate it,
// store it, and compare on return with a constant-time comparison.
const state = base64url(crypto.randomBytes(24));
sessionStorage.setItem('oauth_state', state);

const url = new URL('https://idp.example.com/authorize');
url.searchParams.set('response_type', 'code');     // NOT 'token' (implicit flow: retired)
url.searchParams.set('client_id',        PUBLIC_CLIENT_ID);
url.searchParams.set('redirect_uri',     'https://app.example.com/callback');
url.searchParams.set('scope',            'openid profile email');
url.searchParams.set('state',            state);
url.searchParams.set('code_challenge',   challenge);
url.searchParams.set('code_challenge_method', 'S256');
location.assign(url);

// Sessions. For a browser application, a server-side session is nearly
// always the better choice: the token is not in JavaScript, so XSS cannot
// read it, and revocation is immediate.
//
// Cookie attributes, all four of which are load-bearing:
Set-Cookie: __Host-session="$id.$hmac"; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=604800
//   __Host-  prefix ENFORCES Secure, Path=/ and NO Domain. It is a browser
//           guarantee that a subdomain cannot set a cookie for the parent,
//           which is the session-fixation-via-subdomain attack.
//   HttpOnly  JavaScript cannot read it, so XSS cannot exfiltrate it
//   SameSite  Lax: not sent on cross-site POST, which blocks CSRF for state-
//           changing requests while keeping normal top-level navigation
//   Secure    TLS only, always, no exceptions

// Authorisation: enforce it at the data layer, not only in the route.
// A route check that the query then ignores is a data breach.
//
// ✗ SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1        ← the tenant scope is missing
// ✓ SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2
//   and $2 comes from the session, never from a request parameter.

async function function loadOrder(req: Request, orderId: string) {
  const session = await requireSession(req);       // 401 if absent
  const order = await db.orders.findByTenantAndId(
    session.tenantId,          // ← from the session, not the URL
    orderId
  );
  if (!order) {
    // 404, not 403: do not confirm that someone else's order exists
    throw new NotFound();
  }
  if (!can(session.user, 'order.refund', order)) {
    throw new Forbidden();
  }
  return order;
}

Where a token belongs. HttpOnly cookie for a browser application, because XSS cannot read it. Authorization: Bearer for a machine-to-machine client. Never in localStorage, because any XSS reads it and it has no expiry discipline; never in a query string, because it lands in access logs, referrer headers and browser history. And if you must accept a token from JavaScript, hold it in memory only, with a short access-token lifetime and a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.

11.5 Data layer, caching and background work

The data layer is where correctness is won or lost, and three mechanisms carry almost all of the weight: the schema, the cache, and the outbox. The rest is discipline about transactions and connection limits.

// Connection pooling. The application opens connections far faster than the
// database can accept them. The pooler is not optional at scale, and its
// size is not a number you inherit from a tutorial.
//
// PostgreSQL sizing: total connections ≈ cores × 2..3, split across all
// clients, plus headroom for maintenance. NOT (instances × pool size).
// A 12-instance deployment with a 20-connection pool asks for 240 connections
// against a server configured for 100. That is a 3am incident by schedule.
//
// PgBouncer in transaction mode, which is the only mode that actually helps:
[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
pool_mode  = transaction
max_client_conn = 1000        // what the app may open
default_pool_size = 40           // what the DB will actually see
reserve_pool_size = 5
max_db_connections  = 60
max_prepared_statements = 200    // 1.21+: makes transaction pooling
                                   // compatible with server-side prepared statements

// The transactional outbox. Writing to your database and publishing to a
// broker cannot be one transaction, so make the intent part of the
// transaction and let a relay publish it. At-least-once, so every
// consumer must be idempotent on the event id.
BEGIN;
UPDATE sales_order SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2;
INSERT INTO outbox (id, topic, aggregate_id, payload, at)
VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), 'order.shipped', '$2:$1',
        jsonb_build_object('orderId', $1), now());
COMMIT;
-- Exactly one of the two happened. Both, or neither. Never one.

// The relay, which must be safe to run concurrently in several replicas.
WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id FROM outbox
   WHERE published_at IS NULL
   ORDER BY at
   LIMIT 500
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED            -- the key clause
)
UPDATE outbox o
   SET published_at = now()
  FROM claimed c
 WHERE o.id = c.id
RETURNING o.id, o.topic, o.payload;
-- Publish the returned rows, then they are already marked. A crash
-- between publish and commit re-publishes: at-least-once, by design.

// Caching, from most to least expensive to get wrong.
//   1. HTTP cache headers at the CDN — cheapest, and usually sufficient
//   2. Application cache (Redis) for a computed result
//   3. Materialised view for an aggregate the database recomputes
// Every one of them needs an invalidation path, and a cache without one
// is a correctness bug with a TTL on it.

11.6 Logging, tracing and the operational surface

A backend’s operational surface is the set of facts available when something is wrong at three in the morning. Three signals cover almost everything: structured logs for what happened, metrics for how often and how bad, and traces for where the time went across services.

// Structured logging. One event per line, JSON, with the correlation ids that
// let you join a log line to a trace, a metric and a database row.
{
  "ts": "2026-09-29T05:14:22.418Z",
  "level": "warn",
  "msg": "slow downstream call",
  "service": "orders-api",
  "env": "production",
  "requestId": "01J8Z…",      // → the trace
  "traceId":  "7c1e…",
  "spanId":   "a3f0…",
  "userId": "usr_8817",          // pseudonymised, not raw PII
  "tenantId": "tnt_42",
  "route": "POST /v1/orders/:id/refund",  // the TEMPLATE, not the path
  "status": 200,
  "durationMs": 1840,
  "downstream": { "service": "payments", "durationMs": 1790 }
}
// ✗ "2026-09-29 05:14:22 [WARN] refund slow for order 8817"
//   Unparseable, unaggregatable, and the string "8817" is now unqueryable.

// Metrics: the four that actually change a decision, per service.
//
//   RED:  Rate    — requests per second, per route, per status class
//         Errors — 5xx rate (the SLO signal) and 4xx rate (a client problem
//                      you should be able to see, which is most 4xx)
//         Duration — latency histogram, p50 and p99, not a mean
//
//   plus the saturation metrics that predict an outage before it happens:
//   - connection pool: in_use / max, and wait duration
//   - database: pool exhausted count, query duration, rows scanned vs returned
//   - event loop lag (Node) — the leading indicator of a latency cliff
//   - queue depth and oldest-message age for every async consumer

// Distributed tracing. The one decision that matters is sampling: trace
// everything that is slow or failed, and sample the rest.
// Uniform 1% sampling hides exactly the rare slow request you need.
const shouldSample = isError || durationMs > 1000 || Math.random() < 0.01;
// But keep the decision on the trace, not in the payload, or the two
// disagree and the trace is not reconstructable.

// Propagate context across every hop, including into the queue.
// A message that loses its trace context is a message you cannot follow.
const traceparent = await propagator.inject(context.active());
await broker.publish({
  topic:   'order.shipped',
  payload: event,
  headers: { traceparent },        // re-injected on consume
});

The three questions to answer during an incident. What is broken? — the error rate and the affected route, from a dashboard that is correct within a minute. Who is affected? — tenants and users, from structured logs filtered on status and route. Why? — a trace for a failing request, from the trace ID in one of those log lines. A backend that cannot answer all three within five minutes has an observability defect, and it will be discovered during its worst incident rather than during a scheduled review.

Exercises 11

  1. Design the resource model for a domain you know. Write the full URL space, then mark every endpoint whose purpose is a state transition rather than CRUD. Rewrite the transitions as sub-resources where they create something, and justify each choice.
  2. Build the same two endpoints three ways — REST, GraphQL and gRPC — and measure response size and wall-clock time over a thousand calls with a fixed dataset. Record the compression ratio for each, since that is the number that changes the conclusion for JSON.
  3. Write an error-handling standard for your service: a stable code registry, the status-code-to-retry policy, and a machine-readable body. Then verify that every endpoint in the service returns a code from the registry and nothing else.
  4. Replace offset pagination with keyset pagination on one endpoint. Prove it is immune to concurrent inserts by inserting rows between page requests and showing no duplicates or omissions, which offset pagination cannot do.
  5. Implement an OAuth 2.1 authorization-code flow with PKCE, a __Host- prefixed session cookie, and a state check. Then attempt the three attacks: code interception without the verifier, CSRF with a mismatched state, and a subdomain trying to set a session cookie. Confirm all three are blocked.
  6. Add the transactional outbox to one write path with a relay, then run four relay replicas concurrently and kill one mid-batch. Confirm no event is lost, that duplicates are possible, and that your consumer’s idempotency key makes the duplicates harmless.
  7. Add structured logging with request and trace correlation to one route, plus a RED dashboard and a saturation dashboard. Then deliberately induce a slow downstream dependency and measure how long it takes to identify the cause using only the dashboards and logs.

12 · Web Track: Deployment, Delivery and Operations

12.1 Hosting models compared12.2 Environments and configuration12.3 The delivery pipeline and its gates12.4 Zero-downtime deployment and rollback12.5 DNS, TLS and the edge12.6 Operating it: incidents, runbooks and cost

Web track. Deployment is the point at which the product meets reality. Everything up to this chapter was reversible in the sense that you could delete the repository; from here on, the deployed artefact is the product. This is the part of the web track with no desktop equivalent — the desktop equivalent is distribution and auto-update, covered in chapter 16.

Deployment decisions are dominated by one variable: how long it takes to get a change in front of users, and how long it takes to get it back out. Everything else — build system, orchestration, infrastructure-as-code — is in service of those two numbers. This chapter covers the hosting models, the environment strategy, the pipeline, the mechanics of a zero-downtime release, and the operational practice afterwards.

12.1 Hosting models compared

Five models, distinguished by who runs the machine and how long the process lives. The choice determines the operational work you inherit, and it is much cheaper to change now than later.

ModelYou runCold startBest forWatch out forCost shape
Static hosting + CDNNothingNoneDocs, marketing, SPA shells, any SSG outputNo server logic; anything dynamic needs a separate originBandwidth, essentially free at small scale
Managed platform (PaaS)Config onlySecondsMost products, until they outgrow itVendor lock-in in the config layer; request time and connection limitsPer instance-month plus egress
Containers on a managed orchestratorContainer + manifestsSecondsLong-running services, background workers, mixed languagesYou now own the Kubernetes surface, which is largePer node-hour, which has a floor
Serverless functionsFunction codeMilliseconds to seconds, plus a cold penaltyIrregular traffic, spiky load, event-driven work, glueTimeouts, no state, cold starts, vendor-specific handler model, egress costPer invocation — can be cheaper or far dearer at steady state
Virtual machines / bare metalEverythingMinutesSpecialised workloads, very high steady load, regulated hostingYou own patching, load balancing, TLS, backups, and the pagerPer instance-hour, predictable, and never below the floor
// A container image, built so the deployment is a pull, not a build.
// Multi-stage: the build toolchain is 800 MB and has no business in prod.
// Pinned base digest, not a floating tag — 'node:24' changes under you.
FROM node:24.6-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
# Only the manifest, so this layer is cached until a dependency actually changes.
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

FROM node:24.6-bookworm-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian12 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=deps  /app/node_modules          ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist                  ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/package.json          ./package.json
# Non-root, because a distroless base has no shell and no package manager,
# which is a large part of why it is the right base.
USER node
EXPOSE 8080
# The HEALTHCHECK is what a load balancer and an orchestrator poll. It must
# answer "can this instance serve traffic", not "is the process alive".
#   /livez  → process is up. Never depends on a database: a database outage
#            must not take every instance out of rotation at once.
#   /readyz → can serve. Checks the pool, the cache, and any migration state.
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

12.2 Environments and configuration

How many environments you have, and what may differ between them, is a decision with a real failure mode on both sides. Too few and you cannot test a release; too many and nobody can tell which one is real.

EnvironmentPurposeDataWho can reach itDeploy trigger
LocalDevelopmentSeeded, syntheticDeveloper onlyNothing; runs on the machine
Preview / ephemeralReview a branch, reproduce a bugSeeded, per-branch, destroyed afterAnyone with the URL, often auth-walledEvery push to a branch
StagingVerify the release candidateProduction-shaped, anonymisedTeam, plus automated testsEvery merge to main
ProductionServe usersRealUsersPromoted artefact, never rebuilt
// The rule that makes this work: build once, promote the same artefact.
// Rebuilding per environment means what you tested is not what you ship,
// which voids the entire staging environment's purpose.
//
//   build  →  one immutable image tagged by commit SHA, not by 'latest'
//   stage  →  deploy image sha:9f3c21a to staging, run migrations, smoke test
//   prod   →  deploy the SAME sha:9f3c21a. Never rebuild. Never retag.
//
// Configuration is environment, and it is injected — never baked in.
//   ✗ const dbUrl = 'postgres://prod-user:hunter2@db.internal/prod'  in code
//   ✓ DATABASE_URL from the platform's secret store, read at boot
//
// Validate at startup and refuse to boot on a bad config. A service that
// starts with a missing variable and fails on the first request has turned
// a deploy-time problem into a user-visible one.
const schema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV:        z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']),
  DATABASE_URL:    z.string().url(),
  REDIS_URL:       z.string().url(),
  SESSION_SECRET:  z.string().min(32),          // refuse a weak one
  LOG_LEVEL:       z.enum(['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error']).default('info'),
  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: z.string().startsWith('sk_').optional(),
  // Fail closed on a security setting rather than defaulting it to false.
  SECURE_COOKIES:  z.enum(['true', 'false'])
                     .refine(v => process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' || v === 'true',
                             'SECURE_COOKIES must be true in production'),
});

const config = schema.safeParse(process.env);
if (!config.success) {
  console.error('Invalid configuration:', config.error.flatten().fieldErrors);
  process.exit(1);        // fail fast, fail loudly, at boot
}

Migrations belong in the release, and they are not backward compatible by default. The safe order is: deploy code that can run against both the old and the new schema, then apply the migration, then remove the old schema. That is the expand-and-contract sequence, and for a web deployment the middle step is a separate deploy rather than a step in the same one. Running the migration and the new code simultaneously in one release is the most common cause of a deployment that must be rolled back and cannot be, because the schema has already moved.

12.3 The delivery pipeline and its gates

A pipeline is a set of gates in order of cost to run and cheapness to pass. The design principle is that the cheapest, most-likely-to-fail check runs first, so that most bad commits are rejected in under a minute without consuming a build runner.

# .github/workflows/ci.yml — the ordering is the design.
# Fast and dirty-blocking first, slow and thorough last.
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:                        # cancel superseded runs on the same ref
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  # ── Gate 1: 40 seconds. Type errors and lint. Catches most of what
  #    people actually break, and costs almost nothing to run.
  static:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with: { node-version: '24', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck          # tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run format:check

  # ── Gate 2: 2 minutes. Unit and integration tests with real dependencies
  #    in containers, not mocks. Mocks test your assumptions about the
  #    dependency; a real one tests the dependency.
  test:
    needs: static
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres: { image: 'postgres:18-alpine', ... }
      redis:    { image: 'redis:8-alpine', ... }
    steps:
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test -- --coverage
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: coverage, path: coverage/ }

  # ── Gate 3: parallel, on every push. The expensive suite is sharded so
  #    wall-clock time is bounded by the slowest shard, not the total.
  e2e:
    needs: test
    strategy:
      matrix: { shard: [1,2,3,4] }
    steps:
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4

  # ── Gate 4: the security and supply-chain checks. Cheap, and they catch
  #    the class of problem that is most expensive to discover in production.
  supply-chain:
    needs: static
    steps:
      - run: npm audit --audit-level=high
      - run: npx snyk test --severity-threshold=high
      - run: npx license-checker --production --summary
      - run: npx @secretlint/scanner "**/*"      # committed secrets

  # ── Gate 5: deploy the SAME artefact. Every environment gets the same
  #    image, built once, tagged by commit SHA.
  deploy-preview:
    needs: [test, supply-chain]
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh preview "${{ github.sha }}"

  deploy-production:
    needs: [e2e, deploy-preview]
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    environment:
      name: production
      url: 'https://app.example.com'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh production "${{ github.sha }}"

The gate that people remove first is the one that costs the most later. Flaky tests are the usual reason a gate gets disabled, and a disabled gate is not the same as a fixed test. The durable repairs, in order: quarantine the flaky test with a linked ticket and a date, not by deleting it; fix the source of the flake rather than adding a retry; and give the suite a quarantine budget — if quarantined tests exceed 2% of the total, the quarantine itself is the problem and needs a sprint. A retry in CI masks a real defect and turns a red build green, which is the exact opposite of what a gate is for.

12.4 Zero-downtime deployment and rollback

Zero-downtime deployment is a property of the sequence, not of the tooling. The mechanism is always the same: bring up the new version alongside the old, prove it healthy, and only then remove the old. Anything that tears down before proving readiness is a deployment with a scheduled outage.

// Rolling update, and the three states that make it safe.
//
// 1. READINESS  — "can this instance serve?" Must be false until the app is
//    listening, the pool is warm, and migrations this version needs are done.
//    The load balancer only sends traffic to instances passing this.
GET /readyz
  // 200 only when: server listening AND db pool can acquire a connection
  //           AND no pending migration this build requires

// 2. LIVENESS  — "is the process worth keeping?" Must NOT check dependencies.
//    If liveness depends on the database, a database blip restarts every
//    instance simultaneously, and the restart storm is worse than the outage.
GET /livez
  // 200 if the event loop is responsive. Nothing else.

// 3. GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN — the part that is usually missing. On SIGTERM:
//    a. fail readiness immediately, so the LB stops sending new requests
//    b. wait for in-flight requests to finish, bounded by a deadline
//    c. close the database pool, flush telemetry, exit 0
//    d. if the deadline passes, exit non-zero and be killed — that is fine

process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
  ready = false;                                 // (a) immediately
  const timer = setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25000);  // (d) hard deadline
  server.close();                                 // stop accepting
  await new Promise(r => server.on('close', r));   // (b) drain
  await pool.end();                           // (c) release the DB
  //
  clearTimeout(timer);
  process.exit(0);
});

// Kubernetes: three probes, three different questions.
//   readinessProbe → gates traffic. Slow start, frequent checks.
//   livenessProbe  → restarts the pod. MUST NOT check dependencies.
//   startupProbe   → disables liveness until the app is warm, so a slow
//                   start is not mistaken for a hang and restarted forever.
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 0
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5            # fast: this gates traffic
  failureThreshold: 2
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30       # 30 × 10 s = 5 min of grace
  periodSeconds: 10

// Rollback. The decision must be made in advance, in writing, with a name.
//
//   ROLLBACK TRIGGER: any of these, without discussion:
//     - 5xx rate above 2% for 3 consecutive minutes after deploy
//     - p99 latency above 2× the pre-deploy baseline for 5 minutes
//     - any new error class in the logs that was not present before
//     - a conversion or checkout metric down more than 10%
//
//   ROLLBACK TARGET: the previous image digest, retained for 14 days.
//   NOT 'the last good build' — that is a different thing after a few deploys.
//
//   ROLLBACK TIME BUDGET: 5 minutes from decision to verified recovery.
//   If the command is not in the runbook, the budget is fiction.
kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders-api --to-revision=142
kubectl rollout status deployment/orders-api --timeout=120s

Database changes and rollback do not compose. If the release ran a destructive migration, rolling the code back leaves the new code’s data shape with the old code’s expectations, and the rollback is not a recovery — it is a second incident. This is why the expand-and-contract sequence exists: the destructive step is always a separate release, and the release before it is always fully rollback-able. A team that learns this during an incident has already paid for the lesson.

12.5 DNS, TLS and the edge

The last mile is where most web outages actually happen, and it is the part that feels like infrastructure plumbing until the certificate expires. Five mechanisms, each with a specific failure mode.

// TLS. Two things that are non-negotiable in 2026 and still get missed.
//
// 1. HSTS. Once sent, the browser refuses to ever try plain HTTP for this host
//    again, even if an attacker can inject a redirect. Start with a short
//    max-age and raise it once you are confident, because you cannot undo it early.
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload

// 2. Certificate automation with renewal AND reload. A certificate that renews
//    on disk but is never loaded into the running process is an outage on the
//    day it expires, which is a specific, avoidable, entirely predictable day.
certbot renew --deploy-hook "systemctl reload nginx"

// DNS records and their TTL, which is really the failover latency.
//   A 300 s TTL means up to 5 minutes of stale answers after a change. That is
//   the floor on how fast you can move traffic, and it is worth setting lower
//   (60 s) if you intend to fail over.
//   Low TTL does not mean fast: resolvers cache, and some ignore it entirely.

// Multi-CDN and health-based routing. Failover is a health-check decision, and
// the health check must be run from outside the region that might be failing.
{
  "/* comment": "route on measured origin health, not on DNS TTLs",
  "   originGroups": [
    { "name": "primary",  "targets": [{ "host": "eu-west-1.app.example.com" }] },
    { "name": "fallback", "targets": [{ "host": "us-east-1.app.example.com" }] }
  "],
  "rules": [
    { "condition": { "path": "/api/*" },
      "   "originGroup": "primary",
      "   "healthCheck": { "path": "/readyz", "interval": 10, "timeout": 3,
                            "                 "expectedStatusCodes": [200], "unhealthyThreshold": 3 },
      "   "failover": { "maxRetries": 2, "perTryTimeout": 5,
                           "                  "retryCondition": ["5xx", "timeout"], "retries": 3 } }
  "]
}

// The security headers that belong on every response.
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(self), interest-cohort=()
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp   # only if you actually need it; it has costs

// A CSP with 'unsafe-inline' in script-src defeats most of its purpose. If
// you need nonces, generate a fresh one per response:
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic'

12.6 Operating it: incidents, runbooks and cost

Launching is not the end of the project. The operational practice is what separates a product that works from one that keeps working, and it is a small number of concrete habits rather than a large process.

// Alert on symptoms a user feels, not on causes. Every cause-based alert is a
// page that teaches the on-call engineer to ignore pages.
//
//   ✗ "PostgreSQL CPU above 80%"   → fires on a perfectly healthy replica
//   ✗ "Disk usage above 75%"        → fires on a batch job and is not actionable
//   ✗ "Queue length above 1000"     → the threshold is arbitrary; 10,000 is fine
//
//   ✓ "SLO burn: 2% of requests failing for 5 minutes"
//   ✓ "Checkout success rate below baseline for 15 minutes"
//   ✓ "Oldest unprocessed webhook older than 10 minutes"
//
// Multi-window, multi-burn-rate. Fast and slow alerts from one SLO, so you
// page for the big fires and ticket for the smouldering ones.
name: slo-burn
rules:
  - alert: FastBurn
    # 14.4x over 1 h consumes 2% of a 30-day budget in 1 hour
    expr: slo_error_ratio:rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
    for: 2m
    labels: { severity: page, window: '1h' }
  - alert: SlowBurn
    # 6x over 6 h — real, but not a page; open a ticket
    expr: slo_error_ratio:rate6h > (6 * 0.001)
    for: 15m
    labels: { severity: ticket, window: '6h' }

// The runbook is a page, not a document. Read while panicking.
//
//   SYMPTOM: 5xx rate above 2% for 3 minutes
//   IMPACT:  users cannot complete checkout
//
//   1. Is it us or upstream?
//      kubectl logs deploy/orders-api --since=5m | grep -i error | head -50
//   2. Did a deploy just happen?
//      kubectl rollout history deployment/orders-api | head
//      If yes: kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders-api   ← fix, then investigate
//   3. Is one dependency slow?
//      # in the trace: compare span durations against the 2s baseline
//   4. Is the pool exhausted?
//      SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='active';
//   5. Escalate: #oncall, then the database owner, then the vendor status page
//
//   NOT IN THIS RUNBOOK: restarting things to see if it helps. Every restart
//   destroys the evidence you need and can turn degraded into down.

// Cost. The three that surprise teams, in the order they surprise them.
//
// 1. EGRESS. Free ingress, expensive egress. A CDN in front of an un-cached
//    origin is a way of being billed for every request twice.
// 2. OBSERVABILITY. Per-host metrics and per-span traces at production volume
//    routinely exceed the cost of the application itself.
//    Sample traces; keep 100% of errors.
// 3. IDLE FLOOR. Managed databases and orchestrators have a monthly minimum
//    that does not shrink when traffic does. The right time to notice is before
//    you are paying it.

Web track complete. Where this connects to the Desktop track. Everything in chapters 9–12 assumed a server you control, a browser you do not, and a deployment you push. Chapter 13 begins the Desktop track, where none of those three hold: the application runs on the user’s machine, the update is pulled rather than pushed, the network is an enhancement rather than a prerequisite, and the operating system — not your CDN — decides what your binary may do. The discovery, requirements, design and architecture work in chapters 1–8 applies identically. Nothing else carries over unchanged.

Exercises 12

  1. Build a multi-stage, distroless, non-root container image for a service you own. Measure the final size and the build time, then compare them against a single-stage image and record the difference in both size and attack surface.
  2. Set up three environments with per-branch preview deployments. Prove that the artefact promoted to production is byte-identical to the one tested in staging by comparing image digests rather than git SHAs.
  3. Add a schema-validated configuration check that fails the process at boot, then deliberately remove a required variable and confirm the deployment refuses to start rather than starting and failing on the first request.
  4. Implement the four-stage zero-downtime deployment: readiness gate, health verification, traffic shift, and old-version removal. Then kill the new version mid-deploy and confirm users were served throughout with no dropped connections.
  5. Write a rollback trigger list with numeric thresholds, run it past a peer for a dry read, and time the rollback command. If it takes more than five minutes, that is the finding.
  6. Configure HSTS, a nonce-based CSP, and all the standard security headers. Then measure the report-only violation log after a week of real traffic and fix the sources, so the policy can move out of report-only mode.
  7. Replace every cause-based alert in your monitoring with a user-visible symptom alert, then count the pages received over the following two weeks and compare. The reduction is usually larger than expected.

13 · Desktop Track: Architecture and Framework Selection

13.1 The process model, and what actually differs from web13.2 Native, cross-platform, hybrid and web-tech options13.3 Framework selection matrix13.4 The web-view option and its costs13.5 Multi-process, and where the process boundary goes13.6 A selection procedure

Desktop track begins. From this chapter through chapter 16 the process diverges completely from the web track in chapters 9–12. Chapters 1–8 — discovery, research, requirements, interface design, visual design, architecture — applied unchanged to both tracks and are not repeated. The discovery questions for a desktop product are identical: is the problem real, is it frequent enough to justify a per-user install, and will people pay for a thing on their machine rather than a tab. What changes is everything about how the software is built and delivered.

A desktop application is a program that a user installs, owns a copy of, and runs with the privileges of a logged-in user on a machine you do not administer. Every architectural decision follows from those three facts: you cannot control the environment, you cannot update the user instantly, and you have far more access to the machine — and therefore far more responsibility — than a web page ever has. This chapter establishes the option space and produces a selection procedure.

13.1 The process model, and what actually differs from web

The single most consequential difference between web and desktop is the lifecycle. A web deploy is a push you control; a desktop release is a pull you cannot force, and the user has every reason to be on an old version for months.

DimensionWebDesktopConsequence
Who controls the versionYou do, within minutesYou do not. The user updates when they choose toEvery protocol and schema change must be backward compatible with the oldest version you support, indefinitely
Execution privilegeSandboxed in a browser tabFull user privileges; may be elevatedAny compromise is a compromise of the user’s machine, not of a tab
Memory ceilingTab, usually killed under pressureThe whole system, competing with everything elseA leak is survivable for a long time and then fatal. Memory is a first-class requirement
CPU budgetMostly idle; background tabs throttledYou are competing with the user’s other work, on batteryBackground work must be interruptible and battery-aware, not just off
FilesystemSandboxed origin, quota-basedFull access, and it persistsWhere does the user put 50 GB of documents, and who cleans it up?
DistributionA URLA signed binary, a store listing, or a package managerCode signing, notarisation, and a channel strategy are launch blockers, not details
UpdatesPushedPulled, per user, on their scheduleThere must be a minimum supported version, and a way to enforce it server-side
Install frictionNone — type a URLHigh: download, verify, install, grant permissionsConversion at this step is the largest single drop-off in a desktop product’s funnel
// The consequence that bites first: an update you cannot force.
//
// In March 2026 you shipped v4 and changed the wire format. In July a security
// advisory requires clients to send an auth token with every request. Users on
// v3 are 40% of your install base and they will not update for six months.
//
// Therefore the protocol is versioned and the server accepts both, for as
// long as the old version is in the field:

function authenticate(req: Request): Principal {
  const clientVersion = req.headers.get('x-client-version');  // e.g. "3.8.1"

  if (isAtLeast(clientVersion, '4.0.0')) {
    // Modern clients present a token. This is the preferred path.
    return verifyBearer(req);
  }

  // Legacy clients: the older scheme, with a hard deprecation deadline.
  // Log it, so you can see the population shrink rather than guess.
  metrics.increment('auth.legacy_path', { version: clientVersion });
  return verifyLegacySharedSecret(req);
}

// And the enforcement valve, which is the part most teams never build and
// then all need:
const MIN_SUPPORTED = '3.9.0';
if (isOlderThan(clientVersion, MIN_SUPPORTED)) {
  // Refuse the request, but return something the client can act on. A bare
  // 426 with no guidance produces a support call, not an update.
  return Response.json(
    { 'code': 'client_outdated',
      'minimumVersion': MIN_SUPPORTED,
      'updateUrl': 'https://example.com/download',
      'forceUpdate': true },
    { status: 426, headers: { 'x-min-version': MIN_SUPPORTED } }
  );
}

// The design rule that follows: the client is a distributed system you do
// not control. Treat every version you have ever shipped as simultaneously
// live, and design the protocol so that is survivable rather than exceptional.

13.2 Native, cross-platform, hybrid and web-tech options

Four families, distinguished by what is compiled and where the UI toolkit comes from. Each has a real cost, and each cost is a specific class of problem rather than a vague quality difference.

FamilyExamplesUI isBest atCosts you accept
Native, per platformSwift + SwiftUI / UIKit on macOS and iOS; C# + WinUI 3 / WPF on Windows; GTK 4, Qt on LinuxReal platform widgetsPlatform integration, accessibility, native feel, smallest memory and best input latencyThree codebases. Three teams or three skills. Three release trains. Divergent features within a quarter
Cross-platform, native UI.NET MAUI 10, Flutter 3.4x, Kotlin Multiplatform 3.x, Qt 6, Rust + egui/icedEither real platform widgets, or a drawn canvasOne codebase, native fidelity, one teamThe lowest-common-denominator platform API; widget parity gaps; a new abstraction layer to learn and to debug
Cross-platform, drawn UIFlutter (Impeller/Skia), Tauri 2 with a web UI, Unity for tooling appsA canvas you draw intoPixel-identical across platforms, rich custom graphics, consistent renderingNo real platform widgets. Native accessibility, text input, IME and screen-reader behaviour must be re-implemented per platform, and this is where the work actually goes
Web technology in a shellTauri 2, Electron 4x, Neutralino, Wails 3, CEF/Chromium Embedded FrameworkHTML, CSS, JavaScript in an embedded engineWeb-team skills, instant UI iteration, a huge ecosystem, one renderer processMemory per window, a Chromium update treadmill, and a security surface of exactly the size of a browser
// The Tauri 2 model, because it is the most interesting of the four and the
// decision most teams get wrong. Rust owns the system; the web view is a
// thin presentation layer with no privileges of its own.
//
//   ┌──────────── Rust side ────────────┐  ┌── Web view ──┐
//   │  filesystem, OS APIs, DB, crypto  │⇄ │  HTML/CSS/JS │
//   │  updater, signing, native menus   │  │  no fs, no  │
//   │  no DOM, no Node                 │  │  net, no Node│
//   └──────────────────────────────────┘  └─────────────┘
//
// The capability model is the security model. Nothing is reachable from the
// web view until the Rust side grants it, per window, per command.

// src-tauri/tauri.conf.json  — the allow-list is explicit and narrow.
{
  "$schema": "https://schema.tauri.app/config/2",
  "productName": "Example",
  "version": "1.4.0",
  "app": {
    "windows": [{
      "label": "main",
      "title": "Example",
      "width": 1200, "height": 800,
      "minWidth": 720, "minHeight": 480,
      "titleBarStyle": "Overlay",   // modern Windows / macOS chrome
      "visible": false                          // shown on ready, to avoid a white flash
    }],
    "security": {
      "csp": "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; object-src 'none'",
      "capabilities": ["main-capability"]
    }
  },
  "bundle": {
    "active": true,
    "targets": ["dmg", "msi", "appimage", "deb"],
    "createUpdaterArtifacts": true,          // required for auto-update
    "macOS": { "signingIdentity": "Developer ID Application: …" },
    "windows": { "certificateThumbprint": "…" }
  }
}

// The Rust command. Every one of these is an explicit capability crossing.
#[tauri::command]
fn read_document(path: String, state: State<AppState>) -> Result<String, Error> {
    // Validate the path against the user's chosen documents directory.
    // An unvalidated path from the web view is arbitrary file read, and the
    // capability model does not protect you from your own frontend.
    let allowed = state.documents_root.canonicalize()?;
    let target  = std::path::Path::new(&path).canonicalize()?;
    if !target.starts_with(&allowed) {
        return Err(Error::OutsideSandbox);
    }
    std::fs::read_to_string(target).map_err(Error::Io)
}

// Frontend side: it has no fs, no network and no Node. Everything it can do
// is the set of commands the Rust side registered.
import { invoke } from '@tauri-apps/api/core';
const text = await invoke('read_document', { path: selectedPath });

The honest comparison, scored against the requirements that actually decide desktop projects. Read the right-hand column first: for most products the deciding factor is not the framework, it is whether you can ship a signed, updating build for all three platforms at all.

OptionWindowsmacOSLinuxMemoryNative feelAccess. a11yInstall sizeOne codebase?

.NET 10 + Avalonia 11✓ Best✓ Good✓ Good✓ ~90 MB✓ Good○ Partial✓ ~90 MB self-contained✓ Yes
.NET 10 MAUI 10✓ WinUI✓ Native△ No official△ Medium✓ Good○ Varies△ ~90 MB✓ Mostly
Flutter 3.4x desktop✓ Yes✓ Yes✓ Yes○ ~120 MB△ Drawn, consistent○ Needs work○ ~90 MB + engine✓ Yes

Reading the Linux column carefully. Linux is where desktop projects discover they have no plan. There is no single "the app store", no single packaging format, and the distribution method determines your user base. An AppImage requires the user to make a file executable; a deb requires admin rights and knowledge of the distro; Flatpak and Snap impose a sandbox you must design for and pay a bandwidth cost to; a tarball assumes the user reads documentation. If Linux is more than a few percent of your audience, the packaging and update story needs a decision of its own, made before launch, because retrofitting it means a new distribution channel and a new update mechanism.

13.4 The web-view option and its costs

Embedding a browser engine is enormously productive and has a specific, well-understood cost profile. The cost is not performance in the way people fear; it is that you have taken on the security posture, update treadmill and memory behaviour of a browser while also taking on the full responsibility of an application.

// The genuine advantages, which are large and should be stated honestly.
//
// 1. You get the entire web platform for free: layout engine, text shaping with
//    correct bidirectional and complex-script behaviour, compositing, input
//    handling, IME, and a mature accessibility tree. Reimplementing screen-reader
//    support for a custom-drawn UI is months of work per platform.
// 2. Your existing team already knows it. For a team of web engineers this is
//    the difference between a product in six months and a product in eighteen.
// 3. UI iteration is immediate. No compile, no link, and the dev loop is a reload.
// 4. One codebase reaches three platforms, and the fourth is a build target.

// The genuine costs, and they are structural rather than incidental.
//
// 1. RENDERER MEMORY. Every window owns a renderer. Electron's baseline is
//    ~150 MB for a near-empty window, and it scales with the page. A user with
//    six windows open has spent a gigabyte before doing any work. Tauri avoids
//    this by using the OS's own web view — which reintroduces the renderer's
//    variability, since it is now whatever the user's OS provides.
//
// 2. THE ENGINE TREADMILL. Chromium ships security fixes on a schedule, and an
//    embedded engine must be updated on that schedule or you are shipping a
//    known-vulnerable browser to your users. That is an ongoing obligation that
//    does not exist if you use the system web view.
//
// 3. ATTACK SURFACE. The renderer is the least-trusted component in your
//    process tree, and it is rendering content that may include remote data.
//    Disable everything it does not need. In Electron specifically:
//      contextIsolation: true          ← non-negotiable
//      nodeIntegration: false          ← non-negotiable
//      sandbox: true                   ← non-negotiable
//      webSecurity: true               ← do not disable it for a CORS problem
//    Tauri enforces these by default, which is the substantive security
//    argument for it over a hand-configured Electron app.
//
// 4. NATIVE BEHAVIOUR IS YOUR PROBLEM. Window chrome, menus, accelerators,
//    drag-and-drop with OS file managers, the taskbar, the dock, the tray,
//    file dialogs, drag-and-drop of files onto the icon, and the OS's own
//    light/dark preference all need explicit integration per platform.

// The rule of thumb that survives: choose a web view when your team is a web
// team and your UI is form-and-list shaped. Choose native widgets when your
// product is a first-class citizen of a platform — a pro audio tool, a
// CAD tool, anything where a user will compare it to the platform's own
// applications and judge it on that basis.

13.5 Multi-process, and where the process boundary goes

Unlike a browser tab, a desktop application is not automatically isolated. Where you place process boundaries determines what a crash costs, what a hang costs, and what a user can be blocked from doing. This is a design decision, not a default.

// The three architectures, and what each one costs when it fails.
//
// SINGLE PROCESS
//   one address space; everything shares a heap and an event loop
//   ✓ simplest; lowest memory; easiest to reason about
//   ✗ one slow operation blocks the whole UI and the user cannot even cancel
//   ✗ one crash loses unsaved state, always
//   Use it when the work is genuinely trivial: a viewer, a launcher, a config app.
//
// PROCESS PER CONCERN  (the default for anything real)
//   UI process  — must never block. Zero heavy work, ever.
//   worker(s)   — CPU and IO. One per core, or a pool. Killable.
//   updater     — separate, so an update cannot corrupt the running app
//   ✓ a hung parse takes down a worker, not the window
//   ✓ a renderer crash is recoverable with state preserved on disk
//   ✓ memory pressure in a worker does not freeze the UI
//   ✗ IPC becomes a real design surface: serialisation, backpressure,
//      cancellation, and what happens when the worker dies mid-message
//
// PROCESS PER WINDOW
//   one renderer per window, a shared broker for the state they all need
//   ✓ isolation and memory reclaim when a window closes
//   ✗ every shared value must go through the broker, and the broker is now the
//      single point of contention and failure in the whole application
//   Use it when windows are genuinely independent documents — a tabbed editor,
//   a file manager, a multi-document workspace.

// The rule that actually matters, and it is a UI requirement not a technical one:
//   THE UI PROCESS MUST NEVER BLOCK.
//   If the main thread does disk IO, decompression, parsing or crypto, the
//   window stops responding, the OS offers to kill it, and the user loses work.
//   Every one of those goes to a worker, and the UI process only ever does:
//     - paint and layout
//     - dispatch input
//     - receive already-computed results

// Detecting the violation: instrument the UI thread's longest task.
// A "blocked for 900 ms" in your own telemetry is the defect report.
function watchMainThreadStalls(onStall: (ms: number) => void) {
  let last = performance.now();
  const tick = () => {
    const now = performance.now();
    const delta = now - last;
    if (delta > 50) onStall(delta);      // 50 ms is already a visible hitch
    last = now;
    requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  };
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}

13.6 A selection procedure

Five questions, in order, each with a determinate answer. The first one eliminates the majority of options for most products.

1. Does this need to be a desktop application at all? The honest test is offline, filesystem, or hardware. If the product works fine in a tab and the user will not accept a download, a PWA or a web app is the cheaper answer by an enormous margin, and you have just saved a year of distribution work. Say yes to desktop only if the answer is genuinely yes — this is the question that most often gets answered emotionally.

2. Does it need to interoperate with the operating system in a way widgets cannot? Kernel extensions, drivers, low-latency audio, a global hotkey system, deep filesystem work, a background service that runs when the app is closed. If yes, you need native code on at least one platform and probably all three.

3. What is your team’s actual skill set? Not what you would like to hire. A team of five web engineers will build a better product in Tauri or Electron in six months than in three sets of native code in eighteen, and this is not a close call — it is the difference between shipping and not shipping.

4. Is the user base on Linux, and what share? Under 5%: ship a .deb and an AppImage, document it, and move on. Over 20%: the Linux story becomes a first-class requirement and Flatpak or a system package needs to be designed for, not bolted on.

5. What is the smallest version that could be useful? Write down its feature list. Now check: can you ship and sign and update all three platforms within one quarter? If not, cut platforms from the first release rather than from the second. A Windows-and-macOS product in market beats a three-platform product in a repository.

The most common desktop mistake is the one the framework choice hides. Teams pick a framework, build the UI, and only then discover that updating is unsolved — no updater, no signing identity, no channel strategy, no minimum-supported-version mechanism. By that point the architecture is committed and the update path has to retrofit around a renderer, a process model and a state layout that were never designed with rollback in mind. Choose the updater and signing approach in the same decision as the framework, because they constrain the same things: where state lives, whether the binary is signed, and how a partially-completed update is recovered.

Exercises 13

  1. Take an existing desktop product you use and identify its framework, its process model, and its update channel. Then determine how many weeks of stale versions it is running, from its release history. That number is the strongest argument for or against the architecture.
  2. Build the same single-window application in Tauri 2, in Electron, and in one native stack. Measure idle memory, cold-start time, and install size for each, and record the three numbers side by side. The spread is usually wider than expected.
  3. Write a capability allow-list for a Tauri or Electron application and audit every permission against whether the feature that needs it still exists. Remove the rest, then verify the application still builds and its features still work.
  4. Implement a minimum-supported-version gate on your API, return 426 with an actionable body, and write the client-side handling for it. Then measure what happens when a user on an old version tries to do work: do they get a clear upgrade prompt or a support ticket?
  5. Instrument your application’s main thread for stalls and deliberately introduce a 500 ms synchronous operation. Watch the window become unresponsive and the OS offer to kill it, then move the work to a worker and measure the difference.
  6. For each platform you plan to ship, write down the exact signing identity, the notarisation or store submission process, the package format, and the expected lead time. Sum the lead times. If it exceeds a quarter, that is a launch date you need to know about now.

14 · Desktop Track: Platform APIs, Packaging and Native Integration

14.1 The filesystem, paths and the data directory14.2 Permissions, entitlements and the sandbox14.3 Code signing and notarisation14.4 The updater14.5 Native integration: menus, tray, hotkeys and protocols14.6 Single instance, deep links and file associations

A desktop application runs on someone else’s machine, which means it must be trusted, it must find its files, it must ask permission correctly, and it must update itself without asking questions the user cannot answer. These are the mechanics that separate a program that installs from a product that ships, and every one of them is a launch blocker if it is left late.

14.1 The filesystem, paths and the data directory

The single most common source of user data loss in a desktop application is writing state to the wrong place and then overwriting it during an update. The correct locations are platform-specific, and hard-coding one of them is a bug waiting for a Windows user.

WhatWindowsmacOSLinuxBacked up?Delete with app?
Application codeProgram Files\ (admin)/Applications/usr/lib, /optNoYes
User configuration%APPDATA%\Vendor\App\~/Library/Application Support/$XDG_CONFIG_HOME (default ~/.config)NoNo
User data, documents%LOCALAPPDATA% or the user’s Documents~/Library/Application Support/, or Documents for real documents$XDG_DATA_HOME (default ~/.local/share)NoNo — or you delete a user’s work
Cache, safe to delete%LOCALAPPDATA%\Vendor\App\Cache~/Library/Caches/$XDG_CACHE_HOME (default ~/.cache)NoYes
Logs%LOCALAPPDATA%\…\Logs~/Library/Logs/$XDG_STATE_HOME or ~/.local/stateNoYes
// Get the directories from the platform rather than constructing them. Every
// library here has a "where does this platform want it" function; using it is
// free and constructing the path by hand is a bug on some platform.

// Rust — the directories crate, which implements the XDG spec and the macOS
// and Windows conventions.
use directories::ProjectDirs;

fn data_dir() -> std::path::PathBuf {
    let d = ProjectDirs::from("com", "Example", "Example").expect("home dir");

    // data_local_dir → %LOCALAPPDATA% | ~/Library/Application Support | ~/.local/share
    // cache_dir       → %LOCALAPPDATA%\Cache | ~/Library/Caches    | ~/.cache
    // config_dir      → %APPDATA%         | ~/Library/Application Support/… | ~/.config
    //
    // CRITICAL: create the directory with user-only permissions. On a shared
    // machine a world-readable settings directory is a local privilege
    // escalation, and on macOS it is what the "App Support" ACL exists for.
    let path = d.data_local_dir().join("workspace");
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&path).expect("create data dir");
    #[cfg(unix)]
    {
        use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;
        std::fs::set_permissions(&path, std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(0o700))
            .expect("chmod");
    }
    path
}

// Atomic writes. A power cut during a non-atomic write leaves a truncated
// file, and for a settings or database file that means the app will not start
// and the user has lost their configuration permanently.
fn write_atomic(path: &std::path::Path, bytes: &[u8]) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let tmp = path.with_extension("tmp");
    std::fs::write(&tmp, bytes)?;                 // 1. write beside the target
    std::fs::File::create(&tmp)?.sync_all()?;       // 2. fsync: it is on disk, not in a buffer
    std::fs::rename(&tmp, path)?;                  // 3. rename is atomic on POSIX and NTFS
    // Never truncate the original and write into it. That is the bug.
    Ok(())
}

// The state that must never be in the app directory, because the updater
// replaces that directory wholesale:
//   ✗ Program Files\Example\settings.json    ← gone on every update
//   ✗ the app bundle's own Resources folder     ← code-signed, so writing breaks it
//   ✓ the per-user data directory above

// A versioned directory with a migration, which is what a schema change
// actually looks like in a shipped product.
fn open_store() -> anyhow::Result<Store> {
    let dir = data_dir().join("store");
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir)?;

    // CURRENT names the live directory. A migration is: build the new
    // directory, verify it, then flip a single pointer. If anything fails,
    // the old directory is still the one CURRENT points at.
    //
    //   store/CURRENT          → "v3"
    //   store/v2/              → the old, untouched store
    //   store/v3.tmp/          → being built
    //   store/v3/              → complete, verified
    //   store/v2.bak/          → retained for one release, then removed
    std::fs::write(dir.join("CURRENT"), "v3")?;
    Ok(Store::open(dir))
}

14.2 Permissions, entitlements and the sandbox

The permission model is different on every platform, and the trend is toward more restriction rather than less. A product that is designed as though it has full access will be forced into a redesign by a store review, and the redesign happens after launch.

PlatformModelWhat the user seesDesign consequence
macOSHardened runtime + App Sandbox; TCC prompts for protected folders and device accessA one-time dialog per category, naming the app and the reason, with an "Open System Settings" affordance if deniedEntitlements must be declared at signing time. Plan for the user saying no, and for the denial being permanent-looking
WindowsUAC elevation, plus per-capability ACLs and the Windows Defender Application Control policyA UAC prompt at install if elevated, then a firewall prompt for listening socketsDo not require elevation at runtime. Request it at install, and run the app unprivileged thereafter
LinuxFilesystem permissions, portals (XDG), polkit for privileged operations, package-manager sandboxingVaries by desktop and by packaging. Flatpak and Snap are the most restrictiveUse the XDG portal API for file access, so a Flatpak build works without a redesign
All threeNetwork access, microphone, camera, notifications, accessibility APIsSeparate prompts, each independently deniableEvery prompt is a conversion loss. Ask at the moment of use, never at launch, and degrade fully when denied
// The rule: ask at the moment of use, with a reason, and have a working
// fallback for the denial. Launch-time permission prompts train users to
// to click "deny" without reading, and you have lost the permission forever.
//
//   ✗ on startup:  "Allow Example to access your microphone?  [Allow] [Deny]"
//   ✓ on use:       the user clicks Record. Then:
//                   "Example needs microphone access to record your voice note."
//                   [Allow microphone access]  [Not now]  [How to enable it in Settings]
//
// And the denial path is part of the feature, not an error message:
async function ensureMicrophone(): Promise<boolean> {
  if (await hasPermission('microphone')) return true;

  const result = await requestPermission({
    kind: 'microphone',
    reason: 'to record the voice note you asked for',   // shown verbatim
  });

  if (result === 'granted') return true;

  if (result === 'permanently-denied') {
    // The OS will not ask again. Only a trip to System Settings helps, so
    //   say so plainly and give the exact path, rather than asking again and
    //   appearing broken.
    showDialog({
      title: 'Microphone access is turned off',
      body:  'To re-enable it: System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone, then turn on Example.',
      actions: ['Open System Settings', 'Cancel'],
    });
    return false;
  }

  // A plain "denied" is not permanent. Record that we asked, and offer the
  // feature in a reduced form rather than a dead end.
  state.microphoneDeclined = true;
  return false;   // → caller shows the file-import path instead
}

// The macOS entitlement set, declared at signing time. Anything not here is
