// denied, so this file is a design document, not a formality.
<key>com.apple.security.app-sandbox</key>              <true/>
<key>com.apple.security.network.client</key>            <true/>
<key>com.apple.security.network.server</key>            <true/>   <c>← only if you listen locally</c>
<key>com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-write</key> <true/>   <c>← the open/save dialog, the ONLY way in</c>
<key>com.apple.security.files.bookmarks.app-scope</key> <true/>   <c>← persist access to a chosen folder</c>

The security-scoped bookmark is the feature most products forget. A sandboxed macOS app gets access to a folder the user chose, for that session. To keep it across launches, you must persist a security-scoped bookmark and call startAccessingSecurityScopedResource() on use, with a matching stopAccessing…. Without this, the user picks a folder, closes the app, reopens it, and the folder is simply gone — and because the permission was granted correctly, this failure is invisible in testing on a single run.

14.3 Code signing and notarisation

Unsigned software does not install on modern macOS and is treated as suspect on Windows. Signing is not a launch formality; it is the mechanism by which the operating system expresses trust, and every stage of the pipeline depends on it existing.

// macOS: two separate steps, and confusing them wastes a week.
//
// 1. CODE SIGNING — a cryptographic signature over the binary, made with a
//    "Developer ID Application" certificate. Proves it came from you and has
//    not been modified since.
codesign --force --deep \
         --options runtime \                    <c>← enables the Hardened Runtime</c>
         --timestamp \                         <c>← notarisation requires a secure timestamp</c>
         --entitlements entitlements.plist \
         --sign "Developer ID Application: Example Ltd (TEAMID)" \
         "Example.app"

// 2. NOTARISATION — you submit to Apple, and a human or an automated check
//    confirms the signature is valid and the binary contains no known
//    malware. The stapled ticket is then attached so the app verifies offline.
ditto -c -k --keepParent "Example.app" Example.zip
xcrun notarytool submit Example.zip \
     --apple-id "dev@example.com" \
     --team-id "TEAMID" \
     --password "$APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD" \
     --wait                          <c>← blocks until approved or rejected</c>
xcrun stapler staple "Example.app"
xcrun stapler validate "Example.app"

// Order matters and the failure modes are specific:
//   no --timestamp  → notarisation is refused
//   no --options runtime → Gatekeeper refuses on launch
//   not stapled → the first launch of every offline user is slow and
//                needs network access they may not have
//   inner binaries not signed → the whole bundle is rejected; sign inside-out
//   (frameworks, then helpers, then the app) and use --deep sparingly, since it
//   can mask a wrongly-ordered signature

// Windows: two entirely different signing models.
//
//   Authenticode — a certificate over the executable. Cheap OV certs are
//   widely distrusted and SmartScreen still warns on first download, because
//   reputation is per-publisher and takes downloads to build.
signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 \
         /f certificate.pfx /p "$PFX_PASSWORD" "Example.exe"

//   Store signing — required for MSIX and for Microsoft Store distribution,
//   and it is a different trust relationship enforced by Windows at install.
signtool sign /fd SHA256 /td SHA256 /a /f "Example.msix.pfx" "Example.msix"

// Linux: no equivalent. Package signatures are verified by the package
// manager against the repository's key, and there is no OS-level trust
// prompt at all. Signing is a distribution concern, not a platform one.

// CI: the certificate must never be in the repository or the runner image.
//
//   macOS: import into a temporary keychain, and delete the keychain in an
//     "always" step — a leaked keychain in a cached runner is a leaked identity.
security create-keychain -p "$MACOS_KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD" build.keychain
security set-keychain-settings -lut 21600 build.keychain
security unlock-keychain -p "$MACOS_KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD" build.keychain
security import "$P12_PATH" -k build.keychain -P "$P12_PASSWORD" -T /usr/bin/codesign
security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple:,codesign: \
        -s -k "$MACOS_KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD" build.keychain
#   Windows: the signing certificate in a secret store, with the sign step
#     as a separate, auditable job rather than part of the build.

14.4 The updater

The updater is the highest-stakes component in a desktop product. It runs with the user’s permissions, it replaces the running application, and a failure is a bricked installation on a machine you cannot reach. It must be a separate process, it must be transactional, and it must be able to undo itself.

// The four requirements, and what happens without each.
//
// 1. IT IS A SEPARATE PROCESS. It must survive the app quitting, and the app
//    must not be able to corrupt it. An updater that lives inside the app being
//    updated cannot finish updating it.
//
// 2. THE REPLACEMENT IS TRANSACTIONAL. Old binary is kept until the new one has
//    launched successfully and reported back.
//
//   install/
//     Example.exe            ← the running binary
//     Example.exe.old        ← retained for rollback
//     Example.new.exe        ← staged, verified, not yet in place
//     .update-state.json      ← {"stage":"verified","version":"1.5.0"}
//
//   Sequence on next launch:
//     stage=new_verified  → rename new → current, keep old, record "launched"
//     stage=launched      → app started OK → delete .old, stage=complete
//     stage=launched AND  → the app crashed during startup → restore .old,
//       crash-loop detected      stage=rolled_back, and report the failure
//     stage=staged         → never launched → nothing to do
//
// 3. THE MANIFEST IS SIGNED, and the signature is verified before anything is
//    executed. An update channel over HTTPS is not sufficient: a compromised
//    build server, a hijacked DNS, or a bad CDN edge all deliver a valid
//    download of the wrong bytes.

//    The manifest, signed with a key that is NOT the build server's key.
{
  "version": "1.5.0",
  "releasedAt": "2026-09-28T10:00:00Z",
  "minSupportedVersion": "1.2.0",
  "channel": "stable",
  "mandatory": false,               // forced update, for a security fix
  "notes": "Fixes a crash on export. No migration required.",
  "platforms": [{
    "os": "macos", "arch": "aarch64",
    "url": "https://cdn.example.com/1.5.0/Example-aarch64.dmg",
    "size": 8412893,
    "sha256": "9f3c…",
    "deltas": [                                    // from-version → patch
      { "from": "1.4.2", "url": "…/1.4.2→1.5.0.patch", "size": 412000 },
      { "from": "1.4.0", "url": "…/1.4.0→1.5.0.patch", "size": 418000 }
    ]
  }],
  "signature": "base64:MEUCIQ…"            // over everything above, canonically encoded
}

// 4. IT IS SILENT BY DEFAULT. An updater that surprises the user is worse
//    than no updater. Download quietly, install on a natural boundary
//    (app quit, or idle), and tell the user what changed afterwards.

// Delta updates, and when they are worth the complexity.
//
//   A full 90 MB installer: ~2 minutes on a good connection, and it is the
//   second-largest step in the conversion funnel after the initial install.
//   A 400 KB patch: ~1 second.
//
//   Do NOT invent a delta format. Use a standard block-based one — bsdiff and
//   bsdiff4, or zstd with --patch-from, which is a bsdiff-compatible format —
//   and generate patches for the last N versions only. The economics: below about
//   20% of users, the saving does not justify the generation pipeline and the
//   class of corruption bug it introduces.
//
//   Whatever the format, the patched artefact must be byte-identical to the full
//   artefact. Verify the hash after applying, always, and fall back to the full
//   download on any mismatch. A corrupt patch that installs is unrecoverable.

14.5 Native integration: menus, tray, hotkeys and protocols

The features that make an application feel native rather than embedded. Each is a small amount of platform-specific work, and each is disproportionately visible: users judge a desktop product on whether the menu is where they expect it.

// The application menu, which differs per platform and is checked by every
// user in the first ten seconds. The conventions are not interchangeable.
//
//   macOS: the app menu is first and its title is the app name. Quit is ⌘Q.
//           Window and Help have fixed positions. Preferences is ⌘, (comma).
//   Windows: File/Edit/View/Help, Alt to reveal, and Settings in File.
//            Alt+F4 quits, F1 is help. No application menu at all.
//   Linux: whatever the desktop environment defines, and it varies by DE.
//
// Getting this wrong is a "this feels like a website" signal that costs more
// than any visual decision in this guide.

// System tray, and the three rules that make it acceptable.
//   1. It is an ENHANCEMENT. The app must be fully usable with the tray closed.
//   2. It is NEVER the only way to quit. Users will close the window, assume it
//      quit, and be unable to find it again. This is the single most common
//      desktop support ticket.
//   3. It survives a failed state. If the app is in a broken state, the tray menu
//      is the user's only way to reach the log window and the repair option.

// Tauri: a tray with a menu, and a quit that is always reachable.
#[tauri::menu]
pub fn tray_menu(app: &AppHandle) -> Result<Menu<R>> {
    let open  = MenuItem::with_id(app, "open", "Open Example", true, None::<&str>)?;
    let logs  = MenuItem::with_id(app, "logs", "Open Log Folder", true, None::<&str>)?;
    let sep   = PredefinedMenuItem::separator(app)?;
    let quit  = MenuItem::with_id(app, "quit", "Quit Example", true, None::<&str>)?;
    Menu::with_items(app, &[&open, &logs, &sep, &quit])
}

// Global hotkeys. Register them, and handle the case where the OS already has
// them — a silent failure here means the feature simply does not work for some
// users, with no error anywhere.
#[tauri::command]
fn register_shortcut(app: AppHandle, accelerator: String) -> Result<(), Error> {
    use tauri_plugin_global_shortcut::{Code, Modifiers, ShortcutState};
    let shortcut = tauri_plugin_global_shortcut::Shortcut::from_str(&accelerator)
        .map_err(|e| Error::BadShortcut(e.to_string()))?;
    if shortcut.matches(Modifiers::CONTROL | Modifiers::ALT, Code::KeyS) {
        // Predictively check the common conflicting bindings so you can say
        // something useful instead of failing silently at run time.
    }
    app.global_shortcut().on_shortcut(shortcut, move |_app, _s, event| {
        if event.state() == ShortcutState::Pressed { emit_capture(); }
    }).map_err(|e| Error::AlreadyRegistered(e.to_string()))
}

// Custom URL scheme, which is how another application can open a document in
// yours. It is a deep link and a security surface at the same time.
//
// macOS Info.plist:  CFBundleURLTypes → CFBundleURLSchemes → ["example"]
// Windows:  HKCU\Software\Classes\example\shell\open\command
// Linux:    a .desktop file with MimeType=x-scheme-handler/example
//
//   example://open?doc=abc123&mode=edit
//
// The security rules, because a URL scheme handler is unauthenticated input
// from any application on the machine:
//   1. Treat every parameter as hostile. It is attacker-controlled by definition.
//   2. Never auto-execute anything. Opening a document is fine; "run this
//      command" is not a URL scheme.
//   3. Never pass a raw parameter to a shell. No string concatenation, ever.
//   4. If the URL can name a local file, resolve it and confirm it is inside a
//      directory the user has authorised. Otherwise it is arbitrary file read.
//   5. If the app is already running, do not start a second instance to handle it.
//      See the next section.

14.6 Single instance, deep links and file associations

Three features that are simple individually and interact badly. Together they are the difference between an application that behaves predictably when the user double-clicks a file twice and one that opens eleven windows.

// Single instance. The requirement is not "only one process" — it is "one
// process, and the second launch hands its arguments to the first".
//
//   The user double-clicking a file in a file manager must focus the existing
//   window and open the document there. Starting a new process is the bug.

// Tauri single-instance plugin: the FIRST instance becomes the primary and
// receives the argv of every subsequent launch.
.plugin(tauri_plugin_single_instance::init(|app, argv, _cwd| {
    // A second launch is a request to open something. Focus first, so the
    // window is in front before the document loads.
    if let Some(w) = app.get_webview_window("main") {
        let _ = w.unminimize();
        let _ = w.show();
        let _ = w.set_focus();
    }
    // Then handle whatever the second launch was asked to do.
    for arg in argv.iter().skip(1) {
        // Two forms: a file path (double-click) and a URL (deep link).
        if arg.starts_with("example://") {
            if let Some(doc_id) = parse_deep_link(arg) {
                window.emit("open-document", doc_id);
            }
        } else if std::path::Path::new(arg).is_file() {
            window.emit("open-path", arg);
        }
    }
}))

// File associations. Declared per platform, and the association is with a
// TYPE, not with a specific application. On macOS, in particular, the user
// picks the default app and it is not yours to override.
//
// macOS Info.plist
CFBundleDocumentTypes:
  - CFBundleTypeName: Example Document
    CFBundleTypeRole: Editor
    LSHandlerRank: Owner            ← Owner | Alternate | Default. Getting
    LSItemContentTypes: [com.example.document]     this wrong is a rejection.</c>
// UTExportedTypeDeclarations
    UTTypeIdentifier: com.example.document
    UTTypeConformsTo: public.data, public.content
    UTTypeTagSpecification: { public.filename-extension: [example], public.mime-type: [application/x-example] }

// The trap that costs a day: macOS delivers "open with" for a file the app
// has never seen, from a path it was not given access to. The launch path
// is the Apple Event handler, not argv, and the sandboxed app must have a
// user-selected read-write entitlement AND must have been given the file by
// the Launch Services open call, which it has. If you are reading argv[1], you
// will work for drag-and-drop and never for Finder double-click.

// Windows, the same feature, three mechanisms:
//   1. The registry, under HKCU\Software\Classes\.example
    "Example Document" = "Example.Document.1"
    "Example.Document.1" = {
        (Default) = "Example Document"
        "DefaultIcon" = ""C:\Program Files\Example\Example.exe,0""
    }
    shell\open\command = (Default) = ""C:\Program Files\Example\Example.exe" "%1""

//   2. A file type in the installer. MSIX declares it declaratively, which is
//      why MSIX installs are atomic and per-user by default.
//   3. Command-line argument parsing, which is what a file association produces.
//      GetCommandLineW and parse with CommandLineToArgvW — do not split on spaces.
//      A filename containing spaces is not an edge case; it is most of them.

// The state that must survive all of this:
//
//   A window is closing but the user has 4 unsaved documents.
//   Do not silently save, and do not silently discard. Three options, and the
//   user must be able to tell which one is happening before it happens:
//     - Save all, then close
//     - Close and keep drafts in a recovery folder, with a visible marker on
//       reopen (this is what most editors do, and it is the humane answer)
//     - Cancel, and tell the user what would be lost
//
//   And a crash must not lose the buffer. Write a recovery snapshot on a timer
//   and on every edit debounce, into the app's data directory, never into the
//   install directory, and offer to restore it on the next launch.

Exercises 14

  1. Write a small application that writes to each of the four platform-standard locations, and verify the paths on all three operating systems. Then break it deliberately: put a settings file in the app bundle and run an update, and document what the user experiences.
  2. Replace every non-atomic write in your application with write-to-temp, fsync, rename. Then simulate a power loss by killing the process mid-write, repeatedly, and confirm the original file is always intact and readable.
  3. Request every permission your application uses, one at a time, at the moment of use with a stated reason. Write a real fallback for each denial and test both paths. Record the prompt copy — it is part of the product.
  4. Set up code signing and notarisation for all three platforms in CI. Deliberately build one unsigned and one un-notarised artefact, and record the exact user-facing failure on each platform. That failure is what you are preventing.
  5. Implement the transactional updater with the staged/verified/launched/rolled-back state machine. Test it against: a corrupt download, a full disk mid-extract, an app that crashes on first launch, and a user who quarantines the process mid-update.
  6. Add single-instance handling with argument forwarding, a file association for one custom type, and a example:// URL scheme. Then double-click the file type five times in a row and confirm you get one window with five documents, not five windows.
  7. Build the global shortcut registration and handle the already-registered case. Test it on a machine where another application owns the shortcut, and verify the user gets a clear message rather than a feature that silently does nothing.

15 · Desktop Track: Offline, Synchronisation and Performance

15.1 The offline contract15.2 Local storage and the data layer on disk15.3 Sync engines: last-write-wins, vectors and CRDTs15.4 Conflict resolution in practice15.5 Performance: cold start, memory, input latency and battery15.6 Crash reporting without over-collecting

A desktop application has a network connection that is slow, intermittent, captive, metered and occasionally hostile, and the user knows it. The product’s behaviour on a bad connection is therefore not an edge case — it is the ordinary case, and designing for it up front is far cheaper than retrofitting. This chapter covers the offline contract, the local data layer, the synchronisation design, and the performance budget that a desktop product has and a web page does not.

15.1 The offline contract

"Works offline" is not a feature; it is a set of specific promises, each of which has a different implementation cost. Deciding which promises you are making is the first task, and the answer determines the entire data architecture that follows.

PromiseWhat the user getsImplementation costCorrect for
Offline is an error stateA clear message; nothing works without a connection✓ Almost freeTools with no meaningful local state: a dashboard, a viewer, a chat client with history
Read-only offlineEverything already fetched is readable; writes are blocked✓ Low — a local cache with an expiry policyReference material, documentation, media libraries
Offline write with last-write-wins syncEdits are made locally and pushed when connected; the last edit wins○ Moderate — needs a local store, a queue and a conflict policyNotes, tags, settings, drafts, any field where overwriting is acceptable
Offline write with CRDT mergeConcurrent edits merge without conflict prompts△ High — a data type designed for it, and a real cost in payload sizeCollaborative documents, shared lists, counters, collaborative canvases
Full offline-first with local authorityThe local database is the source of truth; the server is a replica✗ Very high — every read and write goes through the local store, permanentlyOnly when offline is the dominant case, not the exception
// The connection state machine. A desktop app cannot assume a request either
// succeeds or fails: it can hang for two minutes, fail instantly, fail
// with a captive-portal HTML page, or succeed and return nonsense. Every
// request needs a timeout, a retry policy, and a distinction between
// "offline" and "server said no".

type Connectivity =
  | { kind: 'online';  rttMs: number }
  | { kind: 'degraded'; rttMs: number; failures: number }  // > 800 ms or intermittent
  | { kind: 'offline'; since: number; reason: string }
  | { kind: 'restricted' };  // captive portal, or metered

// Detect by actually reaching the internet, NOT by asking the OS whether
// an interface is up. A connected Wi-Fi network with a login portal reports
// "connected" at the OS layer and is not connected at all.
async function probe(): Promise<Connectivity> {
  try {
    const t0 = performance.now();
    const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/ping', {
      method: 'HEAD',
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000),        // never hang on a dead link
      cache: 'no-store',
    });
    const rtt = performance.now() - t0;

    // A captive portal returns 200 with HTML from an unrelated host.
    if (res.headers.get('content-type')?.includes('text/html')) {
      return { kind: 'restricted' };
    }
    if (rtt > 800) return { kind: 'degraded', rttMs: rtt, failures: 0 };
    return { kind: 'online', rttMs: rtt };
  } catch {
    return { kind: 'offline', since: Date.now(), reason: 'unreachable' };
  }
}

// Exponential backoff with full jitter, and a cap. Without jitter, every
// client that went offline at 09:00 reconnects at 09:00:00.1 and knocks the
// server over exactly when it comes back.
function backoffDelay(attempt: number): number {
  const base = Math.min(30_000, 1000 * 2 ** attempt);
  return Math.random() * base;          // full jitter, not "base + random"
}

// The UI consequence, which is the part that matters. Do not show a modal.
// A blocking "you are offline" dialog is a support ticket, because the
// user's answer is "I am not, my train is".
function connectivityBanner(c: Connectivity): string | null {
  switch (c.kind) {
    case 'online':    return null;
    case 'degraded':   return 'Connection is slow. Uploads are paused.';
    case 'restricted': return 'Connect to a network to sync. Everything else works.';
    case 'offline':    return 'Working offline. 4 changes will sync when you reconnect.';
  }
}

15.2 Local storage and the data layer on disk

Desktop storage is not a cache. It is the primary copy of the user’s data, it may be the only copy, and it survives indefinitely. The choice of engine follows from that, not from benchmarks.

OptionWhat it isUse whenFailure mode to plan for
SQLiteEmbedded, ACID, a real relational engine with a single fileAlmost always. Structured data, relational queries, transactions, and the ability to inspect the file with a standard tool when a user complainsOne writer at a time. WAL mode allows concurrent readers with one writer, which is nearly always enough
LMDBMemory-mapped, extremely fast, single-writer, copy-on-writeKey-value caches, config stores, very large read-mostly datasetsNo transactions beyond a single write transaction; the file grows and must be compacted
RocksDBLog-structured, LSM-tree, high write throughputVery large sequential-write workloads, append-heavy event logsCompaction pauses; a much harder store to reason about; no relational queries
LevelDBThe simpler LSM storeLegacy, and in a few embedded scenariosSingle-threaded compaction; corruption on abrupt power loss is documented
JSON or YAML filesA serialised documentSettings, a small fixed set of preferences. Nothing elseWhole-file rewrite for any change; no concurrent access; corruption on a partial write. Chapter 14.1's atomic write makes it survivable, not good
Core Data / Realm / object storesNative object graphs with change trackingApple-platform-only applications, where the platform persistence is genuinely goodTies you to one platform; migration paths are version-dependent and awkward
// SQLite configured for a desktop application, and every setting here is
// load-bearing.
let db = Connection::open(&data_dir.join("workspace.db"))?;

db.execute_batch(
"  -- WAL: concurrent readers with a single writer. This is the single
   --   biggest reason SQLite suits a desktop app at all.
   PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;

   -- NORMAL is the right durability level for a desktop app: a crash of
   --   the process loses nothing, a power cut may lose the last commits.
   --   FULL costs an fsync per transaction and is almost never warranted here.
   PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;

   -- Foreign keys are OFF by default in SQLite. Every release has been
   --   bitten by this and it is still the default.
   PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

   -- 64 MB of page cache. The default is 2 MB, which produces a surprising
   --   amount of I/O for a data set that fits comfortably in memory.
   PRAGMA cache_size = -65536;

   -- A busy timeout so concurrent access waits rather than failing with
   --   SQLITE_BUSY, which is a crash from the user's point of view.
   PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;

   -- Negative means KiB rather than pages. 8 is the recommended page size
   --   for most workloads; 4 KB is safe on every filesystem including
   --   network drives, which some users will point this at.
   PRAGMA page_size = 4096;

   -- Bound the WAL. Without this, a long session with continuous writes
   --   grows an unbounded -wal file next to the database.
   PRAGMA journal_size_limit = 67108864;
   //   And checkpoint on a schedule, from a background task.
)?;

// The schema, and the two columns that make sync and undo possible at all.
db.execute_batch(
"  CREATE TABLE document (
   "    doc_id       TEXT    PRIMARY KEY,
   "    tenant_id    TEXT    NOT NULL,
   "    title        TEXT    NOT NULL,
   "    body         TEXT    NOT NULL,
   "    -- Every row is versioned. 'server_rev' is what the server has
   "    -- acknowledged; 'local_rev' is what we have. Their difference
   "    -- IS the sync queue. Deriving the queue from this is far more
   "    --   robust than maintaining a separate one that can drift.
   "    server_rev   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   "    local_rev    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   "    dirty         INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   "    deleted_at   TEXT,
   "    updated_at   TEXT    NOT NULL
   "  );

   "  CREATE INDEX ix_document_dirty ON document(dirty, local_rev)
   "    WHERE dirty = 1;   -- partial: the queue stays tiny

   "  -- The change log. This is what makes undo, audit and 'what changed'
   "  -- possible, and it is cheap to keep and expensive to retrofit.
   "  CREATE TABLE change_log (
   "    seq        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
   "    doc_id     TEXT    NOT NULL,
   "    at         TEXT    NOT NULL,
   "    field      TEXT    NOT NULL,
   "    old_value  TEXT,
   "    new_value  TEXT
   "  );
"//  CREATE INDEX ix_changelog_doc ON change_log(doc_id, seq DESC);"
)?;

A change log is not optional, and the moment to add it is before the first release. It gives you unlimited undo, an audit trail, a sync queue, a "what changed" view, and crash recovery, all from one table. Retrofitting it onto a shipped application means either an untestable migration or accepting that the first thousand users have no undo. Write the log on every mutation, in the same transaction as the mutation itself — a log written outside the transaction is a log that can disagree with the data.

15.3 Sync engines: last-write-wins, vectors and CRDTs

Three approaches to the same problem, ordered by the consistency they provide and by the cost of that consistency. Choosing wrong here is expensive: a CRDT you did not need is a permanent tax on every payload, and last-write-wins where it was not acceptable is a data-loss bug that users report as "it deleted my work".

ApproachMechanismMetadataConvergenceUser experience on conflictCost
Last-write-winsA timestamp or a server sequence on each field; the highest winsOne timestampGuaranteed, immediatelyOne user’s edit silently disappears✓ Trivial
Server-sequencedEvery write goes to the server; it assigns an order; clients apply in that orderA revision per rowGuaranteed, after the round tripWrites are blocked while offline, or queued and reordered✓ Low, but needs connectivity
Version vectorsEach replica tracks which versions of each object it has seen; on divergence, replayA vector per replica, growingGuaranteed, after a merge passA merge is shown to the user, if it cannot be automated○ Moderate. Metadata grows with replica count
CRDTThe data type carries a merge function that is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas converge without coordinationPer-element state, often larger than the valueGuaranteed, eventually, with no central authorityUsually none — the merge is automatic and correct△ High. A large design commitment
// Last-write-wins, done properly. The important part is per-FIELD, not
// per-row: a whole-row LWW means an edit to the title silently discards a
// concurrent edit to the body, which is a data-loss bug wearing a
// synchronisation costume.
db.execute(
"  UPDATE document SET
      title       = ?1, title_rev       = ?2,   -- separate revision per field
      body        = ?3, body_rev        = ?4,
      local_rev   = local_rev + 1,
      dirty        = 1,
      updated_at  = ?5
    WHERE doc_id = ?6 AND tenant_id = ?7",
  params![title, server_rev, body, server_rev, now, doc_id, tenant_id])?;

// The push. Conditional on the revision we believed was current, so a
// concurrent write is a conflict rather than a silent overwrite.
//
//   POST /v1/documents/:id
//   If-Match: "<server_rev we last saw>"     ← the precondition
//   { "fields": { "title": "…", "body": "…" } }
//
//   200 → applied; response carries the new server_rev
//   409 → someone else changed it; response carries THEIR value and rev
//   412 → our known revision is wrong (we are behind); 409 with full state

// The 409 handler is where the product decision lives. There is no single
// right answer, and it differs per field type.
//
//   title   → last-write-wins is fine. Two people renaming a document is
//              not a collaboration problem.
//   body    → NEVER silently. Present a diff and let the user choose, or
//              merge with a three-way diff, or use a CRDT if this is a
//              collaborative editor.
//   deleted → a delete is a field with a revision like any other. A concurrent
//              edit should resurrect the document, not vanish silently, and
//              the user should be told it happened.

// A CRDT, for comparison, when the requirement genuinely justifies it. The
// merge function is the entire design: it MUST be commutative (a·b = b·a),
// associative ((a·b)·c = a·(b·c)) and idempotent (a·a = a). Any function that
// is not all three will not converge, and the bug is intermittent and
// unreproducible, which is the worst combination available.
class GSet<T> {
  // Add-only set. Trivially convergent, and the metadata is one element per add.
  readonly adds: ReadonlySet<T>;

  add(value: T): GSet<T> {
    return new GSet(new Set([...this.adds, value]));
  }
  // Union: commutative ✓ associative ✓ idempotent ✓
  merge(other: GSet<T>): GSet<T> {
    return new GSet(new Set([...this.adds, ...other.adds]));
  }
}

// A grow-only counter has the same three properties, so three offline devices
// incrementing a counter all converge to the sum with no coordination and
// no conflict prompt. The metadata is a per-device set of observed counts.
//
// The LSEQ counter is the general case: an add/remove set where a remove
// records which adds it observed, so a concurrent add survives. This is the
// most useful CRDT in a note-taking product and the one to reach for first.

Clock skew will break a timestamp-based approach, and it is not hypothetical. Laptop clocks disagree with each other by seconds and with a server by more, and a user who has never enabled automatic time setting will produce timestamps that are days wrong. Any design that compares client timestamps to decide a winner is relying on an assumption you do not control. If you use timestamps, take them from the server — which means the write is not fully offline — or use a hybrid logical clock that mixes physical time with a logical counter, and accepts monotonicity per replica rather than global agreement.

15.4 Conflict resolution in practice

The theory is straightforward; the product design is not. What follows is the set of decisions a synchronisation implementation has to make, each with a default that is wrong more often than it is right.

1. What is a conflict, and at what granularity? Per row, per field, or per character. Character-level is what users intuitively expect for prose and it is the most expensive. Start at field level and be explicit that two edits to the same field of the same row conflict.

2. What does the user see, and when? A silent merge the user does not notice is the best outcome and is only possible when the merge is genuinely lossless. If it is lossy, the user must be told. The failure mode is showing the conflict dialog after the data has already been merged in the background — the user is then asked to arbitrate a merge they cannot see.

3. What happens to a delete during an edit? Three options: the edit wins and the document reappears; the delete wins and the edit is discarded; or a tombstone holds the document for a period so the user can recover it. The third is the humane answer and it costs one table.

4. How long is a tombstone retained? Long enough that every device that has been offline longer than the tombstone lifetime can still learn about the deletion. That is a real, computable number: the maximum plausible offline duration, not a guess. Ninety days is a common answer, and it is arbitrary unless you justify it.

5. What is the identity of a document? If the client generates the id, two devices creating the same logical document produce two documents. If the server generates it, offline creation needs a client id and a reconciliation step. Most products use a client-generated UUID plus a "possible duplicate" detection pass, which is pragmatic and occasionally wrong.

6. What happens when the account is deleted but the device is not? The device has data it may no longer be permitted to hold, and it is a legal obligation as well as a product question. Chapter 12 of the database guide covers erasure; the desktop-specific part is that you cannot reach the device to run the erasure, so the client must perform a crypto-shred: destroying a local key so the data is unrecoverable, and reporting that it did so.

// The sync loop, in the order the steps must happen. Getting the order wrong
// is how a sync implementation duplicates rows or loses changes.
async fn sync_once(state: &mut AppState) -> SyncOutcome {
    if let Connectivity::Online { .. } = state.connectivity { // re-probed, not cached
        state.connectivity = probe().await;
    }

    // 0. Back off. A flapping connection must not produce a request storm.
    if Date.now() < state.next_attempt_at { return SyncOutcome::Deferred; }

    // 1. PUSH local changes first. Applying remote state before flushing local
    //    changes is the classic bug: the remote state overwrites an unsent local
    //    edit and the edit is lost with no record that it existed.
    let pending = local_store.dirty_rows(LIMIT 100)?;
    let mut conflicts = Vec::new();
    for row in &pending {
        match api.push_row(row, if_match: row.server_rev).await {
            Ok(new_rev) => local_store.mark_clean(row.doc_id, new_rev)?,
            Err(ApiError::Conflict { their_value, their_rev }) => {
                conflicts.push(Conflict { row: row.clone(), their_value, their_rev });
                // Leave it dirty. Do NOT mark it clean and do NOT retry.
                // A conflict is a state the user must resolve, not an error to
                // retry. Retrying it unchanged loops forever.
            }
            Err(ApiError::RateLimited { retry_after }) => {
                state.next_attempt_at = Date.now() + retry_after;
                return SyncOutcome::Throttled;
            }
            Err(e) => { log::warn!(?e, "push failed"); }
        }
    }

    // 2. PULL remote changes since the last cursor, including tombstones.
    //    A cursor, not a timestamp: a client clock and a server clock disagree.
    //    The cursor is the last change_log sequence number the server has confirmed.
    let batch = api.changes_since(state.cursor, LIMIT 500).await?;
    for change in &batch.changes {
        //    Never apply a remote change to a row with unsent local changes without
        //    checking the revision. This is the merge gate.
        if let Some(local) = local_store.get(change.doc_id)? {
            if local.dirty && local.server_rev != change.base_rev {
                conflicts.push(Conflict::from(change, local));
                continue;   // diverged, do not clobber
            }
        }
        local_store.apply(change)?;
    }
    state.cursor = batch.next_cursor;      // advance only after applying

    // 3. PULL DELETIONS, including tombstones, in the same pass. Omitting this
    //    is a silent resurrection: a deleted document comes back on the next
    //    device that syncs, with no explanation.

    // 4. Compact. A queue that only grows is a performance problem at month six.
    if batch.changes.len() == 500 {
        state.next_attempt_at = Date.now();   // more to come, come straight back
    } else {
        state.next_attempt_at = Date.now() + 30_000;  // idle poll
    }
    SyncOutcome { pushed: pending.len() - conflicts.len(), conflicts }
}

15.5 Performance: cold start, memory, input latency and battery

A desktop application has four performance budgets, and all four are user-visible in ways a web page’s are not. The first time a user opens the application is the first impression, and it happens before they have decided whether they like the product.

BudgetTargetWhy it is a budget and not a wishWhat usually breaks it
Cold start to interactive< 1.5 s on a 2019-class laptop from a spinning diskThe user’s first judgement of the product, formed before they have read a wordLoading the whole database at boot; a splash screen with no progress; doing work on the main thread before the window is up
Warm start to interactive< 400 msEvery subsequent launch, and the difference between "snappy" and "slow"Re-reading state; not caching the parsed index; a blocking network call at startup
Input latency< 50 ms to visual responseDirectly perceived as quality. Above 100 ms the user stops trusting the interface and starts double-clickingWork on the main thread in a handler; a synchronous layout read after a write; an unbounded list with no virtualisation
Idle memory< 200 MB resident for a utility; < 500 MB for a document editorThe user has twenty applications open. Memory is shared, and yours is not the only one that mattersUnbounded caches; retaining the whole file; a leak per window; logging every event in a ring buffer that never trims
Battery impact< 1% per hour idleAn application that drains a laptop is uninstalled, and the user is right to uninstall itA 1 Hz timer doing work; a sync loop with no backoff; a spinning disk kept awake; an animation running while minimised
// Cold start, budgeted. Every step declares what it is allowed to cost, and
// the budget is enforced rather than observed.
//
//   Phase 0: 0–150 ms    show the window. Never a blank frame.
//   Phase 1: 150–700 ms  chrome, recent documents, last state
//   Phase 2: 700–1500 ms document content, index, search
//   Phase 3: background   sync, telemetry, updates
//
//   Nothing above the line may touch the network. The launch path should be
//   fully functional offline, which means the remote check is always deferred.

async fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let t0 = Instant::now();

    // Phase 0. Paint immediately, with whatever is already known. The window is
    // shown with `visible: false` in the window config and shown here, after the
    // first paint, so the user never sees a white rectangle.
    window.show();
    assert_under(t0, 150, "window visible");

    // Phase 1. Cheap, local, and required for the UI to be usable at all.
    let settings  = settings::load()?;                 // ~1 ms, a small file
    let recents   = recents::load()?;                  // ~5 ms, capped at 20
    ui.render_chrome(settings, recents);
    assert_under(t0, 700, "chrome interactive");

    // Phase 2. Deferred, and the window is already usable while it runs.
    let store = spawn_blocking(|| Store::open(data_dir())).await??;
    ui.set_document_source(store.clone());
    assert_under(t0, 1500, "document interactive");

    // Phase 3. Everything that touches the network or the disk at scale.
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        connectivity::probe().await;                 // not before phase 1
        sync::run_forever(store).await;
        telemetry::start();
        updater::check_later().await;
    });

    Ok(())
}

// Failing a budget in debug builds is worth the noise: it is the only way the
// number stays a budget through two years of feature work.
#[cfg(debug_assertions)]
fn assert_under(start: Instant, budget_ms: u64, what: &str) {
    let elapsed = start.elapsed().as_millis() as u64;
    if elapsed > budget_ms {
        tracing::warn!(?what, ?elapsed, budget_ms, "startup budget exceeded");
    }
}

// Input latency, measured rather than felt.
// The number that matters is the delay between the physical key and the
// frame that shows its effect. Anything over 50 ms is detectable, and over
// 100 ms users start clicking again.
struct InputLatencyProbe { last_key: Option<Instant> }

impl InputLatencyProbe {
    fn on_key(&mut self, t: Instant) { self.last_key = Some(t); }

    fn on_paint(&mut self) {
        if let Some(key_at) = self.last_key.take() {
            let ms = key_at.elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1000.0;
            if ms > 50.0 {
                metrics.histogram("ui.input_latency_ms").observe(ms);
            }
        }
    }
}

// The three fixes that account for most regressions, in order:
//
// 1. Move work off the main thread. Anything over ~8 ms goes to a worker.
// 2. Virtualise long lists. A 50,000-row table rendered eagerly is a
//    4-second freeze, and no amount of main-thread work helps because the
//    layout cost is the problem.
// 3. Batch writes. A keystroke that triggers a database write per character is
//    20 synchronous transactions per second. Debounce to 250 ms, and always
//    flush on focus loss and on quit.

// Battery, which is the budget everyone forgets until review.
//   - No 1 Hz timers. Use an event, or a 30 s timer that early-returns.
//   - Suspend sync, telemetry and the updater when the window is hidden, and
//     when the OS reports a battery saver or on-battery-power state.
//   - Never poll a file you were told about. Use a filesystem watcher, which
//     is an OS notification and costs nothing when nothing changes.
//   - Stop all animation when the window is not visible. A hidden window
//     animating is a measurable flat battery drain.

15.6 Crash reporting without over-collecting

A desktop product cannot be debugged on the user’s machine, so crash reporting is infrastructure rather than a feature. The constraint that makes it hard is that the diagnostic data and the user’s documents live in the same process, and a naive minidump contains memory contents including whatever the user had open.

// A crash report, designed to be useful and to contain as little as possible.
//
//   INCLUDE: app version, OS and version, architecture, the stack of the
//            faulting thread (symbols only), the last N user actions as
//            event names with no arguments, the device model, free disk,
//            and whether a migration or update ran recently.
//   EXCLUDE: file paths, file contents, document text, URLs with query strings,
//            anything typed, environment variables, and memory images.
//
//   A minidump with type information and no private symbols is the right
//   default: it gives you a resolvable stack trace and no memory contents.
//   The temptation to attach a full memory dump in a "just for critical crashes"
//   path is how a diagnostics pipeline becomes a data-protection incident,
//   because a critical crash is exactly when a large document is in memory.

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
struct CrashReport {
    app_version: String,
    os: String,                 // "macos 15.6 arm64"
    device: String,               // "MacBookPro18,3" — useful, not identifying
    thread: String,                // symbolised stack of the faulting thread
    last_events: Vec<String>,       // ["doc.open", "export.pdf"] — names, no args
    recent_migration: Option<String>,
    recent_update: Option<String>,
    free_disk_mb: u64,
    //   No user id. No file path. No document. No environment.
}

// The event log must be name-only, or it becomes a surveillance record of
// everything the user typed. This is the discipline that keeps it useful
// AND collectable.
fn record(name: &str) {
    //   ✓ record("doc.open")
    //   ✗ record("doc.open", path)          → a filesystem map of the user
    //   ✗ record("search", query)           → everything they searched for
    //   ✗ record("field.edit", field_name)  → their data model
    ring_buffer.push(name.to_string());
    if ring_buffer.len() > 50 { ring_buffer.remove(0); }
}

// Opt-in, disclosed, and revocable. Three requirements, and all three are
//   legal requirements in most jurisdictions as well as ethical ones.
//
//   1. OFF by default in every consumer product, and clearly labelled.
//   2. A visible, always-available control to turn it off. Not buried in
//      settings; a menu item is the right level.
//   3. A stated retention period on the server, and deletion on request.
//      "We keep crash reports for 90 days" must be true and enforced.

// The upgrade and migration crash signature, which is the single most
// valuable report a desktop product receives.
//
//   If crashes cluster in the 15 minutes after an app version is installed, the
//   cause is the migration, not the feature. The diagnostic is the correlation
//   of crash time with install time, which means the crash report MUST carry
//   the app version and the report MUST be attributable to an install cohort.
//   Without that, a broken migration looks like a bad release and the team
//   will argue about the wrong thing for a week.

Exercises 15

  1. Write the offline contract for an application you know: which of the five promise levels applies to each feature, and what the user sees in each state. Then implement the connectivity probe and confirm it correctly identifies a captive portal, which is the case a naive implementation gets wrong.
  2. Build a local SQLite store with WAL, a dirty flag, a server revision, a partial index on the dirty set, and a change log. Then simulate a power cut at every point in a write and prove the database is always consistent and the change log always agrees with the data.
  3. Implement push-then-pull synchronisation with an If-Match precondition. Then run two clients against one server, make conflicting edits offline, reconnect both, and prove no row is lost and no edit is silently overwritten. Verify the queue stays bounded over 10,000 operations.
  4. Write a GSet and an LSEQ counter, then prove convergence by applying a random set of operations in a random order on three replicas. Assert the final states are identical, and run it 1,000 times.
  5. Measure cold start, warm start, input latency and idle memory for an application you own, on the slowest machine you can access. Identify the single largest contributor to each and fix it. Re-measure and record the delta.
  6. Audit a crash-reporting pipeline for what it actually transmits. Remove anything that is not on the include list, then confirm the reports are still actionable by resolving a stack trace from each of the three most common crash sites.

16 · Desktop Track: Distribution, Updates and Enterprise

16.1 Distribution channels and their economics16.2 The build and signing pipeline16.3 Phased rollout and rings16.4 Crash-gated rollout16.5 Enterprise deployment, policy and MDM16.6 Deprecation, sunset and forced upgrades

Distribution is where a desktop product acquires or loses its users, and it is the step with the largest gap between what teams assume and what happens. The install conversion rate is the number to model, because every subsequent decision — store versus direct, signing approach, update channel — is made in the context of that funnel.

16.1 Distribution channels and their economics

Each channel trades reach, control, friction and revenue for something different. The right choice depends on your audience, not on which channel is largest.

ChannelPlatformInstall frictionUpdate controlDiscoveryRevenue shareBest for
Direct downloadAllHigh — the user finds a URL and runs an installer✓ Full. You choose timing, staging and rollback✗ None, you bring the traffic0%Products with a web funnel, and anything needing a pre-release build
Microsoft Store (MSIX)Windows 10/11✓ Very low. One click, and it self-updates○ Medium. Staged rollout percentages are supported✓ Store search and recommendations0–15%, or 0 with a qualifying subscriptionConsumer Windows software, and anything enterprise wants auto-updated
Mac App StoremacOS, iOS✓ Very low○ Medium. Phased release over 7 days is supported✓ Store search, editorial features30%, or 15% under the small-business programmeConsumer macOS software. Note the sandbox requirement and the review
Direct .dmg / .pkgmacOSMedium. Drag to Applications, but Gatekeeper warns unless notarised✓ Full, via Sparkle or an equivalent✗ None0%Anything that cannot meet the Mac App Store sandbox
Homebrew CaskmacOS, LinuxLow for technical users○ Via the formula and brew upgrade✓ Great for developer audiences0%Developer tools, CLI products, anything with a technical user base
wingetWindowsLow. winget install Vendor.App○ Via the manifest and the package manager✓ Excellent for technical users0%The Windows equivalent of Homebrew. Far better than an MSI website link
Snap / FlatpakLinuxLow if the user already uses them○ Automatic, via the store✓ Flatpak Flathub is a real discovery channel0%The only credible Linux distribution story at scale
Chocolatey / ScoopWindowsLow for technical users○ Via the package✓ Good for technical users0%Enterprise internal distribution, and developer tooling
// The packaging definitions that are not just a file format. The manifest is
// the product's contract with the platform's update and install machinery.

// ── MSIX: declarative, per-user by default, and the only format that installs
//    atomically and rolls back cleanly if the install fails.
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<Package xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/appx/manifest/foundation/windows10">
  <Identity Name="com.example.app"
            Publisher="CN=Example Ltd, O=Example, C=GB"     <c>← must match the cert exactly</c>
            Version="1.5.0.0" />
  <Properties>
    <DisplayName>Example</DisplayName>
    <PublisherDisplayName>Example Ltd</PublisherDisplayName>
    <Description>…</Description>
    <Logo>Assets\logo.png</Logo>
  </Properties>
  <Dependencies>
    <TargetDeviceFamily Name="Windows.Desktop" MinVersion="10.0.17763.0" />
  </Dependencies>
  <Resources><PackageSize>?</PackageSize></Resources>

  <c><!-- Declares the file type, so double-click works and the shell knows it. --</c>
  <Extensions>
    <Extension Category="windows.fileTypeAssociation">
      <FileType Name="com.example.document">
        <Extension Category="windows.fileType">
          <FileNamePattern Pattern="*.example" />
        </Extension>
      </FileType>
    </Extension>
    <Extension Category="windows.protocol">
      <Protocol Name="example"><DisplayName>Example</DisplayName></Protocol>
    </Extension>
  </Extensions>

  <c><!-- The protocol activation MUST declare the extension on Windows, or the</c>
  <c>    system will not route example:// URLs to the app at all. This is a</c>
  <c>    silent failure: the app builds, installs, and never receives the URL. --</c>
  <Applications>
    <Application Id="App" Executable="app.exe" EntryPoint="Windows.FullTrustApplication">
      <uap:VisualElements DisplayName="Example" Description="…"
                          BackgroundColor="#0F172A" Square150x150Logo="Assets\logo.png" />
    </Application>
  </Applications>
</Package>

// ── Winget manifest, which is a community contribution and has its own rules.
//    Version must be a 4-part number. InstallerSha256 must be the hash of the
//    file AFTER signing, or every install fails with a corrupt-file error.
//    That ordering mistake is the most common winget submission bug.
PackageIdentifier: Example.Example
PackageVersion: 1.5.0
InstallerType: exe                     # or msi, or msix, or inno, or nullsoft
UpgradeBehavior: install
ReleaseDate: 2026-09-28
Installers:
- Architecture: x64
  InstallerUrl: https://cdn.example.com/1.5.0/Example-Setup-x64.exe
  InstallerSha256: 9F3C21A8…
- Architecture: arm64
  InstallerUrl: https://cdn.example.com/1.5.0/Example-Setup-arm64.exe
  InstallerSha256: 7B2E0044…
ManifestType: installer
MinimumOSVersion: 10.0.17763.0

// ── Homebrew Cask. The sha256 must be of the notarised, stapled artefact.
cask "example" do
  version "1.5.0"
  sha256 "9f3c21a8b7e2d4f6a8b0c2d4e6f8a0b2c4d6e8f0a2b4c6d8e0f2a4b6c8d0e2f"

  url "https://cdn.example.com/1.5.0/Example-#{version}-universal.dmg"
  name "Example"
  desc "…"
  homepage "https://example.com"

  depends_on macos: ">= :monterey"
  app "Example.app"
  zap trash: [ "~/Library/Application Support/Example", "~/Library/Caches/Example" ]
  #   The zap stanza is a courtesy, not a requirement. It is also the difference
  #   between a user who will never reinstall and a user who will not upgrade.
end

Ship every channel you can, and make them agree on a version. The failure mode is a 1.5.0 on the website, 1.4.2 in the Mac App Store, and 1.4.0 in winget, with three different update behaviours and a support inbox that cannot tell which one a user has. A single version string, generated once in CI and stamped into every artefact, is the only mechanism that prevents this — and the app must report its version and channel on every support request, so the answer is one field rather than an investigation.

16.2 The build and signing pipeline

The build pipeline for a desktop product is longer than a web pipeline because there are more artefacts, more secrets, and a signing step that must be right in a way nobody tests until it fails at release time.

# One build, many artefacts, one version, stamped once.
name: release

jobs:
  # 1. Version derivation. Never a hand-typed string; it will be wrong.
  version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      full: ${{ steps.v.outputs.full }}
      major: ${{ steps.v.outputs.major }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }        # tags are needed
      - id: v
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          VERSION=$(git describe --tags --abbrev=0 --match 'v[0-9]*' | sed 's/^v//')
          echo "full=$VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "major=${VERSION%%.*}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          # Fail if the working tree is dirty. A release built from an
          # uncommitted change cannot be reproduced and cannot be rolled
          # back to an identical state.
          test -z "$(git status --porcelain)" || { echo "::error::dirty tree"; exit 1; }

  # 2. Build per platform. Matrixed, because they fail independently.
  build:
    needs: version
    strategy:
      matrix:
        include:
          - { os: macos-15, target: aarch64-apple-darwin,  artifact: dmg,  id: mac-arm }
          - { os: macos-15, target: x86_64-apple-darwin,  artifact: dmg,  id: mac-int }
          - { os: windows-latest, target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, artifact: msi, id: win-x64 }
          - { os: windows-11-arm, target: aarch64-pc-windows-msvc,  artifact: msi, id: win-arm }
          - { os: ubuntu-24.04, target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, artifact: appimage, id: linux-x64 }
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run tauri build -- --target ${{ matrix.target }}

  # 3. Sign, per platform, in a job that has ONLY the artefact. Building and
  #    signing in one job means the build environment sees the signing keys.
  sign:
    needs: build
    strategy: { matrix: { include: [ {id: mac-arm, os: macos-15}, {id: mac-int, os: macos-15},
                                     {id: win-x64, os: windows-latest}, {id: win-arm, os: windows-11-arm} ] } }
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v5
        with: { name: ${{ matrix.id }} }
      #    macOS: import the identity, sign, notarise, staple. All four steps.
      - if matrix.os == 'macos-15'
        env: { P12: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_P12 }}, PASS: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD } }
        run: |
          security create-keychain -p "$KEYCHAIN_PW" ci.keychain
          security import "$P12" -k ci.keychain -P "$PASS" -T /usr/bin/codesign
          security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple:,codesign: -s -k "$KEYCHAIN_PW" ci.keychain
          #   Tauri does this for you with signingIdentity set, but
          #   notarisation still has to be invoked explicitly.
          xcrun notarytool submit --apple-id "$APPLE_ID" --team-id "$TEAM_ID" \
            --password "$APP_SPECIFIC_PW" --wait "target/universal/bundle/macos/Example.dmg"
          xcrun stapler staple "target/universal/bundle/macos/Example.app"
      - if matrix.os == 'windows-latest' || matrix.os == 'windows-11-arm'
        env: { CERT: ${{ secrets.WINDOWS_PFX }} }
        run: signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td SHA256 /f "$CERT" .

  # 4. Verify BEFORE publishing. A bad signature discovered by a user is
  #    a support incident; the same discovery in CI is a red build.
  verify:
    needs: sign
    runs-on: macos-15
    steps:
      - run: codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=4 ./Example.app
      - run: spctl --assess --type execute --verbose ./Example.app
      - run: xcrun stapler validate ./Example.app
      - run: codesign --display --entitlements - ./Example.app | tee entitlements.actual.plist
      - run: diff -u entitlements.expected.plist entitlements.actual.plist

  # 5. Publish the update manifest LAST, and only if every artefact verified.
  #    The manifest is what users poll, so publishing it early ships a broken
  #    update to everyone who polls in the meantime.
  publish:
    needs: verify
    if: success()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./scripts/generate-manifest.sh "${{ needs.version.outputs.full }}" dist/
      - run: ./scripts/sign-manifest.sh dist/update.json   # with the UPDATE key,
                                            # which is not the build key
      - run: aws s3 cp dist/ s3://releases/ --recursive
      - run: aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id ${{ secrets.CF_DIST }} \
               --paths "/update.json"

16.3 Phased rollout and rings

A desktop release reaches users on their own schedule, which means a bad release reaches users slowly and separately — and you cannot un-ring it. Phasing exists to bound the population exposed to a defect while the population that would report it is small enough that you can still act.

RingPopulationDurationExit criteriaWhat it is protecting you from
Internal / dogfoodEmployees, always on the buildContinuousNone — this ring never gates a releaseObvious breakage. Its only value is that the team uses the product daily
Opt-in betaUsers who explicitly joined2–8 weeksCrash-free sessions above 99.5% and no P1/P2 reports for a weekBeta-channel users are more tolerant and more technical, so this does not prove much about the general population
1%1% of the stable channel, chosen by a stable hash of install id24–48 hCrash-free sessions within 0.2 points of baseline; support volume flatA migration that only affects 1% of data shapes
5%5%48 hSame, plus no new crash signature above 5 occurrencesA regression that is data-dependent and needs volume to appear
25%25%48–72 hSame, plus support ticket rate within baselineSomething that only a quarter of users encounter
100%Everyone———
// Ring assignment MUST be stable. Hashing the install id means a user stays
// in the same ring across releases, which is what makes the comparison
// meaningful. Math.random() per check means a user bounces between rings
// every hour and every crash report is a coin flip.

// Python: stable, platform-independent, and identical to the server's
// implementation. Note the explicit version salt: change the salt and every
// user moves rings at once, which looks like a mass crash event.
import hashlib

def ring_for(install_id: str, salt: str = "v3") -> int:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(f("{salt}:{install_id}".encode()).digest()
    bucket = int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "big")  # 64 bits, not a 32-bit int
    return bucket % 10000          # 0–9999, so 1% is buckets 0–99

def eligible_for(bucket: int, ring_pct: int) -> bool:
    return bucket < ring_pct * 100

// The server side, so the rollout can be paused without shipping a new build.
// A ring percentage baked into the binary is a value you can only change by
// releasing, and a release is the thing you are trying to avoid.
GET /v1/update/check?current=1.4.2&install=7c1e…&channel=stable
//  200 {
//    "version": "1.5.0",
//    "bucket": 4213,          // so a support ticket can be correlated
//    "rolloutPct": 5,         // controlled server-side, changed in seconds
//    "channel": "stable",
//    "mandatory": false
//  }
//  204 No Content — up to date, or not in this ring. 204 is correct here and
//  is cheaper for both sides than an empty JSON body.

// The client, which must respect a pause without needing an update.
//
//   Check on launch, then at most once every 4 hours, then hourly, then
//   daily. Backing off on failure is what stops a server outage from becoming
//   an app outage.
const CHECK_INTERVALS_MS = [4 * 3600 * 1000, 3600 * 1000, 24 * 3600 * 1000];
let failures = 0;

async function maybeCheckForUpdate() {
  const i = Math.min(failures, CHECK_INTERVALS_MS.length - 1);
  if Date.now() - state.lastCheck < CHECK_INTERVALS_MS[i]) return;
  try {
    const res = await fetch(UPDATE_URL, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) });
    failures = 0;
    if (res.status === 204) return null;
    return await res.json();
  } catch {
    failures++;
    return null;       // never surface this. The app works fine
                                // without an update check, and a modal about
                                // it is the definition of a bad update system.
  }
}

The crash-free metric has to be defined before you launch, not after you have decided the release is fine. "Crash-free sessions" is the fraction of sessions that end without an unhandled crash. The threshold is a business decision — 99.5% is a common floor for a consumer product, 99.9% for a tool people depend on for work. Whatever the number, compute it per ring and compare against the previous version’s rate for the same ring, not against an absolute. A 99.3% crash-free rate is fine if it was 99.4% last week and fatal if it was 99.9%, and only the comparison tells you which.

16.4 Crash-gated rollout

The automatic halt: a release that stops advancing when its own health metrics degrade. This is the mechanism that makes a phased rollout safe enough to run without a human watching, and it is cheap to build once the metrics exist.

// The rollout controller. One loop, one state machine, and every transition
// logged with the numbers that justified it.

enum Stage { Canary, Ring1, Ring5, Ring25, Full, Halted, RolledBack }

struct Rollout {
    version:    String,
    stage:      Stage,
    ring_pct:   u32,
    entered_at: Instant,
}

impl Rollout {
    async fn advance(&mut self, m: &Health) -> Decision {
        // Compare against the SAME ring of the PREVIOUS version. Comparing a
        // new version's 5% ring against the previous version's 100% is a
        // category error and it is how a 2× regression passes a gate.
        let baseline = m.baseline_crash_free(self.stage);

        // Three independent gates. ALL must pass. An OR here is how a
        // // product ships a version that is fast and stable but unsupportable.
        let crash_ok  = m.crash_free(self.stage) >= baseline - 0.002;  // 0.2 points
        let p99_ok    = m.p99_latency(self.stage) <= m.baseline_p99(self.stage) * 1.5;
        let volume_ok = m.sessions(self.stage) >= 10_000;
        //   10,000 sessions per ring: with a 0.1% crash rate you need volume before
        //   the confidence interval on the rate is narrow enough to act on.

        if !crash_ok {
            // Halt, do not roll back. Rolling back loses the ability to
            // diagnose, and some defects are data-dependent and will
            // recur on the next release.
            return Decision::Halt {
                reason: format("crash_free {:.4} vs baseline {:.4}",
                            m.crash_free(self.stage), baseline),
                data: m.top_signatures(5),   // attach now, not later
            };
        }
        if !(p99_ok && volume_ok) {
            return Decision::Hold;   // not enough evidence yet
        }

        match self.stage {
            Stage::Canary => self.to(Stage::Ring1),
            Stage::Ring1   => self.to(Stage::Ring5),
            Stage::Ring5   => self.to(Stage::Ring25),
            Stage::Ring25  => self.to(Stage::Full),
            _ => {}
        }
        Decision::Advance
    }
}

// What an automatic halt does NOT do, and the manual counterpart:
//
//   1. It does not notify anyone. A halt that pages nobody is a halt that is
//      noticed on Monday. Wire the halt to the on-call rotation.
//   2. It does not roll back. A rollback is a decision with consequences, and
//      the person who makes it needs the top crash signatures in front of them.
//   3. It does not stop the version you already shipped. A 25% rollout has put a
//      quarter of your users on a defective build and telling them nothing is
//      worse than the defect.
//
//   The sequence when a halt fires:
//     1. Freeze the rollout at the current percentage. Do not advance.
//     2. Page the on-call with the top five new crash signatures and the
//        affected cohort size.
//     3. Within 30 minutes, either fix-forward and resume, or roll back.
//        "We are investigating" is not one of the options.
//     4. If rolling back, verify the rolled-back population is healthy, and
//        keep the build's artefacts for 30 days for diagnosis.

16.5 Enterprise deployment, policy and MDM

Enterprise buyers are a different customer with different requirements, and the difference is mostly about control: they must be able to deploy without your involvement, configure without your involvement, and audit without your involvement. A product that requires a user to click through an installer cannot be deployed to ten thousand machines.

// The three enterprise requirements, and what each looks like in practice.
//
// 1. SILENT, UNATTENDED DEPLOYMENT. The admin pushes it, not the user.
//    Windows: an MSI or MSIX with per-machine scope, deployed by
//    Configuration Manager, Intune or Group Policy, with no UI.
//
//    <Product Id="…" Name="Example" Language="1033" Version="1.5.0"
//            Manufacturer="Example Ltd" UpgradeCode="GUID-STABLE-ACROSS-VERSIONS">
//      <Package InstallScope="perMachine" Compressed="yes"/>
//      <MediaTemplate EmbedCab="yes"/>
//      <Property Id="ARPSYSTEMCOMPONENT" Value="1"/>   <c>← no Add/Remove entry</c>
//    </Product>
//
//    The UpgradeCode MUST be identical in every version, or the installer cannot
//    find the previous installation and installs a second copy beside the first.
//    This is the single most common packaging bug in a product with a version history.

//    macOS: a .pkg, or better an MDM payload. Note that a signed and notarised
//    .pkg is what allows silent installation; an unsigned one cannot be.
//    Linux: a .deb in an internal apt repository, or a Flatpak with a GPG key.

// 2. CENTRALLY CONFIGURABLE. The admin sets the configuration; the user does
//    not, and the user cannot override it. This is a policy layer, not settings.
//
//    Policy precedence, highest first:
//      1. Command-line flags supplied by the deployment
//      2. Managed configuration file in a system location, written by MDM/GPO
//         (macOS: /Library/Managed Preferences/…; Windows: HKLM\Software\…)
//      3. Environment variables
//      4. User preferences file in the user's own data directory
//      5. Built-in defaults
//    The user layer is LAST, so an admin's policy cannot be silently overridden
//    by a user who changed a setting. Every layer must be reported in
//    "About" so a support call can be resolved in one step.

// Reading the managed layer, and being explicit about who won.
fn resolve_policy() -> Policy {
    //   macOS managed preferences (written by an MDM profile)
    //   Windows: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Vendor\App
    //   Linux:  /etc/example/policy.yaml
    let managed = managed_preferences::load();

    let mut policy = Policy::defaults();
    for (k, v) in managed { policy.set(k, v, Source::Managed); }
    for (k, v) in env::vars()     { policy.set_if_unset(k, v, Source::Environment); }
    for (k, v) in user_settings()  { policy.set_if_unset(k, v, Source::User); }
    //   set_if_unset is the whole point: a lower layer can never win.
    policy
}

// 3. AUDITABILITY AND DATA RESIDENCY. The admin needs to know what the app
//    sends, where it stores data, and how to wipe it on a departing employee.
//
//    - A documented list of every network endpoint, with its purpose.
//    - A proxy configuration that honours the system proxy, including PAC files
//      and per-destination allow and deny lists. An enterprise that cannot
//      route your traffic through their inspection proxy cannot deploy you.
//    - A documented uninstall procedure that removes the per-user data
//      directory, because an MDM wipe must be able to leave nothing behind.
//    - A TLS-only, certificate-pinned client with a documented way to update
//      the pins when the corporate root changes. Pinning without a rotation
//      path is an outage waiting for a certificate renewal.
//    - SOC 2 or ISO 27001, if the deal requires it. Start the audit before you
//      need it; it takes six months and you cannot compress that.

// The single most-asked enterprise question, and the answer must be a document:
//   "Can your application be deployed with no user interaction, configured by
//    policy, and routed through our proxy without modification?"
//   If the answer to any part is no, that is a roadmap item, and it should be on
//   the roadmap before the deal is signed rather than after.

16.6 Deprecation, sunset and forced upgrades

Every desktop product ends, and the decision of how is made long before anyone admits it is being made. The three options are continued support, a paid upgrade for existing customers, or a sunset — and the third one has a set of obligations that are legal as well as ethical, and that are cheapest to plan for at launch.

PathWhat the user getsRevenue outcomeObligationsRight when
Continue indefinitelyEverythingOngoing maintenance cost with no new revenueEvery security dependency must be tracked and patched foreverThe product is profitable and the maintenance cost is small relative to revenue
Paid upgradeA discounted path to the current versionHighest, and it funds the migrationThe old version must keep working while the offer is liveThere is a genuinely better current version and a large installed base
SunsetA date, a reason, an export tool and a refund policyZero, plus reputational cost if handled badlyAdvance notice, working data export, a stated minimum period, refunds for recent purchasesThe product is superseded, is no longer maintained, and the cost of continuing exceeds its value
// Deprecation has to be communicated in the product, not only in an email.
// An email is missed by everyone who did not read it, and the people who
// missed it are the ones who find out when the application stops working.

// The three-tier notice, at intervals, in the application, on launch:
//
//   12 months:  banner in the app, email, a dated page on your website
//    6 months:  banner on every launch, email, changelog entry
//    3 months:  a modal on launch, with a "remind me later" that is honoured
//                 and a "export my data" button IN THE SAME MODAL
//    1 month:   the application enters read-only mode and says so, on launch,
//                 with the sunset date and the export path in the same view
//    0:         it stops running. It must not crash on launch. It must show a
//                 page explaining what happened, where the data is, and how to
//                 get it out.
//
//   That last one is the requirement almost everyone misses. A sunset that
//   makes the application fail to open is a data-loss event, and it will be
//   described as one in every review of your company.

// The export, and it has to be genuinely usable rather than technically
// present. Open formats, not a proprietary archive.
fn export_all(dest: &Path) -> Result<ExportSummary> {
    //   Documents → one file per document in the native format, plus a
    //     manifest.json describing every one, so the set is self-describing.
    //   Settings → a human-readable .ini or .toml, not a binary blob.
    //   Attachments → the original bytes, with original filenames.
    //   Licence and subscription history → CSV.
    //   Analytics or history → CSV, with a documented column meaning.
    std::fs::create_dir_all(dest)?;

    let mut manifest = Manifest::new(app_version());
    for doc in store.all_documents()? {
        let path = dest.join(format!("documents/{}.{}", doc.id, doc.extension));
        doc.write_native(&path)?;
        manifest.add(path, doc);
    }
    settings::export(dest.join("settings.ini"))?;
    manifest.write(dest.join("manifest.json"))?;

    //   Verify the export before telling the user it succeeded. A partial export
    //   discovered a year later, after the data is gone, is the worst outcome
    //   this function can produce.
    let summary = manifest.verify(dest)?;
    Ok(summary)   // shows counts, and the path, in the UI
}

// The forced upgrade, which is the one thing a desktop product genuinely can
// do and a web product cannot. Use it rarely and state it honestly.
//
//   Gate the APPLICATION, not the server, so a user with no connectivity can
//   still work. A forced update check that requires a network is a forced
//   offline for your offline users, which is the opposite of what you wanted.
//
//   Gate criteria: a defect with data-corruption or security consequences, or a
//   version that cannot connect to a service the server has retired.
//
//   Presentation: an explanation, a date, and a "read more" link. Not a modal
//   with no escape and no explanation. A user who cannot work and is not told
//   why will leave a one-star review, and they will be right to.
const MINIMUM_SUPPORTED = "3.9.0";

async fn enforce_minimum_version() {
    if version::current() < MINIMUM_SUPPORTED {
        update::check_and_download_blocking().await;   // show progress, do not exit
        if update::install_and_relaunch().await.is_ok() { return; }
    }
    ui::show_blocking_notice(
        "Example 3.8 can no longer connect to the service",
        "A security fix in version 3.9 is required to continue. "
            "Your documents are unaffected and are saved locally.",
        actions: ["Update now", "What changed", "Read-only mode"],
    );
}

Desktop track complete. Chapters 13 through 16 covered the process model, the framework choice, packaging, signing, updates, offline and synchronisation, desktop performance budgets, distribution channels, phased rollout, enterprise deployment and deprecation. Chapter 17 turns to the quality and security practice that applies to both tracks, chapter 18 to release management and the product lifecycle, and chapter 19 collects the launch checklists and the failure catalogue. Everything in chapters 1–8 was common to both tracks and none of it needed repeating.

Exercises 16

  1. Produce a signed and notarised build for all three platforms, then verify each one the way a user would: Gatekeeper assessment on macOS, SmartScreen on Windows, and an AppImage on a clean Linux VM with no FUSE. Record the exact message shown in any failure case.
  2. Publish a manifest to four channels — direct, Microsoft Store, Mac App Store, winget — and verify the version agrees across all four. Then deliberately publish a mismatch and trace how long it takes before a support ticket identifies the cause.
  3. Implement the rollout controller with the three gates and a stable hash ring. Then simulate a version with a 0.3% crash rate and confirm it halts at 1% with the top crash signatures attached, rather than reaching 100%.
  4. Write a Winget manifest and a Homebrew Cask for the same release. Submit the cask, and time how long review takes. Note the difference in friction between a store review and a formula pull request.
  5. Build the five-layer policy resolution and demonstrate that a user preference cannot override a managed preference. Then write the "About" panel that reports the effective source of every setting.
  6. Write the data export tool, run it, and verify every exported file opens in a standard tool without your application. Then write the three-tier deprecation notice text and the final shutdown screen, and review both for whether a user who missed every email would understand what happened.

17 · Quality Engineering: Testing, Security and Hardening

17.1 Test strategy and the shape of a suite17.2 The test types and what each is for17.3 Test doubles, coverage metrics and legacy code17.4 End-to-end, performance and desktop application testing17.5 Threat modelling and application security17.6 Supply chain integrity and the secure SDLC pipeline

Quality engineering is the discipline of turning an informal claim — “this works” — into an auditable artefact: a test portfolio with a deliberate shape, a set of gates that block a release, and an explicit threat model that the code is designed against. This section argues that the composition of a test suite matters more than its volume, that coverage percentages are a reporting convenience rather than a quality signal, and that the two tracks in this guide — Web (chapters 9–12) and Desktop (chapters 13–16) — diverge sharply at the point where a test must survive a real operating system, a real installer and a real update. It then treats security engineering as part of quality engineering rather than as a separate gate bolted on at the end: threat modelling with STRIDE, the OWASP Top 10 (2025 revision) applied to concrete code, and the software supply chain treated as a first-class attack surface with SBOM generation, provenance attestation and secret scanning in the merge pipeline.
