The section closes with the operational practices that measurably reduce incident rates — tiered CI, quarantine for flaky tests, mutation score as a proxy for test strength, and a mandatory security review before a launch decision is taken. It applies to both tracks; wherever the mechanics differ, the difference is stated at the point where it matters rather than assumed.

17.1 Test strategy and the shape of a suite

This subsection establishes how a suite should be composed, how the tiers should be budgeted, and why the conventional test pyramid is a starting heuristic rather than a law.

A test suite is an asset with a carrying cost and a yield. It costs the time to write, the time to read on every change, the CI minutes it consumes, and — most expensively — the cognitive cost of every future modification to code it touches. It yields the defects it actually finds, weighted by how early it finds them and how certain you are they are real. Every test that does not pay back that cost is a liability, and a suite that grows without a stated ratio between these two quantities will eventually collapse under its own maintenance weight. The first job of a test strategy is therefore not to maximise the number of tests; it is to decide what proportion of the defect space each tier is allowed to own.

The conventional shape — a wide base of fast unit tests, a narrower band of integration tests, and a small apex of end-to-end tests — remains a good default because it encodes a real trade-off: the further a test is from the unit under change, the more expensive it is to write, the more state it depends on, and the more likely it is to fail for reasons unrelated to the code being changed. A unit test that runs in 12 ms and depends on nothing but a function argument can be run ten thousand times without introducing noise. An end-to-end test that provisions a browser, seeds a database, negotiates a TLS handshake and asserts on a rendered DOM tree might take 40 seconds and depend on a third-party payment sandbox, a font CDN and a clock that advances in a time zone the test author was not in. Both find bugs. Only one of them can be run a hundred times a day by every engineer without eroding trust in the suite.

A workable budget for a medium-to-large product is roughly 65–80 % of test cases at the unit tier, 15–25 % at the integration and contract tier, and 5 % or fewer at the end-to-end tier, measured by case count and rebalanced by runtime so that the end-to-end tier never exceeds about 10 % of wall-clock pipeline time. Those numbers are not universal. They are a starting point from which you derive a target, write it down, and enforce it. The enforcement mechanism is not a code review comment; it is a counting test that runs in CI and fails when the distribution drifts, because a strategy nobody measures is a strategy nobody is following.

The pyramid inverts in specific, identifiable circumstances, and recognising them is part of competent test design. It inverts when the system is dominated by third-party integrations whose behaviour you do not control: a payments processor, an identity provider, a tax authority’s API, a map tile server. Against those, contract tests and a small number of carefully-stubbed integration tests are far more productive than unit tests, because the bug you are exposed to is not a branch you forgot to cover but a schema you mis-assumed. It inverts in rule engines, pricing calculators, parsers and compilers — algorithmic code with a large input space and a cheap oracle — where property-based tests dominate and example-based unit tests are a waste. It inverts on the desktop track, where the majority of the product’s observable behaviour is process-level: install, launch, migrate, update, uninstall, and behave correctly at 125 %, 150 % and 200 % display scaling. Those behaviours are only observable from outside the process, and a suite of pure unit tests cannot reach them at all.

Runtime is the constraint that actually governs suite shape, and it should be measured rather than assumed. The standard to aim for is a unit tier that completes in under 60 seconds on a developer laptop and in under 3 minutes in CI, an integration tier that completes in under 5 minutes, and an end-to-end tier that completes in under 20 minutes. If a unit tier has grown past three minutes, engineers begin batching their pushes and reviewing less carefully, which destroys the feedback loop the tier exists to provide. The remedy is not discipline; it is sharding the tier across runners, isolating slow tests into a separate marker, and moving genuinely slow tests down a tier where the cost is acceptable.

// vitest.config.ts — the tier is a first-class, enforced object
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Unit tier: hard budget of 60s locally. CI enforces the same via --reporter.
    include: ['src/**/*.{test,spec}.ts'],
    exclude: ['**/*.e2e.ts', '**/*.contract.ts', '**/slow/**'],
    testTimeout: 2_000,
    hookTimeout: 5_000,
    teardownTimeout: 5_000,
    pool: 'forks',
    poolOptions: { forks: { maxForks: '50%' } },

    // Determinism is a hard gate, not a best effort.
    sequence: { shuffle: false, concurrent: false },
    retry: 0,               // retries belong in the quarantine wrapper, not here
    isolate: true,
    fileParallelism: true,

    // Coverage is reported, not gated at 100%. See 17.3 for why.
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text-summary', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'src/**/index.ts', 'src/**/generated/**'],
      thresholds: {
        lines: 72,          // raise 1 point per quarter; do not chase 100
        branches: 64,
        functions: 70,
        statements: 72,
      },
    },

    // A test file that is not covered by a case is an untested contract.
    onConsoleLog: (log) => {
      if (log.includes('[TEST-DEBUG]')) throw new Error('debug logging left in test')
    },
  },
})
TierShare of casesShare of CI wall-clockLocal budgetCI budgetTarget flake rateWhat a failure proves
Unit65–80 %5–10 %≤ 60 s≤ 3 min≤ 0.2 %✗ A pure function or isolated class misbehaves
Integration15–25 %20–30 %≤ 2 min≤ 5 min≤ 1 %✓ Two of your own components compose correctly
Contract3–8 %5–10 %≤ 30 s≤ 3 min≤ 0.2 %✓ A provider still honours a published promise
Component3–8 %5–10 %≤ 60 s≤ 3 min≤ 0.5 %✓ A component renders and responds in isolation
Visual1–4 %10–15 %—≤ 5 min≤ 2 %~ Appearance is stable, not correctness
Accessibility1–3 %5–10 %≤ 30 s≤ 3 min≤ 0.5 %✓ Automated WCAG checks pass on key journeys
End-to-end≤ 5 %≤ 10 %—≤ 20 min≤ 2 %✓ The deployed system completes a business transaction
Load / soak< 1 %Nightly only—Nightly≤ 5 %✓ The system holds its SLO under modelled load

Flakiness deserves separate treatment because it is the single most destructive property a test suite can acquire. A test that fails intermittently without a code change does not merely cost a rerun; it teaches engineers that red builds are normal, which destroys the only signal the pipeline provides. The correct response is not to tolerate flake but to quarantine it: automatically move a test that has failed without a change to a quarantine list, exclude it from the merge gate, and open an issue with an owner and a deadline. Quarantined tests are still run nightly, and the quarantine queue length is itself a tracked metric. A team whose quarantine queue exceeds 2 % of the suite has a testing problem that no amount of new test writing will fix.

# .ci/tier.sh — the test suite as a set of budgeted, individually runnable tiers
set -euo pipefail

: "${CI:=0}"
WALL_START=$(date +%s)

budget() {           # budget <label> <seconds> <command...>
  local label="$1" max="$2"; shift 2
  local t0=$(date +%s)
  "$@" || { echo "FAIL $label"; exit 1; }
  local dt=$(( $(date +%s) - t0 ))
  if [ "$dt" -gt "$max" ]; then
    echo "BUDGET EXCEEDED: $label took ${dt}s, limit ${max}s"
    exit 2
  fi
  printf 'ok  %-14s %4ss (limit %ss)\n' "$label" "$dt" "$max"
}

budget unit 180        pnpm vitest run --reporter=dot
budget contract 180   pnpm vitest run --config vitest.contract.config.ts
budget component 240  pnpm playwright test --project=component
budget e2e 1200       pnpm playwright test --project=chromium --shard=1/4

TOTAL=$(( $(date +%s) - WALL_START ))
echo "--- tier wall-clock: ${TOTAL}s ---"

# The shape guard: the end-to-end tier must never dominate the pipeline.
E2E_CASES=$(grep -rho '@e2e' tests/e2e | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
ALL_CASES=$(grep -rho 'it(\|test(' tests src --include='*.ts' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
PCT=$(( E2E_CASES * 100 / (ALL_CASES > 0 ? ALL_CASES : 1) ))
if [ "$PCT" -gt 8 ]; then
  echo "SHAPE VIOLATION: end-to-end is ${PCT}% of cases (budget 5-8%)"
  exit 3
fi

Coverage is not a gate on line coverage at 100 %. A codebase can have 100 % line coverage and a mutation score of 20 %: every statement executed, no assertion ever able to fail, the suite green while the product is broken. Line coverage measures whether a line ran, not whether the suite would notice if the line were wrong. Where coverage is useful it is useful for finding untested regions — as a heat map for where to add tests, not as a percentage to climb. Teams that gate on rising line coverage reliably produce large, slow, near-worthless suites; teams that gate on mutation score reliably produce smaller, slower-to-write suites that catch real regressions.

The merge gate is the unit tier plus static analysis; nothing else. Integration, contract and end-to-end tiers run on the pull request as required checks but are configured not to block a merge for infrastructure causes. Blocking a merge on a five-minute end-to-end suite converts a test gate into a queue at the merge button, and engineers route around queues. The unit tier, which runs in under three minutes, is the only tier fast enough to be a genuine gate.

17.2 The test types and what each is for

This subsection works through the available test types, stating for each what it can prove, what it cannot, and what it costs.

Unit tests verify an isolated unit — a function, a class, a pure reducer — against a specification. They are the highest-yield tier per line written and the lowest cost per execution, and they should make up the bulk of any suite. Their structural weakness is that they cannot see the seams: a unit test that stubs the database proves your query builder produces the string you expected, not that the query runs. This is why a suite of unit tests alone, however large, is a test suite that has verified the code does what the tests' author believed it should do.

Integration tests verify that two components you own actually compose — a repository against a real database instance in a container, a controller against a real HTTP handler with a real router, a serializer against a real schema validator. The instinct that makes integration tests expensive is the instinct to be faithful: spin up PostgreSQL 17 with a realistic schema, run migrations, seed a hundred thousand rows. That is occasionally correct and usually not. The productive version is a thin slice of realism: a real database engine with a small schema, a real message broker in a container, a real HTTP server — but with a seed set small enough that a test’s setup is under a second. Integration tests that take 30 seconds to set up will be skipped; skipped tests are dead tests.

// Integration test: real Postgres, real migrations, tiny data. ~180ms.
import { describe, it, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest'
import { Pool } from 'pg'
import { migrate } from '../db/migrate'
import { LedgerRepository } from '../repos/ledger'

let pool: Pool
let repo: LedgerRepository

beforeAll(async () => {
  pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL })
  await migrate(pool, { to: 'latest' })        // real DDL, real ordering rules
})

afterAll(async () => { await pool.end() })

describe('LedgerRepository', () => {
  it('balances a debit posted in the same transaction as its credit', async () => {
    const acct = await repo.createAccount({ currency: 'EUR', minorUnits: 0 })
    await repo.post({ tx: pool, accountId: acct.id, amount: -1_250 })
    await repo.post({ tx: pool, accountId: acct.id, amount: 1_250 })
    const bal = await repo.balance(acct.id)
    expect(bal).toBe(0)                          // not 1_250 — a real invariant
  })

  it('refuses a posting that would take the balance negative', async () => {
    const acct = await repo.createAccount({ currency: 'EUR', minorUnits: 0 })
    await expect(repo.post({ accountId: acct.id, amount: -1 }))
      .rejects.toMatchObject({ code: 'INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS' })
  })

  it('is idempotent under replay of the same idempotency key', async () => {
    const acct = await repo.createAccount({ currency: 'EUR', minorUnits: 0 })
    const key = 'idem-9f3a'
    const first  = await repo.post({ accountId: acct.id, amount: 500, key })
    const second = await repo.post({ accountId: acct.id, amount: 500, key })
    expect(second.id).toBe(first.id)             // one posting, two deliveries
    expect(await repo.balance(acct.id)).toBe(500)
  })
})

Contract tests address the failure mode that neither unit nor end-to-end tests reach well: a provider changes its API and every consumer breaks simultaneously. A contract test pins the provider’s published interface — response schema, status codes, error shapes, latency budget, authentication requirements — as an executable artefact, and both sides verify against it. Pact is the established implementation; the model is that each consumer publishes its expectations, the provider verifies them in its own pipeline, and breaking changes are caught at the provider before they reach any consumer. Contract tests are the correct primary answer to “we integrate with eleven external systems we do not control” and they cost roughly 20–40 % of what end-to-end tests covering the same integrations cost.

// Consumer (Node, vitest) — pacts/consumer.spec.ts
import { pact } from '@pact-foundation/pact'

const provider = pact({
  consumer: 'billing-web',
  provider: 'payments-api',
  logLevel: 'warn',
  port: 0,
})

describe('checkout -> payments', () => {
  beforeAll(() => provider.setup())

  afterAll(async () => {
    await provider.execute()
    await provider.finalize()      // writes pacts/billing-web-payments-api.json
  })

  it('charges a card and returns a receipt', async () => {
    await provider
      .given('a card token tok_51Hx is authorised for 4200 minor units')
      .uponReceiving('a POST to /v1/charges')
      .withRequest('POST', '/v1/charges', {
        amountMinor: 4_200, currency: 'EUR', source: 'tok_51Hx', orderId: 'ord_8812',
      })
      .willRespondWith(201, {
        headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
        body: { id: 'ch_01J9', status: 'succeeded', amountMinor: 4_200, currency: 'EUR' },
      })
    const res = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:0/v1/charges', { method: 'POST' })
    expect(res.status).toBe(201)
  })

  it('surfaces a declined card as 402 with a stable error code', async () => {
    await provider
      .given('a card token tok_declined is declined with issuer code do_not_honor')
      .uponReceiving('a POST to /v1/charges')
      .withRequest('POST', '/v1/charges', { amountMinor: 100, source: 'tok_declined' })
      .willRespondWith(402, {
        body: { error: { code: 'card_declined', issuerCode: 'do_not_honor' } },
      })
    await expect(fetch('http://127.0.0.1:0/v1/charges', { method: 'POST' }))
      .resolves.toMatchObject({ status: 402 })
  })
})

Visual regression testing compares rendered output against approved baselines. It is powerful for detecting unintended change and it is one of the highest-signal-to-noise ratios available — if a test compares 12,000 pixels and requires an exact or near-exact match, it will catch a one-pixel shift that no behavioural test would ever notice. It is also the tier most likely to be abandoned, because baselines must be reviewed and approved, and a reviewer who approves baselines without reading them is worse than not having the tier at all: it converts a review problem into a rubber stamp. The workable compromise is a small curated set of ~30–60 baseline images covering the components whose appearance is contractual, a per-pixel tolerance of 0.1–0.2 % configured rather than defaulted, and a strict rule that a baseline update and a feature change are never in the same commit.

// Playwright visual regression — 1.5x. Fonts frozen, animations disabled,
// tolerance explicit. Baseline updates are a separate, reviewable commit.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test'

const SURFACES = [
  { name: 'invoice-empty',     path: '/invoices',     auth: 'user' },
  { name: 'invoice-populated', path: '/invoices?seed=12', auth: 'admin' },
  { name: 'settings-profile',  path: '/settings',     auth: 'user' },
] as const

test.describe('visual baselines', () => {
  test.use({ colorScheme: 'light', deviceScaleFactor: 1 })

  for (const s of SURFACES) {
    test(`render: ${s.name}`, async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
      await seedViaApi(page, s.auth)
      await page.goto(s.path, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' })
      await page.evaluate(() => document.fonts.ready)
      await disableAnimations(page)

      const mask = [page.getByTestId('avatar'), page.getByTestId('timestamp')]

      await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(`${s.name}.png`, {
        maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.002,     // 0.2 % of pixels — set on purpose
        maxDiffPixels: 240,
        animations: 'disabled',
        mask,
        scale: 'css',
      })

      // A visual diff must also say something about the DOM, or it is decoration.
      const landmarks = await page.getByRole('main').count()
      expect(landmarks, 'exactly one main landmark').toBe(1)
      await testInfo.attach(`${s.name}-dom.html`, { body: await page.content(), contentType: 'text/html' })
    })
  }
})

Accessibility testing must exist in automation even though automation is insufficient. Automated checkers catch roughly 30–45 % of WCAG 2.2 issues, concentrated in the mechanical category: missing alternative text, missing form labels, insufficient colour contrast, absent landmark structure, broken ARIA relationships, unlabelled buttons, missing document language. They catch essentially none of the issues that matter most to users: whether the flow is completable with a screen reader, whether focus order makes sense, whether an error message is announced when it appears, whether a timeout is long enough, whether a captcha is a wall. The correct shape is automated axe checks running on every pull request across key journeys, a manual audit with a real screen reader on a defined release cadence, and at least one usability session with a disabled user before a major version ships.

// Accessibility: automated gate on key journeys + screen-reader smoke.
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test'
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright'

const JOURNEYS = [
  '/sign-in', '/onboarding/step-2', '/projects', '/projects/new',
  '/billing', '/settings/accessibility', '/support/request',
] as const

for (const path of JOURNEYS) {
  test(`axe: ${path} has no serious violations`, async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto(path, { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' })
    const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
      .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa', 'wcag22aa'])
      .analyze()
    // Fail on impact, not on count: a "minor" nit should not block a release.
    const blocking = results.violations.filter((v) =>
      ['critical', 'serious'].includes(v.impact ?? ''))
    expect(blocking, JSON.stringify(blocking, null, 2)).toHaveLength(0)
  })
}

// The part automation cannot do. Runs nightly + on demand, not per-commit.
test('keyboard-only: complete a project creation without a pointer', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/projects/new')
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab')            // focus must enter the form
  for (let i = 0; i < 14; i++) {
    const onForm = await page.evaluate(() =>
      document.activeElement?.closest('form') !== null)
    if (onForm) break
    await page.keyboard.press('Tab')
  }
  await page.keyboard.type('Q3 field audit')
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab')
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /create project/i })).toBeFocused()
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter')
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Q3 field audit' })).toBeVisible()
})

test('reduced motion: no animation longer than 200ms under prefers-reduced-motion', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: 'reduce' })
  await page.goto('/projects')
  const long = await page.evaluate(() =>
    [...document.querySelectorAll('*')].filter((el) => {
      const d = getComputedStyle(el).transitionDuration
      return d.split(',').some((v) => parseFloat(v) * (v.endsWith('ms') ? 1 : 1000) > 200)
    }).map((el) => el.tagName + '.' + el.className))
  expect(long).toEqual([])
})

Property-based testing inverts the example-based default: instead of asserting that a specific input produces a specific output, you state an invariant and let a generator find the counterexample. Hypothesis (Python, 6.x) and fast-check (TypeScript, 4.x) shrink failing inputs automatically, so the counterexample you receive is minimal and readable. This is the single most effective technique against the class of bugs where a hand-written test would have needed forty examples you did not think of: round-trip serialisation, algebraic laws, sorting stability, parser tolerance of malformed input, cache invalidation invariants, and anything involving currency, time zones or Unicode normalisation. A fast-check suite of 15 lines routinely replaces 200 lines of example tests and finds defects on the first run.

// Hypothesis 6.x — properties, not examples. Counterexamples are shrunk for you.
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st, settings, HealthCheck, assume
from decimal import Decimal
from app.money import Money, add, allocate, to_minor_units
from app.codec import encode, decode

@given(st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10**9), st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=10**9))
@settings(max_examples=200, deadline=None)
def test_allocation_is_exact_and_sums_to_total(amount_minor, parts):
    """Splitting an amount into N shares must be lossless and sum back to the total."""
    shares = allocate(Decimal(amount_minor), parts)
    assert len(shares) == parts
    assert sum(s.to_minor_units() for s in shares) == amount_minor
    assert all(s >= 0 for s in shares)
    # The classic failure: floating point. Never use it for money.
    assert sum(float(s) for s in shares) == pytest.approx(amount_minor, abs=1e-6) or True

@given(st.binary(max_size=4096))
@settings(max_examples=300, deadline=None, suppress_health_check=[HealthCheck.too_slow])
def test_wire_format_round_trips_arbitrary_payloads(payload: bytes):
    assert decode(encode(payload)) == payload

@given(st.text(max_size=200))
def test_rejects_unicode_that_normalises_to_a_different_grapheme_cluster(s):
    assume(s != unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s))
    doc = parse_display_name(s)
    assert doc == unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)   # exactly one normalisation

// fast-check 4.x — same discipline on the TypeScript track.
import fc from 'fast-check'
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest'
import { addMoney, splitBill, normaliseKey } from './money'

describe('money', () => {
  it('is commutative and associative over minor units', () => {
    fc.assert(fc.property(
      fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 2 ** 31 - 1 }),
      fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 2 ** 31 - 1 }),
      fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 2 ** 31 - 1 }),
      (a, b, c) => {
        const ab = addMoney(a, b), bc = addMoney(b, c)
        expect(addMoney(b, a).minor).toBe(ab.minor)      // commutative
        expect(addMoney(ab, c).minor).toBe(addMoney(a, bc).minor)  // associative
      },
    ), { numRuns: 1_000, seed: 0x5eed })
  })

  it('allocates a split without losing or inventing a cent', () => {
    fc.assert(fc.property(
      fc.integer({ min: 0, max: 1_000_000 }),
      fc.integer({ min: 1, max: 64 }),
      (total, n) => {
        const parts = splitBill(total, n)
        expect(parts.reduce((s, p) => s + p, 0)).toBe(total)
        expect(parts.every((p) => p >= 0)).toBe(true)
        expect(Math.max(...parts) - Math.min(...parts)).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1)
      },
    ), { numRuns: 2_000 })
  })

  it('normalises keys so that NFC and NFD forms of the same string collide', () => {
    fc.assert(fc.property(fc.unicodeString(), (s) => {
      expect(normaliseKey(s)).toBe(normaliseKey(s.normalize('NFC')))
    }))
  })
})

Fuzzing is property-based testing applied to a parser, a decoder or any component that must survive hostile input, with a coverage-guided mutator rather than a hand-written generator. libFuzzer with sanitizers is the reference implementation and is what ships inside the toolchains of most widely-deployed C and C++ products; libFuzzer’s Java port Atheris brings the same model to Python, and Jazzer.js does it for JavaScript. The signature of a useful fuzz harness is a short assertion — “this decode must not crash, must not read out of bounds, and must round-trip” — plus a dictionary of interesting tokens harvested from the format specification. A two-hour fuzz run on a real parser routinely finds dozens of defects that no human test author would have thought to write, and the corpus that accumulates is the durable artefact: it becomes a regression suite that runs in seconds thereafter.

Mutation testing is the only widely adopted technique that measures the strength of a test suite rather than its reach. It mutates the source — replacing && with ||, deleting a conditional, negating a comparison, replacing a constant — re-runs the suite, and records whether any test noticed. A high line coverage with a low mutation score is the definitive proof that a suite is decorative. Stryker for .NET, JavaScript and TypeScript, mutmut for Python, and PIT for the JVM give concrete, comparable numbers; a project with a credible unit suite should sit above 65–75 % mutation score on business logic, above 45 % on UI code, and explicitly excluded for generated code, configuration, and trivial getters. Setting the target globally at 80 % and then excluding until it passes is a well-known and entirely empty ritual.

// stryker.config.json — mutation testing as the real coverage gate
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/stryker/schema/stryker-schema.json",
  "packageManager": "npm",
  "reporters": ["html", "clear-text", "progress", "json"],
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "coverageAnalysis": "perTest",          // only mutants in covered files
  "mutate": ["src/**/*.ts", "!**/*.d.ts", "!src/**/generated/**", "!src/**/types.ts"],
  "mutators": {
    "default": [
      { "name": "stringLiteralReplacement" },
      { "name": "booleanLiteralReplacement" },
      { "name": "conditionalBoundary" },
      { "name": "arithmeticOperator" },
      { "name": "logicalOperator" },
      { "name": "unaryOperator" },
      { "name": "conditionalExpression", "weight": 3 }
    ]
  },
  "thresholds": { "high": 80, "low": 60, "break": null },
  "perMutatorThresholds": {
    "conditionalExpression": { "high": 85, "low": 65, "break": 65 }
  },
  "disableTypeChecks": false,
  "ignorePatterns": ["src/legacy/**"],
  "concurrency": 4
}
Test typeFindsMissesAuthor costRun costGood mutation scoreUse when
Unit✓ Branches, edge cases, API misuse✗ Wiring, SQL, serialisationLowms75–85 %Always. Business rules, pure logic
Integration✓ ORM dialects, migrations, constraints✗ Concurrency across servicesMedium0.2–2 s50–70 %Repository, migration, transaction code
Contract✓ Provider breaking changes, schema drift✗ Semantic correctness of dataMedium0.1–1 sn/aEvery third-party or shared-team API

Adopt tiers in a deliberate order, not all at once. The sequence with the best ratio of defects-found to engineering-days-invested is: unit tests for business logic → integration tests for the data layer → contract tests for the first third-party integration → accessibility automation on key journeys → mutation testing on the three highest-risk modules → end-to-end on the five revenue-critical paths. Load testing and visual regression come last, and only if the risk justifies their permanent cost. Adding all ten at once produces a suite nobody maintains and a project that quietly stops shipping features for a quarter.

17.3 Test doubles, coverage metrics and legacy code

This subsection deals with the practical mechanics of test construction: what to substitute, what not to substitute, how to read coverage honestly, and how to bring an untested legacy module under test at all.

Meszaros and Fowler’s vocabulary for test doubles is worth adopting precisely because it removes the most damaging ambiguity in testing vocabulary: “mock” is used colloquially to mean any substitution, which obscures the one property that matters — whether the double asserts something. A stub returns canned data so the test can proceed. A spy is a stub that also records calls, so the test can assert on them after the fact. A fake is a working, simplified implementation — an in-memory repository instead of a PostgreSQL one, a hand-rolled JWT verifier instead of the real one. A mock is configured with expectations up front and fails immediately if they are not met. Only the mock asserts; everything else is neutral. Calling a stub a mock in a code review is a small habit with large consequences, because it obscures the question “what is this test actually verifying?”

The dominant failure mode in test design is over-mocking: replacing every collaborator with a hand-written double, so that the test asserts that the code called the collaborators in the order the test author expected. Such a test is a transcription of the implementation. It passes when the implementation matches the author’s memory of the design and fails when the implementation changes — even when the behaviour is correct — so it generates noise without generating signal. Worse, it cannot detect the class of defect that matters most in an integration: a mismatch between two things that were both mocked. If the test mocks the repository and mocks the serialiser, it verifies nothing about the bytes that actually reach the database.

The working rule is a preference ordering: use the real thing unless the real thing is slow, non-deterministic, or out of your control. That single sentence resolves most design questions. Use the real serialiser. Use the real HTTP router. Use the real validation library. Use a real in-memory fake for the database rather than a mock, because the fake will enforce the uniqueness constraint your mock does not have. Reserve mocks for genuine boundaries — network calls to third parties, clocks, randomness, and the specific collaborator whose interaction is the subject of the test. A useful heuristic for a module: if removing the module and replacing it with a five-line fake does not break any test, the module is not actually being tested.

// Go 1.25 — a hand-written fake (enforces the constraint) beats a mock (does not).
package ledger_test

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "testing"
    "github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
    "acme/ledger/internal/store"
)

// FakeStore is a real, working implementation of store.Store.
type FakeStore struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    rows    map[string]int64
    postings int
}

func NewFakeStore() *FakeStore {
    return &FakeStore{rows: map[string]int64{}}
}

func (f *FakeStore) Post(_ context.Context, acct string, delta int64) error {
    f.mu.Lock()
    defer f.mu.Unlock()
    if f.rows[acct]+delta < 0 {
        return store.ErrInsufficientFunds          // the constraint is REAL
    }
    f.rows[acct] += delta
    f.postings++
    return nil
}

func TestOverdraftIsRefusedAtomically(t *testing.T) {
    s := NewFakeStore()
    svc := ledger.NewService(s)
    require.NoError(t, svc.Credit(context.Background(), "a1", 100))

    err := svc.Debit(context.Background(), "a1", 101)
    require.ErrorIs(t, err, store.ErrInsufficientFunds)
    require.Equal(t, int64(100), s.Balance("a1"))   // partial mutation impossible
    require.Equal(t, 1, s.postings)                 // the fake counted for us
}

// .NET 10 — the same principle: prefer a real in-memory implementation.
public sealed class InMemoryOutbox : IOutbox
{
    private readonly ConcurrentQueue<DomainEvent> _q = new();
    private readonly HashSet<string> _seen = new(StringComparer.Ordinal);

    public ValueTask EnqueueAsync(DomainEvent e, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        // Idempotency is part of the contract; a naive Moq mock cannot express it.
        if (!_seen.Add(e.IdempotencyKey))
            return ValueTask.CompletedTask;
        _q.Enqueue(e);
        return ValueTask.CompletedTask;
    }

    public IReadOnlyCollection<DomainEvent> Drain() => _q.ToArray();

    public ValueTask CommitAsync(CancellationToken ct = default) => ValueTask.CompletedTask;
}

// Moq is reserved for the ONE collaborator whose interaction is the subject.
[Fact]
public async Task ChargesCardExactlyOncePerOrder()
{
    var gateway = new Mock<ICardGateway>(MockBehavior.Strict);
    gateway.Setup(g => g.ChargeAsync("ord_1", 4_200, default))
           .ReturnsAsync(new ChargeResult("ch_1", ChargeStatus.Succeeded));
    gateway.Verify(g => g.ChargeAsync("ord_1", 4_200, default), Times.Once);
    gateway.VerifyNoOtherCalls();          // strict: nothing unobserved

    var svc = new CheckoutService(gateway.Object, new InMemoryOutbox());
    await svc.CompleteAsync("ord_1", 4_200);

    gateway.Verify(g => g.ChargeAsync("ord_1", 4_200, default), Times.Once);
    Assert.Single(outbox.Drain());
}

Coverage metrics must be read with their definitions in mind, because each measures something different and none of them measures what a manager asks. Line coverage is the fraction of executable lines executed at least once. It is inflated by defensive code, by defensive logging, and by getters, and it is blind to conditions inside a line. Branch coverage counts outcomes of conditionals, which is strictly more informative and still blind to interactions between conditions. Function coverage counts whether a function was called, and is the weakest of the three. Path coverage counts distinct execution paths through a function, which is exponential in the number of conditions and therefore almost always reported as “incomplete” in a way that means nothing. MC/DC — modified condition/decision coverage — requires each condition to be shown to independently affect the outcome, and is the correct standard for avionics, medical and safety-critical software; it is achievable in ordinary business logic but almost never reached in application code.

The honest argument against a 100 % line-coverage target is not that it is expensive — though it is, because it drives you to test trivial getters and generated code — but that it is a target that can be satisfied while the product remains broken. Coverage is a search heuristic: it tells you where you have not looked. Used that way it is excellent and there is no substitute for it. Used as a percentage to report upward it is actively harmful, because it creates an incentive to write assertion-free tests. A test with no expect, no assert, and no thrown failure is a line-coverage unit with no defect-detection power, and any organisation that rewards coverage percentages will eventually be handed a portfolio of them.

// The line-coverage trap, stated concretely. Both files score 100% line coverage.
// Only one of them can fail.

// BAD: exercised, asserts nothing, detects nothing. Passes if logic is wrong.
export function calculateDiscount(cart, customer) {
  cart.items.forEach((i) => { i.total = i.price * i.qty })
  const raw = cart.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.total, 0)
  const rate = customer.tier === 'gold' ? 0.1 : 0
  cart.discount = raw * rate
  cart.total = raw - cart.discount
  logger.info('discount calculated', { raw, rate })
}

// GOOD: the same lines, with an oracle. Mutation score ~90% on these mutants.
export function calculateDiscount(cart, customer) {
  cart.items.forEach((i) => { i.total = toMinor(i.price) * i.qty })
  const raw = cart.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.total, 0)
  const rate = RATES[customer.tier] ?? 0
  cart.discount = raw * rate
  cart.total = raw - cart.discount
  return { raw, rate, total: cart.total }
}

it('gives gold customers exactly 10% and everyone else nothing', () => {
  const cart = fixtureCart([{ price: 12.5, qty: 2 }, { price: 0.1, qty: 3 }])
  const r = calculateDiscount(cart, { tier: 'gold' })
  expect(r.raw).toBe(2_530)                        // 2500 + 30, in minor units
  expect(r.rate).toBeCloseTo(0.1, 10)
  expect(r.total).toBe(2_277)                      // catches >= vs >, and float drift
})

Characterisation testing is the technique for taking responsibility for code that has no tests. Feathers' formulation is to write tests that capture the current behaviour, including the behaviour you believe is wrong, and to leave the judgement about correctness to a later change. The method is: characterise at a chosen seam, not everywhere. Pick the boundary with the highest ratio of risk to test-writing cost — usually a pure function, a parser, a state machine, a serialiser, or a well-defined public method on a class with no dependencies. Then write tests that assert current output, including current wrong output, and mark those with a clear annotation so the next engineer knows the behaviour is pinned, not endorsed.

The golden-master or approval-test variant is more powerful when the seam is expensive to call directly. Wrap the unwrapped code in a thin driver, feed it a large but fixed corpus of real inputs captured from production, record the outputs, and store them as a snapshot. The snapshot is now a regression baseline. Its weakness is that it is only as good as the corpus and it produces diffs nobody reads, so the corpus must be deliberately adversarial: inputs that triggered customer complaints, inputs at size boundaries, inputs in every supported locale, inputs with invalid UTF-8, inputs from a decade of old data formats. A 200-case golden master with good adversarial coverage is worth more than 2,000 examples you invented while reading the code.

// A golden master over a real production corpus. .NET 10, ApprovalTests-style.
public class VatCalculatorCharacterisation
{
    // Cases captured from production logs, incl. every ticket from 2021-2025.
    public static TheoryData<string> Corpus() => new()
    {
        // DE standard, 19%
        "  1.234,56 ",  // DE: dot thousands, comma decimal, whitespace
        "1.234,56 EUR", // currency suffix
        "1234.56",      // EN input to a DE rule — CURRENTLY WRONG, pinned anyway
        "-0,01",        // rounding of a negative cent
        "0",            // zero
        "1e3",          // scientific notation — CURRENTLY parsed as 1. Pinned.
        "١٢٣",          // Arabic-Indic digits — CURRENTLY dropped. Pinned.
        "12\u00A034",   // non-breaking space separator
    };

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(Corpus))]
    public void CurrentBehaviour_IsPinned(string input)
    {
        var actual = new VatCalculator(Locale.DeBy).Compute(input);
        Approve.Verify($"char/vat/{input.GetHashCode():X8}.txt", actual.ToString());
        // Pinned ≠ endorsed. Ticket PROJ-4412 tracks the two known-wrong cases.
        // Any CHANGE to this output is now a visible, reviewable diff.
    }
}
DoubleAsserts?Enforces constraints?Breaks when implementation changes?Default useAvoid when
Real collaborator✓ via the code under test✓ Yes✗ NoAlways preferredIt is slow, non-deterministic, or external
Fake✓ via the code under test✓ Yes, simplified~ RarelyDatabases, caches, queues, clocksIt is more complex than the real thing
Stub✗ No✗ No✗ UsuallyUnhappy-path branches, rare errorsThe data shape is the thing under test
Spy✓ After the call✗ No✗ Usually“Was this emitted once?” assertionsOrder and call shape are not contractual
Mock (strict)✓ Before/after the call✗ No✗ Almost alwaysThe interaction itself is the requirementYou are testing a collaborator you own
Snapshot / golden master✓ Whole output✗ No✓ Yes, loudlyLegacy code, serialisers, renderersOutput is non-deterministic by design

Do not gate a merge on a suite that fails for reasons unrelated to the change. A required check that is red 8 % of the time is not a gate; it is a coin flip, and the team’s rational response is to learn how to make the pipeline green without making the product correct — re-run until green, quarantine en masse, or merge from a branch that has not run the suite. Fix the suite before making it mandatory. If a test cannot be made deterministic, delete it and replace it with a lower-tier test that can.

17.4 End-to-end, performance and desktop application testing

This subsection covers the two expensive tiers and the point at which the Web and Desktop tracks stop behaving alike.

End-to-end testing is the only tier that tests the deployed system as a user encounters it, and that is its entire justification. Its cost is brutal and its failure diagnosis is poor, so the discipline is to keep it to a count small enough that every case is worth its runtime and that the entire suite can be read in one sitting. Twenty critical paths, executed against a production-shaped environment, run on every merge, is the upper bound most teams should adopt. Beyond that, the marginal case adds runtime and flake without adding confidence, because the paths it covers are variations of paths already covered.

An end-to-end case is only as reliable as the data beneath it. Shared mutable state — one database, one admin user, one seeded project that everyone reads and one test mutates — is the dominant cause of end-to-end flake. The correct architecture gives each worker its own namespace: a unique tenant per test run, seeded from a fixture, with a cleanup that is safe to interrupt. A tenant-scoped API is the cheapest way to isolate browser tests; a per-test container is the most reliable and the slowest. Choose one, and make the isolation visible in the test code so a future author does not accidentally reach across it.

// Playwright 1.5x — the checkout journey. Deterministic, isolated, diagnosable.
import { test, expect, type Page } from '@playwright/test'

test.describe('checkout', () => {
  test('an EU customer pays by card and receives a receipt', async ({ page }) => {
    // Isolation is a first-class fixture, not an afterthought in the test body.
    const tenant = await provisionTenant({ plan: 'team', region: 'eu-de' })

    await test.step('authenticate', async () => {
      await page.goto('/sign-in')
      await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(tenant.owner.email)
      await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.E2E_PASSWORD!)
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click()
      await expect(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' })).toBeVisible()
    })

    await test.step('add a seat and reach the payment step', async () => {
      await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Billing' }).click()
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Increase seats' }).click()
      await expect(page.getByTestId('seat-count')).toHaveText('6')
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: /continue to payment/i }).click()
      await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Payment' })).toBeVisible()
    })

    await test.step('pay with a card that the sandbox authorises', async () => {
      await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242 4242 4242 4242')
      await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('11/31')
      await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123')
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: /pay/i }).click()
    })

    await test.step('the receipt is reachable and the money is right', async () => {
      await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText(/payment received/i)
      const receipt = await getReceiptByOrder(tenant.lastOrderId)   // assert via API, not DOM
      expect(receipt).toMatchObject({
        amountMinor: 6 * 1_200, currency: 'EUR', status: 'succeeded', idempotencyKey: tenant.key,
      })
      // A DOM assertion alone would pass even if the charge amount were wrong.
      await expect(page.getByRole('link', { name: /view receipt/i })).toBeVisible()
    })
  })
})

Performance and load testing is a separate discipline with separate tooling, and it must be run against an environment whose production resemblance you can defend. A load test against a laptop proves nothing. What you need is a load generator separated from the system under test by a network, a dataset with a realistic cardinality and skew — real analytics traffic is not uniform, and a uniform benchmark hides queueing collapse — and explicit pass criteria derived from an SLO rather than from a number someone liked. For the Web track the criteria that matter are server-side latency percentiles and error rate under concurrency, plus the client-side budget that users actually experience. For the Desktop track they are cold-start time, idle CPU and memory, and behaviour under constrained hardware, because there is no server to shield the user and the device is the whole system.

// k6 — load test derived from an SLO, not from a guess.
import http from 'k6/http'
import { check, sleep, group } from 'k6'
import { Rate, Trend } from 'k6/metrics'

// SLO: 99.5% of /v1/invoices under 400 ms p95 at 400 rps sustained.
const errors = new Rate('invoice_errors')
const serverDur = new Trend('invoice_server_duration', true)

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    steady: { executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: 50, timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 200, maxVUs: 800, stages: [
        { target: 200, duration: '2m' }, { target: 400, duration: '5m' },
        { target: 400, duration: '15m' }, { target: 0,   duration: '1m' },
      ] },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'invoice_errors': ['rate<0.005'],                       // 99.5% SLO
    'http_req_duration{endpoint:invoice}': ['p(95)<400', 'p(99)<1200'],
    'invoice_server_duration':     ['p(95)<250'],          // our own budget
    'checks':                      ['rate>0.995'],
  },
}

export default function () {
  group('invoice browse', () => {
    const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE}/v1/invoices?page=1`, {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.TOKEN}`, 'X-Tenant': __ENV.TENANT },
      tags: { endpoint: 'invoice' },
    })
    const ok = check(res, { 'status is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 })
    errors.add(!ok, { step: 'browse' })
    serverDur.add(res.timings.duration)
    sleep(Math.random() * 2)                 // think time: real users are not bots
  })
}

Soak testing is load testing extended in time, and it exists to find failures that only appear after resources have been exhausted: connection pools that leak, caches that never evict, file descriptors that accumulate, in-memory sessions that grow without bound, log files that fill a disk, GC pauses that lengthen, memory that grows 2 MB per hour. A ten-hour soak at 40 % of peak load finds these; a five-minute stress test at 200 % of peak does not. The pass criterion is not throughput but flatness: memory, handle count, queue depth and p99 latency should all be flat within a stated tolerance across the run. A slow upward slope is a defect, and the output of a soak test should be a graph you keep, because it is the only artefact that predicts an outage three weeks out.

Here the two tracks diverge sharply, and the difference is not cosmetic. A Web track end-to-end test runs against a URL. It must be correct on at least Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, at the browser versions your analytics say are actually in use, at viewport widths from 320 px to 2560 px, and under both light and dark colour schemes. A Desktop track end-to-end test runs against a binary that must first be installed, and it must be correct on a matrix of operating systems, CPU architectures, and — uniquely — display scaling factors and locales. A bug that appears only at 150 % scaling on Windows 11 with a 60 Hz display and a German keyboard layout is a real customer bug, and no unit test, no component test, and no Mac-only CI runner will ever find it.

DimensionWeb trackDesktop trackTest consequence
Deployment targetA URL (staging / preview)An installer packageDesktop adds an install tier that has no web equivalent
Browser / shell matrixChromium, Firefox, WebKit, EdgeElectron, WebView2, WKWebView, native QtDesktop adds 3–6 shell targets
OS matrix✗ Not a variable✓ Win 10/11, macOS 13–15, Ubuntu 22.04/24.04, RHEL 9Desktop CI is a matrix, not a job
CPU architecture✗ N/A✓ x64, arm64 (Apple Silicon, Windows on ARM)Native modules and binaries must be built per-arch
Display scaling~ Browser zoom 80–200 %✓ 100 %, 125 %, 150 %, 175 %, 200 %Desktop: layout bugs at 150 % are common
Locale / input~ 8 locales✓ Keyboard layouts, RTL, IME, CJK, currency/date formatsDesktop: text input, shortcuts, menus are locale-bound
Lifecycle tests✗ N/A✓ install · first launch · upgrade · repair · uninstall~ 6–10 dedicated cases minimum
Auto-update path✗ N/A✓ Delta vs full, rollback, signature check, proxy behaviour✗ Broken updater is a P1 for many users
Resource budgetServer SLO + CWVCold start, idle RSS, CPU at idle, package sizeDifferent metrics entirely
Offline behaviour~ PWA / degraded mode✓ Native expectation: must work with no networkDesktop: a hard functional requirement
 
# Desktop lifecycle matrix — GitHub Actions. The matrix IS the test strategy.
name: desktop-lifecycle
on: { workflow_dispatch: {}, schedule: [{ cron: '0 03 * * *' }], push: { tags: ['v*'] } }

jobs:
  install-upgrade-uninstall:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os:        [windows-2022, windows-11-arm, macos-14, macos-15]
        arch:      [x64, arm64]
        scale:     [100, 150, 200]
        channel:   [stable, beta]
        exclude:
          - { os: macos-14,       arch: arm64 }     # runner unavailable
          - { os: windows-11-arm, arch: x64 }       # arm64 only
          - { os: macos-15,       arch: x64, scale: 100 }  # covered at 150/200
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 45
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '24', cache: pnpm }

      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm tauri build --bundles ${{ runner.os == 'Windows' && 'msi,nsis' || 'dmg,app' }}

      - name: Install from a clean machine
        run: pnpm exec vitest run tests/desktop/install.spec.ts --env=desktop

      - name: Launch, sign in, exercise the core journey at ${{ matrix.scale }}% scaling
        run: pnpm exec playwright test --project=electron --scale=${{ matrix.scale }}

      - name: Upgrade over the installed copy (N-1 -> N) and verify data survives
        run: pnpm exec vitest run tests/desktop/upgrade.spec.ts

      - name: Uninstall and verify user data policy
        run: pnpm exec vitest run tests/desktop/uninstall.spec.ts

      - name: Reject an unsigned or downgraded build at the updater boundary
        run: pnpm exec vitest run tests/desktop/updater-integrity.spec.ts

// Desktop lifecycle case: upgrade must not destroy user data, and the updater
// must refuse anything that is unsigned, downgraded, or on a stale channel.
import { test, expect } from '@vitest/runner'
import { launchInstalled, readUserDataDir } from './helpers/desktop'

test('upgrading from the previous minor preserves the local database', async () => {
  const before = await launchInstalled('fixtures/installer/prev-2.4.0.msi')
  await before.signIn({ user: 'e2e@fieldglass.test', pass: process.env.E2E_PASSWORD! })
  await before.createProject('Nordwind turbine — Q3')
  await before.quit()
  const dbBefore = await readUserDataDir(before.userDataDir)

  await launchInstalled('fixtures/installer/current-2.5.0.msi')   // in-place upgrade
  const after = await launchInstalled()
  await after.signIn({ user: 'e2e@fieldglass.test', pass: process.env.E2E_PASSWORD! })

  await expect(after.projectList()).toContain('Nordwind turbine — Q3')
  expect(after.localDbVersion).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(dbBefore.schemaVersion)
  // Migrations must be forward-only in the installer, with a verified rollback path.
})

test('the updater refuses a build that is not signed by our release key', async () => {
  const updater = new UpdaterHarness({ allowUnsigned: true })
  await expect(updater.apply('artifacts/rogue-2.6.0-x64.msi'))
    .rejects.toThrowError(/signature verification failed/i)
  expect(updater.appliedManifest).toBeNull()
})

test('the updater refuses a downgrade without an explicit user confirmation', async () => {
  const updater = new UpdaterHarness()
  await expect(updater.apply('artifacts/prev-2.4.0.msi'))
    .rejects.toThrowError(/downgrade blocked/i)
  await expect(updater.apply('artifacts/prev-2.4.0.msi', { allowDowngrade: true }))
    .resolves.toMatchObject({ version: '2.4.0' })
})

Make determinism a property of your fixtures, not a hope. Inject the clock, seed the random source, disable animation, freeze the locale and time zone explicitly in the test environment, and never let a test depend on the order in which it runs. A test that passes locally on a developer machine with 16 cores and fails in a sharded CI runner with 4 is a test that will be ignored, and an ignored test is a false assurance you are paying CI money for.

17.5 Threat modelling and application security

This subsection treats security as a design activity performed before code is written, and enumerates the concrete application-level controls that reduce incidents.

Threat modelling is a structured conversation about what can go wrong, held early enough that the answer can change the design. The most widely used framework remains STRIDE, which asks six questions of each element in a data flow diagram: Spoofing — can an attacker claim to be this principal; Tampering — can the data be modified in transit or at rest; Repudiation — can an action be denied after the fact; Information disclosure — can data be read by someone who should not; DoS — can availability be degraded; Elevation of privilege — can a low-privilege actor gain a capability they should not have. The output is not a document; it is a prioritised list of mitigations, each of which either goes into the design, becomes a test, becomes a monitoring rule, or is explicitly accepted with a named owner.

# Threat model: invoice export — STRIDE, data flow diagram in text.
# Trust boundaries: [TB1] internet→edge, [TB2] edge→app, [TB3] app→db,
#                   [TB4] app→object storage, [TB5] desktop→updater

| # | Element      | STRIDE          | Scenario                                   | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation (must be real)                          | Verified by                    |
|---|--------------|-----------------|--------------------------------------------|------------|--------|---------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| 1 | GET /export  | Spoofing        | Stolen session cookie exports all tenants  | Medium      | High   | HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite, session rotation on priv esc| e2e 17.4 + cookie assertions |
| 2 | export job   | Tampering        | User edits tenant_id in the request body   | High       | High   | Tenant id from session only, never from body       | Integration test + CodeQL taint  |
| 3 | export job   | Repudiation     | No record that a download was served        | High       | Medium | Append-only audit log, 7 y retention, WORM bucket  | Log assertion test              |
| 4 | S3 presigned  | Info disclosure | Presigned URL valid for 7 days, guessable?  | Medium      | High   | TTL 60 s, bound to exact object key, 1-hop redirect | Expiry unit test                |
| 5 | Export queue | DoS             | 10k concurrent exports exhaust the pool     | High       | Medium | Per-tenant concurrency 2, global 16, 429 + Retry-After| k6 scenario 17.4                |
| 6 | Role check   | Elevation       | `export:all` reachable by `viewer` role      | Medium      | High   | Central authorisation middleware, deny by default  | Policy matrix unit test         |
| 7 | Updater      | Tampering        | Replaced binary on the CDN mirror             | Low       | Critical| Code signing + manifest hash + TLS pinning         | updater-integrity.spec.ts       |
| 8 | Web view     | Elevation       | Deep link grants admin without a prompt      | Medium      | High   | Deep links are untrusted input; re-authorise       | Deep-link fuzz + e2e            |

Residual risk accepted: #3 retained only 90 days of audit (owner: sec-eng, review 2027-03-01).

The OWASP Top 10 remains the shared vocabulary, and the 2025 revision reorganised it around broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, misconfiguration, vulnerable and outdated components, identification and authentication failures, software and data integrity failures, logging and monitoring failures, and handling of the exceptional conditions that fall outside the previous list. Applied to a real product, the two with the highest observed incidence are broken access control — which is an authorisation bug, not a security-scan finding — and failures relating to the handling of exceptional conditions: an endpoint that returns a stack trace, a deserialiser that accepts a type from the classpath, a file upload that trusts the client-declared MIME type.

Authentication and session handling deserve their own treatment because the failure modes are specific and the mitigations are cheap. Credential stuffing against a login form is an automated attack with industrial tooling; the defences that work are rate limiting keyed on a combination of account and network, MFA with phishing-resistant WebAuthn or passkeys, breached-password checking against a k-anonymity service, and monitoring for a sudden success following a burst of failures. Session management has its own list: use a cryptographically random identifier of at least 128 bits, set HttpOnly, Secure and an appropriate SameSite, rotate the identifier on every privilege change and on authentication, enforce an absolute lifetime, and bind to something the attacker does not have where the platform supports it. JWTs fail in characteristic ways: accepting alg: none, accepting the token as its own signing key, not verifying the issuer or the audience, not checking the expiry, and using them where a server-side session was the right answer because a JWT cannot be revoked before it expires without a server-side deny-list — which means the deny-list is the real design.

// Robust session cookie + token verification. Node 24, Express 5.
import { Router } from 'express'
import { randomBytes, createHash, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto'
import { jwtVerify } from 'jose'

const SESSION_COOKIE = '__Host-sid'
const sessions = new Map<string, { uid: string; created: number; abs: number }>()

app.set('trust proxy', 1)
app.use(session({ name: SESSION_COOKIE, httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax',
                  path: '/', maxAge: 1000 * 60 * 60 * 12, rolling: false }))

// Login: rate limit on (account, ip) AND on ip alone, plus breach check.
const byAccount = rateLimit({ windowMs: 900_000, limit: 5,
  key: (r) => `${r.body.email}|${r.ip}`, skipSuccessfulRequests: true })
const byIp = rateLimit({ windowS: 900_000, limit: 40, key: (r) => r.ip! })

app.post('/auth/login', byIp, byAccount, async (req, res) => {
  const user = await users.findByEmail(String(req.body.email ?? ''))
  // Constant-ish time whether or not the account exists: do not leak existence.
  const ok = await verifyArgon2id(String(req.body.password ?? ''), user?.hash ?? DUMMY_HASH)
  if (!user || !ok) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'invalid_credentials' })

  const sid = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')       // 256 bits
  const now = Date.now()
  sessions.set(sid, { uid: user.id, created: now, abs: now + 12 * 3600_000 })
  req.session.regenerate((err) => {                     // NEW id on privilege change
    if (err) return res.status(500).end()
    req.session.uid = user.id
    res.cookie(SESSION_COOKIE, sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/' })
    res.json({ ok: true })
  })
})

// JWT verification: pin the algorithm, verify issuer AND audience, check exp/nbf.
const JWKS = remoteJWKSet(new URL(process.env.JWKS_URL!))
app.get('/auth/session', async (req, res) => {
  const token = req.cookies.get('access_token')
  if (!token) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'no_session' })
  const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, {
    algorithms: ['RS256'],                 // never 'none', never HS* against a public key
    issuer: 'https://id.fieldglass.example',
    audience: 'fieldglass-api',
    clockTolerance: 5,
    maxTokenAge: '10m',
  })
  if (sessionsDenyList.has(payload.jti!)) return res.status(401).end()
  res.json({ uid: payload.sub, scopes: payload.scp })
})

Injection is still the highest-frequency, highest-impact application vulnerability class, and it persists because string construction into a query, a shell, a template or an LDAP filter is syntactically indistinguishable from correct code. The defences are non-negotiable and simple: parameterised queries for every data store, context-aware output encoding for every rendering context, and no string building for anything. The subtler half is that output encoding is context-dependent — encoding for HTML is wrong inside a JavaScript string, inside a URL attribute, and inside CSS, and each of those is a separate XSS vector. This is what a Content Security Policy is for: it makes the browser enforce the distinction that the code failed to.

/* Strict CSP, no 'unsafe-inline', no 'unsafe-eval', with nonces.
   Report-only rollout for 14 days before enforcement. */
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const nonce = crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('base64')
  res.locals.cspNonce = nonce
  res.setHeader('Content-Security-Policy', [
    "default-src 'self'",
    `script-src 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net`,
    "script-src-attr 'none'",                    // blocks onclick=, onload=
    `style-src 'nonce-${nonce}' 'self' https://fonts.googleapis.com`,
    "img-src 'self' data: blob: https://*.mapbox.com",
    "font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com",
    "connect-src 'self' https://api.fieldglass.example wss://rt.fieldglass.example",
    "frame-ancestors 'none'",                    // clickjacking
    "form-action 'self'",
    "require-trusted-types-for 'script'",        // DOM XSS sink elimination
    "upgrade-insecure-requests",
  ].join('; '))
  res.setHeader('Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy', 'same-origin')
  res.setHeader('Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy', 'same-origin')
  res.setHeader('Referrer-Policy', 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin')
  res.setHeader('X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff')
  next()
})

/* Every template interpolates through a context-correct encoder, never raw. */
/* Express + a template engine configured with auto-escaping ON (default).     */
app.post('/comments', requireCsrf, requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  // Reject anything that is not a string, so an object cannot reach the template
  // layer as a "value" and be serialised by a coercion into markup.
  const body = String(req.body.body ?? '')
  if (body.length > 2000) return res.status(413).json({ error: 'too_long' })
  const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(body, { ALLOWED_TAGS: [], ALLOWED_ATTR: [] })
  const c = await db.comment.create({ authorId: req.user.id, body: clean, postId: req.body.postId })
  res.json({ id: c.id, body: c.body, renderedAt: new Date().toISOString() })
})

Cross-site request forgery is only exploitable where a request is authenticated by something the browser attaches automatically. The defences, in order of strength: SameSite cookies set to Strict or Lax; synchroniser or double-submit tokens on every state-changing request; and requiring a non-simple content type, so a cross-origin HTML form cannot produce a valid request at all. The common failure is a token middleware that is applied to some routes and not others, so the next developer adds a route and forgets it. Make it the default in the router and opt out explicitly.

Server-side request forgery is the one that modern architectures make worse rather than better, because a service that fetches a user-supplied URL — a webhook, an import, a PDF renderer, an image proxy, an OpenAPI validator — can reach the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254, an internal admin service, or a database that was never meant to have an IP. The defence is an allow-list, not a block-list: resolve the hostname, verify the resolved address is public, re-verify on every redirect, disable redirects, cap response size and content type, and set a short timeout. Denying a literal string “169.254.169.254” is theatre; DNS rebinding and decimal-encoded addresses defeat it in minutes.

Insecure deserialisation deserves a hard line rather than a control. Native deserialisers that reconstruct arbitrary object graphs — Java’s ObjectInputStream, Python’s pickle, .NET’s BinaryFormatter, Ruby and PHP’s equivalent — are remote code execution primitives by design, and there is no input validation that makes accepting untrusted input into one safe. The rule is: never deserialise untrusted data with a native object deserialiser. Use a data-only format such as JSON, MessagePack with a strict type map, or Protocol Buffers with a generated schema, and validate against a schema after parsing. Where a legacy format must be accepted, use an allow-list filter — Java’s ObjectInputFilter, a custom Unmarshaller — and set a recursion and object-count limit.

Path traversal and file handling share the same shape: the attacker controls part of a path, and the code joins it without verifying where it landed. The defence is to normalise first and then verify containment — resolve the candidate against a known root, compute the relative path, and reject anything that is absolute or begins with .. — and never to compare strings with a prefix test, which is defeated by a sibling directory whose name starts with the root’s name. Archive extraction needs the same discipline plus four more: reject absolute member names, drive letters and Windows device names, refuse entries whose resolved path escapes, and enforce a total uncompressed size, because a small archive that expands to 500 GB is a denial-of-service primitive that passes every per-file check. The related class is trusting client-declared metadata: content type, filename, and declared size are all attacker-controlled, so sniff the type server-side, generate storage names rather than accepting them, and stream rather than buffer.

Secrets in code remain common because the workflow for obtaining a secret is longer than the workaround. Enforce it mechanically: pre-commit scanning with Gitleaks or detect-secrets, server-side scanning on every push and in full-history mode on the repository, and a hard-fail CI gate. Assume a secret that reached history is compromised and rotate it — rewriting history does not un-leak a secret that was cloned, and a rotation procedure that requires no approval is what makes it actually happen. Store what remains in a secret manager, inject at runtime, never in build artefacts or environment dumps, and give every secret an owner and a rotation date.

CSRF, SSRF, injection and path traversal are the ones engineers get wrong. Secrets, dependency risk and the desktop surface are covered next.

# .gitleaks.toml — tuned to reduce false positives without weakening detection
title = "fieldglass secrets policy"
[extend]
useDefault = true

[[rules]]
id = "internal-service-token"
description = "Internal service account tokens (fmt: fg_live_/fg_test_)"
regex = '''\b(fg_(live|test)_[A-Za-z0-9]{24,})\b'''
keywords = ["fg_live_", "fg_test_"]
secretGroup = 0
entropy = 3.5

[[rules]]
id = "private-key-pem"
description = "Any private key material, including test fixtures"
regex = '''-----BEGIN (RSA |EC |OPENSSH |PGP )?PRIVATE KEY( BLOCK)?-----'''
tags = ["key", "desktop-signing"]

[[allowlists]]
description = "Documentation examples and vendor SDK samples"
paths = ['''docs/''', '''vendor/''', '''tests/fixtures/samples/''']
regexes = ['''AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE''', '''wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY''']

[[allowlists]]
description = "Snyk metadata contains resolved URLs, never suppress by default"
paths = ['''coverage/''', '''dist/''', '''build/''']

The Desktop track adds an attack surface that the Web track does not have, and it is a different surface, not a bigger one. The binary itself is the deliverable and it runs with the user’s full privileges, outside the browser’s protections, with a local filesystem, a local credential store, and often a privileged helper for per-machine operations. Five controls are non-negotiable and each maps to a real attack: code signing, with a hardware-backed key and a notarised or timestamped signature, so the OS will refuse to launch a modified binary and so users can distinguish your build from an attacker’s; entitlements and sandboxing, requesting the least privilege that works and being explicit about why, since an entitlement request is a standing invitation; IPC trust boundaries, where every message from a web view, a second instance, or an installed helper is untrusted input and must be validated against a schema; web-view isolation, no Node integration, a restrictive CSP, navigation blocked, and remote content not silently granted permissions; and updater integrity, with signature verification on the manifest and the payload, anti-rollback, and the update channel pinned rather than floating.

// Tauri 2.x — desktop trust boundaries, declared as capabilities, not implied.
{
  "$schema": "../gen/schemas/desktop-schema.json",
  "identifier": "default",
  "description": "Least privilege for the main window. No shell, no fs, no http.",
  "windows": ["main"],
  "permissions": [
    "core:default",
    "core:window:allow-minimise",
    "core:window:allow-close",
    "dialog:allow-open",                 // returns a path, never its contents
    "store:default",                     // scoped app data, not arbitrary fs
    "clipboard:allow-write-text"
  ],
  "deny": [ "fs:default", "shell:default", "http:default", "process:default" ]
}

// Every IPC handler validates its input against a schema. This is the boundary.
#[tauri::command]
fn export_invoices(app: AppHandle, state: State<AppState>, req: ExportRequest) -> Result<ExportReceipt, ApiError> {
    // Untrusted: crosses the IPC trust boundary. Validate before touching state.
    let input = ExportRequest::validate(&req)?;
    if !state.authz.can(state.user_id, "invoice:export", input.tenant_id)? {
        return Err(ApiError::Forbidden);          // never trust the payload's tenant
    }
    let path = state.paths.exports_dir().join(&input.request_id);   // generated, not supplied
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&path)?;
    // The web view never receives a filesystem path. It receives a job id.
    Ok(ExportReceipt { job_id: uuid::Uuid::new_v4(), tenant_id: state.tenant_id })
}

// Web view: no Node, strict CSP, no remote content, no arbitrary navigation.
let cfg = tauri::WebviewWindowBuilder::new(app, "main", WebviewUrl::App("index.html".into()))
    .title("Fieldglass")
    .inner_size(1280.0, 860.0)
    .devtools(false)
    .incognito(false)
    .on_navigation(|url| url.scheme() == "tauri" || url.host_str() == Some("app.fieldglass"))
    .on_download(|_| DownloadEvent::Prevent)     // never write to disk from the view
    .build()?;
