Code signing and auto-update are the same control, and an unsigned updater is worse than no updater. The moment you ship auto-update, you have moved your trust boundary from your HTTPS endpoint to whatever can write to your update manifest. A channel that accepts a manifest over the network without verifying an offline-rooted signature is a remote code execution primitive aimed at every user of the product, and no amount of code signing on the initial download compensates for it. Verify the manifest, verify the payload hash inside the signed manifest, pin the minimum acceptable version, and ship the revocation list.

17.6 Supply chain integrity and the secure SDLC pipeline

This subsection covers the tooling and gating that turns secure development practice into an automated, auditable pipeline.

The majority of components in a modern application are code you did not write, downloaded at build time, from a registry, transitively. OWASP has ranked software supply chain failures as a top-ten class for several consecutive revisions, and the empirical justification is strong: a large fraction of exploited vulnerabilities were present in a dependency the organisation already shipped, and a meaningful minority of intrusions began at the build system rather than the application. The controls below are ordered by how much they reduce risk per unit of friction, and that order is not the order in which they are usually adopted.

First and cheapest is dependency hygiene: lockfiles committed and enforced with --frozen-lockfile, automated updates with review, and a policy that bounds the number of transitive dependencies. Second is continuous scanning: SCA on every push, not nightly. Third is SBOM generation on every build, because the SBOM is what makes every later question answerable — “are we affected by CVE-2026-1187?” is unanswerable without one. Fourth is provenance: signing build artefacts and attesting to how and by what they were built, so that a compromised registry token cannot produce a release. Fifth is the pre-launch review, which is a human process and is the only control that catches a design problem.

// .github/workflows/security.yml — the gates, in the order that actually reduces risk.
name: security
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:
  schedule: [{ cron: '0 5 * * *' }]        # full-history secret scan nightly
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write                             # only for the cosign attestation step
  attestations: write

jobs:
  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }              # full history, or the scan is theatre
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2
        env: { GITLEAKS_ENABLE_UPLOAD: false, GITLEAKS_NOTIFY_WEBHOOK: ${{ secrets.SEC_ALERT }}}

  sca:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions: { contents: read, security-events: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.30.0
        with:
          scan-type: fs
          scan-ref: .
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          ignore-unfixed: true
          exit-code: '1'                      # fail on fixable Critical/High only
          vuln-type: os,library
      - uses: google/osv-scanner-action/osv-scanner-action@v2
        with: { scan-args: '-r --skip-git .' }
      - uses: snyk/actions/node@1
        with: { command: test, args: '--all-projects --severity-threshold=high' }

  sast:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions: { contents: read, security-events: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3
        with:
          languages: javascript-typescript,python,go,java-kotlin,csharp
          queries: security-and-quality
          config: ./.github/codeql/codeql-config.yml
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3
        with: { category: '/language:javascript-typescript' }
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3
        with: { category: '/language:python' }

  build-sbom-sign:
    needs: [secrets, sca, sast]
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    outputs: { digest: '${{ steps.sign.outputs.digest }}' }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '24', cache: pnpm }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm build

      - name: Produce CycloneDX 1.6 SBOM with resolved licences
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/src" cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm:npm \
            --omit dev --output-file sbom.cdx.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: sbom, path: sbom.cdx.json, retention-days: 400 }

      - name: Attest build provenance (SLSA L3, keyless via Sigstore)
        uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v2
        with: { subject-path: 'dist/**' }

      - name: Sign every artefact and emit the digest for the release job
        id: sign
        run: |
          cosign sign-blob --yes --bundle dist/app.msi.b64 \
            "dist/app.msi"
          echo "digest=$(sha256sum dist/app.msi | cut -d' ' -f1)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

SBOM formats worth knowing are SPDX (2.3 and the 3.0 development line), which is the more widely adopted and is the format most regulators and most vendor portals accept, and CycloneDX 1.6, which is lighter, is oriented towards applications rather than packages, and carries vulnerability and licence extensions natively. Generate in CI rather than on a laptop, keep it for the retention period of the artefact, and store it where you can find it by the artefact’s digest — an SBOM that is not indexed by what it describes is not usable during an incident.

Provenance answers a different question from an SBOM. The SBOM says what is inside. Provenance says who built it, from which source revision, with which workflow, using which builder identity. SLSA defines four levels; L3 requires provenance to be generated by a hosted build service in a way that a forge cannot tamper with, and in practice is reached using Sigstore’s keyless signing in a GitHub Actions workflow with workload identity federation — no long-lived secrets, a short-lived OIDC identity bound to the workflow, and a signed attestation that a verifier can check without trusting the CI provider. The practical payoff: when a package registry account is compromised, signed provenance distinguishes the attacker’s tarball from yours without anyone having to trust a checksum file hosted next to it.

DAST complements SAST by testing the running application, and it is the only automated class that sees authentication, session handling, authorisation and configuration together — the class where most real breaches live. Running a DAST scanner on every pull request is usually noise; running it nightly against staging, and weekly against production with safe mode, catches configuration drift and integration-level exposure. ZAP is the established open-source option and its baseline scan is a good default. Two caveats: a DAST result requires a human to interpret, and a scanner finding is not a vulnerability until someone reproduces it.

// Pre-launch security review — the artefact that gates the release decision.
// This is a checklist with an owner and a date, not a document with a header.

SECURITY-REVIEW  release: 2.5.0  candidate-sha: 4f9c1ab  reviewer: sec-eng@  date: 2026-08-14

[ ] 1. STRIDE model re-run against the release delta; all 8 scenarios mitigated
      or explicitly accepted. ......... owner: arch      status: DONE  (2 open, accepted)
[ ] 2. SAST: 0 unreviewed security-and-quality alerts. CodeQL + Semgrep.
      ......... owner: platform   status: DONE  (4 false positives triaged)
[ ] 3. SCA: 0 Critical, 0 High with a fix available. CycloneDX SBOM archived
      under digest 4f9c1ab…  ......... owner: platform   status: DONE
[ ] 4. DAST (ZAP baseline, nightly x7) on staging: no High, no Medium open > 14d
      ......... owner: sec-eng    status: DONE  (2 Medium, MTTR 9d, ticket SEC-311)
[ ] 5. Secrets: gitleaks full-history clean; all rotated keys have a new owner
      and a rotation date.   ......... owner: sec-eng    status: DONE
[ ] 6. Authn/session: passkey + MFA flows re-tested; session rotation verified on
      privilege change; 12h absolute TTL confirmed.  ..... status: DONE
[ ] 7. Authz: policy matrix tests green for all 11 roles x 47 resources
      ......... owner: sec-eng    status: DONE
[ ] 8. Desktop: binary signed with the 2026 hardware key, notarised; updater
      verifies manifest + payload; anti-rollback floor set.  ..... status: DONE
[ ] 9. Web: CSP enforcing (not report-only) for 14 days; HSTS preload eligible.
      ......... owner: web      status: DONE
[ ] 10. Infrastructure: no public S3 bucket, no 0.0.0.0 security group, IMDSv2
      enforced, no default credentials in any account.  ..... status: DONE
[ ] 11. Privacy: telemetry field register reviewed; no PII in events or traces;
      retention 90d; DSR endpoint tested.      ......... owner: dpo  status: DONE
[ ] 12. Third-party DPA + sub-processor register current; pen test summary
      received for any processor handling customer data.  ..... status: DONE

OUTCOME: APPROVE. 2 accepted risks recorded in the release notes and the register.
BLOCKING CONDITIONS (any checked = no-release): 2, 3, 5, 8.
