Sequence the rollout so the cheap controls land first. Secret scanning, lockfile enforcement, and SCA take under a day each and remove the largest share of low-effort risk. SAST and provenance take a week each and need a triage rota with a named owner. DAST and penetration testing need environments and budget. Attempting all ten simultaneously produces a pipeline that is red for a month and gets disabled; landing them in the order above produces a pipeline that is green and improving, and each new control meets a baseline of stability.

Apply every control to both tracks; some have no desktop equivalent and two have no web equivalent. SBOM, SCA, SAST and secret scanning are identical for the Web and Desktop tracks. Code signing, notarisation, entitlements, updater signature verification and the OS-level install/upgrade/uninstall matrix exist only on Desktop. Multi-tenant authorisation testing, CSP and session policy apply on the Web track and, in the Desktop track, apply to any surface the application renders or serves — which for a Tauri or Electron application is the embedded web view, and which is a genuine and frequently overlooked attack surface.

Exercises 17

  1. Produce a written test strategy for one of your current services or products. It must state a per-tier case-count budget, a per-tier wall-clock budget, a flake-rate ceiling, and the specific defect classes each tier is responsible for. Then instrument a counting test in CI that reads your actual distribution and fails when it drifts more than 5 points from the stated budget. Deliverable: the strategy document, the drift test, and a report of the actual distribution on the day you wrote it — the gap between stated and actual is the finding.
  2. Run Stryker (or mutmut, or PIT) over the three highest-risk modules in your codebase and produce a per-mutant report. Identify every surviving mutant in the 20 most dangerous categories (conditional negation, removed method call, arithmetic operator swap, boundary shift) and write a test that kills each one, or record a written decision that the mutation is equivalent. Deliverable: mutation score before and after, plus a per-mutant disposition for the 20, and a short note on which mutants you believe are semantically equivalent and why.
  3. Audit one module you own for over-mocking. Count the test doubles, classify each as stub, spy, fake or mock, and identify every mock of a collaborator whose implementation you also own. For three of them, replace the mock with a real fake and record whether any test failed. Deliverable: the classification table, the three rewrites, and a written rule for your team stating when mocking a first-party collaborator is permitted.
  4. Build a characterisation harness for one legacy module with no tests. Capture 200 real inputs from production logs, a golden-master them through a thin driver, and mark the outputs you believe are wrong. Then deliberately change one line of the legacy code and demonstrate that the harness catches it. Deliverable: the 200-case corpus with provenance, the golden-master test, the ticket list of wrong-but-pinned behaviours, and the demonstration diff.
  5. Complete a pre-launch security review on your product using the twelve-item checklist in 17.6, and independently reproduce two findings with Burp or ZAP. Then measure the DAST-scanner true-positive rate on your own staging environment over 30 days. Deliverable: the completed review with owners and dates, two written reproducers, and a measured true-positive rate that either justifies or retires your DAST gate.

18 · Release Management, Support and the Product Lifecycle

18.1 Versioning: SemVer 2.0 and when it is the wrong model18.2 Release channels and the compatibility contract18.3 Feature flags, progressive rollout and release trains18.4 Telemetry, SLOs and evidence-based decisions18.5 Support engineering and the ticket as a design signal18.6 Product lifecycle, deprecation and end of life

Once software works, the remaining engineering problem is entirely about change: how it is versioned, how it reaches users, how it is observed in the field, what happens when it breaks, and when it is retired. This section argues that the majority of avoidable customer harm in software comes not from defects but from uncoordinated change — a schema migration that runs ahead of the code that reads it, a flag that outlives its experiment, a release that arrives with no rollback path, an end-of-life notice nobody was told about. It covers the mechanics of SemVer 2.0 and, more usefully, the circumstances in which SemVer is the wrong model; the release channel system and the compatibility contract that makes multiple channels safe; the operation of feature flags as an engineering discipline rather than a deployment convenience; telemetry and SLOs used to make decisions rather than to produce dashboards; support engineering treated as a measurement instrument for design quality; and the lifecycle from launch through to a defensible, communicated end of life. It applies to both tracks, and the places where the Web and Desktop tracks diverge — where the update mechanism, the distribution channel and the revocation story are entirely different — are marked explicitly at the point where they matter.

18.1 Versioning: SemVer 2.0 and when it is the wrong model

This subsection establishes a version-numbering policy, defines what each part of a version obliges you to, and identifies the product classes for which SemVer is the wrong instrument.

Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 is a contract, not a syntax. The specification defines precedence — a version has major, minor, patch and optional pre-release and build metadata; build metadata is ignored entirely for precedence; a pre-release version has lower precedence than the associated normal version; identifiers are compared segment by segment, numerically where numeric, lexicographically otherwise, and numeric segments always have lower precedence than alphanumeric ones. Everything else in SemVer is a promise made to a consumer you do not control. MAJOR is a promise that the public API is broken: names changed, arguments changed meaning, a function removed, a serialised format no longer readable. MINOR is a promise that functionality was added in a backward-compatible way. PATCH is a promise that something was fixed without changing the contract. The failure mode is not a wrong number; it is a number that breaks a promise, and it is discovered by a customer rather than by you.

Whether the SemVer contract can be kept is a question about the surface, not the version. It applies cleanly to a published library, an HTTP API, a CLI whose flags are documented, and a configuration file format. It applies with strain to an application, because “the public API” of an application includes everything the user can see, and a change to a settings screen’s meaning is a breaking change even though no signature moved. It does not apply at all to several common product classes, and teams that apply it anyway end up with either a meaningless number or a broken promise.

The clear non-cases are: operating-system and mobile-platform versioning, which is a two-integer scheme controlled by the platform vendor and cannot be changed; hardware and firmware, where a monotonic counter is more honest than a semantic triple; datasheet and document revisions, where a single integer revision is the convention; calendar or date-based versions, used widely in enterprise software where a year-plus-month identifies a support window and maps to a maintenance contract; and internal, single-consumer services, where nobody is parsing your version and the only thing that matters is that the build identifier is unique. There is one more case worth naming: products whose primary consumers are enterprise IT departments, where the compatibility promise is written in a support agreement rather than inferred from a number, and where the number is a label for the contract rather than a description of change.

The alternative that works well for many products is to version the thing, not the product. An application has a marketing version, a wire-protocol version, a schema version, and a build identifier, and they move independently. A release that changes the database layout moves the schema version and may not move the marketing version at all, because no human-visible behaviour changed. A release that adds a column to an API response moves the wire version only if a consumer might break on the extra field. A build that changes nothing but a log message moves only the build identifier. Separating these makes the compatibility promise precise and testable rather than rhetorical, and it makes it possible to state a real support window per version.

// The compatibility contract, stated in code rather than in a wiki page.
// Run on every build. A violation is a release blocker, not a warning.

export interface Versioned {
  marketing: string    // 2.5.0        what humans read; may skip minors
  wire: string         // 1.8          HTTP surface, negotiated explicitly
  schema: number       // 14           DB migrations applied, monotonic, never reused
  build: string        // 2026-08-14T0932Z+a91f0c7   unique, opaque, never parsed
}

const PRECEDENCE = (v: string) => v.split('.').map((n) => parseInt(n, 10))
const isNewer = (a: string, b: string) => {
  const [x, y] = [PRECEDENCE(a), PRECEDENCE(b)]
  return x[0] > y[0] || (x[0] === y[0] && (x[1] > y[1] ||
         (x[1] === y[1] && x[2] > y[2])))
}

const CHANGELOG = yaml.parse(await readFile('CHANGELOG.md', 'utf8'))

export function assertSemVerHonoured(prev: Versioned, next: Versioned) {
  const b = PRECEDENCE(next.marketing)
  const a = PRECEDENCE(prev.marketing)
  const breaking = CHANGELOG.find((e) => e.version === next.marketing)?.breaking

  if (b[0] !== a[0]) {
    if (!breaking) throw new Error(`MAJOR bump to ${next.marketing} without a "breaking" entry`)
    if (isNewer(next.wire, prev.wire) === false && breaking.requiresWireBump)
      throw new Error('breaking change that consumers must handle via wire version')
  } else if (b[1] !== a[1] && breaking)
    throw new Error(`MINOR bump to ${next.marketing} is marked breaking`)

  if (next.schema < prev.schema) throw new Error('schema version decreased: migrations are append-only')
  if (next.build === prev.build) throw new Error('build identifier reused')
  if (next.marketing !== prev.marketing && !isNewer(next.marketing, prev.marketing))
    throw new Error('downgrade in the marketing version')
}

The database is the component that most often breaks the compatibility contract, because a schema change is simultaneously a data change, a code change, and a state that older code will run against. The safe pattern is expand, migrate, contract, and it has three distinct phases separated by at least one full release. In expand, add the new structure — a new column, a new table, a new index — and write so that both the old and the new code paths work against it. In migrate, backfill in bounded batches, with the batch size and the pause chosen so that no single transaction competes with production traffic for more than a defined fraction of capacity. In contract, remove the old structure, which is only safe once no supported version reads it. A release that collapses these into one step is a release with a rollback story that does not work, because rolling back the code does not roll back a dropped column.

-- Expand / migrate / contract, on the same table, across three releases.
-- Releases R, R+1, R+2. R+1 must be able to run against a DB at schema 14 or 15.

-- R   · schema 14 → 15 · EXPAND (additive only; old code unaffected)
ALTER TABLE invoice
  ADD COLUMN total_minor_units BIGINT;                    -- nullable: no default, no lock
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_invoice_tenant_status
  ON invoice (tenant_id, status) WHERE archived_at IS NULL;
-- Note: ADD COLUMN without DEFAULT is metadata-only on PG 11+. With a DEFAULT
-- over 50M rows it is a full table rewrite under lock. This is the difference.

-- R   · dual-write in application code; both fields correct, readers may use either
INSERT INTO invoice (id, tenant_id, total_minor_units) ... -- sets the new field

-- R+1 · schema 15 → 16 · MIGRATE (bounded batches, resumable, observable)
DO $$
DECLARE batch INT := 5000; moved INT;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    WITH cte AS (
      SELECT id FROM invoice
      WHERE tenant_id = ANY($1)
        AND total_minor_units IS NULL
        AND archived_at IS NULL
      ORDER BY id LIMIT batch FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED   -- never blocks the writers
    )
    UPDATE invoice i SET total_minor_units = i.subtotal_minor + i.tax_minor
      FROM cte WHERE i.id = cte.id;
    GET DIAGNOSTICS moved = ROW_COUNT;
    EXIT WHEN moved = 0;
    PERFORM pg_sleep(0.05);        -- yield; stay under 5% of a core
  END LOOP;
END $$;

-- R+2 · schema 16 → 17 · CONTRACT (only when telemetry shows zero old readers)
ALTER TABLE invoice DROP COLUMN subtotal_minor;        -- now irreversible
-- R+1 rollback is still safe: schema 15 code works against a schema 17 database.

The rest of the discipline is mechanical. Derive the version from the change log rather than typing it, so the number cannot disagree with the history. Require that a MAJOR bump be accompanied by a migration guide, because the promise to a consumer who upgrades is not merely “nothing was removed”; it is “here is what to change, here is how long you have, and here is what happens if you do not”. Cap the number of simultaneously supported MAJOR versions at two for published libraries and three for hosted services, and treat exceeding that cap as a defect with a planned removal, not as a surprise. And keep pre-release versions honest: 2.6.0-rc.2 is a candidate, not a release, and a flag on it in a registry defaults to including pre-releases and starts that cascade.

# release-please.yaml — the version is derived, never typed.
{
  "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/googleapis/release-please/main/schemas/config.json",
  "release-type": "node",
  "bootstrap-sha": "4f9c1ab",
  "packages": {
    "apps/api":       { "release-type": "node", "component": "api",
                        "extra-files": ["src/version.ts", "../desktop/tauri.conf.json"] },
    "apps/web":       { "release-type": "node", "component": "web" },
    "apps/desktop":   { "release-type": "tauri", "component": "desktop",
                        "extra-files": ["Cargo.toml", "package.json"] },
    "packages/sdk":   { "release-type": "node", "component": "sdk",
                        "changelog-path": "CHANGELOG.md" }
  },
  "changelog-path": "CHANGELOG.md",
  "changelog-sections": [
    { "type": "feat", "section": "Features" },
    { "type": "fix",  "section": "Bug Fixes" },
    { "type": "perf", "section": "Performance" },
    { "type": "security", "section": "Security" },
    { "type": "perf",  "section": "Performance", "hidden": false }
  ],
  "release-as": "",                     # empty: computed from conventional commits
  "bump-minor-pre-major": false,
  "include-component-in-tag": true,
  "changelog-sections-type": "angular",
  "pull-request-title-pattern": "chore(release): ${version}",
  "extra-scripts": {
    "pre-release": ["pnpm --filter @fieldgl/sdk run build", "bash .ci/assert-semver.sh"]
  }
}

SemVer is a promise about an interface, and you cannot make it about the whole product. The most common abuse is a MAJOR bump for a change that broke nothing in the contract, motivated by a desire to signal importance. That trains every downstream consumer to ignore your major versions, which destroys the only mechanism the version number provides. Equally common is the opposite: a PATCH release that removes a configuration option, shortens a default timeout, or changes the format of a log line that a customer’s parser depends on. If the thing you version is an application rather than a library, version the interface and give the product a separate support-window label.

The Desktop track adds constraints that have no Web equivalent. Installer packages are immutable, versioned, and identified by more than a number: a Windows package has a four-part ProductVersion with a build number that must increase monotonically for every upgrade, an PackageFamilyName and a publisher identity that are part of the upgrade path, and an MSIX/AppImage/dmg that is a different artefact per architecture. macOS enforces that a version number has not been reused in the App Store. A user who installs 2.5.0 and then downgrades to 2.4.0 needs an explicit, separately-signed path, and the schema in Application Support must remain readable by the older build or the downgrade is destructive. Treat installer version rules as part of the compatibility contract and test them in the lifecycle matrix from 17.4.

18.2 Release channels and the compatibility contract

This subsection defines the release channel system, the contract each channel makes to its users, and the data-compatibility rules that make several channels safe at once.

A release channel is a promise about stability made to a named audience. The system that matters is not the set of names but the compatibility relationship between them, because a user on beta and a user on stable may be running the same server and the same database. The standard topology has five tiers. Nightly is every merge to main, optimised for detecting breakage, supporting no guarantees and no data compatibility whatsoever. Alpha is the first build of a new major version, for internal and named testers, explicitly unstable, explicitly unsupported. Beta is feature-complete for a release, still on the old major version where possible, and is the channel on which the team dogfoods for a stated period — two weeks for a web product, six weeks for a desktop product, because the update distribution delay on Desktop means beta users get the build later and keep it longer. Stable is the supported channel. LTS, where it exists, is a branch that receives only security and critical fixes for a longer window, and it exists because a fraction of customers — regulated enterprises, air-gapped installations, offline sites — cannot take major upgrades on the cadence a fast-moving product publishes.

Each channel needs a defined audience, a promotion criterion, a support commitment and a sunset date, and all four are absent from most organisations that use these names. “Beta” with no promotion criterion is a second name for stable. “Stable” with no sunset date is stable forever, which is not a plan. Write the contract down, publish it, and hold the team to it; the moment beta users report bugs and are told “that is what beta means”, the channel has failed regardless of the technical maturity of the build.

ChannelCadenceAudienceSupportData compatibilityPromotion criterionSunset
NightlyEvery main mergeInternal CI✗ None✗ Disposable DB onlySmoke suite greenn/a
AlphaWeeklyTeam + named testers✗ Best effort~ Own sandboxFeature-complete for the milestoneAt beta entry
BetaWeeklyOpt-in customers~ P3, no SLA✓ Schema-compatible with stable2–6 weeks dogfood, 0 P1s openAt GA
StableEvery 2–4 weeks (Web) · 6–8 weeks (Desktop)All users✓ Full SLO✓ N-1 always supportedBeta exit criteria metAfter LTS window
LTSQuarterlyEnterprise, regulated, air-gapped✓ Security + P1 only✓ Frozen; upgrades path documentedDesignated at each GA24–36 months after GA

The compatibility contract between channels is mostly a data contract, and there are exactly two workable strategies. The first is to make the schema changes backward compatible in both directions for the whole window in which channels coexist: expand-only migrations, no dropped columns, no changed types, no changed semantics of existing columns, and code that can read both the old and the new shape. This is the strategy most teams should use, because it means any client on any supported version can be served by the same server, and rolling back the application is always safe. The second is to run separate stacks per channel with independent data stores, which is more expensive and more complex but is the right choice when the version gap is large, when a migration is genuinely irreversible, or when the beta channel is used to test a data model change that the stable channel cannot accommodate.

Regardless of which you choose, an N-1 rule must exist and be enforced: a deployment of version N is only allowed once version N-1 has been fully rolled out and has been serving production for a defined stabilisation period — 48 hours for a web service, longer for a desktop product. This single rule prevents the most damaging class of release incident, which is a partially-completed rollout in which a schema has advanced but half the fleet has not, and a bug that only affects the boundary. The counterpart rule is that a rollback must be a documented, tested operation with a stated time to execute, and that a release which cannot be rolled back within 15 minutes is not ready for a progressive rollout.

# release-channels.yaml — the contract, written down and machine-readable.
channels:
  stable:
    selector: semver '>=2.4.0 <3.0.0' && !prerelease
    audience: all
    support: full
    database: shared-main            # must satisfy N-1 against beta
    min_previous: '2.4.0'           # N-1 rule, enforced by the deploy gate
    stabilisation_hours: 48
    auto_update: true
    rollback_sla_minutes: 15

  beta:
    selector: semver '^2.6.0' && prerelease
    audience: opt-in                 # never the default, never prompted
    support: p3
    database: shared-main            # expand-only, contract deferred
    dogfood_weeks: 6                 # Desktop: update cadence is slower
    promotion_gates:
      - { check: open_p1, max: 0 }
      - { check: crash_free_sessions, min: 99.4 }     # 48h window
      - { check: e2e_suite, min: 100 }                # 0 flakes for 7 days
      - { check: security_review, max_days: 30 }

  lts:
    selector: branch 'release/2.3.x'
    audience: enterprise-contracted
    support: security-only
    database: read-replica-of-main    # never a second writer
    window_months: 30                 # from the 3.0.0 GA date
    fix_policy: [security, data-corruption, p1-crash]
    frozen: true                      # no feature commits, ever
    upgrade_path_docs: 'docs/upgrading/2.3-to-3.0.md'

  nightly:
    selector: branch 'main'
    audience: internal
    support: none
    database: ephemeral-per-run       # nuked at the end; no shared state, ever
    retention_hours: 6

The Desktop track’s channel system is dominated by a constraint the Web track does not have: the update is distributed through the user’s machine, not pushed by the server. That means a Desktop release is not delivered when you publish it; it is delivered when each user allows it, which produces a distribution curve measured in weeks and months rather than hours. Three consequences follow. First, the deprecation window for a Desktop version must be long — a measured 90-day window leaves a median user on a version two majors behind, and a 180-day window is usually closer to correct for a self-updating product with a 30 % population on a managed network that blocks updates. Second, you cannot recall a bad build, only stop offering it, so a signing key compromise or a defective build requires an anti-rollback floor and a revoked-version list that the updater checks before applying. Third, the beta channel is not a channel users visit; it is a channel users are opted into, and the opt-in is itself a support commitment.

# updater-manifest.json — Desktop. Signed; the client trusts nothing else.
{
  "schema": 1,
  "generatedAt": "2026-08-14T09:32:07Z",
  "signingKeyId": "fieldgl-release-2026-07",       # hardware-backed, rotated annually
  "channels": {
    "stable": {
      "version": "2.5.0",
      "releasedAt": "2026-08-14T09:32:07Z",
      "minPrevious": "2.4.3",                    # N-1: updater will cross this
      "floor": "2.4.0",                          # anti-rollback: refuse older
      "artifacts": [
        { "platform": "windows-x64",    "url": ".../2.5.0/app.msi",
          "sha256": "9c1e...a7", "size": 88_412_672, "deltaFrom": "2.4.3" },
        { "platform": "macos-aarch64",  "url": ".../2.5.0/app.dmg",
          "sha256": "4b02...31", "size": 92_118_400, "notarised": true }
      ]
    },
    "beta": { "version": "2.6.0-beta.3", "releasedAt": "2026-08-12T07:10:00Z",
              "floor": "2.5.0", "artifacts": [ { "platform": "windows-x64", "sha256": "..." } ] },
    "lts":   { "version": "2.3.7", "revoked": false }
  },
  "revoked": [
    { "version": "2.5.0-rc.1", "reason": "updater path traversal, CVE-2026-3391",
      "revokedAt": "2026-07-29T18:00:00Z", "minimum": "2.5.0" }
  ],
  "signature": { "alg": "ed25519", "keyId": "fieldgl-release-2026-07",
                 "value": "MEUCIQ...", "signedOver": "everything above except this field" }
}
# Client rules, in order, before any download begins:
#   1. verify signature over the manifest with the embedded offline root
#   2. refuse if version < floor (rollback attack / revoked build)
#   3. refuse if version is in `revoked`
#   4. apply only the artifact whose sha256 matches the signed manifest
#   5. on failure, stay on the current build silently — never half-install

Publish the channel contract and hold yourself to the sunset dates. A channel table that names promotion criteria, support levels and sunsets, published where users and your own team can read it, converts an unwritten cultural expectation into something you can be held to. The value shows up in the crisis: when a P1 arrives, everyone can answer “which channel, which population, what is the rollback, when does beta get it” in under a minute instead of holding a meeting. Attach the contract to the on-call runbook as well as to the status page.

18.3 Feature flags, progressive rollout and release trains

This subsection treats feature flags as a system with a lifecycle, an evaluation model and a retirement policy, and places them alongside the two alternative rollout disciplines.

A feature flag is a boolean, or a small variant set, that separates deployment from release. Its value is that it makes it possible to ship code in one release and change behaviour in another, which decouples a risky change from a risky build and makes a rollback a configuration change measured in seconds rather than a redeployment measured in minutes. Its cost is that it makes the system harder to reason about: the number of distinct code paths multiplies, tests must run with more than one value, and code that is only reachable behind a flag is code that no one is exercising. Used as a temporary operational mechanism with a retirement date, a flag is one of the highest-leverage tools in release engineering. Used as a permanent configuration system, it is a way of shipping untested combinations for the life of the product.

Flags should be classified, because the classes have different lifetimes and different evaluation models. Release flags gate a feature’s first appearance and are deleted within days. Experiment flags select a variant for measurement and are deleted at the end of the experiment. Operational flags — kill switches, rate limits, provider routing, circuit-breaker overrides — are expected to be long-lived and are genuinely configuration, and the right home for them is the configuration system, not the flag service. Entitlement flags are per-customer and are a permanent part of the business model. Conflating the second and third classes is what produces flag debt: an experiment flag is never deleted, its variant becomes a default, and six months later nobody knows whether the flag is still meaningful.

The evaluation model must be decided deliberately. A server-evaluated flag is authoritative, is impossible for a client to bypass, and can be changed instantly, but every request pays a lookup and every un-evaluated code path is genuinely dead code. A client-evaluated flag is cached and offline-capable, which is a hard requirement on the Desktop track, but it is only as fresh as its cache and a determined user can edit it. The correct answer for most products is a hybrid: entitlement and kill-switch decisions are server-side and enforced, while UI presentation and experimentation are client-side against a flag snapshot delivered with the session. Both sides must be documented, and any flag that appears on both sides must state which side is authoritative.

// Flag evaluation: deterministic bucketing, no network call on the hot path,
// and an explicit authority so a client cannot override a kill switch.
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'
import { LRUCache } from 'lru-cache'

type Flag = {
  key: string
  owner: string            // required, validated at registration
  kind: 'release' | 'experiment' | 'operational' | 'entitlement'
  variants: Record<string, unknown>
  rollout: Record<string, number>        // variant → percentage 0-100
  salt: string             // changing the salt re-randomises; use deliberately
  expiresAt: string        // required for release/experiment; CI enforces it
  authority: 'server' | 'client' | 'server-preferred'
}

const cache = new LRUCache<string, Record<string, unknown>>({ max: 10_000, ttl: 30_000 })

export function bucket(subject: string, flag: Flag): string {
  // FNV-1a over (salt, subject). Sticky: the same user keeps the same variant
  // for the life of the flag, so a 10% rollout means the same 10% every time.
  const h = createHash('sha256').update(`${flag.salt}:${flag.key}:${subject}`).digest()
  const n = h.readUInt32BE(0) / 2 ** 32 * 100
  let acc = 0
  for (const [variant, pct] of Object.entries(flag.rollout)) {
    acc += pct
    if (n < acc) return variant
  }
  return Object.keys(flag.variants).at(-1)!
}

export function evaluate(flag: Flag, subject: { userId: string; plan: string }) {
  if (flag.kind === 'entitlement') return flag.variants[subject.plan] ?? flag.variants.none
  const key = `${flag.key}:${subject.userId}`
  const hit = cache.get(key)
  if (hit) return hit
  const value = { variant: bucket(subject.userId, flag), value: flag.variants[bucket(subject.userId, flag)] }
  cache.set(key, value)
  return value
}

// The kill switch is separate, server-authoritative, and checked first. A client
// that says "I am in the new checkout" when the switch is off is told no.
export function gate(flagKey: string, ctx: Ctx) {
  if (killswitches.has(flagKey) && !ctx.staffBypass) return { variant: 'off', value: false }
  const flag = registry.get(flagKey)!
  const ev = evaluate(flag, ctx.subject)
  if (flag.authority === 'server-preferred' && ev.variant !== 'control') ctx.audit('flag_override', { key: flagKey })
  return ev
}

Progressive rollout is a discipline applied to the traffic or the population, and there are four useful forms. Blue-green runs two full environments and switches all traffic at once; it gives a perfect rollback and doubles infrastructure cost, and it does nothing for a database change. Canary runs the new version for 1 %, 5 %, 25 %, 100 % with an observation window at each step and an automatic abort on regression; it is the default for services and it is where the automation from 18.2 lives. A/B testing splits traffic for measurement rather than risk reduction, and it has a different discipline: a pre-registered hypothesis, a fixed sample size, a decision date, and no peeking. Feature-flag rollout ramps a flag for a population and is the Web track’s equivalent, minus the infrastructure. The failure common to all four is a ramp that nobody aborts, so every step needs a machine-checked criterion rather than a human noticing.

Release trains and continuous deployment are the two operating modes, and they are not rivals so much as different points on one axis. A release train batches changes onto a scheduled departure — weekly, bi-weekly, monthly — with a cut-off, a stabilisation window, and everyone on the same train. Continuous deployment releases every merge that passes. The trade-off is exactly the trade-off between batch size and feedback latency: a train amortises the cost of verification across many changes and gives a predictable, communicable cadence, at the price of shipping known-mediocre changes alongside excellent ones and discovering a problem only at batch size. Continuous deployment minimises both batch size and latency, at the price of requiring an automated rollback, a mature feature-flag posture, and a team that can absorb many small releases per day. The pragmatic default for a product team is a train with a hard cut-off and automated progressive rollout inside it, and the migration path from train to continuous deployment is the flag retirement work in this subsection.

# .ci/assert-flag-lifecycle.sh — the gate that makes flag debt visible and bounded.
set -euo pipefail
REGISTRY="config/flags.json"
TODAY=$(date -u +%F)
MAX_AGE_DAYS=45          # release+experiment flags MUST be gone in 45 days
fail=0

# 1. Every flag must have an owner and an expiry.
jq -r '.[] | select(.owner == null or .expiresAt == null)
        | "MISSING META  \(.key)  owner=\(.owner // "-")  expires=\(.expiresAt // "-")"' \
   "$REGISTRY" | tee -a flag-report.txt && fail=1 || true

# 2. Expired flags are a release blocker, not a warning.
while IFS='	' read -r key exp; do
  if [[ "$exp" < "$TODAY" ]]; then
    echo "EXPIRED FLAG  $key (expired $exp) — delete the code, not the date"
    fail=1
  fi
  age=$(( ( $(date -u -d "$TODAY" +%s) - $(date -u -d "$exp" +%s) ) / 86400 ))
  if (( age < 0 && -age > MAX_AGE_DAYS )); then
    echo "OVERDUE       $key  $(( -age )) days past expiry"
    fail=1
  fi
done < <(jq -r '.[] | select(.kind=="release" or .kind=="experiment")
                 | [.key, .expiresAt] | @tsv' "$REGISTRY")

# 3. Count evaluated flags. More than 8 on a request path means combinatorial
#    testing is no longer covering reality and coverage must be restated.
EVALS=$(grep -rho 'gate("[a-z0-9._-]*"' src | sort -u | wc -l)
echo "evaluated flags: $EVALS"
(( EVALS > 8 )) && { echo "FLAG EXPLOSION: $EVALS flags in the request path"; fail=1; }

# 4. Combination coverage is the metric nobody tracks until it bites.
./node_modules/.bin/lcombo --input flags.json --out combo-report.json
COMBO=$(jq '.uncovered | length' combo-report.json)
echo "uncovered flag combinations: $COMBO  (tested in CI against the $EVALS-flag path)"
(( COMBO > 0 )) && echo "NOTE: add $COMBO combination tests to the e2e tier"

# 5. A flag evaluated but never present in the registry is a hard error.
grep -rho 'gate("[a-z0-9._-]*"' src | sed 's/gate("//; s/"//' | sort -u > used.txt
jq -r '.[].key' "$REGISTRY" | sort -u > defined.txt
comm -23 used.txt defined.txt | sed 's/^/UNDEFINED FLAG  /' && fail=1

exit $fail

Flag debt is measured, and the three numbers that matter are: the count of flags defined, the count evaluated on any single request or user path, and the count of flag combinations that no test exercises. A team at 3 flags has no problem. At 12 flags there are 4,096 theoretical combinations; at 20 there are over a million, and no suite covers them, so the real question is not “is each flag tested” but “which combinations are tested and why those”. The tool lcombo generates a set of combinations with maximal pairwise coverage — not all combinations, but a small subset that exercises every interaction of every pair, which for 12 flags is about 50 cases. That is the difference between a maintainable flag system and an untestable one, and it costs one dependency and a CI step.

# release-train-2026-w34.md — the train as an explicit, auditable artefact.
# Everything on this train passed the gate at cut-off. Nothing joins after.

TRAIN:     2026-W34
CUT-OFF:   2026-08-17T16:00Z  (Mon)   — after this, changes go to 2026-W35
STABLE:    2026-08-24T08:00Z  (Mon)   — progressive rollout 5 → 25 → 50 → 100
OWNER:     release-manager@     BACKUP: tech-lead@

## Cargo (17 items)
| ID      | Area      | Change                                    | Risk | Gate         | Rollback |
|---------|-----------|-------------------------------------------|------|--------------|----------|
| FG-2841 | payments  | SEPA instant debit, EUR only                | High | flag 25%→100%| flag off  |
| FG-2877 | invoices  | Expand: add total_minor_units, schema 15   | High | backward ✓   | code only |
| FG-2902 | desktop   | Updater anti-rollback floor 2.4.0           | Med  | matrix 24/24 | manifest |
| FG-2918 | web       | New invoice table, virtualised              | Med  | CWV green    | revert    |
| FG-2933 | auth      | Passkey enrolment                           | Low  | e2e 18/18    | revert    |
| …       |           | 12 more, all risk ≤ Low                     |      |              |          |

## Gates, in order
1.  ./ci/assert-n1.sh                  — 2.4.3 has been stable ≥ 48h        ✓
2.  ./ci/schema-diff --backward        — expand only, contract ≥ 14d out      ✓
3.  ./ci/assert-flag-lifecycle.sh      — 0 expired, 12 flags, 50 combos cov.  ✓
4.  ./ci/security-gate.sh              — SAST/SCA/secrets green                ✓
5.  e2e on beta for 144h               — 0 P1, crash-free ≥ 99.4 %            ✓
6.  release-manager sign-off           — @release-manager 2026-08-19          ✓

## Rollback triggers (machine-watched, auto-abort)
  error_rate > 0.5 % · p99 > 900 ms · crash_free < 99.4 % · any new P1

## Post-train (owner: release-manager, due 2026-08-31)
  - delete flag FG-2841 and its dead branch
  - contract migration for total_minor_units (14-day timer starts 2026-08-24)
  - add the 3 low-risk items skipped this week to the W35 manifest

The most expensive feature flag is the one nobody deletes. Flags accumulate because deleting one is nobody’s ticket: it is untidy rather than broken, and untidy does not page. A codebase with 30 live flags has 2^30 possible runtime behaviours, the vast majority of which are untested, and the resulting bug reports are unreproducible because the reporter and you are running different configurations. Enforce the expiry in CI, as above, and treat an expired flag as a release blocker. A flag that has served its purpose and is still there is a permanent, untested, undocumented configuration surface running in production.

On the Desktop track a flag cannot be the rollback mechanism for a shipped binary. Users install a build; the code for the new behaviour is inside it; and the update reaches them days or weeks later. A server-evaluated flag is unavailable when the machine is offline, which is a normal condition, not an exception. The Desktop pattern is therefore to ship the new code path inert and to control its activation from a signed, cached policy file fetched when online, with a safe default, an explicit expiry, and a kill switch in the policy — never in the binary. Combined with the anti-rollback floor from 18.2, this gives a kill switch that works offline and a rollback that works for a build you cannot un-install.

18.4 Telemetry, SLOs and evidence-based decisions

This subsection covers instrumentation, service and product objectives, error budgets, and the privacy constraints that bound what may be collected at all.

Telemetry is the practice of emitting enough structured observation to answer questions you did not think to ask in advance. The technical choice is settled: OpenTelemetry for collection, with traces carrying the request’s causal structure, metrics carrying distributions, and logs carrying detail correlated to both. The discipline is not. The three failure modes are collecting far more than is useful, which costs money and creates a liability; collecting the wrong things, which produces a dashboard nobody can act on; and, worst, collecting things and then making decisions from them without establishing whether the decision rule was sound.

Service-level objectives and error budgets are the framework that makes telemetry operational rather than decorative. An SLO is a target for a user-visible behaviour measured over a window: “99.5 % of requests to the invoice API return a non-5xx within 400 ms at p95, measured over 28 days”. An error budget is the permitted fraction of failure — 0.5 % — and its purpose is not to be spent but to be governed. A team spending less than half its budget may ship without the full change-review ritual; a team exceeding it halts feature work until reliability is restored. The mechanism works because it converts an argument about risk into a number both sides already agreed to, and because it is asymmetric on purpose: reliability moves faster when it is failing, features move faster when it is not.

// OpenTelemetry 1.7x — Node 24. Traces, metrics, logs, correlated.
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node'
import { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } from '@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node'
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http'
import { PeriodicExportingMetricReader, View, ExponentialHistogramAggregation } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-metrics'
import { ParentBasedSampler, TraceIdRatioBasedSampler } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base'

const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  resource: resourceFromAttributes({
    'service.name': process.env.OTEL_SERVICE_NAME,
    'service.version': VERSION.marketing,     // ties telemetry to the release
    'deployment.environment.name': process.env.NODE_ENV,
    'service.instance.id': process.env.INSTANCE_ID,
    'fieldglass.schema': VERSION.schema,     // so regressions are version-attributable
  }),
  traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter({ url: 'https://otlp.internal/v1/traces' }),
  metricReader: new PeriodicExportingMetricReader({ exportIntervalMillis: 30_000 }),
  // Parent-based + ratio: keep 100% of errors, 5% of successes, and never break
  // a trace into two pieces because a downstream service sampled differently.
  sampler: new ParentBasedSampler({ root: new TraceIdRatioBasedSampler(0.05) }),
  instrumentations: [getNodeAutoInstrumentations({
    '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-fs': { enabled: false },       // huge, low value
    '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http': { ignoreIncomingRequestHook: (req) =>
      req.url === '/healthz' || req.url === '/favicon.ico' },
  })],
})

// Metric hygiene: cardinality is the bill. Never put a user id in a metric label.
sdk.start()

export const httpServerDuration = meter.createHistogram('http.server.duration', {
  unit: 'ms',
  advice: { explicitBucketBoundaries: [5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1500, 3000] },
})
// View: prefer the native exponential histogram, which has ~1 % error at any
// range. Fixed buckets silently mis-measure p99 and are how latency SLOs break.
sdk.addMetricReader(new PeriodicExportingMetricReader({
  views: [new View({
    instrumentName: 'http.server.duration',
    aggregation: new ExponentialHistogramAggregation({ maxSize: 160 }),
  })],
}))

Product telemetry answers a different class of question — did the feature work, did anyone find it, did it help — and it must be separated from operational telemetry in storage, in access control and in retention. The classification is a per-field decision, made before collection rather than during an incident: operational fields (latency, status, version) are unrestricted and short-lived; behavioural fields (which features used, frequency counts, funnel steps) are pseudonymous, aggregate-only, and consented; sensitive fields (anything identifying a person, anything derived from content the user created, anything that reveals health, financial or political information) are not collected at all in an operational system. The practical test for a field is whether the product would be worse if it leaked: if yes, it does not belong in the same pipeline, in the same warehouse, or under the same access policy as error rates.

# telemetry-register.yaml — the field-level contract. Reviewed at launch and quarterly.
# default_action: reject. A field is collected only by being listed here.
telemetry:
  defaults:
    action: reject
    retention_days: 90
    storage: metrics-only
    pii: prohibited

  fields:
    - name: http.server.duration
      class: operational
      action: allow
      source: otel
      dimensions: [route, status, service.version]
      cardinality_budget: 400          # series, not rows. Enforced at the collector.
      retention_days: 30
    - name: feature.use_count
      class: behavioural
      action: allow
      source: client (Web) / local (Desktop)
      dimensions: [flag.key, variant, plan, country]
      consent_required: analytics
      aggregation: daily-count, min_group_size: 20      # k-anonymity floor
      retention_days: 400
    - name: screen.viewed
      class: behavioural
      action: allow
      dimensions: [screen_id, app_version]
      consent_required: analytics
    - name: session.replay
      class: behavioural
      action: allow
      consent_required: explicit-opt-in
      redact: [input, textarea, [data-pii], password, cc-number]
      mask_text: true
    - name: user.email
      class: sensitive
      action: reject                  # joins happen in the product DB, not in telemetry
    - name: invoice.total
      class: sensitive
      action: reject                  # business value, not diagnostic value
    - name: document.content
      class: sensitive
      action: reject                  # content-derived data is the highest liability
    - name: free_text.query
      class: sensitive
      action: reject

  local_only:                          # Desktop: nothing leaves without consent
    - crash.dedupe_fingerprint          # hash of the stack, no user data
    - perf.startup_ms, perf.idle_rss_mb
    - feature.use_count                # buffered locally, flushed on opt-in

# slo.yaml — SLOs as code, reviewed like code, budgeted explicitly.
# Owner: sre@  Review cadence: quarterly  Escalation: #incidents
api_version: slok.dev/v1
service: fieldglass-api
description: Invoice, payment and export surface.

slos:
  - name: api-availability
    objective: 99.9                  # 43m 12s of unavailability per 30d
    window: 30d
    indicator:
      source: otel
      query: |
        sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{
          service="fieldglass-api", route!~"/healthz|/metrics",
          status=~"5..", le="0.5"}))
        /
        sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{service="fieldglass-api", route!~"/healthz|/metrics"}))

  - name: api-latency
    objective: 99.0                  # 1 % of requests slower than 400 ms at p95
    window: 30d
    indicator:
      source: otel
      query: |
        histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_server_duration_bucket{
          service="fieldglass-api", le="0.4"})) by (le)) < 400
    slices: [route]                  # an SLO is only useful if it has slices

  - name: export-completion
    objective: 99.5
    window: 30d
    slo_type: availability
    # A job that starts and never finishes is the failure this exists to catch.

error_budget_policy:
  burn_rate_alerts:                   # multi-window multi-burn-rate (Google SRE)
    - { long_window: 1h,  short_window: 5m,  burn_rate: 14.4, page: true }
    - { long_window: 6h,  short_window: 30m, burn_rate: 6,    page: true }
    - { long_window: 3d,  short_window: 6h,  burn_rate: 1,    page: false }
    - { long_window: 30d, short_window: 1d,  burn_rate: 0.5,  page: false }
  # 14.4x over 1h consumes 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. Page on that.
  policy:
    - if: budget_remaining_pct > 75
      then: "full release cadence, normal review"
    - if: budget_remaining_pct in [50, 75]
      then: "changes require two reviewers; no schema contracts"
    - if: budget_remaining_pct < 50
      then: "freeze non-reliability work until the budget recovers to 75%"
    - if: budget_remaining_pct < 10
      then: "executive incident; all roadmap work halts"
    reviews: weekly

Making decisions from telemetry has its own failure modes, and naming them is part of the discipline. Simpson’s paradox will make a change look like it helped overall while hurting every segment, or the reverse, whenever a mix shift drives the aggregate — a rollout that disproportionately reaches one plan will move the global number regardless of the effect on anyone. Peeking at a result repeatedly and stopping when it looks good inflates the false-positive rate from 5 % to over 50 %; fix the sample size and the end date in advance. Gaming is where a metric becomes a target: if support’s queue length is a KPI, it will be closed with a template reply; if “time to first value” is a KPI, an onboarding step will be removed. The defence is to pair every metric with a counter-metric that would move in the opposite direction if it were gamed, and to review the pair rather than the metric.

// Sentry 2026 — redaction at the edge of the SDK, not in a review of the UI.
import * as Sentry from '@sentry/node'

Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN,
  release: `${process.env.OTEL_SERVICE_NAME}@${VERSION.marketing}`,
  environment: process.env.NODE_ENV,
  integrations: [Sentry.nodeProfilingIntegration()],

  // Error sampling: keep everything P2+, sample the rest. Volume is a cost and
  // a review cost; a sampled error that mattered will recur within hours.
  tracesSampleRate: 0.05,
  profilesSampleRate: 0.05,

  // A failing transaction is a bug we want; a slow successful one is telemetry.
  beforeSendTransaction: (tx) => {
    if (tx.transaction.startsWith('/healthz')) return null
    if (tx.outcome === 'success' && (tx.duration ?? 0) < 2_000) return null
    return tx
  },

  // Redaction happens here, once, and is covered by a unit test. A scrubber
  // configured but untested is a comment.
  beforeSend: scrubEvent,

  sendDefaultPii: false,
  maxBreadcrumbs: 40,
  attachStacktrace: true,
  enableTracing: true,
  tracePropagationTargets: [/^https:\/\/(api|otlp|files)\./],
})

const SENSITIVE = /^(password|passwd|token|access_token|refresh_token|authorization|
  card_number|cvv|iban|ssn|tax_id|secret|api_key|cookie|set-cookie)$/i

function scrubEvent(event: Sentry.Event): Sentry.Event | null {
  if (event.request?.headers) {
    for (const k of Object.keys(event.request.headers)) {
      if (SENSITIVE.test(k)) event.request.headers[k] = '[redacted]'
    }
  }
  if (event.request?.data) event.request.data = '[omitted]'   // bodies, always
  if (event.user) {
    event.user = { id: event.user.id }                       // id only, never email/ip
  }
  if (event.extra) {
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(event.extra)) {
      if (SENSITIVE.test(k)) event.extra[k] = '[redacted]'
      if (typeof v === 'string' && v.length > 512) event.extra[k] = `${v.slice(0, 512)}…`
    }
  }
  return event
}

Write the decision rule before you look at the data. For every question that matters, record the metric, the slice, the minimum effect size that would be worth acting on, the sample size needed to detect it, the date you will decide, and what you will do in each outcome — including “ship” and including “do nothing”. A pre-registration costs ten minutes and converts a post-hoc rationalisation into a test. For the Desktop track, the same discipline applies to locally collected telemetry, with one addition: the opt-in prompt must be offered at install time, defaulted to off for anything behavioural, and the collection must work — buffered, bounded, and dropped rather than uploaded — when the user declines.

18.5 Support engineering and the ticket as a design signal

This subsection describes how a support function is tiered and measured, what a reproducible bug report must contain, and why the ticket volume is a design metric rather than a cost centre.

Support is a measurement instrument pointed at your product. Every ticket is an observation of a path a real person tried and could not complete, and the aggregate is a map of where the product is confusing, wrong or missing. Treating support as a cost centre means paying to absorb that signal; treating it as an instrument means reading it, which is the difference between a support function that reduces ticket volume over a year and one that does not. The mechanism is unglamorous: categorise every ticket at intake, aggregate monthly by category, and require each category over a threshold to produce either a product change or an explicit, written decision not to change the product. The second half is what stops the process degenerating into a wish list.

Tiering separates work by its blast radius. L1 handles known issues, access problems, how-to questions and information requests; it is staffed by people with a runbook and a good search index, and its success metric is deflection and a fast first response. L2 handles reproducible defects, integration questions and environment problems; it needs read access to logs, the ability to reproduce, and the authority to escalate with a complete package. L3 is engineering: the service or application team, engaged by L2 with a reproduction, an affected population count and a hypothesis. The measure of a healthy support function is the ratio of work that L2 can close without L3, and the measure of a healthy product is tickets per active user falling over time. Escalation without a reproduction is not escalation; it is a transfer of cost.

Support SLOs are the mechanism that makes triage predictable, and they are stated as response and resolution targets per priority, with an explicit resolution target meaning “a fix or a documented workaround”, not “the engineer has looked at it”. The targets in 19.2 are a reasonable baseline; the numbers that must be measured rather than assumed are the median first response for P3, and the fraction of P1s that turn out to be something else — a training problem, a data problem, or a misunderstanding. That last number is the most diagnostic one in support, and if it is high the product’s error messages and onboarding are failing before support is even reached.

# runbooks/p1.md — the first 30 minutes of a P1, pre-written so it is executed.
severity: P1
definition: > 20 % of active users cannot complete a core task, or data is at risk
declare_by: any engineer, in #incidents, /incident declare --sev 1
response_required_within: 10m

## 1 · Declare and assemble (0–5 min)
- [ ] /incident declare --sev 1 --svc api --runbook runbooks/p1.md
- [ ] Assign: INCIDENT COMMANDER (does not touch a keyboard)
- [ ] Assign: COMMUNICATIONS (writes every update, does not investigate)
- [ ] /incident status "investigating" --public
- [ ] Post the internal channel template verbatim (below). No improvisation.

## 2 · Establish blast radius (5–10 min) — measure, do not guess
  SELECT date_trunc('minute', ts) AS t,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE status >= 500) / count(*)::float AS err_rate,
         count(DISTINCT tenant_id)                            AS tenants_affected
  FROM   request_log WHERE route LIKE '/v1/invoice%' AND ts > now() - interval '1 hour'
  GROUP  1 ORDER BY 1 DESC LIMIT 5;
  - err_rate now / err_rate 1h ago  = blast radius
  - Compare to SLO 99.9 %: is the 30-day error budget being consumed faster than 14.4x?

## 3 · Mitigation before diagnosis (10–20 min) — in this order
  1. Disable the feature flag most likely involved          ./ops/flag set FG-2841=false --all
  2. Roll back the last deploy if it is < 6 h old         ./ops/rollback --to previous --verify
  3. Roll forward a hotfix if rollback is unsafe (schema)  ./ops/emergency-patch
  4. Shed load: enable the queue, raise rate limits, 429
  5. Fail over the region (Web only)                       ./ops/failover --to eu-west-1
  NEVER: write to the production database by hand. Ever. No exceptions, ever.

## 4 · Communicate every 30 min, even with no news
  "09:14 — investigating. Checkout failures affecting ~14 % of EU users since 08:52.
   Suspect: deploy 4f9c1ab (08:47). Mitigation in progress. Next update by 09:44."

## 5 · Hand over (if unresolved at 30 min)
  - Freeze: no further deploys
  - Write the handover: knowns, unknowns, attempted, ruled out, next hypothesis
  - Re-declare IC if the new person is not the person who built the context

## 6 · Within 5 business days
  - [ ] Blameless postmortem published, circulated, action items with owners+dates
  - [ ] Every action item has a tracking ticket and a DRI
  - [ ] SLO / error budget reviewed: was the alert late? Was the runbook wrong?
  - [ ] Runbook updated with the thing that would have been faster this time

A reproducible bug report is the highest-leverage thing support can produce and the thing most often received as an unusable paragraph. The minimum content is fixed and collected automatically where possible: exact application or bundle version, operating system and build, architecture, display scaling, locale and keyboard layout (Desktop) or browser, user agent and viewport (Web); a timestamp to the minute in UTC; the account or tenant, redacted to a hash; the last known good version; the reproduction steps as numbered imperative sentences; the expected result; the observed result; and a recording or log bundle. Anything less is a triage cost that the reporter has already paid.

// Support bundle — the "attach this" button. Collects locally, redacts, then uploads.
import { arch, platform, release, locales } from 'node:os'
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs'
import { zip } from 'yazl'
import { app } from '@fieldgl/desktop'

const SECRETISH = /(token|secret|password|cookie|authorization|iban|card|ssn)/i

export async function buildSupportBundle(opts: { userConsent: boolean }) {
  const z = new zip.ZipFile()
  const manifest = {
    app: { version: VERSION.marketing, build: VERSION.build, schema: VERSION.schema,
           channel: await currentChannel(), installedAt: await installDate() },
    host: { platform: platform(), release: release(), arch: arch(), cpus: cpus().length,
            memTotalMB: Math.round(totalmem() / 1048576), locale: locales(),
            display: await displayInfo() },        // scale, resolution, refresh Hz
    runtime: { node: process.versions.node, v8: process.versions.v8,
               uptimeS: Math.round(process.uptime()) },
    updater: { lastCheckedAt: await lastCheck(), lastError: await lastError() },
    crash: (await recentCrashes(10)).map((c) => ({ hash: c.fingerprint, ts: c.ts })),
  }
  z.addBuffer(Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(manifest, null, 2)), 'manifest.json')

  for (const f of ['fieldglass.log', 'renderer.log', 'crash/*.dmp']) {
    for await (const [name, stream] of await collect(f)) {
      const redacted = await redactStream(stream)       // tokenised, line-buffered
      z.addReadStream(redacted, `${SECRETISH.test(name) ? 'redacted/' : ''}${name}`)
    }
  }
  // Config: values are whitelisted, not blacklisted. A denylist always leaks.
  z.addBuffer(Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(await exportSafeConfig(), null, 2)), 'config.safe.json')

  if (!opts.userConsent) {
    z.addBuffer(Buffer.from('Session replay and recent documents EXCLUDED: no consent.\n'),
                'EXCLUSIONS.txt')
  }
  return z.end({ forceZip64Format: true })
}

Closing the loop matters more than the measurement. The monthly aggregate should be published, not merely generated, and reviewed with the people who can change the product. Three numbers are worth publishing without fail: tickets per thousand active users per month, the median and 90th percentile time to first response by priority, and the top five categories with their month-on-month trend. When a category is rising, the question is never “how do we close these faster” but “what in the product invited them”, and the answer is usually a specific screen, a specific error message, a specific permission, or a specific missing affordance. Deflection rates are worth tracking but they are a lagging indicator of product clarity: a good knowledge base makes support faster, and a good product makes the knowledge base unnecessary.

-- Support triage: the queries support runs daily. Indexes matter more than cleverness.
-- Q1 · Overnight queue, oldest-first, with age in hours and SLA breach flag.
SELECT t.id, t.priority, t.category, t.subject,
       now() - t.created_at                              AS age,
       (now() - t.created_at) > (t.sla_first_response_at - t.created_at)
                                                     AS response_breached,
       t.tenant_plan, t.app_version, t.locale
FROM   support_ticket t
WHERE  t.status = 'open'
  AND  (t.assigned_to IS NULL OR t.last_activity_at < now() - interval '4 hours')
ORDER BY priority, t.created_at
LIMIT 200;

-- Q2 · Tickets-per-thousand by category, month on month. The design signal.
WITH active AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', ts) AS m, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS mau
  FROM   app_session WHERE ts >= now() - interval '3 months' GROUP BY 1
), tickets AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS m, category,
         count(*) AS n, count(DISTINCT tenant_id) AS accounts
  FROM   support_ticket WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '3 months'
  GROUP  BY 1, 2
)
SELECT t.m, t.category, t.n,
       round(1000.0 * t.n / NULLIF(a.mau, 0), 2)        AS per_1k_mau,
       lag(round(1000.0 * t.n / NULLIF(a.mau, 0), 2))
         OVER (PARTITION BY t.category ORDER BY t.m)   AS prev,
       t.accounts                                      AS accounts_affected
FROM   tickets t JOIN active a USING (m)
ORDER  BY per_1k_mau DESC;

-- Q3 · Is this a version? Correlate with the release calendar before you escalate.
SELECT t.app_version, t.category, count(*) AS n
FROM   support_ticket t
WHERE  t.created_at > now() - interval '14 days' AND t.category IN ('crash','data_loss','perf')
GROUP  BY 1, 2
HAVING  count(*) > 20
ORDER  BY n DESC;
-- 2.5.0 with 340 crash tickets in 6 days is a release defect, not a support load.

-- Q4 · The diagnostic number: what fraction of P1s were not P1s?
SELECT CASE WHEN root_cause_category IS NULL THEN 'unclassified'
            WHEN root_cause_category = 'product_defect' THEN 'real'
            ELSE root_cause_category END AS klass,
       count(*) AS n
FROM   incident WHERE severity = 'P1' AND created_at > now() - interval '180 days'
GROUP  BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
-- A high 'expectation_mismatch' share means the error message is the bug.

Support obligations differ between the tracks in ways that affect the design rather than the process. A Web product’s support load concentrates around browser and version combinations you did not test, and the mitigation is a browser support statement that is enforced by a usage report — publish a policy of “the current and previous two major versions of the evergreen browsers, plus the current and previous two major versions of Safari” and stop investigating a report from a browser you have declared unsupported, politely and consistently. A Desktop product’s support load concentrates around operating systems and hardware you have never seen, managed environments that block your updater, and security software that quarantines your binary. Each of those has a documented answer that must exist before the first report: a minimum supported OS list, a troubleshooting entry for blocked updates, a signed-binary explanation, and a mechanism for the user to send a log bundle without an engineer asking for it three times.

TierOwnsAccessTarget closeEscalates whenMeasured byHealthy value
L1 · Front lineKnown issues, access, how-toRunbook, KB, account readSame shiftNew defect, > 1 recontactDeflection %, FRT≥ 65 % closed at L1
L2 · InvestigationRepro defects, integration+ logs, traces, read-only DB2 business daysNeeds a code change% with reproduction, handoff quality≥ 80 % escalated with a repro
L3 · EngineeringRoot cause, fix, postmortem+ repo, CI, stagingPer SLO✗ TerminalMTTR, escaped-defect rateEscapes < 1 % of releases
Design feedback loopCategory aggregates → backlogMonthly reportNext planningCategory > 5 % of ticketsTickets per 1k MAU, trending↓ 20 % per quarter

Support is the only function that sees every user’s environment. Every ticket describing an OS you never tested, a screen scale you never rendered, a browser version you dropped, or a network that blocks updates is free market research into the environment your product actually runs in, arriving in a form that is already prioritised by a customer who cares. Mine it deliberately. A monthly “unsupported environments” report — grouped by OS, architecture, scaling, locale, screen size — is a better input to the next test matrix than any synthetic compatibility matrix, and it costs nothing beyond asking L1 to tag.

18.6 Product lifecycle, deprecation and end of life

This subsection covers the phases a product passes through, the obligations of each, and the specific mechanics of retiring a version, a capability or a product.

Every product passes through the same five phases, and each has a different engineering obligation. In launch, the obligation is operability: someone must be able to see what is happening, roll back what they shipped, and be woken. In adoption, the obligation is activation — the largest fraction of users will never complete the journey that makes the product valuable, and engineering effort spent raising that number usually beats effort spent on features. In growth, the obligation is scale and reliability, and the risk is that growth arrives as a change in shape rather than a change in volume: a new customer segment with a different access pattern, a new region, a bulk import. In maturity, the obligation is subtraction — the product accumulates features that nobody uses, and maintenance cost rises with the square of surface area while value plateaus. In decline, the obligation is a dignified exit. Products that skip the maturity phase and slide into decline while still being actively developed are the most expensive kind, because they carry a full engineering cost with no corresponding return.

Deprecation is a technical operation with a communication obligation attached, and the two are usually confused. The technical part is well understood: mark the capability as deprecated, add a machine-readable signal to every affected response and payload, emit an event when a client still uses it, and set a removal date. The communication part is where deprecations actually fail, and the reason is almost always that the notice was sent to a mailing list the users do not read. A deprecation notice that does not appear in the product — a banner, a warning in the tool, a line in the CLI, a dialog in the desktop app — has not been delivered, because that is the only channel guaranteed to reach someone currently using the thing.

The standard schedule is four contacts at fixed intervals, and it works because each one is cheap to produce and progressively harder to ignore: 90 days before removal, a machine-readable signal only; 60 days, a notice in-product and by email; 30 days, a direct contact to every account still using the capability, by named human; 14 days, a hard block that returns a scheduled-removal error with a migration link, and an executive escalation for accounts above a revenue threshold. For a hosted API, add the standard HTTP signals so that automated consumers can detect the change without a human: Deprecation and Sunset headers with an RFC 8594 date, and a Link to the migration documentation. For a desktop product, the equivalent is an in-app notice that appears on the affected screen and a version that is the last one supporting it — which is why the deprecation window for a Desktop capability is normally measured in releases, not days.

// Deprecation signals, on the wire, for every deprecated capability.
// RFC 8594 Sunset + RFC 9745 Deprecation + a Link to the migration guide.
import { Router } from 'express'

const DEPRECATED: Record<string, { sunset: Date; replacement: string; doc: string }> = {
  '/v1/invoice/pdf':   { sunset: new Date('2026-12-01T00:00:00Z'),
                         replacement: '/v1/invoice/pdf/v2', doc: 'https://docs.fieldglass.example/m/pdf' },
  '/v1/export/csv':   { sunset: new Date('2027-01-15T00:00:00Z'),
                         replacement: '/v1/export/csv/v2', doc: 'https://docs.fieldglass.example/m/csv' },
}

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const d = DEPRECATED[new URL(req.url, 'http://x').pathname]
  if (!d) return next()
  res.setHeader('Deprecation', d.sunset.toISOString())     // machine-readable
  res.setHeader('Sunset', d.sunset.toUTCString())           // RFC 8594, HTTP-date form
  res.setHeader('Link', `<${d.doc}>; rel="deprecation"; type="text/html", ` +
                        `<${d.replacement}>; rel="successor-version"`)
  res.setHeader('Warning', `299 - "Deprecated, sunset ${d.sunset.toDateString()}"`)
  metrics.deprecationUse.inc({ route: req.route?.path ?? 'unknown', tenant: req.tenantId })
  next()
})

// Three states, and the transition between them is scheduled, not discovered.
const STATE = { SUPPORTED: 'supported', WARNED: 'warned', SCHEDULED: 'scheduled_removal' }

router.get('/v1/export/csv', requireAuth, (req, res) => {
  const days = daysUntil(DEPRECATED['/v1/export/csv'].sunset)
  if (days < 0) {
    return res.status(410).json({
      error: 'endpoint_removed',
      sunset: DEPRECATED['/v1/export/csv'].sunset.toISOString(),
      migration: '/v1/export/csv/v2',
      docs: 'https://docs.fieldglass.example/m/csv',
      // Never remove a response shape abruptly: 410 is explicit, 404 is a lie.
    })
  }
  if (days < 30) res.setHeader('X-Deprecation-Days-Remaining', String(days))
  return res.type('text/csv').send(renderCsv(req.account))
})

# eol-policy.yaml — the rules, versioned, and published to users before they need them.
product: fieldglass
policy_version: 3
published: '2026-06-01'

# Support windows. Desktop is longer: updates reach users over weeks, not hours.
windows:
  stable:   { cadence_weeks: 8,  support: full,        eol_months_after_next_major: 12 }
  beta:     { cadence_weeks: 2,  support: best-effort, eol: at_next_stable }
  lts:      { cadence_weeks: 13, support: security-only, eol_months: 30 }
  desktop:  { cadence_weeks: 6,  support: full,        eol_months: 18 }   # vs 12 Web
  desktop_lts: { cadence_weeks: 26, support: security-only, eol_months: 36 }

# Platform floors, reviewed each release. These are the real deadlines.
platform_support:
  windows:   ['10', '11', 'Server 2022', 'Server 2025']
  macos:     ['13', '14', '15']
  linux:     ['22.04', '24.04', 'RHEL 9']
  announced_removals:
    - { id: macos-12,   notice_date: '2026-04-15', removal_date: '2026-11-01',
        rationale: 'Apple security updates ended 2025-09. Adoption telemetry 3.1 %.' }
    - { id: win7,       notice_date: '2024-06-01', removal_date: '2025-01-14',
        rationale: 'ESOL 2025-01-14.' }              # shipped late; note it in review

# Data obligations, both tracks. The export is the product's last gift.
data:
  export_formats: [csv, ndjson, postgres_dump, parquet]
  export_api: 'GET /v1/tenant/export?format=...'    # self-serve, no support ticket
  export_guarantee: 'full export available for 12 months after EOL announcement'
  migration_assistance_months: 6
  bulk_export_sla: 'P2, 5 business days, human-assisted for tenants > 50k rows'

# Announced EOLs
upcoming_eol:
  - { version: '2.3.x',        eol_date: '2027-03-31', notice_date: '2026-09-30',
      affected_accounts: 34,    named_contacts_sent: 0,  status: notice_pending }

# A removal cannot proceed while any of these is false. Enforced by CI on the
# release that would make the change.
preconditions_for_removal:
  - usage_of_deprecated_surface_below_pct: 0.5     # telemetry, 30-day window
  - named_contacts_sent_to_all_affected_accounts: true
  - in_product_notice_live_for_at_least_days: 30
  - migration_documentation_published_and_linked: true
  - support_acknowledgement_ticket_closed: true
  - export_endpoint_tested_for_affected_tenants: true
PhaseTypical durationPrimary engineering obligationWhat is measuredChief riskWeb vs Desktop
Launch0–3 monthsOperability: paging, rollback, SLOsTime to detect, time to mitigate~ Shipping without an on-callDesktop: installer + updater must be proven first
Adoption3–9 monthsActivation funnel, onboarding, empty statesActivation rate, time to first valueFeature work before anyone is activated~ Same
Growth9–24 monthsScale, new regions, new access patternsSLO burn, cost per active user~ Growth arrives as a shape changeDesktop: auto-update reach % becomes the metric
Maturity1–3 yearsSubtraction, cost reduction, debt paydownFeature usage distribution, maintenance ratioSurface area grows faster than valueDesktop: OS-floor updates consume a major version
Decline6–24 monthsDignified exit, export, migrationRemaining active accounts, EOL comms sent✗ Data stranded; abandonment with no noticeDesktop: unsigned, un-updatable stranded installs

Data export and migration are the obligations that are most often breached and most regretted. Every product that holds customer data must be able to produce a complete, usable, self-describing export without human assistance and without a support ticket, and must continue to be able to do so for a defined period after the end-of-life announcement — twelve months is a reasonable default. The export must be complete, which is a stronger requirement than it sounds: it must include data the customer cannot see in the interface, must use documented stable formats, and must be usable by something other than your product. A CSV of the visible table is not a backup; a PostgreSQL dump plus a schema version plus a data dictionary is. Test the export by having someone who did not build it restore it into a clean environment and verify the row counts — once before launch, and again in the final EOL month.

The end-of-life decision itself should be taken long before it is executed, and made on stated criteria rather than on revenue pressure alone. The criteria worth publishing are: adoption trend over two to four quarters; the cost to keep the product compliant and supported; the strategic fit; and the migration cost imposed on customers. Whatever the decision, three things must never be skipped: a named human contact to every affected account before the change; a data export guarantee that outlives the shutdown by a full year; and a final, tested restore. A shutdown without a tested restore is a data-loss event that has merely been scheduled, and it is the one failure in this entire guide that is genuinely irreversible.
