Make the EOL preconditions a CI gate, not a checklist item. Every precondition in eol-policy.yaml — usage below 0.5 %, named contacts sent to all affected accounts, in-product notice live for 30 days, documentation published, export tested for each affected tenant — is mechanically checkable from telemetry, from the communication ledger, and from the repository. Wiring them into the release pipeline means an irreversible change cannot be merged by someone in a hurry on a Friday, and it means the decision to proceed is recorded as an auditable artefact rather than a memory.

Sunsetting a Desktop product strands installs that can no longer update themselves. If a signed build is already on a user’s machine, that build will keep running and keep failing to phone home after you shut the servers down, and those users have no upgrade path you can reach. Plan for it: ship a final build that disables the affected features gracefully and points at a migration, keep the update manifest and its signing infrastructure alive for the full deprecation window, and monitor the surviving population for at least a year after shutdown. A Desktop product that disappears without a final build is the most common form of silent, self-inflicted abandonment.

Exercises 18

  1. Define a compatibility contract for one of your products and implement it as a CI check. Separate the marketing, wire-protocol, schema and build versions; add a assert-n1 gate that refuses a deploy unless the previous version has served production for 48 hours; and add a schema-diff check that fails on any non-expand-only migration. Then run one deliberately breaking change through it. Deliverable: the written contract, the two CI checks, and a captured screenshot of the pipeline correctly refusing a contract-dropping change.
  2. Publish a release channel contract for your product with the five channels, each with an audience, a promotion criterion, a support level, a data-compatibility statement and a sunset date. Then measure the actual distribution of your users across channels over the last 90 days using your telemetry. Deliverable: the channel contract, the measured distribution, and a written decision for each channel that currently has users on it but no owner.
  3. Audit your feature flags and produce a debt report: every flag defined, its owner, kind, age, expiry, whether it is evaluated on the request path, and which flag combinations your suite exercises. Then install combination-coverage tooling, add the missing combination tests, and delete or justify every expired flag. Deliverable: the audit table, the combination coverage report before and after, and a CI gate that fails on an expired flag.
  4. Define three SLOs for your product’s most important user journeys, with a window, an objective, a slice breakdown, and an explicit error-budget policy with named thresholds for what happens at 75 %, 50 % and 10 % remaining. Compute the current burn rate from your existing telemetry and state honestly which of the three you are meeting. Deliverable: the SLO definitions in a version-controlled file, the burn-rate report, and a written escalation email to your team lead if any are not being met.
  5. Run a retrospective on your last 200 support tickets. Categorise every one, compute tickets per 1,000 monthly active users by category with month-on-month trend, and identify the three categories with the highest cost that are attributable to a product decision rather than a user error. Deliverable: the categorisation, the per-1k-MAU trend table, and three backlog items with the specific screen, message, permission or missing affordance named in each.

19 · Appendices: Launch Checklists, Matrices and Glossary

19.1 The pre-launch checklist19.2 Reference matrices19.3 A worked end-to-end example19.4 Glossary19.5 How products fail, stage by stage19.6 Further reading

Eighteen chapters of process resolve into a small number of things you either did or did not do before launch. This appendix collects them: the checklist in a form you can run, the matrices you will look things up in, one product traced end to end so the sequence is concrete, a glossary, and an honest catalogue of the ways this process fails with the earliest signal that would have caught each one. Track-specific items are marked WEB or DESKTOP; everything else applies to both.

19.1 The pre-launch checklist

Run it as an executable document, not a read-through. An item is done when there is an artefact or a measurement that proves it, never when someone says it is done.

// ── PRODUCT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
//   Each item needs an artefact, not an opinion.
//
[ ] The problem is evidenced, not assumed. Discovery notes exist, are
    dated, and name real people. A document titled "user research" with no
    interviewee identifiers is a wish, not evidence.
[ ] The riskiest assumption was tested BEFORE the build, and the test had a
    numeric pass criterion written down in advance.
[ ] Positioning names the actual alternative the user has today, which is
    usually a spreadsheet and a person.
[ ] Scope contract exists. In-scope, out-of-scope and non-goals are written,
    and "out of scope" is as long as "in scope".
[ ] Success is instrumented: the 2-3 metrics that would tell you in 30 days
    whether this worked. Named, with a current baseline.
[ ] The pricing and billing path is decided, or explicitly deferred with a
    date. "We will add billing later" is the single most common cause of a
    product that cannot be sold.

// ── DESIGN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[ ] The primary flow has been through a usability test with 5 real users,
    with recorded task completion rates. Not 5 colleagues.
[ ] Every screen has designed empty, loading, error and permission-denied
    states. These are the screens users see most and designers skip first.
[ ] Accessibility: keyboard-only completion of the primary flow; a
    screen-reader smoke test; automated axe scan with zero critical issues;
    contrast verified in BOTH themes.
[ ] Design tokens exist and are exported to the code — not a Figma library
    the engineers re-derive by eye.
[ ] Content is written, not placeholder. Lorem ipsum in a launch is a
    statement that nobody has read the product.

// ── ENGINEERING ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[ ] The pipeline builds the SAME artefact it deploys. Image digests match
    between staging and production. No rebuild at the last step.
[ ] Every environment has its configuration schema-validated at boot, and a
    missing variable fails the deploy rather than the first request.
[ ] Zero unhandled exceptions in 7 days of production traffic, verified in
    the error tracker, not assumed.
[ ] Migrations applied to a production-shaped copy with production-like row
    counts. The migration time is known and written down.
[ ] Rollback verified: the previous artefact is retained, and the rollback
    was actually executed once in staging.
[ ] No secrets in the repository. Scanned, and the scanner is in CI.
[ ] Dependency audit clean at the agreed severity, and there is a documented
    process for a critical advisory arriving on a Friday.
[ ] Database backup exists AND HAS BEEN RESTORED, with the elapsed time
    recorded. That elapsed time is your RTO and it is a measurement, not a
    target.

// ── SECURITY ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[ ] Threat model exists for the two or three genuinely sensitive flows
    (authentication, payment, data export). Not a full STRIDE sweep of
    everything — that never finishes and gets ignored.
[ ] OWASP Top 10 reviewed concretely against this codebase, with a written
    disposition for each: fixed, accepted with a reason, or not-applicable
    with a reason.
[ ] Authorisation enforced at the data layer, not only in the route. A
    tenant-scoping test exists and asserts a cross-tenant read returns
    nothing.
[ ] Secrets stored in a secret manager, rotated at least once end to end to
    prove the rotation procedure works.
[ ] Security headers in production, CSP in report-only mode long enough to
    be clean, then enforcing.
[ ] WEB: TLS with HSTS, modern ciphers, and certificate auto-renewal that
    RELOADS the service.
[ ] DESKTOP: binaries signed and notarised on every platform; updater manifest
    signed with a key separate from the build key; verified by a CI job
    before publish.
[ ] Responsible disclosure route exists and is monitored. A security.txt that
    nobody reads is worse than none.

// ── OPERATIONS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[ ] Dashboards: RED per service, plus saturation (pool, queue depth, disk).
[ ] Alerts fire on user-visible symptoms, with a burn rate. Count the pages
    received in the last two weeks — the number should be one per person per
    week or less.
[ ] Runbook exists for the top five failure modes, is one page each, and has
    been read by someone who did not write it.
[ ] On-call rotation exists and the first person on it has been paged
    successfully in a game day.
[ ] Error tracking and crash reporting on, with the retention period stated.
[ ] Status page, even a manual one, and the process for updating it.
[ ] Load tested at 2x the expected peak, with the result written down.
[ ] Incident process: severity definitions, a comms owner, and a template.

// ── COMPLIANCE AND LEGAL ───────────────────────────────────────────────
[ ] Privacy policy and terms drafted, reviewed by someone qualified, and
    consistent with what the product actually does.
[ ] Consent given, collected and stored where the regulation requires it.
[ ] Data inventory: every table and file holding personal data, and every
    foreign key path from a user to their data. Required for an erasure
    request and usually absent until it is urgent.
[ ] Data export works, is tested, and produces files openable without your
    product.
[ ] Retention periods defined per data class, with the authority cited, and
    the deletion implemented rather than documented.
[ ] Sub-processors listed, with a data-processing agreement where required.
[ ] Accessibility statement published, if the product is in scope for it.
[ ] DESKTOP: telemetry is OFF by default, disclosed, and revocable from a
    menu item. Crash reports contain no user content.

// ── GO TO MARKET ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[ ] Onboarding: the first-run experience reaches the aha moment without
    help, measured not asserted. For DESKTOP, install-to-first-value is
    measured, because that is where the drop-off is.
[ ] Documentation: install, first task, and the three most common problems.
[ ] Support: intake channel, severity definitions with response targets, and
    someone on the first week.
[ ] Analytics validated: events fire, are named consistently, and a
    dashboard exists that answers "did the launch work".
[ ] Rollback and kill switches exist and have been tested. A feature flag
    with no tested off position is not a kill switch.
[ ] DESKTOP: staged rollout configured — ring percentages, crash-free
    threshold, and the automatic halt wired to a real notification.
[ ] WEB: cache headers, CDN and TLS configured; a `robots.txt` and sitemap
    if the product is indexed.

How to run it. Put it in the repository as a Markdown file, put it on the release issue as a checklist, and require a link to evidence for every item. The discipline that makes it work is refusing "done" without a link — a dashboard URL, a test name, a document, a measurement. An item with a link is auditable six months later; an item with a tick is a memory.

19.2 Reference matrices

The three tables you will come back to: release channels, support priorities, and version support.

ChannelAudienceUpdate controlSupport promiseData migrations allowedWho can join
Internal / dogfoodEmployeesContinuous, from the branch tipNone. Best-effort triageAnything, including destructiveNobody. It is a deployment target
NightlyTeam plus committed testersAutomated, every nightNoneNon-destructive onlyOpt-in, in exchange for reporting bugs
BetaOpt-in external users, 2–8 weeksWeekly, or a release trainBest-effort, no SLAAdditive only, and reversibleOpt-in, with a feedback link in the app
StableEveryoneStaged: 1 → 5 → 25 → 100%The contractual SLA applies here onlyAdditive only. Destructive is a new major versionDefault. No opt-in required
LTSEnterprise and regulated buyersSecurity and critical fixes only, for a stated periodStrongest SLA, longest support windowSecurity only, and backportedPaid, and contractually committed

The rule the table encodes. A channel is a promise, and the promise gets stronger down the list. Data migrations with rollback are only permitted where the rollback actually works — which is why additive-only is the rule for anything with an SLA attached. A "beta" that silently breaks a customer’s data is not a beta, it is an unannounced production deployment, and the first team to discover that distinction learned it the expensive way.

PriorityDefinitionFirst responseTarget fix or workaroundUpdate cadenceEscalation
P1 — CriticalProduct is unusable or data is being lost or exposed. No workaround15 minutes, 24×74 hoursEvery 30 minutes until resolvedEngineering lead, founder, and the customer is told within 1 hour
P2 — HighMajor feature broken, no reasonable workaround. Many users affected1 hour, 24×71 business dayDailyEngineering lead
P3 — NormalFeature broken with a workaround, or a significant usability problem1 business dayNext release, or 2 weeksWeekly summaryProduct owner
P4 — LowCosmetic, or an edge case with negligible impact3 business daysBacklog, no dateMonthlyNone
Version lineSecurity fixesCritical bug fixesNew featuresPerformance fixesAPI support
Current (N)✓✓✓✓Full
Previous (N−1)✓✓✗✓Full
Oldest supported✓Conditional, per contract✗✗Security only — no new fields
Below oldest supported✗✗✗✗Refused. The app tells the user, with a date and an upgrade path

Write the version-support policy before you need it, and put a date in it. "We support the last two major versions" is a commitment with no end. "Versions released in the last 18 months receive security fixes; anything older must upgrade, and the upgrade is free" is a commitment with a horizon, and it is the version a customer can plan against. The second one also gives you a legitimate basis for the minimum-version gate in chapter 16, which is otherwise an awkward conversation.

19.3 A worked end-to-end example

One fictional product, traced through every stage, with the artefact produced at each step and the number that mattered at each gate. The point is the sequence and the gates, not the product.

The product. A desktop application for clinical trial data entry, used by research coordinators in hospitals. Site staff enter patient visit data on a laptop in a consulting room, often with poor connectivity, and the sponsor needs a clean audit trail. The team is four engineers: two backend, one frontend, one platform. Nobody has built a regulated product before.

Why desktop, and why that is a real answer. Chapter 13's first question is whether it needs to be a desktop application. The honest answer here is yes, for two reasons that a web app cannot satisfy: data must exist on the machine for an audit trail that survives a lost network, and the product must integrate with the hospital’s identity provider through a system-level agent. That sentence is the justification. "Our customers asked for a desktop app" would not have been sufficient.

WeeksStageArtefact producedThe gate, and the number that decided it
1–3Discovery (ch1)14 discovery interviews, transcript summary, opportunity treeSaturation at 11 interviews. The same three complaints appeared unprompted in 9 of the last 6 interviews. Stopped because a 12th produced nothing new, not because of a target
4Problem framing (ch1.1)One-sentence problem statementThe problem is not "entry is slow". It is "a coordinator re-enters the same visit data three times because the form does not survive a page reload". A different problem, a different product
4Assumption map (ch1.4)Four riskiest assumptions, rankedThe riskiest was viability, not usability: would a sponsor pay? Tested with a concierge pilot at two sites for 4 weeks. 2 of 2 signed a letter of intent at $X per site per month. That reframed the whole business case
5–6Feasibility spike (ch2.3)Throwaway spike: offline store + sync + a signed buildTime-boxed to 5 days, then discarded. It proved offline-first was achievable in the chosen framework and that conflict resolution on the visit form was the hard part. That finding shaped the architecture and cost 5 days, not 5 months
6Market (ch2.1)Bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOMSAM from the bottom up, not the top down. 4,000 sites × 8 seats × $X = a number that a top-down analyst figure was 30× larger. Planning against the top-down number would have set an unreachable revenue target
7Scope contract (ch3.3)In-scope, out-of-scope, non-goalsNon-goals included "works on a phone". Writing that down prevented it being added as a feature request in month four, when it would have cost a rewrite
8–10Research and requirements (ch4, ch5)Personas from 14 interviews, 6 user stories with G/W/T criteria, quality attribute scenariosEvery requirement expressed as a testable scenario. "Fast" became "a form save completes in under 400 ms p95 on a 2019 laptop with 20,000 visits loaded". Three requirements had no acceptance test and were cut
9–11Interface design (ch6)Wireframes, one coded prototype, 3 usability rounds5 users per round, 3 rounds, 17 users total. Round 1 found the back-button ambiguity. Round 3 found that the audit trail view was never used and was cut — saving 2 weeks
11Visual design and tokens (ch7)Design system, token export, light and darkTokens exported as the single source. A token change propagated to the build in the same PR, so a contrast fix was one commit rather than a design review
12Architecture (ch8, ch13–15)4 ADRs, process model, sync designADR-002: field-level last-write-wins with explicit conflict on the body. Written because the team disagreed and the disagreement would have resurfaced. The ADR named the cost: an offline concurrent edit to the same field requires human resolution
12–20BuildThe product, in 8-week incrementsWeekly, the two numbers were: crash-free sessions (target 99.7%) and p95 save latency (target 400 ms). Neither was ever above target for two consecutive weeks in the first month
18Compliance design (ch17)Threat model, data inventory, audit trail designThe data inventory came first, and it changed the schema. Finding that visit data was copied into an audit table without a retention policy meant adding a retention column in week 6 rather than after launch
20–21Quality (ch17)Test portfolio, load test, restore drillThe restore drill failed the first time. Restoring the production backup took 3.4 hours against a hoped-for 1. That is the RTO, and it is now written in the runbook rather than the SLA
22Distribution (ch16)Signed builds, notarisation, update channelNotarisation rejected the first submission because the build lacked a secure timestamp. Found in staging by deliberately testing the user install path, not the developer machine
23Launch checklist (19.1)The checklist, with evidence links22 of 31 items had evidence on day one. The 9 without were all in the "operations" and "go to market" groups. The launch date moved two weeks rather than shipping with an unawakeable pager
24LaunchProduction at 5 sitesNot 5% of users — 5 sites, deliberately. Named, reachable, and able to report a bug in a conversation. The rollout percentage came after
2530-day reviewMetrics against the 2–3 chosen at ch3One of the three success metrics was "median time to complete a visit", targeted at under 90 seconds. It came in at 140. That is the finding, and it is a product problem, not a launch problem

What the timeline shows. Twenty-four weeks, of which roughly six were discovery, feasibility and design and eighteen were build. The gate that saved the most time was the scope contract at week 7; the gate that saved the most risk was the data inventory at week 18. The single most instructive failure is the restore drill at week 21 — a test that was run, failed, and changed a number in a contract, four weeks before that number would have been a lie.

19.4 Glossary

Terms used in this guide, defined as the guide uses them. Where a term is used differently elsewhere, the difference is noted.

TermDefinition as used in this guide
Acceptance criteriaThe conditions a change must meet to be considered done, written so a machine could check them. Given/When/Then is the most common form; a checklist and examples-first BDD are the two alternatives that also work
ADRArchitecture Decision Record: a short document recording one decision, its context, its consequences and its status. The value is the record of why, which is the part that is unrecoverable from the code
Assumption mapThe set of things believed true but not yet verified, grouped by type (desirability, viability, feasibility, usability-clarity) and ordered by risk. The output of chapter 1 and the input to validation
Beta channelA release channel with a weaker support promise than stable, admitting opt-in users in exchange for early feedback. Not a euphemism for "unstable production"
BurndownThe rate at which the error budget is being consumed. A 1-hour window burning at 14.4× means 2% of a 30-day budget is gone in one hour. The basis of multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting
Characteristic testA test written against existing undocumented behaviour, to capture it before changing it. The mechanism for safely touching legacy code with no test suite
Concierge MVPDelivering the service manually to a small number of users to test demand before building automation. Tests willingness to pay better than any landing page
Contract testA test that verifies an agreed interface between two independently deployed components. The mechanism that allows a consumer to upgrade without a coordinated release
Core Web VitalsLCP, INP and CLS: three field metrics approximating whether a page felt fast. Useful as a budget enforced in CI, misleading as a target optimised in isolation
CRDTConflict-free Replicated Data Type: a data structure whose merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas converge without coordination. A permanent design commitment, not a technique
Design tokenA named design decision — a colour, a spacing step, a type size — exported as machine-readable data so code and design share one source. The mechanism that makes a design system enforceable
DiscoverabilityWhether a user can find the feature they need without being told. The most common cause of a well-built product being considered badly made
Distribution channelThe mechanism by which users obtain the software, with its own economics, friction and control. For desktop this is chapter 16 and it is a product decision, not a logistics one
Edge renderingRunning the render in a CDN location near the user. A cache with excellent geography; a cache miss is usually worse than not using it
Error budgetThe permitted fraction of failures over a period, derived from the SLO. Its real purpose is to make a judgement about risk explicit rather than to prevent risk-taking
Expand and contractMaking a schema change in phases so each is compatible with both old and new code, with the irreversible step last. The sequence that makes a change safe under live traffic
FidelityHow closely an artefact resembles the final product. The right level answers a specific question: structure, layout, or feel. Choosing wrongly is a signal problem, not an effort problem
Golden pathThe single most common flow through a product, and the one that must be flawless. Every feature that competes with it is a cost
Guardrail metricA metric watched to confirm a change did not damage something else. Rumsfeld’s distinction: a guardrail that fires is not an input to the decision, it is a stop
Jobs to Be DoneResearch framing that asks what a user is trying to accomplish, in their own words, rather than what feature they want. Produces functional, emotional and social jobs, plus a forces diagram
Keyset paginationPagination by a cursor encoding the last row’s sort key, so cost is constant at any depth and concurrent writes do not cause duplicates or omissions. The correct default for anything user-paginated
Kill switchA control that disables a feature without a deploy, tested in its off position. A feature flag that has never been switched off is not a kill switch
MVPMinimum Viable Product. The common confusion is between minimum viable (test the riskiest assumption with the least work) and minimum lovable (the smallest thing users will actually adopt). They are different products
Non-functional requirementA requirement about how the system behaves — latency, availability, memory, install size, cold start — rather than what it does. Fails to be testable when written as an adjective, and "the system shall be fast" is the canonical example
NotarisationApple’s submission and verification of a signed macOS binary, with the result stapled to the artefact so it verifies offline. Distinct from signing, and both are required
Opportunity solution treeA structure connecting an outcome goal to opportunities to it, then to solutions, with evidence attached. Useful because it makes the reasoning auditable rather than implicit
Outbox patternWriting a domain change and an event record in one transaction, with a relay publishing it later. At-least-once, so every consumer must be idempotent. The standard answer to "we cannot transact across two systems"
Performance budgetA numeric limit enforced in CI — bundle size, request count, long tasks, cold-start time. A budget in a document is a wish; a budget that fails a build is a budget
PersonaA description of a real observed user group, built from research. The failure mode is a fictional persona assembled from a stakeholder’s assumptions, which validates those assumptions instead of testing them
Phased rolloutReleasing to 1%, then 5%, then 25%, then 100%, with a defined exit criterion at each step. Bounds the population exposed to a defect while the population that would report it is small enough to act on
Progressive enhancementBuilding so the core function works before any script runs, and adding interactivity after. The only approach that survives a slow network or a script failure, and increasingly rare in practice
Progressive disclosureShowing complexity only when it is needed, so the default surface stays small. A direct defence against the enterprise feature-request pattern
Quality attribute scenarioA six-part statement — stimulus, source, artefact, environment, response, response measure — that makes a non-functional requirement testable. The most useful artefact in requirements engineering
RingA stable cohort of users used for phased rollout, assigned by hashing a persistent install id. Stability is what makes the comparison against the previous version meaningful
Riskiest assumption testIdentifying the assumption that, if false, ends the project, and testing it first with the smallest experiment that could falsify it. The single highest-leverage activity in discovery
SBOMSoftware Bill of Materials: a machine-readable inventory of every dependency in a shipped artefact. Required by regulation in several jurisdictions and cheap to produce during the build
SLIService Level Indicator: the measured quantity — a latency histogram, an error ratio, a success rate. A measurement, not a target
SLOService Level Objective: the target for an SLI over a window, stated with the population it covers. A commitment, from which the error budget is derived
Stage gateA decision point between phases where a defined criterion must be met to proceed. Valuable only when the criterion is written down in advance — otherwise it becomes a meeting
TombstoneA retained record that an entity was deleted, so other replicas learn about the deletion rather than resurrecting it. Retention must exceed the maximum plausible offline duration, which is a computable number
Track-based developmentBuilding and validating one platform path end to end, deliberately incomplete on the others, to find the real risk early. Opposite to breadth-first, and correct for a first release with more than one platform
Trust boundaryA line where data crosses from a context you control to one you do not. Every one needs a distinct validation rule, and the most-missed is the boundary between your own front end and your own back end
Usability heuristicOne of Nielsen’s ten general principles for interface design, used as a review checklist rather than as a design method. Effective because it is a fixed list, which makes review repeatable
Vertical sliceOne complete path through every layer, end to end, rather than one layer across all features. The only way to demonstrate a working system before every feature exists
Wizard of Oz MVPAutomated front end, manual back end. Tests the demand and the interface before the automation is built, and is frequently the correct first release

19.5 How products fail, stage by stage

The catalogue, with the earliest signal that would have caught each one. The signal matters more than the failure, because the failure is usually the end of a chain that started with something small and cheap to notice.

StageHow it failsThe earliest signalThe cheap intervention that would have caught it
DiscoveryBuilding for a problem that was never real, discovered at launchDiscovery interviews where the interviewee describes a different problem than you asked about, three times runningAsk about the last time it happened, not what they want. If nobody can name a specific instance, there is no problem
DiscoveryConfusing a stated preference with revealed behaviourEnthusiasm in interviews that evaporates at the payment stepTest willingness to pay, not interest. A concierge pilot or a pre-order is the only reliable signal
DiscoverySolution-first: five features sketched before one problem is agreedThe roadmap exists and the problem statement does notOne sentence describing the problem, in the user’s language. If it needs a product term, it is not written yet
ResearchFictional personas validating the founder’s assumptionsPersona names, ages and goals with no interview identifiers behind themRequire a quote and a session reference under every persona attribute
ResearchResearch that confirms rather than testsEvery finding supporting the existing planAssign a team member to argue the opposite, and require evidence for it
RequirementsAdjectives instead of numbers, untestable until the end"Fast", "scalable", "intuitive" in a requirements documentEvery requirement needs a number and a measurement point. If it cannot be measured it is a hope
RequirementsScope that grows silently through "small additions"No out-of-scope list, so every request is in scope by defaultWrite the non-goals. Their absence is what makes "no" impossible to say
DesignHigh-fidelity design before the structure is agreedVisual mockups for a flow nobody has tested on paperWireframe before mockup, always. A beautiful screen on a wrong structure is the most expensive artefact in the process
DesignEmpty, loading and error states designed last, or neverA design file with one state per screenAdd the four states to the design system as a default, not as an exception
DesignAccessibility as a final auditA keyboard-only attempt failing at the first dialogSemantic HTML from the first commit and a keyboard-only check each sprint. Retrofitting costs 5–10×
ArchitectureThe irreversible decision made under time pressureA data store, protocol or distribution channel chosen in a single meetingWrite an ADR for anything expensive to reverse. The writing is the value, not the document
ArchitectureBuilding the platform before the productMonths of infrastructure work with no user-visible outputOne vertical slice through every layer, shipped to a real user, early
EngineeringBuilding for scale that does not existSharding, caching tiers and queues with traffic that would not justify themMeasure the current bottleneck. It is nearly always a query, not a capacity ceiling
EngineeringThe migration that runs in the same release as the codeA migration that drops or renames a column, applied with a deployExpand and contract. The destructive step is always a separate release
EngineeringNo rollback, discovered during an incidentA deployment script that only goes forwardRun a rollback in staging as part of every release rehearsal. A rollback never tested is an assumption
QualityTesting the mock, not the dependencyA suite where every boundary is mocked and integration tests are slow or absentUse a real dependency in a container for the tests that matter. Mocks test your assumptions
QualityA flaky gate that gets disabledRetries added to CI, or a quarantined-test count above a few percentQuarantine with a ticket and a date. A deleted gate is worse than a flaky test
SecurityAuthorisation in the route and not in the queryA handler that checks a permission and then runs an unscoped queryScope every query by tenant in the repository layer and assert a cross-tenant read returns nothing
SecuritySecrets committed, then rotated but never purged from historyA key in git, removed from HEAD, still in the logPre-commit secret scanning, and a rotation procedure that includes the history rewrite
LaunchNo staged rollout, so a defect reaches everyone at onceA release process with a single step1% first, with an automatic halt on the crash-free rate. The mechanism is a day of work
LaunchOn-call that has never been pagedNo game day, and the first page goes to someone newOne deliberate page before launch. The failure mode is process, not code
LaunchSuccess metrics chosen after launch, from what is easy to measureA dashboard of activity metrics and nothing about outcomesChoose 2–3 outcome metrics in chapter 3 and record the baseline before you change anything
Post-launchAlerts that fire for conditions nobody acts onMore than a few pages per person per week, and a habit of ignoring themAlert on user-visible symptoms with a burn rate. Delete every alert with no documented action
Post-launchNo deprecation plan, so the product cannot be retired cleanlyNo documented data export that opens without your productBuild the export at launch, test it, and write the sunset policy while you still have users to be fair to
LifecycleFlag debt: hundreds of flags nobody has removedNo owner and no expiry date on any flagEvery flag needs an owner and a removal date at creation. A flag without both is permanent

The pattern across all twenty-four rows. Almost none of these are engineering failures. They are failures to make a small decision explicit while it was still cheap, and every one of the early signals above is visible in the first week of the relevant stage — while the stage is still being planned. The organisations that ship well are not the ones that avoid failure; they are the ones that notice the signal at the moment they can still do something about it, which is to say, early.

19.6 Further reading

A short, curated list of sources that are currently maintained and specific enough to be worth the time. Ordered by where to go next rather than by prestige.

ReadForWhy this and not something else
The official Pro Git book, second editionGit internals, chapters 10–11Free, maintained, and the internals chapters are the only place the object model is explained properly. Everything else about Git on the internet is written for people who have already read these two chapters
git-scm.com/docs — the official referenceExact flag semanticsThe reference is complete and current. When a flag’s behaviour is in question, this is the authority, and it is frequently clearer than blog posts about it
MDN Web DocsWeb platform: rendering, performance, accessibility, HTTP cachingThe most reliable single reference for web platform behaviour. The Core Web Vitals and HTTP caching sections are the ones to read even if you think you know them
web.dev — Core Web Vitals and performance budgetsWeb performance, chapter 10Practical and current, with the budget framework chapter 10 uses
W3C WCAG 2.2Accessibility, chapters 6 and 17The normative text. The success criteria are the checklist; the "Understanding" pages are where the real requirements are explained
PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server official documentationDatabase chapters 11, 12, 17Vendor documentation is the only authority on locking, replication and online DDL, and it is regularly more precise than third-party tutorials. Read the "Notes" and "Compatibility" sections, which is where the real behaviour is
The Twelve-Factor AppConfiguration, deployment, chapter 12Short, dated in places, and still the clearest statement of the config/deploy separation that most teams get wrong
Google’s SRE Book, chapters on SLOs and alertingReliability, chapters 12 and 17The best available treatment of error budgets, burn-rate alerting and the practical limits of monitoring. Free online
Continuous Delivery — Humble and FarleyDelivery practice, chapter 12Long, and worth the time for a team that has not read it. The material on deployment decoupling and the anatomy of a deploy pipeline is directly applicable
Designing Data-Intensive Applications — KleppmannThe architecture chapters, 8, 9, 10, 13The best treatment of the consistency and reliability material in this guide. Read it before touching replication, caching or partitioning in anger
Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Microsoft Fluent Design, GTK HIGDesktop track, chapter 13The only authority on what "native" means on each platform. The difference between the three is where most cross-platform products get it wrong
Apple Developer Documentation — App Sandbox and NotarisationDesktop packaging, chapter 14The sandbox restrictions are the single largest constraint on desktop architecture, and the docs state them precisely
OWASP Top 10 and Cheat Sheet SeriesSecurity, chapter 17Current, free, and specific enough to act on. The cheat sheets on session management and authorisation are the two most useful documents in application security
Observability-engineering — FfosdemObservability, chapter 11Free online, and the clearest available argument for logging events rather than metrics. Directly applicable to the instrumentation in chapter 11

If you read only three. Read this guide end to end once, then Designing Data-Intensive Applications for chapters 8–12, and Google’s SRE Book for the alerting chapters. The first will change how you make architecture decisions, the second will change how you reason about data, and the third will change how you spend your on-call hours. The rest can wait until you need it, and the list above tells you when that is.

Exercises 19

  1. Run the chapter 19.1 checklist against a product you have shipped. Count the items with evidence, and identify which of the four groups the gaps cluster in. That group is where your process is weakest, and it is usually not engineering.
  2. Write a version-support policy with explicit dates for your product, then implement the minimum-version gate your policy implies. Verify that a client below the floor receives an actionable message rather than a failure.
  3. Trace a product you know from idea to launch in a one-page table, with a week number, an artefact and a gate for each stage. Then identify the three gates that saved the most, and whether you or your predecessors ran them.
  4. Pick five rows from the failure catalogue and design a specific check for each — a CI assertion, a design review question, a dashboard panel — that would surface that signal. Implement the two cheapest.
  5. Choose one item from the further-reading list that answers a question you currently have, and apply exactly one idea from it to a real decision in the next week. Write down the decision and what changed.
